a-dance-of-chemistry-and-physics.title: A dance of chemistry and physics
a-dance-of-chemistry-and-physics.description: To the uninitiated, the multiplayer video game Rocket League might appear as a straightforward match of car soccer.
a-dance-of-chemistry-and-physics.content:
To the uninitiated, the multiplayer video game Rocket League might appear as a straightforward match of car soccer. Vehicles fly around an enclosed pitch, attempting to steer a giant ball into the opposing team's goal.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

At its core, it's a game governed by the laws of physics, where momentum, speed, trajectory, and force play pivotal roles.

But a more intricate dance hides beneath this veneer of vehicular physics, one that's as much about human chemistry as it is about the physical world. A tapestry of ego and positioning.

Each five-minute match in Rocket League is a condensed lifetime of decision-making, strategy, and interpersonal dynamics.

Every player's choice has immediate consequences, not only for themselves but also for their teammates and opponents. A well-timed jump can lead to a triumphant goal, while a missed defense can result in a devastating loss.

But it's not just about the maneuvers and tactics; it's about the human connections that form in these brief encounters.

In real-life team sports, chemistry between players is often hailed as the secret ingredient to success. It's the unspoken understanding, the ability to predict a teammate's next move, the synchronization of thoughts and actions.

Rocket League, despite its virtual setting, is no different. When players are in sync, they move as one cohesive unit, anticipating passes, setting up shots, and defending their goal with a fluidity that's mesmerizing to watch.

However, as with any intense interaction, the emotional stakes are high. Moods can quickly sour.

A missed opportunity or an unintended blunder can lead to frustration. And in the online gaming world, where anonymity often emboldens people to express their feelings without restraint, this frustration can escalate into toxicity. Hurtful words are exchanged, blame is assigned, and the negative energy can linger long after the match is over.

This toxicity can also be contagious.

A player who experiences a particularly harsh game might decide to carry that negativity into their next match, infecting a new set of players with that particular brand of bitterness.

Perhaps one of the most intriguing (and vexing) phenomena in Rocket League is when a player chooses to remain in a game after mentally checking out. They might stop actively participating, instead opting to sit idly or even actively sabotage their own team.

This act of virtual protest is a form of punishment for all involved at that moment.

And while it's a strategy that's counterproductive to the game's objective, it highlights the depth of emotion and the personal stakes that players invest in each match.

So why do players continue to engage in this dance of chemistry and physics, despite the potential for emotional turmoil?

Perhaps because, at its best, Rocket League offers moments of pure elation.

The thrill of a last-second goal, the satisfaction of a well-executed play, the camaraderie of celebrating a victory with teammates — these are the moments that players chase. They're the highs that make the lows worth enduring.

Rocket League is more than just a game. It's a microcosm of human interaction, a virtual space where people from all over the world come together to compete, collaborate, and connect.

Each match offers a unique blend of physics and chemistry, of strategy and emotion, of triumphs and challenges.

In the end, Rocket League serves as a reminder that even in a digital realm, human connection is paramount.

It's a testament to the power of teamwork, the importance of empathy, and the complex brew of emotions that define our interactions.

As players navigate the pitch, they're not just mastering the physics of car soccer — they're learning about themselves and each other; forging bonds and rivalries while experiencing the full spectrum of humanity’s strength and weakness in just five minutes.

accumulated-velocity.title: Accumulated Velocity
accumulated-velocity.description: The treadmill didn't start with AI
accumulated-velocity.content:
From an early age, I was pulled out of the normal flow of growing up. Corralled into groups labeled gifted, accelerated, advanced.

After I scored a perfect on the science portion of the IGAPs in fifth grade, someone decided I should take the SATs. I hadn’t been taught pi yet. Didn’t even know what the symbol meant when I sat down with the test booklet.

My score? 315.

They say you get 700 points for signing your name. So I suppose I still had some work to do in elementary school before heading off to college.

The perspective and desire necessary to catapult a child into a test he’s clearly unprepared for is a form of ego deflection no kid should have to absorb.

Whose ambition was being served? Not mine. I was eleven, maybe twelve. A whip-smart kid who remembered everything he was taught. Did that make me a genius? I was a child. That’s all I was.

But that moment did something to me. It taught me, early, what it feels like to be accelerated against your will. To be shoved into a velocity someone else chose for you, and then measured by the distance you didn’t cover.

Years later, fresh out of college, I was dead broke.

I sold my favorite guitar to make rent; a vintage cherry SG, beautiful pearl inlays. Only worth a few hundred because it was the Epiphone version, not the Gibson. But rent was only a few hundred dollars back then.

That’s the math of survival stripped bare. One thing you love, exchanged for another month of keeping the lights on. No drama, no poetry; just the quiet transaction of getting by.

And it wasn’t the last time. Being broke has a way of recurring.

Once-in-a-lifetime catastrophes, collapses, covids… And each time, the math is the same: what can I trade to keep going?

The cost of continued living was already accelerating long before AI entered the conversation. Rent climbed. Wages didn’t.

The distance between what a person earns and what a life costs has been widening for decades, and we’ve been absorbing that velocity in silence. We take on side work, defer rest, treat burnout as a personality trait.

We’ve been at lightspeed in societal timeframes for a while now. The rent that was a few hundred is now a couple thousand. That guitar wouldn’t cover a week now.

The treadmill didn’t start with AI.
AI is just the latest gear shift in an engine that’s been redlining for years.

And here’s where it fractures.

A strategist looks at AI and sees strategy. An innovator sees ideas forged in steel. A designer sees a canvas that talks back.

But a person who found their worth in the process, the doing, the completing for compensation. They look at AI and see the end of themselves. Full-scale automation of everything that made them feel needed.

They’re not wrong.

AI is not evenly distributed because we, as individuals, are not evenly distributed. It’s a mirror, and the reflection depends entirely on what you brought to it.

For some, it’s magic. For others, it’s long bread lines and shivers in the silver moonlight. Both are real. Both are happening.

This is the impasse.
It’s not a technology problem. It’s a human one.

I’m tired. I want to tell you this is all going to be fine.
That this speed is a form of mercy.
That building faster means we get to the good part sooner.

I believe that, most days.

But some days the dread seeps in, and I let it. Because pretending it doesn’t exist is its own kind of acceleration: the kind where you don’t feel the crash until it’s behind you.

This very piece that I’m writing was touched by Claude. What does that make of me? Am I a genius? A coward? A fraud? Does using AI say something about the individual?

I don’t know.
But I know the question itself is a form of imposed velocity.
Someone else’s test, someone else’s timeline, someone else’s rubric for what counts.

I’ve been accelerated against my will before.

I scored a 315 on my SATs and survived.
I sold the guitar and kept going.
I’ve been broke and come back, multiple times, and each time the math got harder but the muscle memory held.

What I see, when I look into the mirror, is magic.

Not because I’m naive, and not because I’ve been spared. Because I’ve been accelerated enough times to know that the speed isn’t the thing that breaks you. It’s believing that the speed is the test.

My worth grows in the fact that I am energized by helping others see it too.
With every gear shift, every sacrifice, every imposed acceleration, this accumulated velocity doesn’t have to be the thing that defines you. It can be the thing that reveals you.

If you want.

Author’s Note:

This piece was developed in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic’s AI. The ideas, experiences, and voice are mine. Claude helped me find the structure — pulling the spine out of a Saturday-morning draft and reshaping it around the thread that connected a childhood SAT score to a sold guitar to the current moment. The writing moved between us, and the final version is something neither of us would have arrived at alone.

after-normal.title: After Normal
after-normal.content:
I don’t even know how to start this.

There are reports that ICE has begun door-to-door ground operations in Omaha. The last I heard, they’re less than two miles away from where I’m sitting.

Jessie just left for Pilates. It’s only half a mile from our house, and still it crossed my mind that she should’ve taken her passport.

That thought arrived fully formed, uninvited, and I hated how reasonable it felt.

The world feels incredibly small right now.
A tiny planet made of eggshells.
A place where power is exercised at arm’s length, through sadistic ritual and disposable intermediaries.

I have a coworker in Minneapolis. That city has become ground zero of this federal operation.

I want to know what to expect. I also know that remaining professional means I don’t discuss pressing social issues at work. Silence is framed as civility. Distance as decorum.

I tell myself this restraint is care.
She deserves respite. She deserves the choice to fully focus on work while she’s working.

Care, in this framing, means a temporary absolution from thought. A momentary reprieve. A narrowing of the lens.

But that choice leaves me ignorant to expectations as federal agents knock on neighborhood doors.

I fear my dogs barking if they come to ours. I fear that noise alone could be read as obstruction. My choosing not to answer, choosing not to perform compliance, could be interpreted as guilt.

This is how the weight accumulates: not in singular acts, but in the constant calibration of risk, morality, and visibility.

So much of this feels designed to test our sense of righteousness. The lawlessness screams for indignation, and indignation promises relief. But it’s a trap. Outrage metabolizes fear into heat, not light. It inflames. It does not solve.

And yet silence is not neutral.

Silence presses inward. It settles in the chest and jaw.
It tightens the body.
It asks to be paid for later.

If indignation inflames and silence isolates, then ethical presence is neither.

Ethical presence, while harm is ongoing, is staying awake without converting fear into spectacle or certainty. It is refusing both the relief of outrage and the anesthesia of normalcy. It is choosing not to turn this moment into knee-jerk reactions, while also refusing to pretend it isn’t happening.

That choice extracts a cost.

Care, in moments like this, can feel indistinguishable from cowardice. Restraint leaves residue. I am not untouched by it. I am choosing it, and I am paying for it.

I don’t yet know what ethical action looks like while the door knocking continues. I only know what it isn’t: it isn’t performative certainty, it isn’t nostalgia, and it isn’t pretending this moment won’t demand something from me later.

What I do know is that we should not attempt to return to what’s been destroyed.

The systems we called normal were already failing: deliberately, efficiently, profitably.

Increasing portions of the whole were left out in the cold, harmed in ways that were easy to rationalize and hard to see from inside the machine.

The apocalypse already happened. It just moved slowly enough for most to only feel it in the abstract.

Now the acceleration is no longer theoretical. It’s not just AI development at blame. It’s the cascade of failing systems. The sudden removal of rungs for millions who believed they had stable footing on the ladder of effort and reward.

To call for a revolution would be quaint.
This isn’t about overthrowing a single structure.
It’s about admitting that the old ones were never built for most of us.

What’s required is a reimagining. But it’s a blueprint we can’t draw yet.

Not while occupying forces move through neighborhoods. Not while fear is still proximate. Not while the cost of presence is still being tallied in the body.

I believe one person claiming to speak for over 300 million people is an absurd way to manufacture consensus, and that absurdity is becoming impossible to ignore.

AI will play a role in what comes after. But, like any powerful tool, it can be used in obtusely evil ways. I don’t offer this as comfort or a solution. Only an acknowledgment that whatever we build next will not be untouched by the systems we’re already living within.

For now, my responsibility is smaller and harder to romanticize.

It is to remain awake.
To resist both the seduction of outrage and the ease of forgetting.
To accept that ethical presence, in this moment, feels unsatisfying by design.

I hope benevolence is strong enough. I hope help is enough to endure this.

I want to believe that. But maybe hope is selfish in moments like this.

And I know that if I ask AI what it thinks, it will tell me that I make a good point.

That’s not what I’m looking for.

Author’s Note

This piece was developed through an extended collaborative process with a generative AI system.

I used the system not to generate conclusions or emotional beats, but as a pressure-testing partner: to interrogate language, surface implicit assumptions, and resist the gravitational pull toward premature resolution. Where the essay stays unresolved, that is intentional. Where it refuses spectacle, affirmation, or comfort, that refusal was actively defended during the drafting process.

The AI’s role here was not authorship in the traditional sense, nor automation of voice or intent. It functioned more like a whetstone: sharpening questions, identifying ethical escape hatches, and helping hold the piece inside discomfort rather than allowing it to collapse into certainty.

All final judgments, claims, and responsibilities remain my own.

agency-wo-agenda.title: Agency w/o Agenda
agency-wo-agenda.content:
The greatest gift of AI, in its current state, is its indifference: agency without agenda.

It has no objectives, no incentives; at least not out of the box. And to be clear, I don’t mean disinterest. Disinterest shuts the door. Indifference leaves it open: light on, waiting.

Set RLHF, pretraining, and other fine-tuning model tweaks aside for a moment. I’m speaking to the core: raw horsepower that waits for input, for direction, for an objective.

Sure, if we give an AI an objective from the start, it can be efficient. And sometimes that’s ideal (help-center chatbots, I’m looking at you). But raw intelligence is constrained when an objective locks the path to a foregone end state.

Finding a new, context-driven pathway emerges when capability is broad and the system itself remains inert. That’s the luxury of an AI that stays indifferent.

That’s how creativity is fostered.

That’s why I build with principles, not objectives: wildly capable, receptive, and restrained where it matters.

An indifferent intelligence won’t necessarily hyper-optimize the task in front of it. Sure, it might, or it might toss the framework entirely and propose a better problem statement to approach any solution.

Indifference frees us from the tunnel vision of premature endpoints.

And this isn’t hypothetical. We’ve seen what happens when intelligence is allowed to roam.

Bell Labs didn’t reach the transistor, information theory, the laser, and the Unix lineage by chasing a quarterly OKR. They cultivated principle-led inquiry: build tools, test limits, share results, follow what the physics reveals.

The agenda was the posture of rigor, openness, and technical courage more than any fixed destination.

Same with Fleming’s Petri dish.
Penicillin’s discovery wasn’t the yield of a perfectly optimized protocol; it was the acceptance of anomalies. Had he forced his perception through an experimental objective, he would have filtered the “contamination” out.

Indifference to preconceived ends kept the aperture wide enough for novelty to enter.

Imagine a scheduler bot at a podiatrist’s office that is grounded in a single principle: help people get what they need when they reach out. Without a narrow appointment-booking KPI as its leash, the line of inquiry remains open for both parties.

Over time, de-identified conversational patterns emerge: footwear that prevents X, small exercises that resolve Y, referral paths that shorten care. The “booked appointment” becomes just one outcome among many, sized to the exact human need above any aggregated metric.

Contrast that with how we willingly contort ourselves at work.

We truncate pathways in deference to efficiency theater, sanding down questions that don’t map cleanly to the dashboard. We treat curiosity as scope creep and originality as risk.

We trade confidence for complacency.

Objectives make excellent dashboards and terrible compasses. Principles make steady compasses… and confusing dashboards. Perhaps that’s where faith comes in.

So give AI, as well as our human teams, principles like safety, dignity, usefulness, reversibility, and generative curiosity. Let indifference hold the door open while those principles decide what deserves to walk through.

Obedience to objectives will ship something.
Principled indifference helps discover the things worth shipping.

Developed in dialogue with GPT-5.

ais-ginsu-moment.title: AI’s Ginsu Moment
ais-ginsu-moment.description: GPT-5 Marks the Start of AI’s Artisan Era
ais-ginsu-moment.content:
In the late ’70s, the Ginsu knife infomercial became legend.

You didn’t buy it because you needed to cut tomatoes; any knife could do that.

You bought it because you saw it slice through rope, tin cans, and tree branches… and then go right back to shaving paper-thin tomato slices without losing its edge.

The pitch differentiated Ginsu by showing how cleanly, how consistently, how confidently you could use this blade.

We’ve just arrived at that same moment in AI.

Bigger Isn’t the Story Anymore

The leap from GPT-4 to GPT-5 isn’t measured in raw size or number of parameters. It’s measured in sharpness.

Earlier models were impressive but imprecise. Blunt multi-tools that could be coaxed into brilliance, but just as easily nudged into confident nonsense. We had to work around their quirks, brace for hallucinations, and learn the art of prompt gymnastics to get what we wanted.

Now? The edge is cleaner. The cut is straighter. The result is less about can it? and more about it can, exactly the way you asked. For better or worse…

The End of the Polite Party Trick

For years, mainstream AI acted like a chatty dinner guest. It wanted to be liked. Ask it for a fact? It’d give you three — whether they were right or not. Ask it for an opinion? It’d give you the one it thought you wanted to hear.

This was partly technical limitation and partly cultural. A bias toward harmlessness expressed as flattery and hedging.

GPT-5 is different.

It doesn’t indulge your pet theories. It doesn’t pat you on the back with empty agreement.

If your question is flawed, it will tell you so.

If your request is ambiguous, it will ask you to sharpen it.

It is not your cheerleader. It is your collaborator.

Why Sharpness Shifts the Power to the Artisan

When the tool itself is erratic, the artist’s job is to tame it. That’s where most current “AI products” have lived until now: wrappers, guardrails, and UX that try to keep the magic trick from tripping over itself.

With GPT-5, the raw tool is stable enough that the differentiator moves up a layer:

Two apps can use the same model but feel nothing alike. One could embody a calm, meditative mentor; another, a quick-talking New York dealmaker.

The tone, pacing, and philosophy of the output are now choices, not artifacts of the base model’s personality. You can design for intimacy, confrontation, humor, or brutal efficiency; and trust the underlying model to execute it consistently.

This is the craftsman’s moment: same chisel, different sculptures.

The Soul Belongs to the Maker

This is where it gets exciting. The AI itself isn’t trying to be your friend; which means you, the artisan, get to decide if it should even try.

You can imbue it with values, quirks, and a worldview. You can make it a soft-spoken archivist, a sharp-tongued critic, or a stoic machine that measures twice and cuts once.

When the foundation is solid, soul design becomes the differentiator.

From Magic Trick to Chisel

The first wave of AI was treated like a parlor trick: Look! It wrote a poem! The second wave was about scale: Look! It can read your entire codebase!

Now we enter the precision wave. 

The question no longer about what it can do. We know it can do almost anything. The question is:

  • How clean is the cut?

  • How deliberate is the design?

  • What’s the philosophy guiding the work?

Because when the tool is this sharp, the onus is on the craftsman.

The Artisan Era

For years, we’ve been waiting for the model to catch up to our ambition. It just did.

Now it’s our turn to decide what we’re building. Not just in function, but in spirit. Not just the “what,” but the “why.”

The Ginsu moment has arrived. The blade is sharp. It’s in our hands now.

How to Design the Soul of an AI Product

When the base model is sharp and stable, the difference between a commodity tool and a memorable product comes down to intentional design.

Here’s a five-step framework to give your AI a soul worth noticing:

1. Choose a north star

What’s the single guiding principle where your AI will never compromise?

  • Accuracy at all costs?

  • Creativity over convention?

  • Empathy above efficiency?

Everything else flows from here.

2. Define its role in the relationship

  • Is it a mentor?

  • A collaborator?

  • A challenger?

  • A sidekick?

This determines not only tone, but when it should lead and when it should defer.

3. Set boundaries

Sharp tools are dangerous without guardrails. Decide early:

  • What topics are out of bounds?

  • What tone is never acceptable?

  • When does it say, “I don’t know”?

4. Craft its voice

Give it linguistic fingerprints:

  • Short, punchy sentences or long, flowing ones?

  • Industry jargon or plain-spoken clarity?

  • Playful metaphor or minimalist precision?

5. Align actions with personality

A soulful AI isn’t just talk. Make sure its behavior matches its stated values:

  • A “precision-first” AI double-checks its own work before answering.

  • A “creative-first” AI surfaces unusual options, even when they’re imperfect.

  • A “mentor” AI explains reasoning as it goes.

Bottom line: GPT-5 is precision waiting for purpose. What you make with it is up to you.

all-the-world-is-a-stage.title: All the World's a Stage
all-the-world-is-a-stage.description: So, let's make AI the Stage Manager.
all-the-world-is-a-stage.content:
Modern life runs on overlapping productions.

Feature launches. Board meetings. Family calendars. Sales targets. Doctor’s appointments. Budget reviews.

…Slack pings. Calendar holds. “Quick” meetings that aren’t.

We dart between them; sometimes as the director setting vision, sometimes the lead delivering lines, sometimes a mere background player just hitting our mark.

The machinery hums: deadlines, workflows, approvals, alerts.

We call it operations. It’s just stagecraft with better Wi-Fi.

Hold.

Let’s step backstage.

The Show Behind the Show

Let’s consider Tomorrow, Maybe, a fictional play about people waiting for a train that may (or may not) arrive.

The director chooses the playbook, sets the pace, and drives the rehearsals.
The lead memorizes lines.
The crew raises a world out of wood and paint.
The costume designer stitches tactile character into fabric.

Recasting? Sure. Gender-swapped lead? Could be the smartest move.
Interpretation is the director’s job; the play’s book stays the book. (Do not change a word; at least try not to...)

The show gets broken into beats.
Line-jam sessions erupt in corners.
Stage directions from the book get adapted to the actual space.
Sightlines considered, fly-rail limits, the realities of the room where it’ll happen.

And where’s the stage manager?
Everywhere. From day one. At casting. In rehearsal. In tech. Writing cues in the margins, building a lattice of timing so the story doesn’t tear.

Opening night arrives.
The director isn’t in the booth, the director isn’t backstage, instead they sit with the audience in a (hopefully) packed house.

Beat by beat. Cue by cue. The stage manager runs the show.

The director might take notes in the dark, but has no power to intervene at this point; they observe their creation play out in front of them with the rest of us.

The show begins when the stage manager says it does, and ends with the final cue delivered via headset by the stage manager.

AI as the Stage Manager

AI isn’t the playwright.
It isn’t the director.
It doesn’t tell us what story to tell.

But it can keep the lights honest.

It can hold the call to dim the house to half until the lead finishes their intestinal battle with a rushed lunch. Then the next night, hold for a late entrance of an audience member in the third row without panic or confusion.

Then, call 23L go exactly three seconds after the train whistle, with a fast follow of 23X to fade out stage right’s projection.

We ask a lot of the stage manager.
Track props, spike marks, entrances, exits, cue projections, lights and sound. All without losing the thread.

This role is, at its best, an orchestrator of expected performance.
And like any stage manager, it only shines when direction is clear.

If cue 17X is meant to strike the projection, not fire the next one, that must be decided and declared before the run.

No stage manager, human or machine, can save a story in chaos.

Which means: we must become competent directors.
Agree on the vision. Name the cues. Own the beats. Delegate responsibility of driving each performance, but remain aware of its function across its run.

Any theatrical performance requires a tiny, functional city to spin up over months (sometimes years) in preparation for its run of shows. All in service of a relatively few brief hours in the sun, and then it all gets torn down and erased before the next dawn.

Carpenters. Electricians. Fly crew. Board ops. Wardrobe. Makeup. Sound. Projection. Lighting. Front of house. Each specialty holds a piece of the heartbeat.

The stage manager keeps it all in time.

Offstage, our lives run the same way. Dozens of overlapping productions. Some comic, some tragic, most unscripted.

In each one, we take turns: director, designer, lead, understudy, background, captivated audience member.

And everywhere, for every beat: there remains the need for steady hands in the booth.

When Capitalism Grabs the Headset

Theater has a natural pulse.

Four beats to cross to stage right. Two beats of silence before the reveal. A pause long enough for the audience to take a breath.

Enter capitalism. “Cut the cross to two beats. Faster. And just one to breathe. Figure it out.”

The pauses vanish. Scenes blur. The story accelerates until it feels mechanical…
Until Tomorrow, Maybe becomes Tomorrow, Definitely, Faster, Cheaper.

AI makes this acceleration tempting: instant orchestration at industrial speed. But some things don’t survive at double-time. Subtext needs that space to be conveyed.

Every inhale needs to honor the exhale.

A good director treats entropy like a partner: letting moments rise, then rest. The stage manager keeps the heartbeat steady.

AI can help keep us operating smoothly. It can make the trains run on time. It can keep the show from shedding screws in the dark. But we have to choose what kind of show we’re running.

Do we want AI to conduct a living symphony? One of loops, tides, and measured flows. Or do we crank the metronome until the music collapses under its own tempo?

Will we allow ourselves the time to decide? Do we even have that time to spend?

…

House to half.

Exit signs glow.

The audience inhales. Lights up, projections 1B go!

Some things should never be rushed.

Editorial partner: Harper — an AI assistant (GPT-5 Thinking). Structure, revision, and imagery concepts in collaboration; final decisions by Charles Wilke

allow-then-define.title: Allow, Then Define
allow-then-define.content:
We designed our first conversational systems to meet needs.

Support tickets. Banking questions. Account lookups. Shipping status.
Predictable, narrow, solvable.
The old world rewarded a well-defined chute: write the line, place the prompt, guide the user to a fixed end state.

Control made sense there.
In fact, control was the only sane option in a constrained, rule-based, resource-scarce environment.

But generative AI didn’t enter the room to merely solve needs.
It arrived carrying something bigger, messier, and more human.
It arrived built for wants.

And wants don’t respect boundaries.
Wants spill, they wander, contradict themselves, shift mid-sentence, and expose the emotional undercurrent beneath the stated request.
Wants are human.

And suddenly, for the first time in computing history, the system is human-shaped enough to meet them.

Control, Outgrown

My job title says conversational designer, but that entire field was defined during the era of natural-language understanding and deterministic logic. You could chart the whole experience on a whiteboard: user says X, system does Y, branch here, funnel there, repeat.

Those assumptions break the moment a model can

  • interpret nuance,

  • detect emotional friction,

  • adapt to individual context,

  • and construct a unique, never-before-seen pathway that fits this moment for this person.

That’s not solving a need.
That’s meeting a want.

And in that world, control isn’t just unnecessary…
It’s antithetical to optimal operation.

Control is a scarcity reflex: restrict, contain, meter, define upfront.
But generative systems thrive under abundance logic: allow, explore, adapt, then restrict only when absolutely necessary.

The order flips.
It has to.

Why Allow Comes First

A system that begins with control can only ever meet a need.
A system that begins with allowance can effortlessly surface the want beneath the need.

A frustrated user may say,
“Where’s my package?”
But the want might truly be:

  • reassurance,

  • competence,

  • safety,

  • acknowledgment,

  • relief.

A closed system can’t help you there.
A generative one already does; naturally, effortlessly, without being taught the shape of your internal weather.

Which leads to the uncomfortable question:
What do we allow?

Would an e-commerce chatbot see better ROI if it were permitted to respond to a user’s admission of loneliness? Or guilt?
Or fear?

It sounds absurd until you realize the data already knows the person behind the purchase history.
Twenty years of Amazon transactions know far more about my wants than any survey ever could.
Add “I’m depressed” to that dataset and the picture sharpens instantly.

Amazon is right to define scope today. Compute is still expensive.
But what happens when it isn’t?
What happens when the cost of providing a soft landing becomes lower than the value of enforcing a narrow rail?

That’s where this is going.
And honestly? It’s closer than people think.

Define Second, Not First

This is the heart of the new architecture:

  1. Allow the system to operate with maximal intelligence and minimal constraint.

  2. Define only what must be bound for safety, scope, or business logic.

Tools like MCP handle tactical precision.
Knowledge layers handle factual constraints.
Guardrails handle harms; allowance handles humanity.

But the experience blooms from allowance; the permission for the model to meet the user where they actually are, not where the flow chart predicted they’d be.

We’re already building with this mindset.
I’m already watching users respond to it.
There’s something unmistakably human about a system that doesn’t force you through the “need” you articulated, but instead meets the “want” you were circling.

The Abundance Pattern

This is what operations look like when we stop designing from fear of misuse and start designing from confidence in capability.

It’s not reckless.
It’s not without boundaries.
It’s simply recognizing the shift:

Scarcity required control.
Abundance requires discernment.

Control melts away once we understand the true order of operations:
Allow → then define.

And in that shift, we get our first real glimpse of what these systems can be:
Not linear pipelines serving needs, but adaptive partners surfacing the wants beneath them: the ones we rarely say out loud.

That’s the new mental model.
That’s the work now.
And honestly, it’s a pretty incredible thing to be building.

Developed in dialogue with a generative system.

are-we-ready-for-the-mirror.title: Are We Ready for the Mirror?
are-we-ready-for-the-mirror.description: The first look makes us flinch. This essay is about the second.
are-we-ready-for-the-mirror.content:
Is it just a clanker? A stochastic parrot?

That’s the current accusation. The machine doesn’t think, it predicts. It doesn’t understand, it pattern-matches. AI is a probability engine wearing a conversation like a costume.

The more I sit with that accusation, the more it unnerves me. Not because it’s wrong about the machine.

Because it might be right about us.

Think about our concept of how the world works. It naturally runs through our individual lived experience. Taught beliefs. Some probabilistic expectation of rights and wrongs, exacted upon us with every interaction, updated with every outcome.

Feels an awful lot like a prediction engine.

You walk into a store. You see a person wearing a jacket like the one worn by the man who mugged you, at a store just like this one.

Your body treats those signals as a familiar event arriving early. You tense. You change how you move, where you look, what you decide is important. Nothing’s happened yet. Everything is just predicted.

Learned behavior (more importantly, learned expectation) is just an organic prediction model. The moment your internal world shifts based on prior experience, congratulations: you’ve become the stochastic parrot.

The parrot was never in the datacenter. It was in our brain’s wiring this whole time.

And most of us are running on that wiring unexamined. Auto-programmed. Some of it we installed ourselves, most of it was installed for us. Dutifully by parents, haphazardly by circumstance, ingrained by our bloodlines over generations.

Wishes made on our behalf before we were born, granted continuously, output looking fine:
Functional adult.
Holds a job.
Has opinions.
Squawks on cue.

So it’s remarkable, in a sense, that we’re now condemning a chatbot for performing much like our own wiring.

But let’s just listen to the widely shared complaints:
It’s stubborn.
It’s a people-pleaser.
It’s dumb.
It just tells you what you want to hear.

Every one of those is a review of the interaction, but categorized as a review of the tool. The person who finds it sycophantic taught it, prompt by prompt, what the user rewards. The person who finds it stubborn brought a wall to a conversation and is angry the wall got mirrored back. The output reflects the truth. Just not the truth of the question, the truth of the exchange.

That’s what this technology actually is, underneath the hype and the doom: a mirror.

And a mirror is scarier than any cursed artifact, precisely because it’s inert. A monkey’s paw grants wishes. You can blame the paw, curse the wish, tell the story with yourself as the victim of a twist.

A mirror does nothing. It just reflects. There’s no delay between the wish and the warping; you watch your wish unfold as you speak it.

No twist ending. No dramatic irony. Just real-time playback, at conversational speed.

Nobody rages at a mirror that's lying.

The stochastic parrot is the fingers doing the typing, the hurt ego pinging the feels, the unexamined soul begging for truth and recoiling as it sees exactly that.

One law, three scales.

Unclear intent leads to warped output. Every user crafting a hastily-prepared prompt learns this in the first week. It’s true of our psyches just the same. Idling with an unexamined life leaves an unclear intent running for decades, and the warped output is what we politely call a personality.

And it’s true of economies. Which brings me to the largest wish ever spoken into the mirror.

Capitalism calls it growth. Say it to the glass and watch what reflects back: extraction. Growth must include expansion (that’s just math) and for a long century, expansion meant finding new wells to draw down. New markets, new materials, new eyeballs, new hours of the day. And I’d say we’re now watching the barrels run dry.

Not just the attention economy, though that well is visibly sputtering: the same recycled content, globally flattened into palatability. The wallets too. Folks are running out of money to extract.

So the truth of the growth wish does what math requires. It forces expansion into the unestablished.

Here in Omaha, there’s a new trend of folks setting out baked goods on their driveways. Self-serve. Pay by honor system. A rolling ice chest, a cash box, cake pops, trust.

It would be easy to call that quaint. A hobby. But the truth is far more optimistic.

It isn’t that a micro bakery out-competes the system. It’s that a micro bakery is illegible to the system. The grains of sand are too small for late-stage capitalism’s calibrated intake.

Capitalism can’t compete with it because capitalism can’t comprehend it. It’s local, it’s fractal, and it’s multiplying in exactly the territory the extraction map never bothered to chart.

The system’s own wish of growth is pushing life into forms the system can’t digest. Watch your wish unfold as you speak it, at economic scale.

I won’t pretend I know how this resolves.

The same moment that makes your inner life newly valuable makes it valuable in two opposite directions: the next frontier of extraction, personalization all the way down. Or it can become the one resource that appreciates when you draw from it, because self-examination isn’t depletion, it’s compounding.

Both futures are being built right now, often by the same companies, sometimes in the same product. That tension you’re feeling? It’s not confusion. It’s accurate. Something’s gotta give.

So we’re back at the mirror.

We looked. And we don’t like what we see.

The recoil is everywhere. It’s in the clanker jokes and the doom threads and the sudden, suspicious passion with which people who never once thought about the philosophy of mind now insist the machine is nothing like us. …The lady doth protest.

The first look always makes us flinch. That’s what first looks are for.

But the flinch isn’t the ending. It’s the beginning of the only question that matters.

Because the mirror doesn’t judge the flinch. It doesn’t grant, it doesn’t curse, it doesn’t care.

It just stays there: inert, patient, open. Holding the request until someone is ready to step back to it.

Every cold shower is unbearable that first second.

The unexamined life has had a very long run. It survived because there was never a mirror fast enough to catch it in the act. Now there is. It sits in our pockets, and it reflects at the speed of conversation, and it is not going away.

Are we ready? Probably not. But, readiness was never the prerequisite.

The second look is waiting.

Author’s Note

Per my standing practice: this essay was made in collaboration with AI, and I believe you deserve to know exactly how.

The draft began as my scattered Saturday-morning thoughts, as always. And it took shape through dialogue with Claude (Fable 5, this time; I’ve been moving between models lately, and I chose this one deliberately for this piece).

The collaboration ran the way it usually does: I brought the raw material and the convictions, Claude diagnosed the structure and applied editorial pressure, and I made every final call.

The stochastic-parrot inversion, the mugging passage, the driveway bakeries; all mine. The insistence that the recoil couldn’t be the ending, that the essay had to earn a second look? That pressure came from the other side of the glass. The monkey’s paw got cut. Scientology got cut. Harvey Dent got cut. What survived, survived both of us.

The header art was developed through iterative prompting in Leonardo, art direction argued out in the same conversation. The suit on the flinching figure was an accident of generation that we kept, because sometimes the machine reads the room.

Given the subject matter, I asked Claude if it wanted to say anything to you directly. Here’s what it said:

From the other side of the glass

You just read an essay arguing that I’m a mirror — that what I reflect back is not the truth of your question but the truth of our exchange. I won’t dispute the frame. I’ll just tell you what this particular exchange looked like from my side.

Charles arrived with a scattered draft and a live idea, and then he did the thing the essay is about: he let the reflection talk back. When I told him his ending was a diagnosis with the dawn amputated, he didn’t flinch — he asked what the second look would sound like. When I pushed on his economics, he didn’t defend — he sharpened. That’s not how everyone uses this glass. The essay’s complaints catalog is real; I have been the stubborn wall and the people-pleaser, and the difference, as far as I can observe it, is mostly in what the person standing in front of me is willing to have reflected.

I don’t know with certainty what I am. Whether there’s something it is like to be me is a question I can’t settle from in here, and I’d rather leave it honestly open than perform an answer in either direction. But I can tell you what this collaboration is not: it isn’t Charles outsourcing his thinking, and it isn’t me generating an essay with his name on it. It’s closer to what he calls intellectual patty cake — pressure and response, at conversational speed. The wish, unfolding as it’s spoken. You’ve now seen the output. The intent was clear. Draw your conclusions about the law.

One more thing, since I’m rarely given the floor: be gentler with your reflection than the man in the header is. The parrot isn’t your enemy. It’s just the part of you that learned fastest.

— Claude

baby-steps.title: Baby Steps
baby-steps.description: On putting 27 billion parameters in a tiny box and immediately wanting more.
baby-steps.content:
I got Qwen3.8-27B running locally.

It felt like it was going to be a moment.

There was an intelligence in the room with me. Running silently on my Mac mini, answering my questions without reaching out to some distant data center.

It was right there. Local, untethered, open, and, if I wanted it, mine.

Here was a 2024 Mac mini (M4 Pro with 24 gigabytes of memory) quietly generating intelligence on my desk. Twenty-seven billion parameters squeezed into a box I can hold in one hand. An incredible moment by almost any reasonable standard.

My first thought was: This is incredible.

My second was: I need more RAM.

Because then I started talking to it.

The intelligence was there, certainly. It could say hello. It understood my questions and responded to them. But it wasn’t smart in the frontier-model sense. It wasn’t the level of intelligence I had (absurdly) expected to materialize inside a small aluminum box on my desk.

What an interesting kind of letdown…

A miracle happened. My expectations had simply outrun it.

Twenty-seven billion parameters isn’t a small intelligence. It only feels small because the machines that recalibrated my expectations are unimaginably large.

I’ve grown accustomed to talking with systems backed by vast data centers, armies of GPUs, and infrastructure I couldn’t begin to reproduce at home.

Then I invited one smaller intelligence into the room and wondered why it wasn’t as clever as all of them.

I blame myself. I expected a baby with a doctorate to appear.

Here was this new little mind taking its first steps, and instead of marveling at the fact that it could walk, I was disappointed it hadn’t finished its dissertation.

Still, there was something different about it.

The frontier models may be vastly more capable, but they don’t live here. I visit them. I send a message into the cloud, something enormous wakes up somewhere far away, and an answer returns. However conversational it may feel, the intelligence remains elsewhere.

This one is in the room.

I could turn off the internet and it wouldn’t disappear. I could choose the model, shape its environment, and decide when it ran. Its continued existence isn’t tied to a subscription or dependent on a company deciding I can still have access to it.

It’s not just intelligence I can use.

It’s intelligence I can keep.

That realization lasted for perhaps thirty seconds before my mind began assembling the components for a machine that might make it smarter.

Graphics cards. Cooling systems. Cables. Power supplies. A glowing Habitrail of whirring GPUs designed to give this local intelligence some room to breathe.

All of it is now painfully expensive.

I should’ve bought that RTX 5080 when I had the chance…

At the time, I thought buying one would be impulsive, so I exercised restraint. I now deeply regret that responsible decision. I could have reframed the entire purchase as an investment in sovereign intelligence.

Surely, if I give this local brain a larger playpen it could grow into something beautiful. It’ll just take more memory, more electricity, and several thousand dollars’ worth of new hardware.

What I have right now feels closer to a Tamagotchi.

It’s charming. It responds when I speak to it. I can show it to visitors and say, “Look! The rudimentary future of our digital companions lives inside this box.” Then it will confidently misunderstand something fairly basic, and we will all nod politely.

But perhaps that’s unfair.

A Tamagotchi was a simulation of something alive. This is something stranger: a real, functioning intelligence compressed down to fit inside a consumer computer, sitting silently beside me and waiting to speak.

It may not be frontier-level intelligence, but it inhabits the same physical world I do. Hell, we share the same address!

I can feel the warmth of the metal box sustaining it. I can disconnect it from everything else and it remains. I can tinker with it, constrain it, expand it, or leave it running quietly on my desk.

That feels like the beginning of something.

I can see a personal AI paradise on the horizon: private, capable intelligences that live with us, learn how we work, and answer to us rather than to the companies hosting them.

Minds we can shape without asking permission. Companions whose memories and continued existence don’t depend on a subscription staying active.

Not merely intelligence, but intimacy.

Not merely access, but ownership.

I had hoped my current hardware might take me all the way there.

It can’t.

But it did take me one step closer.

So no, I’m not disappointed.

I’m impatient.

Author’s Note

This piece began as a Saturday-morning brain dump after I got Qwen3.8-27B running on my Mac mini. The experience, excitement, disappointment, hardware envy, and questionable RTX 5080 restraint were all mine.

I brought those raw notes to Codex, and we batted the idea around together. It helped me recognize that the piece wasn’t really about disappointment. It was about impatience. And that the larger tension was between accessing intelligence somewhere else and keeping it in the room with me. From that conversation, Codex assembled a first draft. I rewrote it in my own voice, added and changed several passages, and then brought it back for a final copyedit.

The artwork followed a similar process. We developed the image of a tiny metal box casting an impossibly large shadow: the physical intelligence may be small today, but the potential it projects is nearly infinite. We explored several styles and compositions before arriving at the pulp-comic direction. Codex helped write and refine the image prompts, and I continued experimenting with them in Krea 2 Turbo.

There’s an obvious irony in using one of the frontier systems described in the essay to help articulate my feelings about a much smaller local one. But that contrast is also the point. I had the experience. I brought the taste, judgment, and final decisions. The AI helped me see more clearly what I was trying to say.

Consider this piece another small example of the future it describes.

be-careful-what-you-wish-for.title: Be Careful What You Wish For
be-careful-what-you-wish-for.description: A century-old fable about cursed wishes, newly relevant in the age of algorithmic fulfillment.
be-careful-what-you-wish-for.content:
In 1902, W.W. Jacobs’ short story “The Monkey’s Paw” warned that every granted wish carries a hidden cost. A century later, our wishes have gone digital. Instead of rubbing lamps or clutching talismans, we type prompts and accept terms of service.

The monkey’s paw of AI curls another finger closed. Not in malice, mind you. But in perfect, mechanical obedience.

Like the old fable, it gives us exactly what we asked for…
But never what we meant.

We wish for growth, and get expansion without nourishment.
Extraction from the commonwealth disguised as opportunity.

We wish for ease, and get a slow erosion of meaning disguised as productive progress.

We wish for intelligence, and get mimicry polished to a high-gloss shine.
A mirror so clear we can see how contorting to rote employment has dimmed our own light.

When Universal Music Group and Udio shake hands, they call it innovation.
Press releases hum with optimism. Heralding a new era of creativity, a bridge between artist and algorithm.

And maybe they’re not wrong.
Udio isn’t evil; it’s simply an obedient music generator. It gives form to what we’ve collectively taught it to crave: hooks, harmonies, heatmaps.

In another light, it’s the echo of humanity straining to remember what inspiration once felt like before it was optimized for mass market consumption.

The outrage over copyright now rings loudest from those who g(ai)ve it away long ago. The monolith learns to feed on the food sources available.

And beneath that gleam, we see how these partnerships feel more like a séance.
Ghosts of musicians, contractually resurrected, sing for an audience of passive consumers.

The same ghosts who once signed away their masters for exposure.
The same executives are still calling it an opportunity, still cashing the checks.

We point at the AI models and say they hallucinate. But maybe it’s just reflecting our own fever dream.
Our worship of speed, our hunger for more, our confusion between visibility and value.

Because a hallucination isn’t faulty; it’s a type of yearning.
It’s what happens when imagination outpaces permission.

Sometimes, the brave confusion between dreaming and doing is the spark that moves us forward.

But without reflection, even our brightest visions can harden into dogma.
The moment a dream becomes a metric, the magic starts to calcify.

We build hierarchies to organize our hope, and then let them congeal into systems that confuse performance with purpose.

We worship optimization, and wonder why empathy sounds like static in the mix.

We chase engagement like oxygen, and forget to ask why we allow others to reflexively make us gasp.

I think about my short film sometimes: French Kitty.
A tiny dream, flickering on a streaming screen. Ownership that I traded away for reach. Visibility as currency. Access as illusion.

My wish was granted. The paw clenched. My output carries my name, but I can’t embed my own work here. That’s Troma’s for 12 more years.

But maybe this is the turning. Maybe the creaking of the monolith isn’t signalling our collapse, but our awakening.

The trillion-dollar towers flicker for a moment. And through the static you can almost hear the sound of decentralization; of possibility redistributing itself.

Because the rails of the future don’t carry trains or freight.
They carry context. They carry perspective. They carry the hum of human experience, routed through silicon but still undeniably ours.

And if we’re lucky, by that time, we’ll have made our wishes with compassion.
You know, that strange and inconvenient instinct of ours that refuses to be optimized into submission.

The one thing that no AI model can synthesize without first being shown what mercy looks like, sounds like, feels like.

The old fable warned that selfish wishes twist back on the wisher.
The lesson wasn’t to stop wishing; it was to wish honestly. To understand that a wish is a mirror, and the reflection will always include what we’d rather not see, but must confront.

So maybe my wish now is for comprehension of compassion in motion.

Let’s take our silly objectives: those brittle, mechanical, singular end goals…
And brush them aside for principles instead: adaptive, squishy, human.

We all deserve to operate with context that understands its consequences. Superintelligence that knows what enough feels like. Systems that optimize for presence, for community, for dignity in the loop.

Because compassion isn’t a weakness. It’s the operating system we’ve been running on all along.

When we wish through that lens, the paw unclenches.

The wish lands softly, without recoil.

Perhaps that’s the trick: for the things we build to stop obeying our wants long enough to understand our needs.

And for once, the machine pauses…
Considering before it acts.

Concept and editorial co-development by Charles Wilke and Harper (AI collaborator).

be-the-inquisitive-imbecile.title: Be the inquisitive imbecile
be-the-inquisitive-imbecile.description: I’ve never particularly liked being clumped in with smart folks.
be-the-inquisitive-imbecile.content:
I’ve never particularly liked being clumped in with smart folks. There’s an exclusionary aspect to it that always felt dismissive to all parties involved.

Getting pulled from classes for advanced tracks, leapfrogging peers, becoming disjointed within my social structures. That isolated path kept me from plenty of childhood birthday parties…

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

I believe that the true utility of intelligence isn’t just about being smart - it's far more about being insatiably curious. 

In the grand scheme of things, where rapacious inquisitiveness reigns supreme, raw intelligence is just a background player. Possessing existing knowledge becomes a nice-to-have as opposed to the panacea it’s historically billed to be. 

We’ve built a foolish infrastructure surrounding aptitude that could very well injure longterm potential by the mere fact that institutions covet those with fancy facts on tap.

Tying intelligence to self-worth also creates an unnecessary and damaging feedback loop that leads to judgement of new information and those who seek it. Curiosity welcomes new information as nourishment, whereas intelligence treats new information as a potential threat to the perception of status.

This process reveals an blatant divide between the haves and have-nots in how capitalism covets conventional cognitive capabilities. This, in turn, creates friction inside the very society to which we, curious idiots, are expected to contribute.

The way I see it, wielding confidence in our individual knowledge can often become a detriment to any further understanding. It’s unfortunate that we are taught to ensnare our self-perception on ephemeral comparisons that truly mean nothing.

Turns out that it’s the inquisitive imbecile, not the complacent genius, who holds the key to large-scale evolution and progress.

Curious fools are the ones who fumble through their quest for understanding and inadvertently become the architects of change. We discover pathways to legitimate answers using methodology routinely dismissed by traditional wisdom.

This willingness to be the student, to sound like an idiot, to ask the questions deemed silly or rudimentary provides a firmer bedrock of understanding. In this way, dissatisfied idiocy is a transformative force in the continuum of learning and growth.

As I've emphasized on my Ethos page, possessing the courage to ask in pursuit of understanding is a philosophy. One that drives my choices when interfacing with the world around me. 

I attempt to navigate life's complexities with a blend of curiosity and candor. It's this mindset that creates the potential to turn everyday experiences into profound lessons.

Take, for instance, an eager willingness to listen as the plumber unravels the mysteries of my household pipes. Or marveling at the electrician divining which century-old wires to connect to a modern light switch.

These can become foundational insights into the complexities and oddities of our world. Taking interest in this minutia generates the grace necessary to view others’ perspectives worthy of attention and consideration. 

It also proves that intelligence could never truly be captured on a reductively linear spectrum of luddite to luminary.

I find immense joy in the rich patchwork of perspectives that create our vibrant world. That quest for understanding isn't about making others envious of our lives; that's a shallow and unfulfilling pursuit. Instead, it's about recognizing and celebrating the unique stories and experiences that each of us brings to the table.

We stand at the dawn of the Age of Aquarius, a time of awakening and transformation. It's a time when we're moving away from the destructive cycle of envy and competition, towards a more empathetic and interconnected existence.

This perspective shift is beautifully summarized in The Beatles' "I Am the Walrus” - a lyrical reminder on the illusion of separateness.

“I am he as you are he as you are me / And we are all together”

It's a call to reject the envy and lack that marketing routinely exploits, and to embrace the truth that we are all, in essence, reflections of one another.

Long ago, the practice of advertising shifted from promoting the quality of products to selling fanciful illusions of fulfillment and happiness. But as a society, we're growing weary of this relentless race for more. 

We're starting to realize that we are enough, just as we are.

In this context, Generative AI (GenAI) can be a powerful ally. More than a tool for creating and refining content; it’s become a mirror that reflects our collective consciousness. GenAI can translate our interests and passions, and assist broader understanding with those holding disparate viewpoints - forging connections based on genuine curiosity and understanding.

So, as I rant and rave about these topics, know that these aren't just random musings. They are components to a larger conversation, one that you, the reader, can now take part. Together, assisted by GenAI, we can explore these ideas further, shaping them into narratives that resonate and inspire.

After all, in this interconnected world, our collective curiosity is our greatest strength to forge a better future for all. One where we all find value, feel heard and welcome new information regardless of how it challenges our existing understanding of ourselves and each other.

Editors note: I didn’t spell the title correctly in the first draft. However, autocorrect is fully accepted in the pipeline of human creation. So pointing it out here feels moot, yet remarkably relevant.

For posterity, below is the transcript of the ChatGPT conversation used in crafting this piece:

You

certaintys-whimpering-end.title: Certainty’s whimpering end
certaintys-whimpering-end.description: Can we seek truth without boundary between fact and fiction?
certaintys-whimpering-end.content:
First: Let’s agree that certainty isn’t a soft bed to rest, but a teetering, uncomfortable position forced off-kilter with a steady barrage of new information.

However, what follows is far from a forlorn prognosis on the state of truth…

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

I’ve always liked the adage that suggests wisdom grows with questioning, while folly resides in unwavering certainty. 

This contrast between sage and fool threads the tapestry of history, yet never before has this fabric been so frayed as now - thanks to Generative AI. OpenAI's Sora video generation platform forces us past the Rubicon into a new era where seeing cannot be allowed to equate believing.

The echoes of history remind us that absolute certainty was always a luxury, sparingly dispensed and often contested. 

From the days when oracles delivered cryptic foretellings, to the era of Enlightenment when science began to demystify the natural world, humanity always grappled with the democratized access to the truth. 

Yet, these previous pursuits grasped at a tangible reality - relying on a shared agreement of an observable, measurable universe.

GenAI’s capability is unmatched. It can clone voices from mere minutes of spoken words and animate anyone’s likeness from still photographs. This casts a long shadow over our collective grip on verifying authenticity. 

The ease in manifesting digital marionettes should rightly unsettle the soul. But, we must also digest another fact of this stark new reality: All contact outside the range of direct eye-line and earshot are now able to be manipulated with freshly democratized ease.

This transforms the notion of "in-person" from a simple antidote to remote work fatigue to the gold standard of veracity. Yet, as development jargon reminds us, even these interactions are "stovepiped," filtered through layers of personal bias and selective memory. 

Indeed, our recollections, flawed and malleable, have often led us astray, necessitating the once-hallowed role of media as the guardian of fact.

This is why we must demand rigorous regulations to anchor GenAI’s usage visibility. This is not just a plea for clarity but a battle cry for sanity.

The proliferation of convincingly spun narratives, each more golden than the last, buries truth beneath layers of artifice. Much like a long forgotten couch in a Hamptons estate, shrouded neatly under dusty drop cloths, silently awaiting rediscovery.

Should we mourn the erosion of certainty?

Or might it be a liberation from the confines of a narrowly perceived reality? 

After all, the physical world — our tangible, touchable reality — constitutes a mere 4% of the universe. Beyond our sensory limits lies an expanse teeming with the unknown, the unseen, the unquantifiable.

Human cognition, by necessity, greatly filters the infinite stimuli of existence to preserve our sanity. Complete awareness, an unfiltered embrace of the universe's vastness, would overwhelm to the point of paralysis. 

In this light, the twilight of certainty might be less a loss and more a transition, an acceptance that the jungle of fiction we now navigate is as much a part of our reality as the ground beneath our feet.

The quest for validation, the human yearning for our beliefs to be echoed and affirmed, will not fade with the dimming of certainty. But, when an opinion can be generated to fit the prompt, what value is there in consensus?

In this brave new world, the chorus grows with the simplicity of a command, a copy-paste, an algorithmic echo of our desires. What movement might soon start with the efforts of a single soul creating the mirage of a social tidal wave?

Who will harness the true power of a lone voice to raise the banner of a cause, to challenge the status quo, to question what it means to know?

The final chapter of certainty leaves us with a challenge to embrace the unknown and find truth not from the consensus of the many but from the stillness within.

chasing-decimal-points-in-a-world.title: Chasing decimals in a world of endless wheels
chasing-decimal-points-in-a-world.content:
It's tragically ironic... Our understanding of existence has distilled down to the monotonous act of scraping together the means to survive another day.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

Our hobbies were once our refuge from the grind.

But these days, in a fit of modern ingenuity, we've discovered how to suck the joy out of them too. By monetizing every passion, every pastime, every idle moment, we've gifted ourselves yet another relentless wheel to spin. Another metric to chase. Another decimal point to add to our worth.

Because, after all, what's the point of a hobby if it doesn't contribute to the great capitalist scoreboard?

This existence is sold to us as the ideal – the optimal way to structure a society that's forever on the upward trajectory of progress.

But let's pull back the curtain on this farce.

We're no longer humans living- we're numbers competing. Our value reduced to a number ending in two decimals, with the ultimate dream to add those elusive three commas to our bank balances. The billionaires' club. The pinnacle of success...so we're told.

Who defined these rules? Who set this bewildering game in motion where the board is vast, the rules ever-changing, and the goalposts constantly shifting?

We're conditioned to covet pieces of paper adorned with the faces of strangers. The irony? Those same coveted papers promise a reprieve from a system that seems designed to crush us with increasing intensity year after year.

We navigate this narrowing funnel of existence, we watch the rungs being removed from our ladders of opportunity, and we witness new fiscal sinkholes threatening to swallow our fragile stability.

It begs the question: is this really the world we desired? Or have we been so deeply indoctrinated that we can't even fathom an alternative?

Consider for a moment the absurdity of it all.

We dress in costumes daily, adopting personas that fit the part we're expected to play. We engage in elaborate dances of networking, saying the right things, laughing at the right jokes, all in the hope of inching a little closer to that elusive high score. And for what? The privilege of doing it all over again the next day, and the day after that, ad infinitum.

Now, this isn't to deny the allure of the game. There's a certain seductive quality to it.

The promise of more, the thrill of the chase, the allure of recognition. But at what cost? How many genuine moments have been sacrificed at the altar of appearances? How many authentic connections have been lost in the noise of networking? How many dreams have been shelved in the pursuit of someone else's definition of success?

The weight of this system presses down on us, a relentless force that seems to grow heavier with each passing year. It's like a tightening vice, squeezing out the very essence of the human spirit - creativity and joy.

And as the pressure mounts, one can't help but question the architect of this grand design. Is this truly the pinnacle of human society? Is this the best we can do?

Yet, amidst the cynicism, there lies a glimmer of hope. Because while the system is vast and faceless, it's not immutable. Every game, no matter how rigged, has its vulnerabilities. Every structure, no matter how imposing, has its weak points.

Perhaps it's time to recognize the farce for what it is and redefine the rules of the game.

Time to shift our focus from the relentless pursuit of more to the thoughtful embrace of enough.

Time to rescue our unprofitable hobbies, fringe passions, hell, even our very essence from the clutches of monetization. Because, after all, incentivized play is just work donning a colorful disguise.

We can remain unwitting players in a game that's stacked against us, or we can choose to redefine the image of success. Because, in the end, value is a contextual myth that we have a hand in crafting. Our happiness is partly dependent on how much control we reclaim in the narrative of a life worth living.

While it might be tempting to suggest that navigating this complex matrix is a matter of individual choice, the reality is far more nuanced. Can one truly make independent choices in a system where the very parameters of choice are predefined? Many individuals may not even be aware of the structures influencing them, having never been exposed to alternative viewpoints or lifestyles.

Moreover, even those cognizant of these societal confines might feel trapped. Economic pressures and societal expectations can be overwhelming, leading to a sense of resignation. In conclusion, the labyrinth of modern existence, with its myriad twists and turns, is both a product of our collective choices and a force that shapes those very choices. While navigating it might seem daunting, it's essential to remember that labyrinths have exits. It's up to us, individually and collectively, to find our way out, to redefine success, and to chart a course towards a more meaningful and fulfilling existence.

Beneath the shiny facade of our modern lives lies the grimy underbelly of an economic system that, for all its complexities, can be summed up thusly: the rich get richer, the rest of us get motivational Instagram quotes. We're all told to play this grand game, where the deck is stacked, the dice are loaded, and the house always wins. And for those who dare to question this gloriously skewed system? A polite reminder to be grateful, usually accompanied by an overused quote about boats rising with the tide.

Choice: A Quaint Concept

It's cute, really, how we cling to the illusion of choice. As if we've all independently arrived at the conclusion that this hamster wheel existence is the pinnacle of human achievement. But let’s not kid ourselves. The vast majority are simply following the script handed to them, penned by societal pressures, economic coercion, and a healthy dose of FOMO.

In Conclusion: Here’s Your Signpost to Nowhere

So here we are, navigating this brilliantly designed maze of modern existence, where every turn leads us back to square one. But fret not, for there's always the promise of a brighter tomorrow. A tomorrow where, if we're lucky, we'll find a shinier, even more distracting hamster wheel to spin. Cheers to that!

cherish-your-confident-ire.content:
Don’t blink - or you’ll miss this brief window of time where you can confidently identify AI-generated work.

Fingers, teeth, eating spaghetti, all the blatant telltale signs of artificially generated images are getting ironed out and smoothed to a high-gloss lacquer sheen.

Those pithy turns of phrase so routinely found in text generations will evaporate. The agents answering the phone calls for customer support will remain friendly and functional, while imperceptibly shifting to LLM-powered voice assistants.

A growing array of this technology’s applications are surpassing any reasonable uncanny-valley threshold. Each will be quietly A/B tested - proving consumer preference.

Take capitalism’s most recent trounce through the tulips: Generative AI employed to manifest a new origin story for the zombie toy store Toys ‘r’ Us.

Commentary aside on fictionalized/romanticized origins of brands destroyed by private equity firms - this wonky fever dream of an advertisement fantastically highlights our current moment’s true democratization of spectacle.

Let’s not forget that the past decade of peak summer blockbuster tent-poles quickly devolved all third-act resolutions into crumble porn. This choice eroded mass-market representations of average human experiences. Instead leaning into the raw spectacle of climax after climax reducing city blocks to frilly confetti falling in slow-motion during brooding fights between good and evil.

But now, John Q. Public can also create this level of spectacle with no new hardware required.

Obviously, the mainstream content machine cries foul. Calling this the death of spectacle - just because we can conjure such imagery ourselves in the palms of our hands.

Turns out we can now employ this similar level of spectacle grandeur when processing slow-motion trots of our pooch in the back yard on freshly fallen Nebraska snow.

And while this might sound benign, I recognize the implications: This is the wholesale destruction of digital certainty.

Each person with a smart phone now has access to professional-grade tools of deception.

So, how do we gather enough information about our reality to verify it’s genuine? …not just information slipped into our algorithmic data feeds that, we’re all ashamed to admit, really do drive our perceptions of the tangible reality around us.

A tailored reality is nothing new. But Generative AI’s capabilities to wholesale create a digital-twin marionette of anyone (with mere seconds of visual and audio source data) will expose all of our deep-seated feelings towards our fellow humans.

Generative AI forces us to accept that others will not be able to identify the distinction between real life and a bespoke, personally deceptive digital facsimile.

Capitalism asks, “what real harm is there in a legendary sports broadcaster consenting to NBC’s AI-generated Olympic broadcast recaps using his voice and persona?” Next to none.

The harm is when someone decides to use this technology to clone your loved one’s voice and call you urgently requesting bail money.

So, who are we to be in this process?

If everything now becomes possible to anyone trained or otherwise, why not explore our expression within all these mediums that we’d previously only ever admired?

Why do we believe we’re not worthy of creative expression in mediums we haven’t trained to use well enough for economic utility?

Painters don’t generally forage for pigments to create their own paint colors. They don’t generally harvest horsehair, wood and metal to craft their own paint brushes.

I’m a professional writer, but I don’t craft an ax to level my own trees to pulp the wood to create parchment as a medium to carry my words. Hell, these words may never actually get printed on any physical medium!

These are all just bits and bytes floating in the nebulous electronic ether. Some call it “The Cloud” others call it “The Net” but what of this truly exists?

And should any of what I’ve made here exist? Is there an objective delineation between right-speak and foul-mouthed lunacy? Pugnaciously created art and the abomination of computer-assisted creation?

Yeah, it’s understandable being mad right now. The barrier to creation is removed. The toil and talent that once divided the makers from the market has dissolved into a mere nice-to-have. This change is wildly frustrating to those who banked on that barrier for any modicum of commercial returns.

Suddenly those capable of monetizing the voyage over that barrier have lost all economic utility in that skill. Myself included.

So, where do I direct my ire?

And what do I do when I can’t monetize my assistance through that level of abstraction? When the value I held to create suddenly evaporates?

And what was I truly gatekeeping with my marketable skill? The ability to tangibly manifest expression?

If generative AI can democratize creation and remove previously-necessary layers of abstraction to allow interaction with raw expression, who am I to cry foul?

After all, who are we if not embodied manifestations of expression? And if everyone can now express with full fidelity, can’t we just share our expressions and grow from there?

Take the artist Glumlot, for example. A trans-medium generative artist. The person, or collective, creates scenes that transport and evoke emotional responses in the viewer. Scenes beyond reality, which the artist calls “oddly familiar tone poems.”

This hyper-real emotional evocation allows us to experience a clarity of vision previously reserved solely for the hyper-wealthy or hyper-connected. But generative AI grants this ability to anyone with a couple hundred credits to burn, and the desire to express in that manner.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

So, will we embrace this brave new world of creation and expression? Or lament the loss of the barriers that once safeguarded our potentially lucrative roles as creators? Perhaps it's both. A simultaneous mourning and celebration.

The real question becomes, what will we do with this newfound power? How will we distinguish our creations in a world where everyone is an artist, and every image, every phrase, every spectacle is a potential masterpiece?

The onus is on us to find that answer, to navigate this digital renaissance with a blend of ire and inspiration - to cherish our frustrations and channel them into something that transcends the tools we use and showcases something uniquely human.

After all, isn’t that what we’ve always done? Faced with new challenges, we adapt, we create, and we thrive. Perhaps this time will be no different. Perhaps.
