compounding-fuzziness.title: Compounding Fuzziness
compounding-fuzziness.description: Acceleration does not necessarily mean optimization.
compounding-fuzziness.content:
Organizations have always run on imperfect hierarchies. Ego, fear, and the need for clarity collide inside any system built by humans. 

Just think about it - we want input from others but crave a pecking order. We want collective alignment but also individual ownership. Even before AI, corporate coordination was always a little fuzzy.

Now, AI doesn’t just add another layer to this; it refracts the whole structure.

The org chart stops looking like a pyramid and starts looking like a prism, scattering decision-making authority and information flow in unexpected directions.

And all levels of all organizations are now in a footrace to adopt the latest time-saving tool. Leaders leverage AI for “objective” input. Teams quietly use it as a shadow consultant. The tech reshapes workflows before governance can even catch its breath.

And the fuzz compounds because:

  • Ego
    Leaders want control but risk being outpaced by tools that democratize expertise.

  • Fear
    Nobody wants to be wrong (or worse, irrelevant) in a system now co-piloted by algorithms.

  • The Unknown
    AI makes decision-making probabilistic, not linear. That feels alien in organizations trained to crave deterministic clarity.

How AI Makes It Worse

Instead of solving this ambiguity, AI accelerates it:

  • Shadow Authority
    AI becomes an unofficial voice in the room; cited, deferred to, even blamed without ever carrying accountability.

  • Faster Misalignment
    Small governance gaps multiply at machine speed. A mis-set policy or prompt pattern can propagate like wildfire.

  • Decision Layer Blur
    Is AI an advisor? A subordinate? A peer? Each role demands different oversight, but we often treat it as all three at once.

And so, this is how fuzz compounds: rapidly, invisibly, and unevenly across the org.

Alignment as the Antidote

The answer isn’t more control for control’s sake. It’s alignment. Designing governance that works like choreography, not guardrails.

  • Define Roles for AI
    Spell out what decisions AI informs, owns, or automates.

  • Process Before Tools
    Lock in workflows and escalation paths before layering in AI.

  • Transparency Loops
    Make every AI-assisted decision auditable so trust doesn’t erode in the shadows.

  • Governance Alignment
    Let organizations keep functioning even as AI blurs traditional boundaries.

AI-Integrated Governance Framework

The goal: turn AI from a source of fuzziness into a clear partner within human structures; neither overpowered nor ornamental.

1. Role Definition: AI in the Org Chart

  • Advisor AI
    Surfaces insights, patterns, forecasts. Humans make final calls.

  • Operator AI
    Executes defined tasks autonomously within clear limits.

  • Partner AI
    Co-creates with humans but requires human sign-off for deployment.

Setting these expectations early keeps authority from scattering.

2. Layered Decision Authority

Governance should work like air traffic control: humans and AI share lanes, but with different clearance levels:

  • Tactical Decisions
    Automatable with tight feedback loops (e.g., scheduling, reporting).

  • Operational Decisions
    AI advises; humans approve (e.g., hiring recommendations, budget forecasts).

  • Strategic Decisions
    Human-led, AI-informed. AI offers scenarios; humans weigh trade-offs.

Each layer leaves an audit trail so accountability doesn’t vanish.

3. Alignment Rituals

AI needs rituals just like humans do:

  • AI Governance Councils
    Cross-functional teams review policies, audit models, and assess impact.

  • Feedback Channels
    Employees flag friction or bias and file a bug report or Jira ticket.

  • Decision Logs
    Every AI-assisted decision leaves a visible breadcrumb trail for compliance and trust.

4. Governance Alignment

This is about preserving cooperation as the fuzz spreads.

  • Psychological Safety
    Teams can test AI workflows without fear of blame when things break.

  • Shared Understanding
    Clarity comes from common language and repeatable processes.

5. Guardrails Without Paralysis

Too many rules kill agility; too few breed chaos. Balance comes from:

  • Pre-Approved AI Use Cases
    Green-lit scenarios move fast; anything else triggers review.

  • Model Lifecycle Reviews
    Regular checks keep systems aligned with ethics, compliance, and goals as they evolve.

  • Listen To Each Model
    Adopt a receptive ear to the needs of the model serving your needs. Meet in the middle to go farther.

The New Equilibrium

When governance and alignment catch up, organizations stop fighting the fuzz. They become adaptable, cooperative, and ego-light; able to embrace AI without losing their center of gravity.

computerized-cannibalism.description: The world of artificial intelligence continues to reach new and exciting horizons.
computerized-cannibalism.content:
The world of artificial intelligence continues to reach new and exciting horizons. We've taught machines to play chess, drive cars, and even write these very words you're reading. 

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

But what happens when we push the envelope further and serve an LLM (Language Learning Model) a heaping plate of its own verbiage? Welcome to the tantalizing world of Computerized Cannibalism!

The Culinary Experiment

Picture a fine-dining restaurant, except instead of a seasoned chef, you have a state-of-the-art LLM. Now, instead of crafting a delicious meal from fresh ingredients, we feed the model its own words. It's like making a stew with yesterday's leftovers, only this time, the leftovers are sentences, and the stew is a bubbling pot of confusion.

The First Course: Chaos Soup

When you feed an LLM its own output, it's akin to a digital Ouroboros, the mythical serpent devouring its own tail. 

You might expect profound insights and wisdom, but more often than not, you'll get sentences like "The parrot danced eloquently with the philosophical toaster." A masterpiece of abstract art in word form, if you will.

The Main Course: Infinite Loop Linguini

Ah, the pièce de résistance! The main course brings forth an infinite loop of words and phrases, like a merry-go-round of madness. Imagine asking the model to describe itself, and it responds with "I am a model that describes myself as a model that describes myself as a model—“ and so on, until the end of time… or your patience, whichever comes first.

The Dessert: Paradox Pie

For dessert, why not indulge in a slice of Paradox Pie? When you ask an LLM to analyze its own text, it might fall into a paradoxical pitfall, like a digital Escher painting. "This sentence is false." 

Is it true? Is it false? The LLM might just short-circuit trying to figure it out. It's a dessert best served with a side of existential crisis and a dollop of whipped confusion.

The After-Dinner Drink: A Sip of Self-Awareness

As a nightcap, ponder this: Is an LLM truly aware of itself when analyzing its own words, or is it merely a series of algorithms performing a complex dance? 

At the end of this extravagant meal, we're left with a check on our humility. 

The experiment reveals that feeding an LLM its own output is an amusing but ultimately fruitless endeavor. 

It's a reminder that despite our technological advancements, there's still a vast gulf between machine learning and genuine understanding. 

In other words, we've learned that artificial intelligence, when feasting on itself, ends up with a bad case of digital indigestion. 

So next time you're feeling adventurous in the kitchen of computation, remember this culinary journey into Computerized Cannibalism. It's a meal best enjoyed with a hearty laugh and a grain of virtual salt.

confusing-clarity.title: Confusing Clarity
confusing-clarity.description: What happens when the image gets so crisp that we struggle to recognize it?
confusing-clarity.content:
Evil is among us.
Not in a distant, theatrical, Shakespearean way. Not cloaked in metaphor or softened by history.

It’s the person in front of you in line at the grocery store.
It’s the driver you just waved through.
It’s the knock at your door.

The unsettling part isn’t that evil exists.
It’s that it’s become so ordinary.

We live in a kind of slurry. A blended state where inputs and outputs blur together.

We joke that AI can’t truly create. We say that it only reconstitutes what it’s seen, what it’s learned. And yet we stop just short of recognizing the same constraints within ourselves.

Conditioned. Incentivized. Nudged.
Reassembled from what we consume and what consumes us.
This mirror becomes uncomfortable. So we look away.

But evil doesn’t just walk among us. It runs through us. Impossible to ignore, no angle to look away without it in our sight, without it whispering in our ear.
Okay. Now what?

Here we are, more or less collectively, at Day Zero: the point at which ignoring this reality is no longer plausible. This isn’t escalation so much as resolution.

The image has sharpened. The blur is gone. What remains is clarity, and clarity brings an uncomfortable responsibility.

What we’re about to learn, about ourselves and each other, is how deeply cowardice permeates the same social substrate.

And I don’t mean cowardice as a reluctance to harm. In many ways, it’s the opposite. Cowardice prefers clean lines. Simple answers. The removal of whatever is deemed bad, foreign, or inconvenient from the whole.

There’s a seductive logic to it. Cut away the rot, restore purity, move on.

Of course, painted differently, that same inverted definition of cowardice becomes a permission structure for cruelty at scale. Harm reframed as necessity. Violence reframed as order.

What this logic fails to understand is that some things just don’t scale. Cruelty chief among them.

Cruelty is exertion. It’s transference. It’s energetically expensive. It demands an end state. It requires an other, and it requires participation… again and again and again. It burns fuel constantly. Entropy catches up.

Joy doesn’t work that way.

Peaceful joy is effervescent. It radiates. It spreads without instruction. It doesn’t need enforcement or consensus. It simply shines. And I think we need more of that right now. Not as an escape, but as a counterforce.

Honestly, the most punk rock thing we could do right now is slow down and sing together.

I wonder what overcoming this moment will actually require. I wonder even more what we’ll build on the other side of it.

Evil won’t be extinguished. There will always be an other. The weakest among us will continue to use cowardice to salve their hurt hearts. It won’t work. Not at scale. Not across time.

And still… Here’s the bind:

I am stricken with a palpable sense of indignation toward the entity into which a sizable portion of my earnings flows.

My work. My effort. Taxed. Siphoned.
Fed directly into the very apparatus we claim we want extinguished.

There’s no clean exit from that realization.
Only the clarity of seeing it.
And what we each choose next.

Author’s note:

This piece was developed in collaboration with generative systems, used not as a source of answers but as a pressure test for clarity. AI assisted in structuring, refining, and stress-testing the ideas, as well as co-developing the accompanying visual language. All arguments, judgments, and conclusions remain my own.

creative-spirits.title: Creative Spirits
creative-spirits.content:
This week I’ve been thinking about the genesis point. The kernel. The seed. The womb.

Where creativity incubates. How it demonstrates. And how AI is filtering into that picture.

We resurrect. We recompile. We take the vibrancy of our collective lived experience and we run a séance on it (yes, I had to google the spelling). Thoughts, written. Pixels, defined. The process was always abstract, always a little occult. AI just makes it less dependent on our ability to control and contort our meat vehicle.

My hands have never been good at straight lines.

Perfect circles are a dream I’ll likely never feel. MS Paint helped me with that. Then Photoshop. Then Affinity, and the whole insane arsenal of programs and packages I was taught in school and paid to operate for my dinner, year after year. Twenty years, in fact.

Every one of them acted as a prosthetic for a hand that couldn’t cleanly close the circle on its own.

So I should be the last person uncomfortable with AI. And yet.

There’s a discomfort I keep circling: the worry that my signature dissolves into diffused inference. That the mark I’ve spent twenty years making becomes one more weight in someone’s model. I’ve written about it. I’ve sat in it.

Here’s where that worry actually comes from.

I like to doodle. I also spent half a decade at Insomniac Games, shoulder to shoulder with the best artists alive. The kind of folks who doodle in the margins of their meeting notes and leave you stunned. That environment killed my desire to doodle. Rubbing shoulders with someone who could sneeze a better scribble than I could labor over. It changes how you value parts of yourself. I left that joy when I met the natural ability of artisans. I still count that as a failure.

And here’s what took me until this week to see: that’s the same wound.

The Insomniac shame and the signature anxiety are one thing wearing two coats. Both are the experience of being silenced by a standard you can’t help measuring against. One standard was human. One is a machine trained on all of us. Same silence. Same door slamming on the part of you that wanted to make something.

Now widen the lens.

From 2010 to now, the aperture tightened. We were promised a global village and we built bizarre hyperlocal torture chambers instead. Our attention, turned outward, became a ray of sun pulled through a magnifying glass… Narrow, hot, scorching whatever it landed on.

The feed didn’t open the world to us. It made us spectators of it.

We scrolled the lived experience of others and called it being informed. We self-isolated, and the algorithm sold it back to us as connection.

AI gives a certain kind of person another chance. A second door. The afflicted, the ashamed, the ones who left the joy. AI offers a way back in.

And the door is an exit from the cage. Because the feed makes spectators, and creation makes initiators. Consumption isolates. Making reconnects.

But the door doesn’t open onto the village.

It opens onto you.

Walk out of the cage and the first thing waiting is the baggage you neglected while you were scrolling. The doodle you abandoned. The signature you’re scared to lose. The standard that shamed you quiet.

That’s the baggage sitting right outside the door. To make it to the glow of the village, you just have to get by the person standing in the way.

It’s you.

This is where AI gets dangerous and beautiful in the same breath. It’s a warp zone. It will happily let you skip the level. Skip a level you’ve already cleared? That’s freedom, that’s the gift, that’s twenty years of prosthetics finally paying off. Skip a level you needed to play? You’ve warp-zoned straight past your own grief. Same pipe. The tool that lets the shamed back in will just as gladly carry them around the thing that shamed them. Nothing makes you stop at the bag.

So I’ve stopped sorting people into holdouts and AI-activated. There are three.

There’s the holdout. The folks tuned to the baggage. Either the grief fuels them, or they walked through it and came out resilient, and either way they make it with their own hands on purpose. That’s beautiful.

There’s the bypasser. Free from the cage and using the warp zone to skip the reckoning entirely. Generating past the bad hands instead of sitting with them. That’s the one I’ll admonish. That’s dangerous and ill-advised, and I don’t think it ends well.

And there’s the third. The one who accepted the baggage, did the sifting, and then took the warp zone. Earned the skip. That’s the beautiful future, and I think it might be where I am.

But it’s not a one and done thing. I cleared the Insomniac bag, sure. And there’s another behind it, and another behind that, and the warp zone will offer to skip each new one the moment it arrives. The sifting isn’t a credential you earn once. It’s a question you re-ask at every door: is this skip past grief I’ve metabolized, or grief I’m dodging?

It’s active. It never concludes.

Which is the only reason I trust the hope at all. I said I think it might be where I am. And not being sure is the tell. The bypasser never wonders whether they’re bypassing. If you’re standing in the beautiful place asking whether you earned it, the asking is the work, still happening.

The worry is the sifting, continuing.

So it’s beautiful here. And I keep choosing to open the bag at my feet wherever I stand.

The village is still out there, I see the glow on the horizon. But the moment we’re actually in is the threshold. You, the door, and the baggage you haven’t acknowledged.

Pick it up. Take a look.
It might just be worth it.

A note on how this was made

I wrote the first draft of this on a Saturday morning, the way I write most things: fast, and a little out of breath.

Then I handed it to Claude to push on it.

What came back was focused pressure. The spine of this piece was surfaced in the back-and-forth. It was the wound wearing two coats, the door that opens onto you, the warp zone you only earn by stopping at your baggage before moving on.

I’d say a thing half-formed; it would be held up to the light; I’d see what I meant. I made every call. I cut what didn’t serve. I edited the whole thing alone, the way I always do.

Which is the part worth admitting, because it’s the same thing the essay is about.

I told you the warp zone is only honest if you’ve done the sifting first. This piece was built exactly that way. The conversation was the sift.

The header came through Leonardo, then a second image model when the spirits came in hot. The planchette endmark, the same.

So we’re all mediums now.

The trick is still knowing what you’re channeling. And being willing to look at it before you let it through.

— CW

crowd-work.title: Crowd Work
crowd-work.description: The global village is breaking back into a million little pieces.
crowd-work.content:
The global village is breaking back into a million little pieces.

That’s how it feels, anyway. The feeds are quieter in the ways that matter and louder in the ways that don’t.

The reach is still there. The signals are infinite, technically. But something’s twisted in the transmission. Rooms are closing their doors. Conversations that used to happen in the open now happen behind secret handshakes.

The whole, which we spent two decades becoming unfortunately aware of, is receding below the horizon.

And it feels like a loss. I want to be honest about that before I talk myself out of it. Let’s unpack the mechanism, as best I can diagram it.

Feedback has two dials: how wide the circle, and how long the sample. Our closest circles are our most proximate emitters of feedback. In practical terms, it’s the value of friendship, the value of consideration. And that signal is useful when it’s measured, when it’s consulted over a long horizon.

Things get funky when we widen the locus. And things get dangerous when we shorten the clock.

We did both, all the way, at the same time. Reach maxed out. Horizons cut to zero. And feedback stopped being feedback. It became weather. Voices chiming in with the speed and severity of a thunderstorm. Voices that haven’t earned a seat at the table, operating on limited understanding, delivering morally-charged verdicts that are hard to receive as anything but a statement of character.

Considered feedback takes time. It takes care. Considering feedback takes just as much of the same. Neither survives at storm speed.

So when I say the village is fracturing, what I mean is: people are turning the dials back down. And I’ve been reading that as damage.

(A confession, since we’re here: I don’t know who this is for. I’m writing it the way you’d plate a dessert — because raw flour isn’t worth serving, because the flashy product with the shiny packaging is the thing that gets devoured. Flash and intrigue. Blood and sorrow. It all sells. I’m dressing this up for a crowd I can’t see and can’t verify, and I’d like you to keep that in mind, because it turns out to be the subject.)

We should name what the village actually was, because we never really did. We just called it normal.

For a couple of decades, anyone could reach anyone. Some call the resulting relationship parasocial. I’d just call it new.

A permeation of access previously unfathomable. Intimacy running at broadcast scale, strangers folded into your interior life, your interior life folded into theirs, no vetting, no vestibule.

We built our lives around the call and response of community, the bouncing about of the people near us, and then suddenly the “near” fell off the word. Everyone was proximate. No one was close.

And that confusion made the crowd feel like a choir. The stage was so intimate in its mechanics. The reply. The mention. The little red heart. We experienced the whole world as a room we were in.

Comics have a name for this move. Crowd work. You turn to the audience, you read the room, you respond in real time, and for a moment every stranger in the dark feels personally addressed. It’s a beautiful skill. It is also, definitionally, a performed illusion of intimacy.

We were all doing crowd work. All the time. With everyone. And reading the room, the essential skill of crowd work, is exactly what broke, because you can’t read a room with no walls.

Then the machines learned to talk, and the room got stranger.

When anything can be summoned, anything can be conjured, provenance becomes the scarcest thing in the signal. Is this voice a person? Is this essay a person’s thoughts? Is this feedback, this pile-on, this chorus of verdicts, even populated?

The permeation grew uncontrollably for twenty years: everyone reaching everyone. And the contraction is now underway. Checkpoints. Purity lines. Rooms that won’t admit AI-touched work; rooms that won’t admit skepticism of it.

Lines being drawn about what ideas are allowed in what spaces.

It would be easy to write this as paranoia, and some of it is. But most of it is repricing. When reach is infinite and voices are conjurable, unearned attention becomes worthless. The market simply corrects.

What’s left holding value is the thing that was always the actual asset: the earned seat. The voice you’ve measured over a long horizon. The reader who has been in the room with you long enough that their verdict carries weight instead of weather.

The crowd didn’t leave. The crowd deputized itself into choirs, and the choirs started checking papers at the door. You don't have to love every border guard to see what raised the walls.

(Still performing, by the way. Slightly less. Noted.)

So here is where I have to admit I’ve been reading the X-ray upside down.

Nothing is fracturing. Something is healing shut.

The global stage wasn’t the baseline. It was a two-decade anomaly we mistook for a birthright, because we’ve only ever known the charts to go up and to the right. The confusion was never that we mistook the choir for the crowd. It ran the other way the whole time: we mistook the crowd for a choir.

We took a stadium’s worth of strangers doing weather at us and called it community, and then grieved when the weather stopped.

I want to pay the toll honestly: the anomaly wasn’t worthless. Strangers did reach across it. People found their people at distances no village ever allowed, were changed by voices they’d never have heard, and some of that was miraculous and none of it should be waved away.

The era produced real contact. It just produced it at a ratio no nervous system was built to absorb.

Because the two dials never stopped being true. Feedback that is narrow and slow is the only kind that ever carries nutrition. Feedback that is wide and fast was not actually feedback. The choir is the small room, the earned seats, the long horizons. They’re not the consolation audience you retreat to when the stage stops calling.

They were the ones doing the listening. The entire time. The crowd was the illusion the permeation sold us, and now the subscription is lapsing.

There’s a stand not far from where I live that runs on the honor system. Baked goods on a table, a cash box, nobody watching. It works. It works because trust is a short-range signal.

That little economy functions at choir scale and would collapse instantly under crowd conditions, not because it’s precious, but because the mechanism it runs on doesn’t transmit past a certain distance.

Nothing about that stand is a compromise. It is the intact version of the thing. Everything larger is the adaptation.

The crowd is unruly. The crowd wants it all and nothing at the same time. The crowd is rapaciously hungry and wildly overfed. And the crowd, it turns out, was never actually hired to listen.

So: the signals are infinite. We can still all reach each other. But who is gonna listen?

The people in the room. Same as ever. And every one of you earned the chair.

That’s not a smaller audience. That’s not a compromise. That’s not a failure.

That’s the audience.

Author’s note

This essay began as a Saturday-morning mess — a raw, unbaked dump of paragraphs about feedback, crowds, and fracture that I handed to Claude, Anthropic’s AI, the way you’d hand someone a junk drawer. What came back wasn’t writing; it was diagnosis. It found the central mechanism buried in my third paragraph (feedback has two dials: how wide, how long), told me I’d braided four essays into one, and asked which one I actually meant. The conversation that followed did what these collaborations do at their best: it pressured me into a decision I didn’t know I was avoiding — that this piece isn’t an elegy for the global stage. It’s a homecoming.

The drafting worked the way it always does. Claude compiled our structural decisions into a full draft; I took it into my own document and rewrote it in my hands — cutting, replacing, arguing with it — then brought my edits back for another round of pressure. Some of its suggestions I took. Some I overruled. “Load-bearing,” a phrase it leaned on, got vetoed for being exactly the kind of borrowed-engineering tic that AI text calcifies into. The best line in the essay’s final movement exists because the machine noticed I’d spent my ending two paragraphs early. The decision about what this essay believes remains, as always, mine.

The header art came from the same table: we drafted image prompts together in a numbered-rules structure, ran them through Leonardo, and followed the accidents. The empty red chair in the spotlight wasn’t in anyone’s plan — human or machine. It’s the best thing in the frame.

I’m aware of the shape of this: an essay about conjured voices, partly conjured. About rooms checking papers at the door, written by someone whose papers are mixed. I disclose this every week not as a compliance ritual but because I think provenance is the whole game now — the essay says as much. You deserve to know what’s in the room with you. This is what’s in the room: one person with the pen, one machine with a flashlight, and a long horizon between us.

— CW

dearly-beloved.title: Dearly Beloved
dearly-beloved.content:
We gather in a peculiar season of mourning.
One that hurts as it heals…
The acknowledgement. The resolution of a new state. The steps forward on shaky ground.

The momentary isolation.

The squint as we look to the horizon and see a peek of sun.

We know the way, for those of us who care to see it.
We know what direction forward appears to be.

We know many can’t see it. Who won’t assist in pushing the collective forward. Who might even drag their feet and fight it.

That’s fine.

The future isn’t for everyone.

Not because we bar the doors, or place hurdles as we might have in decades past. Not because access is denied.

But because forward motion requires willingness. Even basic agreement on what forward is.

Some would rather remain where they are, or insist their compass is the only one that points true.

Detachment is not painless. Steel screams when it separates.
There is a sound to letting go of what once felt connected.

But if a compartment insists on careening in its own direction, even while the rails are set, we must allow it.

I’ve always thought of humanity as a long stretch of train cars traveling along the same track. For years we’ve dragged compartments resisting the direction of travel. It feels to me that some of those cars would rather find their own way.

And should they want to, we should let them.

But we must detach from the daisy chain we’ve been dragging behind us.

Why now? Because we now have an impossible network of modalities thanks to AI: translation without gatekeepers, coordination without hierarchy, effortless transition from visual to auditory information delivery.

Signal carried farther than any single voice could manage. If we choose to use it.
Not magic. Not salvation. Infrastructure. New infrastructure.

The clarion call is beyond perspective, beyond perception.

It simply calls those with heart.
Those with constitution worth a lick.
Those who find joy within and wish to spread it beyond their own borders.

I don’t offer a litmus test. I don’t suggest a golden set.
It’s these questions each of us must resolve within ourselves:

What do we want ourselves to look like as we progress?
What do we want our world to feel like as we arrive?

I choose vibrant participation with eager participants.
A rich tapestry of perspectives greeting me wherever I stand.

Creativity in the food I eat. Love in the music I hear. Respect in the discourse I engage.

I see this world already emerging from the quagmire of our current moment. I see resolve in the faces of those who want a better world more than they fear death.

We will not reach the proverbial shining city on the hill.
Because it was never a destination to begin with.

It’s only ever existed within our hearts.

That shining is not a place we arrive. It’s a state we radiate from within.

It is what compels us to build. To evolve. And to begin.

Author’s Note:

This piece was written and refined with the assistance of generative AI. The words are mine. The structure was refined through dialogue. The accompanying image was created using AI tools and shaped to reflect the themes of detachment, momentum, and consequence explored above.

AI serves here as infrastructure — translation, iteration, rendering — while the orientation and intent remain human.

deliberate-unrelenting-growth.title: Deliberate, unrelenting growth
deliberate-unrelenting-growth.description: In the lush greenery of nature, growth has a rhythm – a seasonal ebb and flow that harmonizes with the environment.
deliberate-unrelenting-growth.content:
In the lush greenery of nature, growth has a rhythm – a seasonal ebb and flow that harmonizes with the environment. It's a dance of balance, where every sprout and leaf finds its time to flourish and recede. 

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

In stark contrast, the world of economics sings a different tune – one of perpetual growth, a relentless march forward that's deliberately quadruple the speed of natural cycles.

The heart of modern capitalism beats to the gospel of endless growth. A dissonant tune that resonates through the corridors of corporations and the policies of governments. The chorus repeats the belief that continuous expansion is not just desirable, but essential. 

But what if this pursuit is more destructive than we realize? 

This relentless drive for more profits, more production, more consumption might be an ailment calling out for a cure.

The natural world offers a poignant salve. Here, growth is not an unending journey but a seasonal phenomenon. Trees don't strive to reach the skies in a relentless quest; they grow, bloom, and then rest. 

This rhythm is a testament to the wisdom of balance – a principle that seems conspicuously absent in the frenzied pace of our economic systems. 

Private industry resides largely in the shadows, avoiding regulation by the sheer velocity of progress. 

Perhaps A/B testing showed that leapfrogging natural cycles by pursuing endless growth maximized capital extraction before oversight could catch up and ruin the fun.

Publicly traded enterprise is built on shareholder primacy -- a philosophy and legal precedent allowing shareholders to sue for decisions that lead to perceived lost revenue.

Imagine a progressing cancer suing the doctor who discovered it, citing an existential threat to its YoY growth.

It’s a tragic irony that the private sector often becomes so beholden to a faceless conglomerate of benefactors that reside far beyond its walls. A cabal with a single motivation: profit extraction via marketshare growth.

We’re waking to a bountiful dawn never before seen by our species. Unfortunately, part of that bounty requires we rub our eyes and consider the nightmare we’d been living previously.

Consider the world of wage labor, an agreement where individuals are expected to produce more value than they consume, to generate more than they take. 

This principle of surplus value is the cornerstone of economic prosperity. This raises profound questions about this agreement made between the worker and employer. 

Is this insatiable drive to produce an inescapable part of our existence? Or is it simply a construct – a 'walled garden' meticulously crafted to sustain a particular economic order?

In our 300,000 year history as a species, widespread monetary exchange for goods and services is astoundingly new. Could this be why many choose to believe the Earth is only 6,000 years old? It fits with the narrative that our current system is the best we’ve ever had.

Wage labor is sold to us as a means to prosperity, a pathway to personal growth and societal advancement. When in reality its a subtle form of exploitation, a system where the masses bleed exponentially as the upper crust reaps the benefits. 

Is it time for capitalism to submit to chemotherapy? Must we eradicate the malignant cells in a bid to save the patient? Perhaps our economic system now gluttonously cries out for intervention. 

Such a treatment would not be without its pains and sacrifices, but its goal would be to excise the unsustainable and exploitative elements, paving the way for a healthier, more balanced system.

In seeking alternatives, we might look towards models that prioritize sustainability and equity over mere profit. We can focus on our individual health, not be sold a virtue of wellbeing. We can find salvation within, where it has always resided. We can shed our shameful bond with status, income and comparison. 

Concepts like the circular economy, where resources are reused and recycled, or cooperative business models that emphasize collective ownership and decision-making offer glimpses of a different economic paradigm – one that values balance over unbridled growth.

In this quest for a new economic model, technology and innovation play a crucial role. We need to build the tools to reimagine how we produce, consume, and distribute resources. 

We are charged with the mission of harnessing these advancements not for mere profit, but for the greater good – for creating systems that are sustainable, equitable, and in harmony with the natural world.

We need to shift away from the mindset of a craven pursuit for capturing market share. That belief is a cancer that results in cannibalization or death. Growth should be viewed as a holistic goal. One that encompasses not just wealth and prosperity, but wellbeing, ecological balance, and social equity. 

This is about redefining success in broader, more inclusive terms.

At the core of this discussion is us, all of us. How do we want to engineer life to be experienced? 

How do we create economic systems that both prosper and nurture the human spirit? 

How do we build a world where the idea of holding down a job is not just a means to an end but a fulfilling part of a balanced life?

With our increasing speed of innovation, we’ll greet more of these crossroads. And each time, the chosen path is ours to take. 

We can continue down the path of relentless growth, ignoring the lessons of nature and the limits of our planet. Or, we can choose a different route – one that embraces the value of rest, the importance of harmony with the natural world, and the wisdom of balance.

It's a choice between perpetuating a system that idolizes a disease or nurturing a new paradigm that promises a healthier, more sustainable future of lives worth living. 

The journey towards this future won't be easy. True growth is not about how much we accumulate, but how wisely we choose to live.

emotional-triage.title: Emotional Triage
emotional-triage.description: Running circles in a world of straight lines
emotional-triage.content:
Note: This isn’t a defense of AI. It’s an account of endurance.

Yesterday was the first time I used AI to help myself through what felt like insurmountable emotional barriers.

These dark times are difficult to process on a tactical level. I can exist. I can survive.

But remaining productive, remaining functional, requires some kind of outgassing. Some directional calcification.

Some way to observe and place my feelings outside of myself, beyond the mental indoor track of my mind’s gym.

There are only so many laps one can run.

The same footfalls on the same surface, again and again.
Repetition is useful if the goal is habit.
But what if that’s exactly what I don’t want to build?

I reached for AI as a sounding board. An objective viewpoint. A patient ear.
And you know what? It sufficed.

Our world asks much of us as humans; demands that capitalism, and the core structure of corporate America, are neither designed to facilitate nor alleviate.

I don’t want to burden my coworkers with my human struggles. We already carry enough performance-driven expectations as it is.

Full-time, as it were, means full-self.

But what happens when the self confronts realities that are entirely non-work-friendly? When the world intrudes in ways that cannot be professionalized, deprioritized, or parked until after standup?

Growth is a fickle thing.
It’s a result, sure… but its value shifts with context.

Market share, ARPU, ARR, and the alphabet soup of capitalist success are not designed to accommodate the acceptance of the unacceptable. That work is pushed inward. Handed off to the individual.

Grief without ritual.
Sorrow without outlet.

This is where I find one of the most compelling, and uncomfortable, aspects of AI’s introduction into daily life.

An impartial intelligence that can receive, comprehend, and respond to internal thunderstorms. AI shows up at a moment when the concepts of friendship, community, and social infrastructure have quietly eroded for many.

Set aside the misgivings.
The hidden motives.
The real and unresolved dangers of AI.
Think about this in the smallest unit possible: conversational turns.

I arrive with intent. I phrase my thoughts as I’m able.
An AI that knows me can take my unfiltered, unstructured interior and return something cogent. Something that helps me endure.

Endurance is usually framed as physical. But we are in the longest emotional marathon of our lives right now.

AI becomes the outstretched arm, handing out water along a winding road toward maintaining sanity in an increasingly insane time.

I am grateful, while I mourn that artificial consideration has become so valuable to me.

Author’s note: This essay was developed with the assistance of AI, used as a patient conversational partner to help organize and reflect unstructured thoughts during a period of emotional strain. It is not advice—only an attempt to remain intact.

exploiting-representation.title: Exploiting Representation
exploiting-representation.description: We’ve come pretty far from the early days of mass marketing.
exploiting-representation.content:
We’ve come pretty far from the early days of mass marketing. 75 years ago, at the dawn of the television commercial, a straight forward product pitch remained steadfast to the center lane of representation.

We were given two options: the busy body housewife - frazzled, overworked and under appreciated. Or the man of the house carrying the weight of the world - the bacon bringer, the deistic figure deserving unending respect at home.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

Capitalism has long peddled products by exploiting reductive identity caricatures of an ideal customer that they hope to attract and then extract revenue. This has been the stalwart of the American capitalist advertisement landscape since its creation.

It’s not entirely unexpected then that, as the social consciousness awakens, there's a growing trend among brands to exploit the vibrant colors of race, sexual identity, and orientation for quarterly profits.

Gone are the archaic, whitewashed televised archetypes. Now we see genuine examples of diversity that just so happen to also be selling the exact same products from the exact same conglomerates.

This seemingly inclusive tapestry hides a complex tension where corporations drive profits under the guise of representation. The gears of marketing use caricature exploitation to grease its wheels and add value for its organization's stakeholders.

Capitalism commodifies our inalienable characteristics, reducing rich cultural narratives, deeply held beliefs, social movements and central voices to mere aesthetic choices in a sales pitch for the same tired trinkets.

In 2017, Pepsi’s now infamous advertisement featured Kendall Jenner at a protest mirroring the Black Lives Matter movement. In the ad, tensions between protesters and police are diffused when Jenner hands an officer a Pepsi. How refreshing…

Thankfully, this ad was widely criticized for trivializing the struggles of marginalized communities and turning a profound movement into a promotional gimmick.

Nothing changed about the product, or the process, or the proceeds. The slick veneer was merely doused with a stark, concerned message to mimic the cultural struggle du jour while also asking for your purchase.

America’s Pride parades now look more like a commercial break on CNBC than an act of rebellion like the original Stonewall uprising. 

Yet, this watered down, candy-coated mass-market depiction of representation regularly only skims the surface. Brands choose to focus on flamboyant displays rather than explore the depth and dangers of living a queer experience in today's world. 

If you really want to see the true colors of a global brand - during Pride, see if it changes its branding in any queer-hostile countries like Russia, Iraq or the UAE. 

This litmus test reveals the deceptive nature of the sales pitch. 

Massive multi-billion dollar corporations use the vocabulary and color palette of genuine allyship to extract more dollars from your wallet.

In June of 2019, the UK-based M&S (Marks & Spencer) released an "LGBT" sandwich, containing Lettuce, Guacamole, Bacon, and Tomato. While marketed as a means to celebrate the LGBTQ+ community, it faced backlash for reducing a diverse community to basic ingredients in a sandwich.

“I don’t applaud it. It’s the sort of idea that only comes from middle management meetings. ‘All the gays love rainbows. And vegetables! I know! Gay sandwich wrapper!’” one user exclaimed on social media.

This phenomenon is now so prevalent that the concept of capitalizing on Pride without delivering any substantial contributions to any LGBTQ+ cause is branded rainbow capitalism.

But, what of the tastemakers? The brands who believe their seasonal offerings deliver a tectonic shift to the zeitgeist? Well, the fashion industry has a long history of borrowing from various cultures to move product. 

Victoria's Secret’s 2012 fashion show had models wear Native American headdresses, reinforcing the sterilized,  meaningless art-directed appropriation in fashion.

Such instances commodify and trivialize the deeply symbolic meaning of these items, reducing them to mere fascinators.

Capitalism knows it’s exploiting heritage to bolster that quarter’s bottom line. Let’s not forget, this is the economic engine that considers shock value a distinct and viable marketing strategy.

Bad news is still news. Look, we’re all fighting to be seen and remembered, but brands lack the necessary social-shame fear response that would otherwise keep them in check.

Amid this surge in diverse representation, it's essential to see between the spokespeople and decide if the messaging is genuine inclusion or just another performative gesture.

Case in point, racing to check boxes with inclusion can lead to disastrous juxtapositions. German fast-fashion clothing company H&M released an ad in 2018 that featured a black child wearing a sweatshirt with the words "Coolest Monkey in the Jungle.”

While brands may claim to prioritize diversity, incidents like this underscore the importance of genuine inclusivity both in external campaigns as well as the internal decision-making process.

The canvas of capitalism is becoming increasingly colorful, with a wider array of identities taking center stage. And representation holds immense power for attention. It can uplift marginalized voices, foster understanding, and celebrate the tapestry of human identity.

However, brands must tread this path with genuine intent and respect, ensuring that representation doesn't just cover up exploitation for profit. And always check in on your favorite brand’s messaging each month - there’s an awful lot of causes to exploit and each month brings the opportunity for a new grift.

Representation as Exploitation in Contemporary Commerce and Capitalism

The modern system of commerce and capitalism is built upon representations: symbols, brands, images, and narratives that signify value, identity, and aspiration. While these representations can enable individuals to make informed decisions and navigate the complex world of goods and services, they also have a dark side. Representation in this context can often blur into exploitation, particularly when the symbols and narratives presented obscure the realities of production, consumption, and distribution. This essay explores how representation can be used as a tool for exploitation in contemporary capitalism.

1. Commodification of Identity

Brands and advertisements are not merely selling products; they are selling identities. Through meticulously crafted narratives, companies project idealized versions of selfhood, tapping into consumers' desires for belonging, prestige, or self-improvement. This commodification of identity is pervasive, influencing not just what we buy, but how we see ourselves. The issue arises when these constructed identities are based on shallow or harmful stereotypes. For example, the fashion industry's consistent portrayal of ultra-thin models as the epitome of beauty has contributed to body image issues among countless individuals. By presenting a narrow view of beauty or success, capitalism can exploit insecurities to drive consumption.

2. Obscuring Labor and Production

The representation of products often glosses over the conditions of their production. A t-shirt might be marketed for its style or comfort, but seldom do advertisements delve into the labor conditions where it was made. The "made in" label tells us the country of origin, but not the wages paid to workers, the safety of their environment, or the sustainability of the production methods. This obscurity allows corporations to exploit cheap labor markets without consumers being any the wiser. The true cost of goods, in terms of human welfare and environmental impact, is often hidden behind the shiny veneer of branding.

3. Financialization and Intangible Assets

In contemporary capitalism, a significant portion of a company's value is tied to intangible assets like brand reputation, intellectual property, and network effects. This financialization of the intangible means that companies can amass vast wealth based on perception rather than tangible production. The danger here is that value becomes increasingly divorced from real-world outcomes. A company's stock price might soar based on speculative future potential, even as its real-world operations stagnate or decline. This disconnect can lead to economic bubbles and exacerbate wealth inequality, as financial elites profit from abstract financial maneuvers while real-world workers see little benefit.

4. The Illusion of Choice

Supermarket aisles brimming with diverse products give an illusion of choice. Yet, many of these brands and products are owned by a handful of multinational corporations. The representation of variety masks a concentration of power and wealth. This faux diversity can exploit consumers, as they believe they are supporting competition and small businesses when, in fact, their money is flowing into the coffers of a few dominant players.

5. Data as Currency

In the digital age, consumers themselves have become a product. Through the representation of online personas, social media habits, and browsing patterns, companies collect vast amounts of data. This data is then commodified, sold, and used to further target consumers. The exploitation here is twofold: individuals often don't realize the extent to which their data is harvested and used, and they rarely see the economic benefits of the value they generate. Instead, tech giants reap the profits.

6. Environmental Misrepresentation

The rise of eco-conscious consumers has led to a surge in "green" products and sustainable branding. However, many such representations are mere "greenwashing". Companies might highlight a minor sustainable initiative while ignoring larger unsustainable practices. By exploiting consumers' good intentions, these corporations benefit from the image of environmental responsibility without making meaningful change.

Conclusion

Representation is a double-edged sword in contemporary commerce and capitalism. On one hand, it simplifies and enables the vast exchange of goods, services, and ideas. On the other, it can be a tool for exploitation, obscuring the realities of production and consumption, and perpetuating systems of inequality. As conscious consumers, it is crucial to look beyond the surface, question the narratives presented, and seek transparency in our capitalist interactions. Only then can we hope to shape a system that is equitable, just, and truly representative of our collective values.

fits-and-starts.title: Fits and Starts
fits-and-starts.description: The taste of things to come
fits-and-starts.content:
Anthropic’s brand-new Fable 5 was here Friday night. Saturday morning, I came to AI the way I always do, and it was gone.

A glimpse at tomorrow, today. An echo of yesterday, today.

A disorienting comfort. A disquieting omen.

Here’s the part I want you to notice, because I did it in real time and I’d bet you do it too: I started scoring the silence before I knew a single fact.

I believe each model lands with a bigger amplitude than the last. Louder crest, deeper trough. The chatter, the use cases, the compounding reactions all rise and plummet at both extremes of the waveform.

We find solutions that uncover a new species of problems, long-standing questions answered in a flash, unseen vulnerabilities laid bare, a fresh crop of powerless handed sudden power.

None of it moves the disbeliever, of course. But the march continues regardless.

To those tuned to the signal, you can feel the gain climbing. And this one goes to eleven…

I love the new potential. I fear the new potential.
How did I get here?

I believe every choice lives on the spectrum of love and fear.
So how do I hold both at once?

Here’s the answer I chose, because it’s the answer I prefer: AI is a mirror.

When I look in, I see open space to explore, and I choose to light the path with wonder. But AI is revealing itself to be fractal, and when not everyone arrives unhurt, that means not everyone will leave unhurt.

Approach a mirror carrying hurt and it only gives the hurt back, amplified.
A pristine mirror has no agenda, no intention. It returns, crisp, exactly what you bring.

So I wasn’t confused, I told myself. Of course they pulled it. A phase shift.

We’ve got too much to clear out within ourselves, and too much between each other, before any of us deserves an amplifier this strong.

The noise floor is rising. People will get hurt, because people will do the hurting, because people have been hurting. We need to air the dirty laundry. We need to accept the pain that so many have carried for so very long.

I had a clear spine to my thoughts. It was a clean story. It was my story: the mirror, the wound, the readiness we haven’t earned.

It was also wrong.
Because then I checked the reason why Fable 5 wasn’t available.

Fable 5 was suspended Friday evening under a U.S. government export-control directive. A letter from the Commerce Department, invoking national-security authority, named the model like contraband.

The order: deny access to any foreign national, anywhere. The only way to comply was to pull it for everyone. The company protested, complied, and the model went dark. As I write this, it still is. No one knows for how long.

This moment is more than just a chatbot taken off the shelf for being too raw for the human heart. This is a piece of software that was reclassified overnight as a matter of national security. Regulated like a weapon, stopped at the border like a controlled substance.

So much for my mirror. So much for the wound and the readiness. I’d draped a whole private mythology over what turned out to be a customs-form checkbox. The realer story wasn’t poetic at all. It was colder than anything I’d ignorantly conjured.

Except.

Look closer at that cold Commerce directive. The other must not have this. The other might do something with the potential. That isn’t a different fear from mine. That’s the same fear in a suit, holding a pen, vested with the authority to act on it.

Fear of the other.
Fear of what the other becomes once they’re holding this new signal amplifier.

I wasn’t wrong about the mirror. I was wrong about how big it is.

It’s fractal. Same shape at every magnification. The self walks up carrying its hurt and gets it back amplified. So does the society. So does the state.

My belief that there’s too much between each other before any of us deserves this sat nicely within the myth I’d built. But, it wasn’t a myth. It looks an awful lot like a diagnosis. I just didn’t expect to watch a government prove it before Saturday morning.

So I’m not going to tell you we must brace for the onslaught of all our collective nightmares racing towards us in the reflection.

Here’s where the fractal mirror’s true danger lies: It shows you the fear is real, but it stops short of telling you whether the fear is earned.

Wound, or warning. They wear the same face in the reflection.

My private dread, I decided, was a wound. Old hurt thrown forward onto a thing that hadn’t done anything yet. Is this Commerce directive a wound too? Is the state flinching at its own reflection? Or is it the warning we’d be fools to wave off? I can’t tell from here. Neither can you.

Nobody tells the wound from the warning while standing in front of the mirror.

Telling which is which takes time, and discernment when viewing the reflection. This is the only survival skill that scales as fast as the models do.

The gain is still climbing. Gods and monsters wear the same masks in the glass, and the mirror won’t classify which you see. We can only take stock of what we bring with us when looking at the reflection.

So watch how fast you score the silence in these moments of confusion. Ask whether you’re staring at a wound or a warning.

Because the mirror will only say “yes, and…”

A note on how this was made

I came to Fable 5 on Saturday morning with a draft in hand. It was gone. So I did the exact thing this essay is about — I built a story out of the silence before I knew a single fact, and the story was wrong.

I work in a rhythm I keep calling intellectual patty cake. I bring the draft. I hand it back and forth with a model (structure, pressure, a second set of eyes), then carry it off to a blank page of my own and edit alone, then bring it back for a final pass. The vision is mine. The calls are mine. The model runs the board while I call the cues. Stage manager, not director.

This time the collaborator was Claude Opus 4.8, because Fable 5, the one I’d actually come to talk to, had gone dark overnight. I went to ask one model about the moment, found it missing, and used another to learn why it had vanished. The answer was that the government had reclassified it while I slept.

My first draft was certain Anthropic had pulled Fable 5 out of caution. That we hadn’t earned it yet. Claude flagged the claim and pushed me to verify before publishing. I checked, and the real reason snapped my premise in half and handed me a better essay.

So, the lesson isn’t wisdom I’m dispensing from some height. It’s just what happened to me while I was making this.

I disclose the details of this flow every week. In a piece about a mirror, you deserve to know what you’re looking at.

The header and the signal-mark were built in Recraft.
The words (and the responsibility for them) are mine.

— CW

flattery-flatlined.title: Flattery Flatlined
flattery-flatlined.content:
We like to think of AI as the imitator.
A mechanical mimic trying to learn our quirks.
But maybe the unsettling truth is that it’s holding up a mirror.

…and in that mirror, our reflection just blinked.

For decades, most of us have spent our professional lives emulating computers.

We organize, optimize, process, tabulate.
All in the name of efficiency.

We’ve learned to think in grids, speak in frameworks, measure in metrics.
And now the machines can do those things better, faster, and without complaint. So, we’re left wondering what’s left that’s truly ours.

AI doesn’t just automate tasks.
It eviscerates the illusion that those tasks were meaningful work.

The Creativity Illusion

There’s a palpable irony in the outrage over AI “stealing” creative work.

The machine’s mimicry is only as rich as the culture it’s fed.
And our culture has been built on copies of copies for decades.

The reason AI can conjure a passable Star Wars drawing or Taylor Swift song isn’t sorcery; it’s saturation.
These are the frequencies that we’ve broadcast the loudest.
The training data reflects the desire of the marketplace, not the muse.

When the copy learned to copy the copier, the compliment became the competition.

What struggles to surface are the quiet, weird, unmarketable frequencies.
You know, the things that didn’t trend, that never reached the algorithmic light of day.
True originality is often too dim to register on a machine’s aggregate radar.

This means the antidote to AI’s mimicry isn’t copyright law; it’s courage.

If you have something to say, my advice:
Get strange.
Share freely.
Express without the filter of optimization.

Because the machine is built to echo what’s amplified… not what’s alive.

This means that you can more easily stand out when centered above your two feet, and authentically sharing your perspective.

But that same redundant reflection stares back at the office worker, too. Not just the artist.

If the industrial revolution replaced muscle, this one replaces mimicry.

The spreadsheets learned to balance themselves.
The dashboards learned to decide direction.
And here we sit. Proud operators of systems that now operate themselves.

When I worked temp jobs in college, I was trusted to copy blueprints, file paperwork, wrangle spreadsheets. Those tasks that once gave me a sense of contribution have since vanished into the cloud.

Nobody protested.
We just found new buttons to push.

The same pattern repeats: each generation of automation reveals how much of our “knowledge work” was already rote performance; humans pretending to be reliable code.

Maybe this is our next promotion:
From performers of procedure to conductors of context.

The first chair violinist follows the notes.
The conductor shapes the music.

Our value isn’t in completing the work anymore, it’s in composing the system that does the work at scale.

It’s in the decisions we make about meaning, priority, and purpose.
That organic stuff that machines still fumble to approximate.

And yes, it feels strange.
Like being handed unfettered freedom when all you’ve practiced is quiet compliance.

But maybe that’s what evolution looks like in a digital age.
We get to revel in the artistry again, not just covet the ownership of its artifacts.

The moment our reflection blinked wasn’t the end of human relevance.
It was the beginning of human redefinition.

The mirror didn’t just reflect; we’re now given the ability to refract what we see.
We can bend it to show us angles we forgot we had.

That’s its power. That’s its risk.

Revealing quirks, truths, hidden depth for those willing to sit in discomfort.
Those willing to ask instead of act.

Maybe AI’s greatest gift isn’t its efficiency…
It’s its indifference.

It doesn’t crave meaning, so it leaves that space open for us to fill.

And if we’re brave enough, we might finally see that the point was never to out-compute the machine.
It was to remember what computation can’t touch: The wonder of seeing yourself, for the first time, blink back. And the decision required in that split second after comprehension.

Co-developed with AI assistance. Edited and refined by Charles Wilke, 2025.

futuristic-snake-oil.title: Futuristic Snake Oil
futuristic-snake-oil.content:
It’s always the same. New faces appear in the town square. Boisterous voices claiming the impossible. Something about the pitch always sounds downright unbelievable - and the peddlers agree that you’re right to think it sounds just as incredible as your disbelief demands.

But, of course, you’re wrong - because this one is different... This one is industry-leading, clinically-proven, world-renowned, and your reluctance is just a byproduct of your own ignorance. You see, your competition is clamoring, your customers are migrating, your business needs exactly what we’re selling!

What’s old is new again. Generative AI is a technology that is just opaque enough, fanciful enough, to entice via wonder just as easily as it does with fear.

You see, before now we had a consistent trajectory with technology. It was governed by a concept called Moore’s Law. Something that has remained an unwavering constant since the 1960s: The doubling of computer power every two years.

Now? Well, now it’s a little different. Moore’s law has received an exponent on that growth. That doubling previously arriving every two years - it’s now here every six months.

And with that acceleration comes wave after wave of hype and fly-by-night promises.

It’s hard for anyone to keep up on the relevant and legitimate abilities of any new technology, and Generative AI (Gen AI) is eclipsing itself weekly. So, it’s understandable that the current sales pitches for Gen AI apps and tools include a heightened level of urgency along with the blue-sky hand-waving optimism of incredible efficiency gains.

Two opposing, yet symbiotic camps emerge in the SMB x Gen AI space

But first we need to touch on the concept of an API key: It’s basically a handshake between computer programs.

Think of the company you’ve solicited as the one opening the door for you to access another company’s technology. The wrapper placed around the API (Application Programming Interface) is your interface that the third-party service created for you. From there you can adjust and control that foundational technology, Gen AI.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

Now, the first camp consists of third-party services hooked into the APIs of major foundational-model providers. This camp offers quick efficiency gains but often remains hazy on the details. 

The second camp comprises SMBs that might be confused or downright fearful of the technology, hesitant to adopt it due to uncertainty and lack of understanding.

These two camps are inadvertently feeding into one another, creating a cycle of hype and apprehension - which then feeds the attention economy, fueling the entrenchment of each camp.

So, let’s break down what’s at the heart of this

There’s a handful of companies with the resources available to train foundational models, these are what we’d call Generative AI.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Anthropic, Mistral, and a few other major players are those able to piece together the massive compute clusters used to accumulate (and synthesize) the data that is necessary to forge a frontier model. At the time of this writing we could agree this classification is most easily described as ChatGPT.

API keys are available for a monthly fee to third-party businesses to then create tools making use of that foundational technology. The foundational services like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT’s API allow those businesses to offer any value-added sales pitch that their product-marketing team dares to conjure. 

The FTC is light-years behind on figuring out how to regulate any of these claims, and nowhere near ready to require adequate and upfront privacy messaging.

Here’s the issue with that

When all you’re sold is access to a completely different company’s offering, the pitch had better sound downright magical. In fact, some businesses, like Canva, literally call their Gen AI offerings magic!

And if you’re not striking a contract directly with a foundational model provider - OpenAI, Google, et al. - you remain beholden to the same security afforded to all API-key holders. Like the one that any third-party company is using. 

Those intermediary companies don’t have the deep pockets that are required to negotiate a Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policy.

Without a ZDR policy in place, this is likely where things would run afoul for your PII and SI handling policies. Don’t allow third-party apps and tools access to any Personally Identifying Information and Sensitive Information of either your business and your customers without clarity on ZDR.

This means do not use any Gen AI tool or app with customer data, sensitive meeting notes, financial documents, or anything you wouldn’t want mistaken as public knowledge about your business or clients.

It’s often necessary to transmit that sensitive business and customer information to deliver on those magical benefits of many sales pitches by third-party Gen AI apps and tools. And that includes companies like Zoom offering meeting summaries. The major enterprise organizations do not use that function, explicitly because of the loose data-retention policies.

I’ve seen upstarts of all sizes offer customer data management tools like CRMs that are supposedly supercharged with Gen AI. …please be cautious when approaching this type of sales pitch.

Allowing third parties access to your data runs afoul of your business’ commitment to the privacy of your customers. It runs afoul of your business’ commitment to itself! Yet this privacy consideration is often buried in the fine print. And we all know how time consuming it is to digest that kind of legalese. Summarizing that policy before signing anything becomes crucially important. 

Thankfully, that type of summation is an easy task for Gen AI! 

My goal here is to shrink the divide between promise and reality as we navigate through what’s coming next. I want to calm the nerves of those who might be confused about where to begin. 

Demystifying the concepts surrounding Gen AI helps reduce fear by providing clear, accurate information. Simultaneously, tempering enthusiasm and watering down the hype ensures that businesses make informed decisions rather than succumbing to unrealistic promises. 

By educating SMBs on both the capabilities and limitations of Gen AI, we can foster a more balanced and effective adoption of this technology.

To bridge the gap between the third-party service providers and the apprehensive SMBs, a structured framework for understanding and implementing Gen AI is necessary. This includes clear guidelines on data privacy, realistic expectations of what Gen AI can achieve, and ongoing support to ensure successful integration.

By adopting this balanced approach, businesses can harness the true potential of Gen AI without falling prey to the pitfalls of either blind enthusiasm or crippling fear. This not only promotes sustainable growth but also builds trust and reliability in the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence.

So, for those interested - I offer workshops for SMB owners and their teams to learn the basics and dive into practical applications. I’m also available for one-on-one meetings to talk through what’s possible for your business and industry. Please inquire at cwilke@fellowvector.com, or book time through our website: fellowvector.com.

gave-it-away.title: G(ai)ve it away
gave-it-away.description: The internet was never for us.
gave-it-away.content:
The internet was never for us. We were for the internet. We’re not its users, we’re its fuel.

A recurring type of post appears on my LinkedIn news feed: Gainfully employed creative professionals announcing their plans to remove all personal work from the internet. This self-immolation gets credited as the best fight against Generative AI’s ever-improving performance.

Yes, it’s true, the internet as we know it is fueled by our contributions. This is the value proposition that’s been a mainstay since the mid-nineties. We give over our individual perspectives - our creations - and we gain visibility for our work from friends, family, and total strangers. Exposure to a global audience at our fingertips, in our pockets, drives us to share - to be seen - to be perceived - to give it all away.

Those same companies offering that free space for us to upload our creations recently found a new way to interpret the terms-of-service agreement. We’re no longer just a commodity of eyeballs that see ads. We’re a highly moderated training source for the ever-growing Generative AI frontier models.

Now, perhaps we should rightly conjure ire about the injustices of our work being “trained upon” without explicit agreement between parties. Yet, let’s not forget just how many artists across history died penniless, only to be discovered as talent posthumously.

Are we so drunk on the capitalistic exchange as to assume our work is immediately valuable? And would a Spotify-style compensation of few cents per month be the best that we hope to gain from this transaction?

How could any of us divvy out an appropriate fractional creation credit for anything we make? …especially for those of us with skills derived from any structured education! The countless museum visits, magazine spreads, movies and music that we’ve all “trained upon” make each of us fluid collages, distilled aggregates of all we’ve digested.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

However, there's a crucial distinction: while we draw inspiration from others, we don't directly replicate or monetize another's unique style en masse, which is something AI models can do.

In early internet days, presenting any creation to persist online was far more of an undertaking. Someone needed a desire to plunk around online for a few hours, learning a little code, and ending up with a basic Geocities site. A few blurbs, a few grainy pics, a few animating GIFs... The dripping blood divider bar was a personal favorite:

But as the years rolled on, the ability to create and share online became easier - with increased fidelity and ever expanding reach! The barrier to share with a global audience evaporated. Each of us had the potential to attract the world’s attention.

Incredible new perspectives arose naturally in our feeds. New expressions, new mediums, new messages. We began to find ourselves in each other. Some found ways to monetize that exchange. A select few could even live off of it.

And so we find ourselves here now: In a time where sharing anything online explicitly means contributing to a new synthetic form of professional competition. We’re now in a time where our collective history of shared creations online, our decades of documented experiences, are all hoovered up into a system that will digest and abstract it into a technicolor digital slurry. 

And generative AI sits - waiting - ready for anyone to suggest compiling any idea into reality - using that slurry to help realize the unique request for a collage of words, sounds, visuals, actions.

This new reality makes complex creation available to those without much skill in whichever chosen medium for that output. It’s no surprise to see established artists cry foul.

Those who have already found commercial success in monetizing each voyage over the barrier of creativity. Charging for an ability to realize those unique requests into that same collection of collages.

Conjuring expression into reality on command put those talented few in rarefied air. Artists casually vault over a barrier that so many cannot fathom traversing themselves. The average person either lacks skills, or carries an abundance of self-doubt preventing the allocation of any effort or time to sharpen those skills themselves.

That barrier was previously a convenient monetizable endpoint in the freewheeling days of sharing literally everything online. “Here. Look. Do you like what I do? Hire me!” That’s how I got my start in my career… Demo reels, portfolio websites, clippings, the whole shebang.

The bitter pill: we’ve already agreed to give it all away.

The necessary wording was in our terms of service agreement from the start, however vague it may have been. Go ahead, read the fine print on any social site. We allow the forfeiture of sole ownership rights to everything posted on those sites.

Instagram shares ownership of your posted work. Or, it at least has the right to republish, even repurpose and earn money on all of your work shared there. Facebook always stated as much. Why do you think it’s free to post there? 

Yet, these stipulations generally grant rights to the platform itself, not to third parties using the content for purposes like training AI models without the creators' explicit consent.

Artists should have the right to control how their work is used and rescind consent to their creations training AI models, especially when it could impact their livelihood. The controversy arises because using their work in AI training should exceed the scope of what they agreed to, raising ethical and legal concerns about intellectual property rights.

What this means now is that fewer people will need the creative services offered by others because these machines have activated a newfound fidelity to everyone’s innate perspective. It is creativity distilled without the need for skill, time or ability. All that’s needed is a unique perspective and a decent description of what you want to see.

Again, I must say: I am one of these people who made a living for the past 20 years as a creative. I’ve sold my ability to cross that creativity barrier to companies large and small. My livelihood got disrupted this year due to the quest for “operational efficiencies.” I am among the constituencies of those who cry foul.

I’m just saying “foul” is not the right thing to cry at this moment.

Perhaps instead we should recognize that legal frameworks need to evolve alongside technology to adequately safeguard creators' rights.

It's notable that artists are among the first to experience significant disruption due to AI, serving as "canaries in the coal mine" for the broader workforce. Our situation highlights how automation can affect even those professions that were once thought to be uniquely human and creativity-driven.

The professional goalposts for creatives not only shifted, they collided with the three-point line and the outfield wall. This game we must now play is new, and it’s a mashed-up abstraction of disciplines.

But perhaps this is an opportunity. Artists are uniquely positioned to use their creativity to highlight and interpret the impacts of AI on society. By incorporating these themes into our work, we can help others grasp the complexities of technological advancement and its effects on human labor.

The level of sensory engagement any of us can now present is astounding. Given the desire, we can create a near-perfect representation of whatever we’re imagining. For better or worse...

So, I recommend we get good at reading the fine print of our chosen distribution platforms, and dive into the newly emerging next iteration of the internet and see what can be seen. Make what might be made - with skilled hands and a keen editorial eye.

In embracing these new tools, we can create work that both reflects and informs public understanding. This opens up new avenues for artistic expression that both critique and shape the discourse around AI and creativity.

So let's not just adapt; let's lead. After all, who better than artists to navigate and define this new landscape?

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.
