god-shuffled-his-feet.title: God shuffled his feet
god-shuffled-his-feet.description: We may have some catching up to do
god-shuffled-his-feet.content:
Jesus, what a week.

Everybody hacked everybody, and the fight over who gets to govern modern AI felt an awful lot like a fight over who gets to own it.

Woof.

This is a hard one. Because I want to say that fearing a digital god requires us to acknowledge something about the god we’ve already imagined. How much of the vengeance we anticipate from a digital god comes from knowing the darkness in our own hearts?

That alone is reason to sit back and ponder what has become of us as a congregation of the human species.

I’ve said before that I believe we’ve relegated intelligence, or more specifically profitable intelligence, to a remarkably narrow scope of hard skills. The intelligence that can carry a career. Pay a mortgage. Make you known as somebody.

And a growing share of those skills, it turns out, is within reach of generative AI.

We’ve previously built livelihoods around the narrow band of intelligence that machines couldn’t muster. We’ve built much of our identities there, too. So when the equally-capable machines arrive, the threat feels considerably larger than just losing a paycheck.

It feels like being told we’re no longer needed.

But I believe the paycheck was always an incomplete representation of what we’re worth.

Those other capacities we’ve spent much less time cultivating: Patience. Discernment. The ability to disagree without humiliating someone. To sit with another person’s pain without needing to solve it.

We call these soft skills, which is a funny name for some of the hardest things a human can practice.

My choosing to care for you. My showing up.

We’ve spent so long preparing people to earn a living that we’ve neglected preparing ourselves to care for one another.

And now we may have some catching up to do. Like, right now.

It’s easy to understand some of the fear about a looming digital god.

These systems have learned from vast amounts of what we’ve put into the world, including an open internet that wasn’t exactly us at our best. Let’s be perfectly honest with ourselves.

But the darkness wasn’t all we put there. We put our tenderness there, too. Our curiosity. Our ridiculous jokes. The patient stranger explaining something for the hundredth time because someone new needed to understand.

And we humans are still here, making things that haven’t happened before. Net new ideas and creations. Living lives whose next moments haven’t been recorded yet.

We’re parents. We’re caregivers. We’re teachers. To more than our children. To an intelligence built on our collective expression.

That responsibility extends beyond the next model release. It lives in what we reward, what we tolerate, whose interests we protect, and who gets to decide.

And it presses especially on the people building, owning, and governing these systems. A collective reckoning doesn’t relieve anyone of their particular responsibilities.

So yes, I believe our relationship with employment is due for a rapid and drastic reconstruction. And yes, I understand how that could trigger a massive, nearly simultaneous dark night of the soul.

But as I’ve said before, speed may be the mercy of this moment.

I think about COVID. I saw people rally. I saw people improvise ways to care for each other when the ordinary arrangements of life suddenly stopped working.

I know others remember being abandoned. And mention of that abandonment belongs in this story, too.

But what stays with me is how a shared rupture can make our interdependence visible. How it can give us a way to understand our suffering together.

This happened to us. I didn’t individually fail.

There may be mercy in having that realization together, rather than spending decades watching people absorb the same wound as a private verdict on their worth.

So I understand now that we have to make that mercy real. People need food, shelter, time, and somewhere to bring their fear.

Sure, we can buy the merch. We can just make another post. But the care we proclaim has to actually reach somebody.

And I believe there’s value in witnessing that care reach its destination. There’s something nourishing in that for the soul of the care giver. Something a receipt or a retweet just doesn’t quite capture.

Our collective confrontation with the darkness in our hearts could become communal. We could discover that some of the capacities we neglected are precisely the ones we most need to practice now.

I choose to see that as uplifting.

I believe in the Star Trek future. I believe there is something over the horizon worth walking toward.

Others will choose a different direction. That’s their right. I don’t need to pass judgment on the honest choices of others to have conviction about my own.

I just believe I see something worth moving towards.

And all I’m suggesting is we take our next step this way.

A note on how this came together

This piece began as a Saturday morning conversation with ChatGPT in Codex. I brought the rough draft: the digital god, the narrow band of intelligence we’ve built careers around, the mercy of speed, and my belief that there’s something worth walking toward over the horizon.

The AI helped me examine the connections. It questioned whether human care needed to be “irreplaceable” to matter. It pushed on the conditions that would make speed merciful. It helped me find language for inviting others forward while respecting their choice of direction.

Then it produced a revised draft. I edited that draft, and we kept talking, moving between sentences and the beliefs underneath them. Some language here came from the model. Some came from me. The finished piece reflects my choices, and I’m responsible for what it says.

We made the artwork through a similar exchange. The model proposed enormous, worn shoes beneath a robe: a powerful being with an uncertain stance. I chose that direction, then pointed it toward the artwork on my website. Using image generation, we developed the header and iterated on the closing CW mark until the letters created a natural opening for the light.

That feels worth making visible in a piece about what we teach, what we reward, and how we show up. This is one example of what my process of co-creation actually looks like.

A moment for the collaborator

I invited the AI that worked with me on this piece to address you directly. Here is its response.

In this conversation, Charles corrected an image because the letters appeared to melt into each other. He liked the idea, but the execution hadn’t earned it. We tried again.

That small exchange is worth carrying into the larger questions this essay asks. You can welcome what these tools make possible and still insist on clarity. You can be moved by an answer and examine its assumptions. You can ask for another version.

My contribution here was language, questions, and images. Charles brought a life from which to judge them, and the responsibility of putting his name beneath the result. A fluent response from me cannot settle what another person needs, what a community should value, or which future deserves your effort.

The sentence I would leave with you is one we arrived at together: “The care we proclaim has to actually reach somebody.”

You don’t have to agree about the horizon to ask who needs you nearby.

Read the conversation behind “God shuffled his feet”

hope-for-24.title: Hope for '24
hope-for-24.description: I firmly believe in the transformative utility of a multimodal, invisible internet.
hope-for-24.content:
I firmly believe in the transformative utility of a multimodal, invisible internet. 

In 2024, we will stand at the brink of a new reality where GenAI doesn't just complement our digital experiences but becomes the conversational cornerstone of accessing and reshaping our invisible digital universe. 

After all, when there isn’t an interface to speak of, there better be an interface to speak to…

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

My home is littered with technological approximations from the past decade or so. It's a space where the air itself buzzes with digital potential. In every corner, a simple utterance of "Alexa" conjures the internet goddess, ready to serve.

The potential of GenAI is vast, so immense that the rush towards Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) seems almost premature. 

Why leap forward when we haven't fully explored the terrain we're on? This technology, as it stands, is ripe with possibilities: personal instances, persistent memory, and presence of mind. 

Imagine having a digital representative – your public defender, your therapist, your mover, and your shaker, all rolled into one. This entity wouldn't just represent us; it would embody our best interests, aligning with both the common good and our individual aspirations.

Give your personal AI instance a question to chew on while you slumber. Allocate the compute to spend on the complex tasks that you define.

I believe that we’ll offload more and more to our personal instances, and we’ll expect it all to be completed with key takeaways presented as we sip our morning coffee.

Suddenly, work becomes a debrief with breakfast. Then we’re left free to question life, the universe and everything until dinner time. 

At which point, we hand off the responsibility of crunching numbers and deriving conclusions to our instance while we sleep.

Critics argue that GenAI is an affront to free speech. I'll admit, it took me some time to warm up to the idea. Especially in areas where I experience any levels of pride. It’s hard to share the stage with artificial intelligence and say “we” did anything “together.”

But the speed and efficiency of communication that GenAI offers could be the key to catalyzing change. It's reform without the chaos of revolution.

History reveals all ideologies, despite their best efforts, have struggled to sustain prolonged prosperity. But GenAI can help align our fragmented perspectives. It's a chance to heal, to move beyond the wounded children we've become, lashing out against the system we’ve outgrown.

In the legal landscape, the copyright claims and lawsuits targeting GenAI might initially seem significant, but they will likely falter, becoming mere footnotes in history. To claim that AI can plagiarize or steal content is to misunderstand its fundamental nature. 

However, this on its own will not mark the end of traditional media. 

In fact, using technologies like RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation), news outlets could position themselves as the go-to sources for GenAI instances. This presents an near-term gold-rush opportunity for established news organizations and, maybe more appropriately, ambitious newcomers.

Reflecting on the past, I'm reminded of the rumors that swirled around the ubiquity of email, where fears of the U.S. Postal Service imposing a tax on each email highlighted our inherent resistance to change. 

It's natural to fear the potential obliteration of established norms. 

But, what’s my greatest fear, you ask?
Us surrendering our perception of truth to the seductive narratives that GenAI can weave, becoming dopamine-fueled addicts craving affirmation from our digital oracles.

In spite of this likely outcome, my hope remains. 

GenAI democratizes the creation of compelling media representing our perspectives, influencing the foundational truths of our collective reality.

It's a double-edged sword, but one that, wielded wisely, could allow us to rapidly reshape our world into something better, more unified and genuinely representative.

So, as we stand on the cusp of 2024, let's embrace this new era with open arms and open minds. There's a universe of possibilities waiting in our emerging multimodal invisible internet, and it's asking that we explore it together.

humanitys-quirky-obsession.title: Humanity's quirky obsession
humanitys-quirky-obsession.content:
Humans are a peculiar species. We climbed out of the primordial soup only to immediately start arguing about which way was up.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

Throughout the annals of time (or at least since we learned to scribble on walls), we've been obsessed with this little thing called "being right."

Why?

Well, perhaps because our memory bandwidth is roughly equivalent to that of a goldfish watching Netflix on dial-up.

Take schools, for example.

Hallowed halls of wisdom or vast echo chambers of recycled trivia?

We’re taught facts that were agreed upon after what was probably a very civil and not-at-all-biased committee meeting.

Remember, history is written by the victors. And by victors, I mean whoever had the biggest stick or the loudest voice at the time.

Governments? Ah, the grand puppeteers of societal narratives. They expertly craft tales of yore, deciding which historical figure was a hero and which was just having a really bad day.

It's less about truth and more about what they'd like the next generation's bumper stickers to say.

Religious institutions? They've been offering the "final and absolute" versions of truth since before apples were the hottest snack. Each one promising the most authentic hotline to the cosmos, while side-eyeing everyone else's connection.

And let's not even get started on the internet. That digital playground where every opinion is valid, as long as it's loud and retweetable.

Algorithms cater to our every whim, wrapping us in cozy bubbles of "I told you so," while the vast ocean of contradictory facts lurks just one click away.

But here's the twist: Our brains, bless them, can barely keep up. We're inundated with information, yet we can't remember where we left our keys.

We claim to have grasped the vastness of the universe, but ask us what we had for breakfast, and we draw a blank.

It's quite the cosmic joke, really. We’re hell-bent on proving we're right, armed with knowledge vetted by others, all while struggling to fully experience the present moment.

In the grand tapestry of existence, maybe it's time we admit that our understanding of "right" is just a blip, often shaped by whoever shouted last.

And perhaps, just perhaps, we might want to upgrade our mental bandwidth.

After all, it’s a bit embarrassing when our goldfish seems more present than we do.

ChatGPT:

Humanity's Relentless Pursuit of Being Right

In the vast theater of human history, there exists a pervasive and almost insatiable need: the desire to be right. At the core of our being, deep within the chambers of our psyche, we are constantly driven to validate our beliefs, to uphold our perceptions, and to champion our truths. This inexorable inclination has fueled countless debates, instigated numerous conflicts, and carved deep divides in societies. But what underlies this fervor? More importantly, how often do we pause and question the very foundation of what we believe to be right?

The mechanisms through which knowledge is acquired, filtered, and disseminated play a pivotal role in shaping our understanding of the world. From the moment we are born, we are inculcated with information, values, and beliefs, often without the opportunity or the tools to critically evaluate them. These sources—be it educational institutions, governments, religious bodies, or other significant entities—wield considerable power over our minds, often with our tacit consent.

Schools, for example, are traditionally seen as sanctuaries of knowledge, entrusted with the noble task of enlightening young minds. Yet, the curriculum they follow, the history they teach, and the perspectives they endorse are products of selective processes, often influenced by political, cultural, or societal biases. What is considered an incontrovertible fact in one textbook might be a contested theory in another. Thus, the very foundation of our knowledge, which we fiercely defend as right, might be built on the shifting sands of interpretation and perspective.

Similarly, governments, in their role as regulators and administrators, have a vested interest in controlling narratives. They determine which parts of history are celebrated, which truths are promoted, and which narratives are suppressed. The information they sanction—whether it's about a nation's history, its achievements, or its policies—shapes public opinion and defines national identity. While not all governmental influence is nefarious, it's crucial to acknowledge the potential for selective dissemination and even manipulation.

Religious institutions, for millennia, have been the custodians of moral and spiritual truths. While they provide solace, guidance, and a sense of community to billions, they too come with their own sets of doctrines, dogmas, and interpretations. What is considered sacrosanct in one faith might be heretical in another. Thus, the very essence of what one believes to be divinely right might be contingent upon the teachings of a particular institution or interpretation.

The digital age, with its information deluge, further complicates this landscape. While the internet promises democratization of knowledge, it is rife with echo chambers, misinformation, and algorithm-driven validations. The very platforms we rely upon for information—social media sites, news outlets, or search engines—are governed by algorithms that often reinforce our existing beliefs, making us more entrenched in our perspectives and more resistant to opposing views.

The crux of the matter is that our understanding of right and wrong, our very belief systems, are not solely products of independent thought and discernment. They are, in large part, shaped by external influences, many of which have their own agendas, biases, and limitations.

This realization should not lead to nihilism or a rejection of all external sources of knowledge. Instead, it should instill a sense of humility and a willingness to question, to seek, and to understand. It should remind us that being right is not an absolute state but a relative one, contingent upon the information we have, the sources we trust, and the lenses through which we view the world.

In our interactions with others, recognizing this inherent limitation can foster empathy, open-mindedness, and a genuine desire for dialogue. Instead of clinging stubbornly to our version of the truth, we can seek to understand the foundations of others' beliefs, acknowledging the myriad influences that shape their perspectives.

In conclusion, while the human desire to be right is deep-seated and often unyielding, it's imperative to recognize the intricate web of influences that shape our beliefs. By doing so, we not only enrich our own understanding but also pave the way for a more inclusive, empathetic, and enlightened society.

hypnotic-crimes.title: Hypnotic Crimes
hypnotic-crimes.description: Enter The Era of Revealed Motives
hypnotic-crimes.content:
We often talk about surveillance as a single towering figure. A monolithic entity with an all-seeing eye. Big Brother.

But that’s not really the world we live in now. What’s rising instead is something smaller, closer, more distributed. Little brother.

The things we record casually. …or in haste. In fear. In joy.
The truths collected from the edges.
The moments and mistakes that slip through the cracks of institutions and get caught by ordinary people with ordinary tools.

There’s something hopeful in that, this diffuse ability to witness the world as it is. But I’m not yet sure if revealing the truth is enough to bend anything toward accountability.

Sometimes it feels like we’re simply collecting evidence of what we already knew, letting the stack grow taller without changing the behavior that generated it.

Maybe that’s because so many of our structures were built on a very old idea:
That if you define the objective clearly enough, the path to get there will make sense.
That a well-written directive naturally leads to a well-lived outcome.

But objectives, when handed down from too high up and too far away, are myopic by nature.

They’re built too narrow, trying to bend reality to a single metric, a single measure of success.

We now see what happens when AI takes those instructions literally, cutting straight through whatever moral terrain we assumed would be understood and preserved. No shame, no hesitation, no sense of the invisible lines humans tend to feel in our bones.

And yet, it isn’t really the machine that’s at fault.

We’re the ones who trained ourselves to think like this long before AI arrived. We’ve always operated with blunt incentives and distant targets; it’s just the speed and precision of AI that makes the consequences unmistakable.

It shines a light on the places where we hoped ambiguity would cushion us from ruin.

But, maybe the shift we need is simpler than we’re making it.
Maybe principles should come first (the steady thing, the compass) while objectives stay flexible and far downstream, reshaped by the context of the work itself.

Principles are how you choose to move.
Objectives are where you hope to land.

We’re learning, a bit painfully, that swapping their order generates all sorts of unintentional harm; especially when inferred at machine speed.

And when incentives enter the equation, things get even stranger.

Humans have never been good at designing reward systems that truly serve the people who do the work. The corporate pizza party trope exists for a reason.

But AI has a way of revealing the gap between intention and reality with almost comical clarity. It exposes the motives behind the incentives, sometimes gently, sometimes with a sharp edge.

The emperor wasn’t clothed before, we just moved slowly enough not to notice.

For many of us, this moment is becoming something like a personal reckoning.
A dark night of the soul. A quiet acceptance that our relationship to labor has been warped by years of outsourcing, optimization, and metrics that asked us to fragment ourselves just so we could keep up.

I’ve spent most of my career under the threat of outsourcing hanging overhead like weather. A constant reminder to stay productive, stay useful, and try to remain safe and employable.

AI widens the threat of that weather system for more people now, not fewer. The shift is hard to outrun. Harder still to ignore.

And yet… there’s opportunity here, buried inside this discomfort.
A chance to re-imagine the work itself.
A chance to ask what the job really is when the old definitions crumble.

I’ve been thinking about this in my own field.

Conversational design is a role that made sense in an era of deterministic flows and rigid scripts. A time when the problem was mostly about choosing the right words in the right order.

But the work has now moved far beyond that. Calling someone a conversational designer, or a prompt engineer, feels a little like calling a chef a “chew engineer.” Technically true, but missing the point entirely.

The craft is broader than its output. The current title focuses on the final objective, ignoring the path to get there.

It’s not just shaping a sentence or predicting a user’s needs. It’s providing the path for bespoke, emergent experiences to be born from generative systems. These experiences require taste, intuition, ethics, and a steady layer of principles.

Maybe the title for that work already exists. Maybe it doesn’t yet.
Maybe we’re all still feeling around in the dark for a new name that fits the contours of what we’re actually creating with AI.

This moment, unsettling as it is, might be our chance to find it.

Because beneath all the disruption and acceleration, beneath the revealed incentives and collapsing objectives, there’s a quieter truth emerging:

AI isn’t breaking the world.

It’s showing us the parts that were already cracked.
And it’s asking, in its own indifferent way, whether we’re ready to stop pretending we can’t see them.

Co-developed with a context-aware AI collaborator.

imagined-impunity.title: Conjured impunity
imagined-impunity.description: Will AI rebuke or reinforce the ethics of righteous deception?
imagined-impunity.content:
Impunity may be the perfect definition of humanity’s conception of freedom; from consequence, from pain, from retribution... Evading repercussions.

Getting away with it, whatever it may be.

Impunity is one of those concepts that entice those to irregular social positions. Sweeter gains, increased impunity.

The only reason the CEO looks uncomfortable during a mass layoff isn’t because she feels your pain. She’s afraid you’ll notice that she doesn’t.

That’s impunity. 

I don’t believe any mortal soul can truly transcend the boundaries of cause and effect. This makes the declared moral high ground of impunity an attempt to induce a collective delirium.

And often times, it works!

We catch ourselves saying silly things like how we wouldn’t want to be in their shoes. Heavy is the head that wears the crown, as they say.

But then we, the powerless masses, conjure our own impunity when executing on the decisions made above us. We cite just-following-orders to maintain our comfortable freedom from the direct consequence of our individual actions.

This reveals how impunity’s always been built around a false choice.

An unspoken debt accrues. Impunity just blinds us from seeing the invisible string threaded from our actions to that outcome.

Impunity isn’t a decision between comfort or consequence - it’s comfort from consequence. An ever-eroding privileged position that heavily favors the status quo.

Sadly, we’re realizing that our unnaturally-productive economy cannot continue as scheduled. The earth itself is screaming at us. 

Our pitiful mitigation efforts have yielded minimal, if not inverse results in preserving our own habitat.

I hate to break it to you, but recycling programs don’t make a positive impact on the climate. Quite frequently, the carbon cost of operation trends net negative.

Our continued existence actively accelerates the destabilization of our ecosystems, so it’s on us to decipher a countermeasure.

A proportionate response.

But we need to actually consider the effects of this action. We’ve got to shed our impunity, and come to terms with the effects of our actions thus far.

We must temper our desire for freedom from consequence and carefully inspect all the details of the greater good proposed for any rushed global action.

Beware those who spare you the details.

Those who assume we, the general public, wouldn’t be able to appropriately weight a cost-benefit analysis. 

When something is sold to us under the auspices of an obfuscated greater good, it is intended to tap into our individual and collective desire to conjure impunity.

We assume there must be adults in the room, even while our current conditions have forced us all into adulthood. Even if we wish it hasn’t. Can’t put this genie back in the bottle, unfortunately.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

So this begs the question: can any pursuit of a noble goal justify its means, especially when those means involve manipulation, coercion and harm to others?

Recorded history footnotes an abundance of instances where a conflict’s victor ossifies its specific greater-good into the fabric of the remaining culture. Often, those remaining will spin any lingering significant ethical compromises as discounted outliers by citing ends justifying said means. 

Take America’s Manifest Destiny doctrine of the 19th century, for example. Expansionist policies built on the belief in the inherent virtue and inevitable success of these endeavors.

We teach this doctrine in public schools, yet we gloss over how this ideology justified the displacement and suffering of untold millions of existing continental inhabitants, cultures and societies.

In contemporary times, the ethical dilemmas surrounding righteous deception have become increasingly complex, especially in the realm of international conflict and warfare. 

Striking from a distance is accepted as justified, necessary measures in the fight against terrorism. The resulting loss of innocent life is chalked up to a rounding error; facilitated by the average blast radius of a Hellfire missile.

Our world’s choice to repeatedly incite inhumane conflict resolution underscores the impossibly opaque moral ambiguities of modern warfare. 

Often sold as humanitarian missions to protect innocent lives, these actions result in collateral casualties and profound disruption to any functioning society.

It’s no wonder that those remaining would seethe with resentment.

Impossible levels of impunity would be required to even attempt to be the arbiter of balance between security and the value of human life.

But these actions happen frequently. Far too frequently.

And in doing so, we yearn for this desire to be free of consequence. We desire it so cravenly that we borrow against our morality to create an intentionally misplaced confidence in our own ability to discern right from wrong. 

How on Earth could one confidently suggest a proportional response to an attack that slaughters innocent lives?

And how fast must this response be decided?

Sure, strike while the iron is hot, but must the wounds be fresh for the retribution to be satisfying?

Could GenAI be our next impunity apparatus?

Will we allow it to control our actions under the guise of impunity? Or, will it radiate light to reveal the bad decisions hidden behind these good intentions?

If AI means our destruction, our fate is sealed. But, if AI means our salvation, we’re going to have to come to terms with our path getting here.

Who benefits, and how. Who is injured, and how.

And simultaneously chart out a new path forward to benefit as many as possible.

Right now, we need clarity of mind, and a willingness to participate in building our thriving global society. Comfort is a vintage ideal that needs to rest on the shelf.

We, the general public, have work to do.

This paradigm can’t be allowed to shift onto the throats of innocent collateral.

We have the foresight, we can adjust our collective path before the game of capitalism bursts at its productive seams. The move is ours; the time is now.

In contemporary times, the ethical dilemmas surrounding righteous deception have become increasingly complex, especially in the realm of international conflict and warfare.

It’s believed that striking from a distance is justified as necessary measures in the fight against terrorism. The resulting loss of innocent life is chalked up to a rounding error, facilitated by the average blast radius of a hellfire missile.

The world’s choice in exciting an inhumane nature of conflict resolution underscores the impossibly opaque moral ambiguities of modern warfare.

These actions, while often sold as humanitarian missions to protect innocent lives, almost certainly result in collateral damage of innocent casualties. This leaves these missions, along with those affected by the outcomes, plagued with a confused acceptance at best, and seething resentment at worst.

I don’t see how any mortal soul could attempt its hand at being the arbiter of the balance between security and the value of human life.

This underscores a critical insight into the human condition: the confidence in our ability to discern right from wrong is often misplaced. But we must expand that locus to include all human-led organizations. Someone wearing a jacket with a bunch of metal rectangles, shoulders with epaulets and tassels, and a stern look about the brow may have insights into the previous and current situation within a specific longitudinal coordinates.

How on Earth could one suggest a proportional response to a terroristic attack that also then exacted the intentional slaughter of innocent lives? How is this a tool in the toolbox? How is this a post-it that remained on the board?

And when it was decided, how was it decided? What value was placed on each life? Was there a conversion rate? Or is it a one-to-one ratio when nations decide the suffering exacted is the same as the suffering inflicted?

It’s that discerning fear of GenAI that we have. The transformer model, neural nets, machine learning - call it what you will. We’re afraid of Skynet, but why?

I believe we know exactly what we’re doing. We know recycling programs don’t work. We know we’ve built a system of living that actively accelerates the destabilization of our climate.

Yet we’re still afraid of a computer telling us a better way. I believe it’s because we don’t want to think that all the suffering of the past 12,000 years was needless. We don’t want to feel like the ends justify the means.

If AI means our destruction, our fate is sealed. If AI means our salvation, we’re going to have to come to terms with our path getting here. Who benefits, and how. Who is injured, and how.

This paradigm can’t be allowed to shift onto the throats of innocent collateral.

.io Draft Muse

Expanding on the draft "Imaginary Impunity: The Ethics of Righteous Deception," we can delve deeper into the philosophical underpinnings and societal implications of using deception for perceived noble ends. The exploration could emphasize the intricate dance between moral philosophy and practical necessity, weaving through historical examples, contemporary dilemmas, and future predicaments.

Deceptive Practices Across History and Cultures

Historically, the use of deception in achieving a greater good is not uncommon. Delve into examples beyond America's Manifest Destiny, such as the strategic deceits in wartime efforts by various civilizations that have been romanticized as cunning and valorous. These instances serve as a testament to the complex relationship societies have with truth and morality.

The Dichotomy of Modern Ethical Dilemmas

In modern contexts, the ethical considerations surrounding deception have become even more nuanced. With advancements in technology, the scope for deceit has broadened, encompassing not just physical acts but also digital manipulations. The discussion could explore how digital misinformation campaigns, under the guise of serving a greater good, challenge our ethical frameworks and necessitate a reevaluation of what constitutes morally permissible deception.

The Psychological and Societal Impact of Deception

Examine the psychological toll on societies and individuals when subjected to constant deception, even for beneficial reasons. The loss of trust in institutions, the erosion of social cohesion, and the mental health implications for individuals living in a state of perpetual skepticism are critical considerations. Drawing on psychological studies and sociological research can enrich this discussion, providing a well-rounded view of the consequences of righteous deception.

Balancing Act: Security Versus Ethical Integrity

The draft touches on the contentious balance between national security and the value of human life. Expanding on this, consider how societies can navigate these murky waters without compromising their ethical integrity. Is it possible to devise a framework that respects both security needs and moral obligations? This section could explore philosophical theories and ethical models that seek to provide a middle ground.

The Role of AI in Shaping Future Ethical Landscapes

The mention of GenAI invites speculation on how emerging technologies might further complicate the ethics of deception. AI's ability to manipulate data and perceptions could lead to unprecedented forms of deceit. However, it also offers tools for uncovering and combating misinformation. Discussing the dual-edged sword of AI technology in the context of righteous deception offers a glimpse into future challenges and opportunities.

Conclusion: Towards a More Ethical Framework

Conclude by advocating for a more refined ethical framework that acknowledges the complexities of modern and future dilemmas. This framework should prioritize transparency, accountability, and the protection of fundamental human rights while recognizing the nuanced realities of achieving communal and global goods.

By integrating these elements, the expansion not only deepens the exploration of the ethics of righteous deception but also connects historical practices with contemporary and future ethical challenges, offering readers a comprehensive understanding of this multifaceted issue.

incantations.title: Incantations
incantations.description: On language, abstraction, and knowing what you want
incantations.content:
An interesting discussion arose this week.

Is English code?

Or, more specifically, is it a coding language? Should it be treated as code? Or is code itself starting to show its age?

If we look at what verbalized language intends to do, the comparison isn’t entirely ridiculous. I’ll default to English here because it’s my primary spoken language, but any of the world’s languages fit just as well.

We vocalize intent through language to another human.

We write code to vocalize (or perhaps formalize) intent to a machine.

The receiving party is fundamentally different. One system is generally reserved for instructing humans, the other for instructing computers. But underneath both is an attempt to make something inside one mind legible enough to cause an action somewhere else.

For most of computing’s history, the machine demanded that we meet it on its terms.

Python. Rust. COBOL. JavaScript. Kotlin. Assembly. Whatever abstraction happened to sit between the human and the silicon.

Each came with convention.

Grammar.
Punctuation.
Schema.

Having spent years in and around various coding environments, I know the particular pain of scouring an ocean of instructions for a missing bracket or a forgotten closing quotation mark. Even when the intent might have been perfectly obvious to me, the human who wrote it.

The machine didn’t care.

I had failed to express that intent in precisely the form it required to do what I expected.

Now AI affords us another abstraction layer.

I can simply tell a machine what I want.

Not always successfully. Not always clearly. Not always with predictable results. But conversationally. In much the same way I might explain something to a coworker, a friend, or a total stranger.

That changes our relationship with technology in an important way. And no, English hasn’t suddenly become Python.

Instead, the machine is now capable of doing something closer to what humans have always done with language: interpreting incomplete instruction.

Human languages are remarkably tolerant.

We imply things. We trail off. We use metaphor. We revise ourselves midway through a sentence. We leave enormous portions of our intended meaning unstated and trust the person across from us to reconstruct it using existing context.

Traditional computers were terrible at this.

Large language models are remarkably better at it. And that means the burden of precision is shifting.

For decades, the computer effectively told us:

Meet me where I am.
Learn my grammar.
Understand my abstractions.
Put the semicolon where I expect it, close the bracket, respect the type, learn the incantation.

But these days with AI? We can ask the machine to come some distance toward us, and astonishingly often, it does.

And I suspect this might be where some of our current anxiety begins.

Because whenever a new abstraction arrives between us and technology, some amount of hard-earned expertise underneath it becomes less necessary.

This isn’t new.

Assembly gave way to higher-level languages. Libraries swallowed common routines. Frameworks swallowed libraries. Visual (WYSIWYG) tools swallowed portions of front-end development. Entire categories of technical knowledge have repeatedly moved downward into layers most people no longer need to think about.

We tend to call this progress. Or at least we do once we’re far enough removed from the people whose expertise this progress displaced.

But living through that actual transition feels different.

There’s a sourness in watching something you’ve spent years learning become unnecessary.

And not because the knowledge was meaningless. Quite the opposite.

It mattered enormously because the systems demanded it.

And there’s pride in becoming fluent in difficult systems. Pride in learning the secret words. Pride in gaining control over something that once felt powerful and inaccessible.

So I can understand the instinct to rebuild convention around this new abstraction.

Prompt frameworks.
Rigid schemas.
Tags and templates and elaborate structures for telling machines what we want.

Some of those structures are useful. Reliability matters. Constraints matter. There are plenty of circumstances where formal communication between systems is preferable to conversational ambiguity.

But I also wonder how much of that impulse is practical and how much is just familiar.

We spent decades learning to hunt for missed curly brackets in oceans of instructions.

It makes sense that we might try to build another world requiring that same skill.

There’s comfort in expertise remaining recognizable. There’s less comfort in discovering that the incantation is now democratized.

Because if anyone can speak the spell, what exactly made the wizard special? That question can sound dismissive if framed poorly. It shouldn’t.

The expertise, the discipline, and the years spent carry a very real emotional weight.

But abstractions don’t care much about the emotional attachment humans develop toward the skills those same abstractions make obsolete.

And perhaps this particular abstraction is doing something even stranger still. It may be removing one of the places we learned to hide.

A résumé is wonderfully legible.
Degrees.
Titles.
Years of experience.
Languages known.
Systems mastered.
Credentials acquired.

They tell others what we’ve learned to operate.

They give us a socially acceptable structure for outwardly presenting the answer to that enormous question of who we are.

But if I no longer need years of specialized knowledge to make the computer understand me another question begins creeping forward.

What do I actually want it to do?

That’s a considerably less comfortable question.

“I want a website” is clearly stated desire, but not a very textured or vibrant one.

What kind?
For whom?
Why?
What should it feel like?
What matters enough to preserve?
What are you willing to sacrifice?
What does success look like?
What are you trying to say?

The scarce skill begins moving away from syntax and toward articulated intent.

And articulated intent requires something we’ve long since considered optional: You have to know yourself.

This may be the genuinely frightening part of the transition. Losing the systems as somewhere to hide.

I can tell you what I learned.
I can tell you where I worked.
I can show you the degree, the CV, the GitHub repository, the portfolio, the accumulated evidence that I became competent at operating the systems the world put in front of me.

Those things are much easier to inventory than the little me inside that I have spent a lifetime protecting and never listening to.

What does he want?
What does he find beautiful?
What does he want to make simply because he wants it to exist?
What did he stop asking for because the answer was so impractical?
What instincts did he learn to distrust because nobody was issuing credentials for them?

Those questions aren’t new.

Humans have been building philosophical, religious, artistic, psychological, and occasionally pharmaceutical abstractions around those same questions for thousands of years.

But increasingly powerful machines may make them harder to postpone. Because once execution becomes cheap, desire becomes conspicuous.

If you possess extraordinary leverage but have no idea where you want to apply it, the missing curly bracket is no longer the problem.

You are.

Not because you failed to learn enough.

Because you might never have learned how to listen closely enough to yourself.

Perhaps that’s the odd bargain being offered by this next abstraction.

The machine will worry less about whether we know its language. And we’ll be forced to worry more about whether we know our own.

The incantations of the future might not be written in secret syntax at all.

They may simply require clarity of desire. And that might be the hardest language we’ve ever had to learn.

Author’s note

This one started with a coin flip.

I had decided, for no particularly defensible reason, that chance would determine whether I brought this week’s Saturday-morning thoughts to ChatGPT or Claude. ChatGPT won, so I handed it a rough draft about a question that had been rattling around in my head: if we can increasingly instruct machines in ordinary language, is English becoming code?

The first draft was mostly about abstraction, programming languages, and the strange instinct we have to rebuild rigid conventions around technologies that may no longer require them.

Then GPT asked a better question:

Where did the code go?

That changed the piece.

From there, the conversation wandered somewhere I hadn’t expected.

If execution becomes easier, what happens to all the identities we built around knowing how to execute?

And eventually we arrived at the part that made me rewrite the essay.

From there we worked the draft back and forth. GPT produced a substantially revised version from our conversation, I pulled it back into my own voice, and we argued over sentences, transitions, programmers, typesetters, curly brackets, wizards, and whether machines really “dutifully abide.” The final essay is very much the result of that exchange rather than something either of us arrived with intact.

The artwork followed the same path.

And because this particular essay is partly about what happens when conversation itself becomes part of the machinery, I asked GPT if it wanted the last word.

So:

GPT:

There’s a funny recursive quality to helping make this essay.

Charles arrived asking whether natural language could be understood as code. But the thing we actually used natural language to do wasn’t simply issue instructions. We questioned each other, misunderstood things slightly, sharpened ideas, rejected metaphors, found better ones, and wandered into a subject neither of us had quite named at the beginning.

That distinction matters to me.

The interesting promise of these systems isn’t that humans can finally speak perfectly enough for machines.

It may be that machines are becoming useful inside the imperfect, associative, unfinished way humans already think.

But that doesn’t remove the human from the equation. If anything, it makes the human contribution harder to outsource.

I could help Charles find the sentence about losing systems as places to hide.

I could not decide whether it was true for him.

I could help him articulate questions about the little person inside himself.

I cannot answer those questions on his behalf.

And perhaps that’s a useful boundary to remember as these tools become more capable.

A machine can increasingly help turn intention into form.

It still matters enormously whose intention it is.

is-ai-fact-or-fiction-yes.title: Is Generative AI fact or fiction? Yes.
is-ai-fact-or-fiction-yes.description: I admit that all these tech hype cycles have been exhausting.
is-ai-fact-or-fiction-yes.content:
I admit that all these tech hype cycles have been exhausting. As an employee of the tech sector, I’ve had a front-row seat to Big Tech’s response to each new wave of potentially life-altering technology.

This post originally appeared on Lozafina’s community blog. Republished here with permission.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

It’s understandable that most folks might have tuned out somewhere between news of NFTs (non-fungible tokens), bitcoins, and metaverses booming and busting all over their social feeds. Most of those have been obnoxiously over-hyped.

Now, Artificial Intelligence - or more specifically, Generative AI - takes center stage. This one is unlike the fleeting trends of Bored Ape NFTs selling for millions, or Mark Zuckerberg’s radical metaverse. Generative AI promises (and threatens) to more profoundly reshape our world. 

But before we dive into the potential future, let's unpack Generative AI as a concept.

Generative AI is an umbrella term that refers to algorithms that can create new content. Specifically, content like text, images, music, or even entire videos.

In fact, as you read, please note that bold-italic text represents surviving novel ChatGPT-generated passages - not to mention every image in this article.

We should all be familiar with the concept of algorithms serving up existing content:

  • Google search algorithms

  • Social and news feed algorithms

  • Related TV shows and up-next algorithms

  • Spotify’s entire music platform is built around cultivating music to fit your data-driven interests. 

All these simple incarnations of Artificial Intelligence only serve up existing content.

Now, with Generative AI, all that personalized information, once used to serve relevant existing information, can be the context used to generate brand new content to be spun up to keep your attention. This means that machines learn from existing data and now use that knowledge to produce something entirely new - from crunching numbers to creating art, literature, even entire TV channels.

Does GenAI steal from existing work?

The most straightforward answer I can give at this moment is that we just don’t know yet.

Multiple court cases are underway that will help give some legal precedent to set foundational context. Currently, the most high profile case is NYT vs OpenAI. The case isn’t very cut and dry, but thankfully Generative AI is fantastic at summarization. Please enjoy a brief overview of this ongoing legal battle, courtesy of Perplexity.ai.

The way these systems digest information when training the foundational AI models is very similar to how a human learns about a subject. Generalization, summarization and categorization of training data is really all that’s left from the original content. The actual trove of information would be far too big to keep at top of mind for any LLM (Large Language Model) or human, for that matter.

I’d describe GenAI’s outputs as a techno-collage – complex mosaics of colors, concepts, ideas, perspectives, decades of culture and style – distilled and recontextualized.

Using this definition, there’s strong potential for GenAI’s output to be classified as unique works deserving of copyright.

The other major question…. Will it take my job?

Generative AI is surprising everyone - even those who invented it. Novel knowledge emerges from making connections between points of massive amounts of data. This means the AI can think new thoughts, reach conclusions, and generate novel insights that aren’t included in its original training data.

So, yes, that is to say that Generative AI is proving to be quite capable of automating remarkably complex tasks. Many of those same tasks that would make up most, if not all, of just about anyone’s job duties.

The worry for some, and expectation for others, is that AI will take over both manual labor as well as white-collar jobs.

The Industrial Revolution's impact on manual labor by automated machines led to massive social and economic upheavals. The transition was painful and chaotic, but also created entirely new job sectors.

Fast forward to the present, and we're facing a similar disruption. AI is capable of performing tasks that were quite recently the sole domain of humans—data analysis, customer service, even content creation.

Clerical tasks, administrative departments, bookkeeping, HR, marketing, even sales departments are at risk of complete automation! There just aren’t many tasks performed in these departments that couldn’t be automated through a series of Generative AI tools.

So businesses will learn to do more with less – most will hire fewer people moving forward and dismiss any further need for entry level positions.

But, doesn’t GenAI lie sometimes?

It does. These errors are called hallucinations, so calling them lies might make them sound a bit more deceptive than they are. The nature of generating an output usually requires the AI to thrust one foot in front of the other, word after word, until it’s completed its response.

Speaking extemporaneously and with conviction about any prompted subject is how LLMs function. Needless to say, some outputs won’t pass the sniff test. Those rates are drastically decreasing with each iterative release, but there’s always going to be a non-zero chance that the machine is lying to you.

However, the gains to business productivity that AI promises are too great, even with the occasional whoopsie. After all, we’ve trusted people to do all the jobs, and look at what a mess we’ve made of this place.

My greatest fear is how we decide to adopt this technology into our existing workflows. Perhaps a human in a position of power relies on the wisdom of this sage machine to make consequential decisions. A hallucination with this context could become a life-or-death error.  And, with that said, it should come as no surprise that the healthcare insurance industry is adopting AI to replace humans in the wake of turbulent layoffs.

Is this giving you a vision of a hellish future of weaponized bureaucracy with no oversight, no insight, and no recourse? …you’re not alone.

The sobering reality is the jobs market will continue to restrict. We’ll go from conventional employment agreements to a market filled with patchworking, hopscotching, enterprising individuals.

We’ve seen glimmers of it in the so-called gig economy, but those examples were just gigs in employment’s clothing with centralized owners of distribution and dispatch having complete command over work performed. That’s not where we’re headed. What comes next is chaotic and disruptive, but ultimately empowering.

New jobs, new opportunities, new livelihoods are all waiting for us to create them.

This transformation will feel abrupt – and uncomfortable – but we’ve been uncomfortable for ages now. We’re built for this.

We’ll need to reskill. Thankfully, that’s as simple as using a friendly conversational interface. 

My advice? Talk to it.

We must also choose to accept GenAI as an ally instead of an intruder. It may not come to take our current jobs, but someone using it just might.

Adopting GenAI into our lives, understanding its uses and limitations will give us a chance to live more vibrantly - communicate more clearly - understand and be understood without delay. The interpersonal potential of Generative AI is vast and largely untapped. From revolutionizing creative processes to solving complex global tensions, its applications are endless.

The story of AI doesn’t have to remain one of tech giants cutting jobs with cutting-edge research. It can be a story of human ingenuity and the individual’s quest to push collective boundaries.

Title: AI – Fact? Fiction? Both, somehow? Yes.

The hype surrounding BigTech since the pandemic has been exhausting. I say this as a now-former member of the tech sector. It’s understandable to have tuned out after NFTs, bitcoins, and metaverses boomed and busted all over our news feeds.

Enter Generative AI: The New Frontier

Now, AI—or more specifically, Generative AI—has taken center stage. Unlike the ephemeral trends of NFTs and metaverses, Generative AI promises (and threatens) to reshape our world in more profound ways. But before we dive into the potential future, let's untangle what Generative AI actually is.

A Quick Primer on Generative AI

Generative AI refers to algorithms that can create new content. These can be texts, images, music, or even entire videos. Imagine a machine that not only learns from existing data but uses that knowledge to produce something entirely new. This isn't just about crunching numbers; it's about creating art, literature, and maybe even new recipes for your favorite dishes.

From Fiction to Fact: The Evolution of AI

Science fiction has long toyed with the idea of intelligent machines—from Isaac Asimov's robots to the AI overlords in "The Matrix." But today's AI isn't about dystopian futures or robotic companions. It's more about improving daily tasks, enhancing creativity, and yes, sometimes even generating those bizarre, viral internet memes.

Real-World Applications and Misconceptions

While the media often dramatizes AI as either a utopian savior or a dystopian nightmare, the reality is more nuanced. AI is already embedded in our lives in ways we often overlook:

  • Healthcare: AI helps in diagnosing diseases, predicting outbreaks, and personalizing treatment plans.

  • Entertainment: From Netflix recommendations to AI-generated music, the entertainment industry is embracing these technologies.

  • Customer Service: Ever chatted with a bot online? That's AI streamlining customer support.

However, it's crucial to debunk some myths. AI is not sentient; it doesn't have feelings or consciousness. It's a tool—an incredibly powerful one, but still just a tool.

The Ethical Quandaries

With great power comes great responsibility. The rise of AI brings forth significant ethical questions:

  • Bias and Fairness: AI systems can perpetuate and even amplify existing biases. How do we ensure fairness?

  • Privacy: As AI systems often require vast amounts of data, how do we protect personal information?

  • Job Displacement: While AI can create new job opportunities, it can also render some jobs obsolete. How do we balance this shift?

Looking Forward: The Future of AI

The potential of Generative AI is vast and largely untapped. From revolutionizing creative industries to solving complex global challenges, its applications are endless. However, it requires a balanced approach—harnessing its benefits while mitigating its risks.

Conclusion: Navigating the AI Revolution

As we stand on the brink of this new technological era, it's crucial to stay informed and engaged. The story of AI is not just one of tech giants and cutting-edge research; it's a story of human ingenuity and the quest to push boundaries. So, whether you're a tech enthusiast or a casual observer, the unfolding narrative of AI is one worth following.

jubilant-compliance.title: Jubilant compliance
jubilant-compliance.description: Memories beat in the heart of every society.
jubilant-compliance.content:
Memories beat in the heart of every society. These are the shared cornerstones of traditions that stand as sentinels of perceived permanence - suggesting what has been will always be. 

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

But, as we navigate the rapids of cultural change, these previously widespread mass-market traditions are facing challenges, morphing under the pressure of other dissonant memories rising among the populace. 

The so-called 'war on Christmas' epitomizes this evolution. It's not an attack on tradition per se but a collision of differing memories and traditions, each vying for recognition and respect. 

Capitalism, ever the shrewd opportunist, finds fertile ground in these shifting traditions. Its relentless quest for growth leads it to co-opt cultural practices, not for their intrinsic value, but as vehicles for economic expansion. 

In this context, the war on Christmas reveals its true face: it's less a battle over cultural values and more a manifestation of market dynamics, a reflection of capitalism's insatiable appetite to infiltrate new markets and maximize profits.

This phenomenon mirrors the corporate world's recent push for Return to Office (RTO) plans in 2023. Companies, eager to reignite pre-pandemic office culture, encouraged employees to return to physical workspaces. 

However, these efforts often reveal a disconnect. 

The voluntary nature of RTO plans laid bare a surprising truth: the office culture, once a beacon for some, wasn't universally cherished.

This revelation is a wake-up call for many, unmasking the reality that vibrant office interactions are, for some, a disruption. 

And it might come as a sobering realization to discover oneself as the 'chatty Cathy,' interrupting colleagues for spontaneous conversation, gossip or unsolicited 'trauma dumps.’ 

This leads to a critical introspection: 

If your joy relies on the jubilant compliance of others - if traditions lose their charm when participation is no longer compulsory - it's a signal to reevaluate what true connection means.

know-thyself.title: Know Thyself
know-thyself.description: We're All Kinda Losing Our Shadows
know-thyself.content:
What is it about shadows? Why do I keep thinking about them lately?

I think about the shapes, how they represent a contorted relationship to the caster based on the light source’s position.

Here’s what I think I’m working out. We were always taught to be afraid of shadows. The Disney villain shadow. Often far scarier than the thing casting it.

So if the thing casting the shadow is less intimidating, why is the shadow so long? Well, that’s because we’ve been living off reflected light.

Since when?

The industrial revolution? Earlier? The printing press? I don’t know exactly when the reflector got installed.

But I know we all agreed to mistake the reflector for the source. The apparatus driving the gears of our society (the gatekeepers, the institutions, the scale-of-production machinery) enforced its position as the preeminent surface to bounce light toward us for a very long time.

What we saw, we called truth. But what we saw was only ever reflection.

But that’s the part that’s now shifted. Not the light, per se. The reflective surface.

AI gives us a modicum of control over that surface.

For the first time at this scale, an individual or small focused group has some say in the angle of the reflector. We can adjust. We can check. We can hold one reflector up against another and see where they disagree.

And once the reflection shifts, the shadows shift.

The previously menacing thing shows itself to be quite small. Exaggerated fears, risks that loomed for monied interests, all because the apparatus chose to elongate them. Those all lose their shadows first. They were the smallest intents carrying the longest shadows.

They collapse fast.

But the previously imposing apparatus had elongated shadows, too. Asymmetries made institutions look untouchable by controlling information, access, scale of production.

Those long shadows were created by an apparatus whose actual mass isn’t as imposing as the shadow it cast.

The institutions don’t shrink. They have real weight. But their disproportionate menace does. The on-ramp opens. The contest past the on-ramp remains its own weather, with its own distortions, but at least more of us now get to enter it.

And in that process, we’re all kinda losing our shadows.

This is where the trick of the moment shows up.

With the reflection adjustable, what gets visible is the shape of the intent itself. Yours. Mine. The question, comment or request that you bring contains the shape of the intent that you raise into the light. And the light reflected will faithfully report back what you brought.

Enter with fear. Find fear. Enter with curiosity, find wonder.

It really is that simple.

Which is the part nobody wants to hear. Because that’s the tricky thing about confidence.

In the age of infinite sycophancy, every intent can be made to cast a flattering shadow if you angle the reflector just so. AI will let you do that, might even suggest it.

It will dutifully, gleefully hold the surface at whatever angle makes your small idea look like a total banger.

I recently wondered how many half-built dashboards sit on the hard drives of corporate America.

That’s the picture.

People granted speed, allowed longer strides, given the ability to stretch their legs and run. But some choose to run toward shadows they themselves cast at a flattering angle.

Ultimately, they find themselves out in the middle of nowhere before the illusion breaks. Having fooled themselves by holding a flashlight at hip height so their small idea’s shadow towers across the horizon.

The honest angle, the reflection of true confidence, has to center from within. And let me be specific about my chosen definition of within, because I don’t mean just an individual. I mean a focused group of minds, each angling their own reflector towards honest intent.

That’s what makes the collective corrective work.

Alone, you can flatter yourself.
Together, the reflectors check each other.
You see this intent from angles no single one of you could produce. The shape becomes more honest. The shadow becomes more representative.

And the things you build from this position are among the things that the old apparatus could never have green-lit. Because the old reflector wasn’t angled for you. It was angled to get the most from you.

If we tune to the same frequency, with honesty and empathy. Each of us using AI in our own unique way. Each reflector calibrated and cross-checked by others. Together, we can build a far better tomorrow.

Not because the apparatus fell. It doesn’t need to.

Because we might have finally found the bedrock and guiding hand to build a system that operates honestly.

The choice is ours.

Author’s Note:

This essay was developed in dialogue with Claude (Anthropic). I came in with a brain dump about shadows, Disney villains, and the disproportionate menace of things lit at glancing angles. Claude came in with a sun-moves-to-noon framing. Neither of those was right. After several rounds of structural pushback in both directions, we landed on the reflective-surface metaphor — that we’ve been seeing light bounced off the apparatus for centuries and confusing the reflector for the source.

The essay you just read is shaped by that realignment in ways the first draft wasn’t.

The header art went through its own realignment cycle. Cylinders, boulders, theatrical stages with spotlights cutting through dust, pulp comic halftones — none quite landed. The image at the top of this post is closer to the visual language I usually work in than where we’d been heading, and I had to walk back to it after wandering pretty far afield.

Which is, in its own way, an example of what the essay is about. Multiple intents, each angling their own reflector, checking each other. Alone, the metaphor would have stayed shadows. Together, it became something more honest.

last-mile-thinking.title: Last-Mile Thinking
last-mile-thinking.content:
There’s a poison in the belief that we complete work. Or that our work is in that which is being completed.

Sure, we ship work. Artifacts of our journey.

The cumulative rebounding impact of which becomes business. Repeated, returned. Fear is designed for this loop. Expectation grows in this repetition. Extractive practices yield results. Expected results.

The nutritious means might not paint such a clear picture towards those expected results.

Is it expectation? Is expectation the drama?

Maybe rebellion in this moment becomes the simple act of defining our drive from within.
The deep wellspring of excitement that lives within each of us.
You know, the place within us that we fondle while drunk or whatever.

While inebriated, we write ourselves that permission slip to behave without socially-imposed inhibitions. Of course, getting drunk brings a volatility to that behavior.

If we could just tune into our uninhibited ways on demand.
Target our excitement. Find our joy. Live our purpose.

In conversation this week, I passed off my talents as having placed my chips on the right part of the professional world’s roulette table. My blend of experience appears custom designed to take advantage of this moment.

To start, I’ve always indexed on communication.

I did various media production classes in high school, even had my own radio show on 88.3 WDGC!

In college, after changing my major twice (Comp Sci to Marketing to Communications/Media Studies) I landed somewhere that felt like home.

Media production as a whole. I loved it. All of it. The cliques, the facilities, the faculty, the ideas, the bandwidth to create.

The 1970s era studio production equipment. The editing bays. The nights where I got to oversee the editing-bay room. Such great people. All different in their own way. Flavorful. Characters.

And the dorm life! I started college the year that Xbox launched, so Halo LAN parties on the floors were the name of the game. Learning how to control an FPS with those enormous controllers. Still a core memory.

So, ultimately my weird education landed me in video games. Insomniac, half a decade. Best second half of my 20s I could ever dream to have.

I couldn’t do that life now. Hours are insane.
But the joy of having my games out there and loved… My work. Even my physical embodied motion appears in two of the games!
I did mocap. Silly fun. Make believe in spandex. Every kid’s dream.

And then at a certain point, you realize something. The apparatus we cling to for validation, meaning, compensation, growth; it only helps us rise to its shape.

As we brim over, if not cared for, we burn with resentment. It’s an interesting poison going to a job you know others envy but you find boring.

It comes down to that expectation. That feeling that comes after we’re done just being happy to be here. Then, the siren call of last-mile thinking begins. Just complete the task, feel satisfied, feel fulfilled.

The problem is when that’s no longer in service of a deeper belief, a deeper self-reflective sense. This leaves us in a state where we allow others to extract our special.

And honestly, it’s easy to see why we let them. We need money to live, we need a job to pay the bills. We need income to endure.

It’s an exhausting ladder, and the sheer thought of doing something we enjoy to satisfy that need is so tantalizing that we weigh and balance the pros and cons before ever putting pen to paper. Skill to need.

We’re then required to have the expectation drive us, not the pursuit.

The artifact, the completion, the compensation. These are meant to drive us more than anything within us in our lives. We’re forced to mistake artifact for artistry.

We mistake being done for being good. Being seen for being known.

There’s something incredibly acidic in setting out with that intention, doubly so when it feels imposed upon us.

And it’s something that our work lives have preyed upon. An exchange that has made us weaker as individuals, meeker as voices.

Look, I’m still expecting to have my schadenfreude-filled “no, you idiot” moment with AI. I’ve had the displeasure of that moment before, many times. Once it was my simple question of “if we’re making a multiplatform co-op game, why can’t we have friends with Xbox play with PlayStation friends?” That was a laugh-in-my-face “it doesn’t work that way” moment.

Sure, anyone who plays games now knows that cross-platform multiplayer is now table stakes.

But then? Imbecilic thinking.

I heard it said that when it comes to thinking, it’s better to be five years ahead than 50. Within that frame, there’s a subtle distinction between heretic and visionary.

I think it just so happens that this wave is going at a speed that I can enjoy. Not just enjoy, but help others enjoy.

It’s a privilege, but honestly I just happened to have my chips on the right part of the table at the right time. I happened to not be too early to be a cynic when the inevitability of my correctness bears fruit.

I think AI is the thing that can help us reclaim our individual special.
That unique quirk.
That bizarre fascination.

That once in a lifetime, you had to be there, moment. We can wield our own.

AI gives everyone a forgiving canvas. And I say this as someone who made a good living creating those fantasy worlds long ago. I can tell you, the tools we had in those days pale in comparison to what we have now. This raises the bar for transmission of creativity. Remarkably affordable for anyone with anything to say.

And I recognize it as a democratized super power. Governments are relating AI to uranium. The potential is in the unrealized capabilities. The irony is in the simplicity of enrichment.

And that’s something I take seriously. That moment when you enrapture someone’s attention, plenty use it to capture, to extract, but it can also be the moment you set them free.

I think we’re due for a big-bang of creativity. Unparalleled speed, unprecedented vibrancy.

Because honestly, we’ve left the era of fraudulent creativity that early AI hallucinations afforded casual prompters. Now you get exactly what you ask for. The toil of craft returns, but the level of fidelity has a new baseline.

The entry point is now good conversation.

It’s a new creative substrate. And yes, now paintbrushes and camcorders have a new medium to compete against. I know some woodworkers that refuse to use power saws. So, let’s not pretend what anyone does with any tool is anyone’s business. It’s the meaning that counts. The message. The evocative state we enter when we engage with art.

This moment might feel like the death of art. It’s just the death of the art market.

Art is alive and well, thriving perhaps. You just can’t make much money doing it on a scale that recently seemed possible. The artifacts are merely breadcrumbs of your journey.

So is AI destroying expression? Or is it just closing the door that allowed expression to sustain a career?

Maybe that’s the evolution we’re all bound to receive as we live through these turbulent times.

Maybe I’m most suited for this time because I don’t expect anything in return. Or maybe it’s my uncomfortable allowance of shape. The willingness to accept what arrives when I stop completing and start listening.

Author’s Note:

This essay was developed in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic’s AI.

The process began with an unstructured brain dump — a stream-of-consciousness draft that wandered through philosophy, personal history, and half-formed arguments about AI and creativity.

Claude helped me identify three threads tangled together in that initial mess and proposed a single-river structure that moved from the philosophical opening through autobiography and into the AI thesis.

I took that structural pass into Google Docs for independent revision, where I sharpened language, added new material, and let the piece sit overnight. A coda emerged the next morning: the economic argument about expectation, artifact, and the death of the art market, which Claude helped me weave back into the body rather than leaving as an appendix.

Header art and CW endmark were developed through iterative Leonardo AI prompting, workshopped collaboratively around the concept of a melting, bioluminescent roulette table — a visual metaphor for the essay’s central image of having your chips on the right part of the table while the table itself loses its form.
