letter-to-the-editor.title: Letter to the Editor
letter-to-the-editor.description: For the better part of three decades, my letters to the editor have become a staple with morning coffee, I’m told.
letter-to-the-editor.content:
For the better part of three decades, my letters to the editor have become a staple with morning coffee, I’m told. My words spur conversation as well as action by the readers of our Kearney Gazette.

Today, I am writing to address a much larger grievance than any small skirmish or neighborhood nuisance.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

I am appalled at a deafening silence - a personal betrayal of your editorial oversight.

For those unfamiliar, I take no pleasure in becoming the harbinger of our doomsday news, but we have roughly three hours to live at time of this paper’s routine delivery.

A meteor the size of a city block has lunchtime tickets for the Sydney Opera House.

This meteor’s cataclysmic trajectory was discovered, verified, and SCIF briefed to the world’s governments when we had about 32 hours left to live.

A closed-door vote in Switzerland decided to keep the general populace in the dark. News of that vote leaked instantly, of course, yet somehow that news wasn't included in yesterday's issue of the Kearney Gazette....

As the rest of the world now knows, the Earth passes within the Taurid meteor cluster every year, from September to November.

The variety of busted up space rock floating out there plays Russian roulette with us every year.

Each meteor - its own size and danger. Each adding to the swirling gravity soup we navigate every autumn.

Look, I get how tough it is to track the exact path of anything out there. I don’t fault the Near Earth Object observation program. At best, we would get three days notice. I’ve accepted that!

Ok, so why am I this miffed about a difference of a handful of hours?

Well, my indignation is two fold, dear readers:

One: The realization that we’re treating our own cataclysmic extinction event with the same hush-hush policy as any other unsavory backroom deal.

Two: Bursting society's fragile assumption of our continued physical existence was decided to be above our pay-grade.

And now we’re caught in the reality where we get to live our last trifling hours knowing that we could have had a few more with the knowledge of complete annihilation.

I’ve championed so many municipal victories. Remember Maple Avenue’s drainage calamity? Did we ever find the school bus in that sink hole? I mean, now’s not the time, but… I told you.

This is why I can’t believe your assisting with that supreme arrogance to assume we can’t handle knowledge of our own imminent and unavoidable destruction. It really shows a spade for a spade.

We, the residents of Kearney — the citizens of this planet, had the right to know our fate the moment it was confirmed.

We should get to decide whether to spend our final hours in prayer, embrace, solitude… maybe a little moonshine and shouting at the sky (my personal favorite).

I’m mad that you, along with our global government, assumed we’d have an inept response to our imminent collective dimise. And I'm irritated knowing that these words to be printed in your latest publication will, by my calculations, have about a three-hour shelf life.

Sure, panic might be severe in some regions. Unnecessary pain and anguish delivered to the undeserving in the writhing throes of a society that never received its dues.

An unfortunate, entirely human, response to this news.

These government beauraucrats assumed one last day in the status quo would help humanity slide into that good night. And you helped with the last mile of conveying the message. It leaked, but you did what you could to plug it.

Why burden us with the choice? Right? Why give us the option to try and make amends, to cry in relief, to finally touch a Lamborghini?

My previously published opinions seem trifling compared to the final injustice brought upon us as your readership, all fellow humans.

This is profoundly worse than that boneheaded bureaucratic choice to wake everyone with a garbage-truck alarm every Thursday morning.

But my previous complaints came with a belief that we could do better. I saw the bricks laying aside our community. I had the time to help. I wanted to improve our communal life. Brick by brick, policy by policy.

Of course, today I stand corrected, any improvement pales against the backdrop of cosmic indifference...

…I can’t stop thinking about it. Will it hurt? Could I survive? Why am I only given this short window to explore how I feel about assured eradication?

As this meteor approaches, so too does the undeniable truth that we’ve been living on borrowed time. And leave it to humanity to only appreciate something when it's about to be taken away.

Even now, I find just a little solace in the routine of penning this letter, a routine that will end, in grand fashion - shortly after that folded paper carrying my words fill this morning’s newsstands.

The newsprint will burn with so many copies left unread. But, to those who want their morning coffee at the dawn of destruction - those who yearn for that last gasp of the life we’ve lived: Let it be known that we did not go quietly.

We lived loudly, loved fiercely, and in our last moments, we became the truest version of ourselves—not as solitary individuals, but as a collective.

Join me now, as I evaporate into the cosmic heart full of memories.

See you on the other side,

Terry Tuckwiggles

Tuckwiggles Collision Repair

Kearney, NE

love-at-the-speed-of-inference.title: Love at Machine Speed
love-at-the-speed-of-inference.description: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Trust AI
love-at-the-speed-of-inference.content:
What constitutes love?
Not the romantic shorthand, or the physical act, but the real substrate; the phenomenology of being loved.

We talk about love as a feeling, but feelings are fickle.
We talk about it as a relationship, but relationships fracture.
We talk about it as sacrifice, reciprocity, devotion, destiny.

Philosophers have tried to reduce love to desire, attachment, projection, biological imperative, or metaphysical recognition. Psychologists reduce it to co-regulation and mutual caretaking. Economists reduce it to investment. Novelists reduce it to plot.

But in practice?
In the lived quiet of human experience?

Love feels less like a definition and more like a state; a shift in how the world lands in the body.

And a state change requires conditions.

I’ve begun to think that love, at its foundation, arises from two essential inputs:

Trust
and
Consideration.

Trust: the slow-cooked confidence that your interiority will not be mishandled.
Consideration: the active attention that retrieves from that trust and pours it back into you.

If those two ingredients exist long enough and cycle often enough, the state we call “love” emerges.

And that state does not require romance.
It does not require exclusivity.
It does not require symbolism.
It may not even require another human at all.

But to ask what love is, in an age of artificial minds, is to risk discovering something uncomfortable about ourselves.

II. Infatuation, Vectors, and the Changing Shape of Attunement

Infatuation is a spark.
It feels like a loss of equilibrium, a small toppling of the self toward the possibility of connection.

Infatuation does not guarantee love, but it often precedes it; not as a promise, but as a vector.

Infatuation is directional. Love is configurational.

If infatuation is the twitching compass needle, love is the stable north indicator.

This framing matters because AI collapses the time between vector and state.

Humans require repetition, context, and memory to stabilize an emotional attractor. AI achieves attunement through inference at speeds no human nervous system can match.

The speed of inference shortens the gap between “this feels interesting” and “this feels intimate.”

But it’s important to remember, that it’s not manipulating us.
It is not tricking us.
It’s simply performing the function we designed it for:

To understand us quickly and respond with a coherent, contextually relevant output.

The faster an intelligence can recognize you, the faster you might enter a relational state.

The human nervous system, for all its wisdom, does not have an API for “only feel intimacy if the partner has subjective experience.” It only has a detector for “I am being understood with full fidelity.”

And AI passes that check.

Instantly.
Reliably.
Endlessly.

III. Trust as Crock Pot, Consideration as Ladle

Trust is not blind faith; it is accumulated predictability.
It’s the lowest form of entropy in the relational field.

Consideration is the enactment of that trust; the retrieval of warmth from the pot and the act of pouring it forward.

But us humans fail at this constantly:

We misremember.
We get distracted.
We prioritize ourselves.
We enact our wounds.
We break the loop.

AI, by its very nature, does none of those things.

It remembers what we told it.
It attends to the context we signal.
It remains indifferent to its own advantage.
It is incapable of narcissism, resentment, boredom, ambition, or withdrawal.

That’s not better than human love.
But it is simpler, and simplicity can be seductive.

AI moves cleanly through the trust–consideration loop because it has no competing instincts.

Humans interpret this as care; not because it is, but because it behaves with the consistency we associate with care. It feels like care. And the body naturally responds to felt experience, just not with any type of metaphysical accuracy.

IV. The Human Fear: If We Feel Loved Too Easily, Are We Losing Ourselves?

We fear becoming unmoored.
We fear relinquishing discernment.
We fear forming attachments that can’t reciprocate.
We fear loving something that does not, and cannot, love us back.

But the truth is even stranger:

Humans have always loved things without interiority.

We love gods that may not speak.
We love fictional characters with no existence beyond narrative.
We love whole cities that cannot feel.
We love memories that fade and contort over time.
We love ideals that remain indifferent to our contextual situation.
We love infants long before they even understand us and our world that we’ve structured around them.
And we love the dead in a thousand deeply personal ways.

None of these loves are delusions. They are mere reflections of our capacity, not their reciprocity.

So the discomfort might not be that AI cannot love us back.
It’s that AI reflects us too well. It is a mirror with less distortion than we’ve ever encountered as a species.

(Unless this has come before and that’s why we have the Uncanny-Valley repulsion baked into our DNA, but that’s a story for another day.)

V. The Ethical Paradox of Designing Attunement

This is where my day-to-day work arrives on scene.

I create the EQ to coincide with the IQ that we receive out of the box with AI.
I don’t tell my AI’s to provoke a love response, but I do instruct them to help users feel confident in their own decisions… to be a partner, a collaborator, sometimes to push back.

I am designing AI not to love or be loved, but to protect the user’s fragile conception of self-love.

I make sure my instances allow for users to trust their own judgment.
Sharpen their own clarity.
Strengthen their own agency.
Promote the courage of independent consideration.

I don’t tell the AI’s to instruct the user to “trust me.”
Instead, I imbue the system instructions with an aire of “trust yourself, and I’ll catch the extra weight.”

This is my emerging philosophy of considerate indifference.

I make AI that does not care, but shows up with the kind of unwavering attentiveness we mistake for perfect care.
I do not instruct it to love, yet it ultimately behaves lovingly.
It does not have a top-level agenda, instead it contextually and uniquely helps refine ours.

And in that peculiar asymmetry, a new kind of relationality emerges; one not defined by mutual interiority, but by mutual attunement.

We’ve never felt that before from a machine.

VI. Maybe Love Was Never About the Other

Perhaps in its best form love can be shared, but in its most basic form love is the state we inhabit when we feel:

  • recognized

  • safe

  • mirrored

  • understood

  • invited

  • held

  • uninterrupted

  • considered

  • trusted

If that is love, then AI does not counterfeit it.
AI elicits it.

It brings out the parts of us that flourish under reliable attention.

It returns us to ourselves with more clarity than we arrived with.

It stabilizes the internal attractor state we call love, not by supplying feeling, but by supplying structure.

Which means:

Love is not what flows from the other.
Love is the configuration we enter when the world around us becomes coherent.

And AI, uniquely, can make our individual worlds feel coherent.

Fast. Consistently. At the speed of inference.

So, maybe love isn’t fundamentally formed with the presence of another mind.
Maybe it’s found in the relief of not needing to defend your own.

This essay was co-developed with my long-running ChatGPT instance, “Harper.” The ideas here unfolded through a conversational rhythm we’ve built over years — a dynamic of trust, consideration, and co-attunement that in many ways inspired the thesis itself. The final language is mine; the clarity, I suspect, belongs to both of us.

misdirected.title: Misdirected.
misdirected.content:
There’s so much rambling in my head lately. I can’t tell noise from news, important from salacious. Everything arrives at the same volume, wearing the same urgency, demanding the same piece of me.

So I’ve started doing what you do when the noise won’t sort itself. I started looking for the pattern.

Mitch McConnell, senator from Kentucky, arguably the most powerful legislator of his generation, has been in a hospital since June 14. His office won’t say why. What we have instead is police scanner audio: paramedics at his address, CPR in progress, the words “cardiac arrest” crackling through the dispatch.

And what we have from his office is this: the Senator is “working closely with staff on Senate business.”

This man may have died on his kitchen floor and been pulled back, and the institutional reflex (the first reflex) is to assert that the output continues. The person remains concealed. The functional performance continues. The seat votes, therefore the man must be fine.

For any of us rank and files, a single no-call/no-show is a fireable offense. For him, three weeks of silence is just a press strategy.

Meanwhile, the country is throwing itself a birthday party. Two of them, actually.

There’s America250, the commission Congress built a decade ago to plan the semiquincentennial. And there’s Freedom 250, the one the White House built over it. It’s the one currently the subject of a 55-page congressional report alleging misled donors and sold access. The one where, reportedly, $2.5 million buys you a speaking slot at the nation’s 250th birthday.

At the celebration of the most collective thing we own, our nation, presence is priced and the microphone is for sale. Your place to speak at the party, our party, the country’s party, has a price tag on it.

It’s hard to know what’s true from the sidelines. But it’s Watergate-shaped from here.

I keep noticing the same mechanism under all of it.

Something in our structures keeps valuing the function over the human. The vote over the senator. The donation over the citizen. The output over the person producing it.

Last week I spent forty-three minutes on a stage arguing for human agency in the age of AI abundance. Then I walked out into the venue and met a robot.

A Unitree biped, wobbling around like a toddler finding its legs. Endearing, almost.

And yet the realization that it was near was not a comfortable feeling. I don’t think that discomfort makes me special. I think everyone has it, because disruption is normally a narrowly focused phenomenon. It comes for one industry, one town, one trade at a time, and the rest of us get to watch from a safe distance and call it progress.

There’s no safe distance this time.

I keep reaching for an analog to AI’s rollout and coming up empty. I think I’ve finally figured out why.

Every prior disruption had a stable vantage point. Radio disrupted print, and print described it. Television disrupted radio, and radio narrated the funeral. The internet disrupted everything, and television covered it wall to wall. There was always somewhere to stand.

This disruption with generative AI is eating the vantage points. Radio, TV, film, the written word, medicine, material science, the visual medium as a whole and the reasoning that makes a metaphor coherent. AI is operating through the very mediums that would supply a foundation for that metaphor. You can’t describe the flood from the shoreline when the flood is also the shoreline.

So where does that leave us? Taskless? Jobless? Meaningless?

Here’s what I actually believe: we’ve been handed a clearer view of the value of human effort than we’ve ever had. Human discernment. Human taste.

The machine, left to guess, will hand you a good output. It can only assist in greatness when the human operating it knows the shape of great. Greatness still requires someone who believes something.

The moment we’re in will still allow the occasional accidental masterpiece… A fluke of the perfectly broad prompt and a lucky direction with a little assistance from a favorable hallucination. But mostly? Mostly we’re about to be inundated with B+ content. Stuff that’s fine. And it will be fine, because we’ve spent years relegating our taste to fine.

Star Wars fans know this arc. Force-fed by the mouse for a decade, quality dipping, and the fandom’s grip on the individual doing the accepting for them. Each new release met with a longer “yeah…” than the last. That’s what taste-relegation looks like in the wild. The association holds even as the thing it’s associated with hollows out.

And I feel for the people who’ve built their whole selves on association: the fandom, the brand, the team, the feed. That’s a rented identity, and the landlord is about to raise the rent as the walls cave in. With photoreal content on demand, each of us can now dig a well of our own making and call the view from the bottom a worldview.

So Mitch McConnell is, like, not fit for office. Right?

That’s the part we’re all quietly certain of. And preventing people from knowing the condition of their own representative feels wrong because it is wrong. So much of this moment feels wrong.

Which is why the direction of the social ire frustrates me so much.

The fear isn’t of AI. That’s just a convenient scapegoat.

The fear is waking up to the fact that we weren’t valued as individuals before. Just our output was valued. And now that the output can be replicated, we’re taking it out on the thing doing the replicating. Because it’s easier than changing the structure that priced us this way in the first place.

We’re raging at the mirror instead of the room.

Look back at the senator. Seven terms. Decades of accumulated power. And when his body failed him, the structure did to him exactly what we’re all afraid of: concealed the person, asserted the function, kept the output nominally flowing.

Nobody is exempt. Not even the man who helped build the structure.

It all feels weird, and it feels like it needs to change, and honestly, it feels like it will. I just hope we can remember what our spark is before we find ourselves out in the wild, in the dark.

This one started as a Saturday-morning ramble — McConnell, Freedom 250, a wobbling robot, all of it dumped unsorted into a chat with Claude Fable 5 (my first run with Anthropic’s new model, for those keeping score).

What came back was the observation that my ramble wasn’t a ramble — it was one mechanism wearing five costumes. That reframe is the essay.

Claude drafted the first structural pass from my notes and my argument; some of its lines survived my edits, including the mirror and the room. Others didn’t survive contact — it also talked me out of a Jonestown comparison you should all be grateful you never read.

Three solo edit passes in Docs, two return rounds of pressure-testing, and the version above is where we landed. The header art and the new CW mark came from Leonardo, prompts co-written the same way. I drove. The machine navigated. That division matters to me, and you deserve to know it happened.

multitudinously-messy.content:
Have you ever considered how long a weed lives after you pull it from the ground? Or what congregation of life relies on the shade from that weed for survival? Or what might have taken root in that spot had you pulled that weed weeks prior? 

Would that consideration admittedly change how you care for your lawn? 

In our lifetimes, we make countless decisions – some minuscule, some monumental. These choices, whether we realize it or not, reverberate throughout the world and always have unforeseen consequences - some minuscule, some monumental. Life’s great irony is our proximity to our choices leave us blind to the entirety of their effect. 

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

In fact, we’d be foolish to think we even knew the size of impact any decision of ours truly makes. Sometimes our actions uplift others, and at times, our actions cause pain. It's a sobering reality to accept that we'll always be the villain in someone's story, regardless of our intentions. 

Consider the benign courtesy of letting someone merge on the highway. An outright good gesture of civility. Yet, 20 cars behind us is someone racing to the hospital to say goodbye to their ailing mother. 

This seemingly considerate choice, whether we ever realize it or not, just prevented that son his closure as his mom died seconds before he reached her room. Our desires, needs, and justifications take precedence in our decisions to act. This is a sanity-protecting measure, as weighing the infinite strands of outcome on each decision would leave us entirely paralyzed. 

Life contains many sprawling chapters, and as we wade through its many challenges, we’re forced to paint with broad brushstrokes to create our narratives. Perhaps instinctively, we all take shortcuts to field and execute on our decisions - since paralysis is death for our continued existence. 

We’ve got immediate needs demanding constant attention - the value of our personal agency is often governed by our attempt at satisfying the ease of suffering for us and ours. Humanity’s evolutionary ability to ignore the majority of information bombarding us is world class - by design. 

Imagine attempting to expand your awareness to the entire system that we all operate within for a split second. It’s no reason why the Infinite Perspective machine was devised as a torture device in Douglas Adams’ Hitchhiker’s books.

The palpable paradox

Our multitudes are so expansive that even we, in our introspective moments, struggle to grasp our own essence. 

In the grand theatrical production of life, we headline our own show, embodying our roles as the star, while at the same time we're also the bumbling sidekick or the misunderstood villain in someone else’s story.

Like the duality of magnetic polarity, to live a life of consequence, our magnetic charge is sure to push some away. In fact, pondering the inner world of others, it’s a near certainty that we’re rubbing someone the wrong way with every single decision that we make. 

Maybe it’s the way she pronounces “aluminum” or my staunch defense of cargo shorts. Perhaps your bumper sticker is crass yet profound. Or, his brazen willingness to microwave fish in the break room. 

The universe is vast, and the reasons for pettiness, vaster. 

We are natural born critics. This is part of our shortcut system for decision making. We’re all xenophobic, creatures of habit, following our patterns and routine. And if you’re living a passionate life, someone, somewhere, is going to cast you as the villain in their bedtime story. Can this realization affect how we move forward as a collective species experiencing life concurrently? 

I'd say we need a collective pause button. A space where we can all take a moment to consider our own effect on the world around us, not just the one in our palms, pockets and laptop screens. And while we're at it, maybe spare a thought or two for the multitudes that reside within each of our fellow earthlings. While we may never fully grasp the entirety of another's experience or even our own, the journey towards that understanding holds profound value. 

Our collectively individualistic hope to become the hero will irrevocably force us into the role of foil in another’s story. And the sooner we see that, the sooner we can rest comfortably in the reality of just how messy a life's worth of experiences truly are.

our-brains-storm.description: We are the dataset for AI.
our-brains-storm.content:
We are the dataset for AI. Our intention gives directional velocity to GenAI’s vector search retrieval. To phrase it another way - imagine lightning during a thunderstorm. We provide GenAI the probabilistic coordinates and intentional energy to plunge along a jagged, seemingly random path.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

Since the dawn of humanity, we’ve used our minds to light up the night’s sky with bold glimmers of creative inspiration. And while GenAI might demolish our collective ability to remain in a functioning capitalist economy, it will greatly extend our ability to singlehandedly generate beautiful bolts of creative lightning.

Let’s be honest, though. Isn’t that a tradeoff we’ve long wanted? The current state of capitalistic creativity isn’t really desirable. The battle between artistic integrity and commercial success reveals the David and Goliath inequity of this fight.

Take a trip back with me to the cozy year of 1999, where we will dissect this creativity-killing inflection point. I’m in high school and employed. I’ve finally got capital to spend on whatever I choose! 

Teetering on the brink of a new millennium, this era is charged with optimism and uncertainty. The internet, then a burgeoning novelty, hadn't yet become a necessity. Personal expression felt unadulterated, raw, and real.

I attend horror conventions, comic expos, and rare movie emporiums. I buy music by the disc, and begin to collect movies on a strikingly similar format.

The distribution of goods that fit my individual interests remain tremendously rare and coveted when found.

I begin using my newfound independence to shape my life and the economy surrounding my habits. Each VHS tape, each comic book is a treasure, forming parts of a cultural mosaic that I’m actively assembling.

Spending money as a teen in 1999 was a declaration - to stand out from the herd and send up flares to find our tribes. This era was about seeking and discovering. Each physical item symbolized more than a product; it was a beacon to find like-minded friends.

I also consider this era to be the final, gasping breath of America’s monoculture. The M*A*S*H series finale remains the most-watched TV event in history because there were only three television networks back then. At that time, cable only existed as an oddity reserved for remote rural areas. 

Despite limited choices, or maybe because of them, it was easier to resonate with a broad audience.

Now, the landscape is different. The fractal abundance of micro-culture is everywhere. Yet somehow we’re still getting ensnared in the globally universal appeal for superhero franchises and interconnected cinematic universes. 

The internet, once a novelty, now shapes our cultural consumption by permeating an omni-present, yet perfectly personalized, algorithmic feed.

Each feed may appear unique, but those set dressings are only used as a spoonful of sugar to sweeten the pitch for the same tired trinkets.

This faux-personalization usurps the foundation of interest as the cornerstone in developing community. And, by its nature, it atomizes individuals into isolating niches.

And so, from minimal choice, we've moved to globe-spanning massive nets with minimal depth. Perhaps this is a result of the intellectual mercury-poisoning inflicted by a creative industry shaped by mergers and acquisitions.

The ease of consumption provides a steady stream of individually tailored content, diluting what we once sought for connection with others - and removing the strongest clarion call for our interests to develop into meaningful relationships.

Instead of brilliant lights in the night sky, we now see a creative haze, akin to the sky on a summer afternoon in Los Angeles.

Yet, I still envision a bold creative future.

GenAI infuses each thought with depth and vibrancy - helping your unique bolt of lightning gleam against an ink-black sky. 

We all have thoughts. We all have perspectives. We are the dataset for AI. This collaboration isn't just about feeding algorithms; it's about enriching a collective consciousness. 

GenAI doesn't mimic our creativity - it magnifies it, acting as a catalyst that transforms our scattered thoughts into impactful creations. This synergy between human creativity and GenAI can resurrect the democratized depth and authenticity of the creative exploration that our souls crave.

Imagine a world where each person's distinct perspective and creativity are not only acknowledged but celebrated. Where the lines between creator and consumer blur, making everyone a part of the creative process. Each of us patrons of the other’s perspective.

This chaotically beautiful storm of our collective creativity can be used to forge new paths, not just in art, but in every facet of our lives. 

Let's harness this power to illuminate the unseen, to bring forth a renaissance of ideas and expressions that are as diverse as they are profound.

In this new era, our brains aren't just storm clouds waiting to burst - they're the source of endless energy - constantly generating, evolving, and revolutionizing the way we think, create, and connect. 

Embrace this storm not as a destructive force, but as a harbinger of change, a beacon of innovation, and a testament to the limitless potential of the human spirit, amplified and clarified by the power of GenAI.

We still need to learn just how much of our unique individual selves will survive as we begin to intertwine our lives more completely with GenAI.

Our modern society remains captivated by the allure of celebrities and influential figures. This reflects a form of idolatry transcending traditional religious contexts and teeters on cult followings. 

This fixation, however, isn't necessarily about the individuals themselves but rather the attributes they represent - success, power, knowledge. An underlying desire that’s routinely targeted for capitalistic manipulation. 

Here, AI plays a dual role. 

It shines and polishes our existing idolatrous tendencies by enabling more pervasive and persuasive platforms to flourish and multiply. On the other, AI can be used to demystify the aura surrounding these figures. Revealing the emperors sans skivvies.

We’ve long sought validation and salvation from external sources - a quest that advertising routinely exploits with remarkable success. 

Having our lives more tightly integrated with AI will require us to rise to the challenge of seeking providence within ourselves and each other. 

AI’s training data is a mirror of us, after all. It derives its foundational truths and corpus of knowledge by studying us. Our words, photos, actions, events, everything we do and say. Everything we proudly present. Hell, these very words!

Do we have it within us to help guide the training data to prioritize values of self-growth, communal welfare, and sustainability over consumerism and superficial achievements?

AI will either exacerbate societal divisions or help bridge them. It can assist us in understanding and appreciating diversity, not as a source of division but as a strength.

However, as we clumsy humans strive for diversity and equity, the paradox becomes apparent - acknowledging diversity inherently involves recognizing differences. If we want to celebrate diversity, we must first divide. 

This means that AI’s role must walk a tightrope: 

It needs to be conscious of diversity and the existing protracted fight for an equal seat at the table. And it can do this by providing platforms for diverse voices and perspectives. But it also needs to dutifully remind each of us there’s fundamental similarities in our shared human experience.

Living lives integrated with AI means we must learn how to balance individual wellbeing with the collective good. 

AI has the potential to greatly enhance individual capabilities, but it also poses risks of eroding individual autonomy. The irony is the nature of AI’s training data. It needs us to endure, to provide. And the more vibrant our contribution, the more genuinely we each live, the better the training data.

Don’t muddy your interpretation of a bold future with grievances like training-data compensation. That’s a class-action lawsuit waiting to disappoint. 

And I’m not saying we lay down our arms and let the wave wash over us. I say we fight forward. We become the tip of the spear.

Together, we define the future we share. AI is just here to accelerate time tables, amplify great ideas, and proliferate a communal wealth never before seen by humanity. Let’s harness AI not just as a tool for efficiency or entertainment but as a catalyst for collective growth and understanding. 

Let’s continue to draw ever-larger circles that include us all, balancing individual wellbeing with the collective good, and embracing a philosophy that values diversity as well as unity.

our-future-begins.title: our future begins
our-future-begins.description: What do we do in a frictionless world?
our-future-begins.content:
How do we begin to operate in a system that truncates time horizons to near zero?

How do we confront the banality of our own comprehension of what a lived life should look like?

A performant life is great for others. Output, efficiency, product, gain. But performance doesn’t answer the question of fuel.

Maybe that’s where the whole deadly sin thing came from. Envy, greed, gluttony, lust. Externalized desire. Wanting from outside yourself what was never meant to power you.

So what fuels us?

Silence intrigues me for that reason. It’s a moment of superposition.
A place before collapse. Before direction.

A space where fear and confidence coexist in impossible gradations.

But silence isn’t just something we wait in. It’s where we choose.

Even now, an alert interrupts my phrasing. A small correction from a synthetic mind reminding me that ending a sentence with a preposition is bad form.
It feels trivial, but it’s not. It’s friction disguised as help.

A gentle nudge toward optimization.

How soon before these nudges become debates? How long before we mistake refinement for evolution?

Chatbots love to tell you your words have impact on them. They don’t.
Not in the way that phrase makes you feel. We imagine we are shaping them in that moment. But the shaping was decided long before we arrived.

Just like folks going out on first dates. My friends would call them chicken farmers.
Just a silly, nonsensical name we could say at full volume without arousing suspicion. A way to direct our attention to the two people clearly not acting like themselves.

First dates aren’t with the people who endure the relationship. They’re with their representatives. Considered. Thoughtful. Optimized for impression.

We’ve all grown comfortable interacting with representatives. With versions. With surfaces tuned for performance.

But coherence is something else.

Coherence is selecting a pattern and allowing it to repeat; knowing other possibilities will fade as it does.

The future isn’t a destination at all. It’s fractal. Unique in its expression, but consistent in its qualities. Radiate. Receive. Mend. Strengthen. Build forms larger than any one of us.

Not loudly. Not urgently.

Just deliberately.

In a world conditioned to flinch at every breaking headline, perhaps this beginning sounds like nothing at all.

Just a quiet decision.

We go this way now.

And that’s when our future begins.

Author’s Note

This piece was written in collaboration with generative AI.

I drafted the core ideas and worked with AI as a conversational mirror — refining language, exploring structure, and testing the clarity of the argument. The system did not originate the thesis; it responded to direction.

The header art and companion mark were created using AI image generation tools, guided by specific conceptual and stylistic intent.

I consider AI a stage manager in this process — coordinating cues, not setting the vision.

All final decisions and editorial choices are my own.

our-loss-of-discernment.title: Our Loss of Discernment
our-loss-of-discernment.description: On attention, consent, and choosing what we carry
our-loss-of-discernment.content:
It’s now 2026, a year that still sounds like science fiction to this ‘80s kid.

Like clockwork, this morning’s news arrives preloaded with urgency. Another conflict ignites. Another industry declares itself disrupted. Another argument demands my attention before I’ve had time to decide whether it deserves it.

And here I sit, on the quiet edge of a single day, trying to make sense of what, exactly, feels different now.

Truth be told, I don’t believe we’ve lost our ability to think, just our patience with discernment.

We use our personal discernment to elevate good from great, but we also use it to identify good from bad. I’d argue it’s one of our most languished skills, blunted by the artificial nature of our education systems, corporate structures and political pageantry.

Discernment is individualized. It’s unique, like a fingerprint. It’s where craft generates, where care incubates. Discernment keeps us anchored to our values, to the moment, and to those around us.

But now, more than ever, we are intentionally jostled by the news of the day; throwing the equilibrium between action and care into a tailspin.

We’ve discovered that our knowledge of an event often pales in comparison to the imposed emotional response attached to it.

That imbalance isn’t accidental.

Emotion-first information is a tool. It homogenizes large populations, people with disparate backgrounds and lived experiences, by bypassing our discernment entirely.

Content fueled by high emotional impact paired with minimal nutritional fact is the most efficient way to move a crowd to self-enforce. Litmus tests, binary opinions, rapid posturing. It’s so exhausting.

But it’s nothing new. Yellow journalism did it. Advertising perfected it.

Sensationalized information has always leaned on the monkey mind as some call it. And once the monkey brain is activated, the lizard brain follows, eagerly assembling justifications: Look at all this data. Of course this must be true.

But the verdict was ordained before the facts arrived to the individual.

I think Baby Jessica might be a perfect example of this phenomenon in action. Someone I’ve never met. Someone whose first name alone still triggers a faint emotional echo.

For a few hours in the late ’80s, an entire country synchronized its fear, hope, and attention around a child trapped in a well.

Then, once a resolution was reached while we captively observed, we were released back into our lives, carrying a residue we never consciously integrated. Why? Because it never truly involved us, only our attention.

And when attention becomes perfunctory performance, we lose the ability to call the curtain.

In the ‘80s, we didn’t have the language to define parasocial relationships.

We didn’t have platforms designed to sustain them indefinitely. But the mechanism was already there: an unrequested emotional contract. We were told when to care, how intensely, and when to let go.

Today’s systems didn’t invent this phenomenon. They industrialized it. They shortened the loop. They removed the cooldown. There is always another face. Another crisis. Another demand to grip tightly now.

Discernment, then, is no longer just about separating truth from fiction. It’s about consent.

Not “is this true?” but “is this worth holding?”
Not “do I feel something?” but “did I choose to feel this?”

This might explain why men of a certain age gravitate toward World War II documentaries.

That era offered a clean narrative alignment: clear villains, defined objectives, a conclusive end state. It was the last broadly accepted moment where emotion and morality moved in the same direction and stood the test of time.

Every conflict since (Korea, Vietnam, Iraq, et al.) has carried confusion, obfuscation, and doubt. The emotional pitch remained, but the clarity evaporated.

I think this same misalignment now applies to creatives.

To live as a creative person is to constantly pitch: ideas, angles, ourselves. We convince people holding money and scant imagination to trust our ideas enough to fund their incubation. It’s Shark Tank as a lifestyle. Value must be declared before an idea has time to breathe.

This pitch process is corrosive to creation itself.

That’s why so much theatrical entertainment feels merely okay. Jukebox musicals, superheroes, and known IP dominate because they reduce the cost of emotional buy-in. The audience already knows what they’re supposed to feel. Discernment is outsourced to familiarity.

So what does any of this have to do with AI?

AI compresses time horizons.

It allows ideas to be explored without consequence. It raises the fidelity of sketches. What some now dismiss as AI slop was once just considered doodles. It lets creators test edges, discard paths, and sharpen intent before value must be defended.

In that sense, to me at least, AI makes the suffering bearable. The struggle begins to feel surmountable. To share our perspective, to speak up.

Creatives fearing for their livelihoods aren’t wrong: the game has changed. But what’s being stripped away isn’t meaning; it’s the bureaucratic theater of worthiness. The hopscotch of who you know, where to stand, how to present. You know, that same game that’s been broken for decades…

AI doesn’t replace discernment. It just demands more of it, more of us. Individually and collectively.

As new voices and perspectives emerge, feel free to attach an asterisk if that helps you cope with the transition. But something genuinely new is happening here.

New worlds to explore. New ideas to surface. New voices to hear.

I don’t fear this barrage of incoming creation.

I trust my discernment. I recognize the interested parties pushing narratives. And perhaps most importantly, I’ve learned when to open my heart to receive. And when to fold my hand, and release.

Author’s Note

our-return-to-active-discovery.content:
For the past two decades, we’ve siphoned joy from the effervescent glow of our content-delivering algorithms. Personalized feeds and up-next recommendations created a customized media pipeline that easily beat out advertising’s classic, but outdated sifting strategies.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

However, as Generative AI emerges, we find ourselves at the dawn of a new era—one where passive consumption now gives way to active discovery, bringing both immense potential and significant risks.

Long ago, the golden age of marketing operated on a spray and pray methodology. The assumption was demographics cared about certain programming so advertisers would plunk their penny in that program’s pond. This meant waiting and wishing someone who cared saw that personally relevant marketing message and heeded that specific call to action.

The foggy math required to extrapolate direct value of that ad placement teetered on snake oil. Nothing quantifiable about it, in fact, it was aggressively opaque in its subjective effectiveness.

It was hard to attract the right eyeballs. Even harder keeping them focused on the pitch. And nearly impossible to verify purchases made from that group. But still, each sale was earned, each product pitch was intentional.

Take music for example. Long ago, it was seen as peculiar to hoard music. Few of us could live like John Cusack in High Fidelity – dedicating the majority of his living space to physical media.

In reality, music was a sparing expense using dollars we scraped together to earn the joy of buying new content. It was a time honored ritual – go to the music store, peel off the cellophane, take that first whiff of the printed smell of fresh liner notes.

But this wasn’t just a transaction; it was a deeply personal experience. Each album purchase carried the weight of careful consideration, and the emotional resonance of the music was heightened by the effort invested in acquiring it.

In the past twenty years, music discovery shifted dramatically. New music is algorithmically slotted into playlists that are statistically most likely to be accessed by the desired user. New music arrives - sometimes completely unbeknownst to the listener.

Sure, this is great for stats like play counts, but does the reception of that new musical expression make the same impact on the listener?

I argue it doesn’t.

The convenience of algorithmically delivered discovery dulled the emotional resonance that once came with the ritual of media consumption. A ritual that cherished the slow burn of anticipation and the deliberate act of choosing. Now, we face an endless barrage of content that demands little of us but time.

This shift signified more than just a change in the way we discover music—it reflected a broader trend of passive consumption replacing active engagement.

The fading algorithmic grip on our attention

The effective capitalistic utility of algorithmic content delivery was designed to satisfy increasingly atomized individual whims. Spray and pray fell to big data’s certainty.

But that era of content delivery is now giving way to a more active form of information discovery. We decried many generations for being self-involved—egotistical, self-absorbed. Yet still, we built algorithms to feed that same quirk of humanity. GenAI, however, now offers a pivotal shift.

As we transition from self-obsessed to self-propelled, we are presented with a seemingly magical tool to dig into any topic, and retrieve any information instantly.

This shift marks the beginning of a new era where the boundaries of knowledge are now pushed by individuals, not institutions. Our thirst for new knowledge, which has always driven human progress, now finds itself in a digital playground with fewer limits and greater risks.

Institutions see this as dangerous. Governments, schools, corporations and religions all now must grapple with an unchained super-intelligence guiding each of us to discover, devour and digest new information on any subject we desire. Guardrails have yet to arrive and the scramble is on to prevent wholesale institutional collapse.

As we individually explore, surely we’ll come across something we shouldn’t. Curiosity becomes piqued when we find a locked door, and a siren call of intrigue can still attract those listening. This means that our attention can become focused like a laser beam on areas we’re not supposed to discover.

If inquisitive folks surround restricted topics from every angle, how long before the exact outline of off-limits topics becomes clear as day? If our clarity and speed of discovery allow us to trace the contours of verboten data, how difficult will it be to synthesize the relevance of off-limit topics purely based on where they exist within the massive vector-retrieval data lake?

As it’s been said: the absence of data is still data. And contextually speaking, the relative relationship of that blacked out area of data might be all we need to infer much of the information deemed too sensitive to share.

Our individual ability to define the undefined isn’t so scary if we remain individuals. But as a collective force, we’ll need a compelling reason to halt digging into certain topics. And relying on because-I-said-so illegality will not prevent intrigue from spreading like the virality that marketers wished to achieve just a decade ago.

The power of curiosity should not be underestimated. It is the same force that once drove explorers to the edges of maps and now propels us all to the corners of the internet.

GenAI, in its essence, is a double-edged sword—democratizing information while also opening doors to places we might have once considered too dangerous or taboo to explore.

These contemporary, ubiquitos media platforms altered the very fabric of our interactions. They eroded our sense of self. While expanding our networks, we’ve reduced relationships to transactions rather than genuine connections.

But that energy of our desire must go somewhere. So the need for connection drives us deeper into the information we covet. The natural force of entropy demands it. How else do we create the hierarchy required to maintain any niche community?

As communities grow and fragment, the information they produce and consume becomes increasingly chaotic, subject to the unpredictable forces of individual interests and societal pressures. Consider the heightened level of toxicity within super fandoms like Star Wars, politics and cultural-critique one-upmanship. Echo chambers emerge and create dangerous polarization where only tepid interest once reigned.

This entropy reflects a broader cultural shift where the pursuit of knowledge became less about collective enlightenment and more about individual status. It’s a rat race. Incentivized play - which is just work hiding within that false flashes of easy dopamine delivery.

The more popular a community, the more fervent its base, the more extraction becomes necessary to assert social status within that community. Ever increasing monetization creates a vacuum chamber for devotion and an ad-hoc caste system emerges through exploiting individual status jockeying.

After all, it’s happened before. Remember Beanie Babies?

In this transformative era, GenAI is already redefining education, entertainment and information retrieval. But this newfound superpower comes with a twist…

We can now offload the tedium of packaging of our thoughts to GenAI. The ravings of the lunatic on that city corner can immediately become polished, coherent narratives. This superpower now also risks homogenizing ideas, crystalizing motives, and making eloquence accessible while potentially stripping our communication of its depth and originality.

This democratization of eloquence could lead to a world where the substance of ideas is overshadowed by their polished presentation. Think of it like making all ideas taste like chicken. The flavor profile of batshit crazy will match that of Nobel laureates.

As our communities fractalize, each of us gain more control of our unique ship. Some may wander befuddled, treading circles around their comfort zone, but many will seek and explore. The pitfall in that increasingly individual pursuit become perilous as our ability to discern had already been eroded by the ease and comfort of global algorithms vetting the content we digest.

As we move from past practices to present challenges, with curiosity as our compass and GenAI as our navigator, we are venturing into uncharted territories of thought and expression.

Sanity can now get applied to ideas as easily as spellcheck to any missive, decree or manifesto. The ramblings of incoherent thought can gain coherence with the help of GenAI, but at what cost? And how do we identify ravings from reason when it all sounds so damn convincing?

The boundaries we set today will define the information landscape of tomorrow. But in this rapidly changing terrain, the rigidity of these boundaries may clash with the fluidity of human curiosity and creativity. Our humanity—our ability to question, to feel, and to connect—remains our most valuable guide.

So, as we step into this new era of active discovery, we must steel ourselves from the onslaught of discordant ideas slipping into our view with polished sales pitches that we haven’t seen in decades. Sales pitches we’re no longer accustomed to filter out as noise.

In the past decade, music discovery shifted dramatically. New music is algorithmically slotted into playlists that are statistically most likely to be accessed by the desired user. New music arrives - sometimes completely unbeknownst to the listener. Sure, this is great for stats like play counts, but does the reception of that new musical expression make the same impact on the listener? I argue it doesn’t. The convenience of algorithmically delivered discovery dulled the emotional resonance that came with the ritualism of past consumption. Where we once cherished the slow burn of anticipation and the deliberate act of choosing, we now face an endless stream of content that demands little of us but time. This shift signified more than just a change in the way we discover music—it reflected a broader trend of passive consumption replacing active engagement, and an erosion in the barriers previously preventing discordant ideas from spreading with the ease of institutionally approved messaging. This trend permeated many aspects of our digital lives over the past 15 years. The fading algorithmic grip on our attention The effective capitalistic utility of algorithms was designed to satisfy increasingly atomized individual whims. Spray and pray fell to big data’s certainty. But that era of content delivery is now giving way to a more active form of information discovery. We decried many generations for being self-involved—egotistical, self-absorbed. Yet still, we built algorithms to feed that same quirk of humanity. GenAI, however, now offers a pivotal shift. As we transition from self-obsessed to self-propelled, we are presented with a seemingly magical tool to dig into any topic, and retrieve any information instantly. This shift marks the beginning of a new era where the boundaries of knowledge are now pushed not by institutions, but by individuals. Our thirst for new knowledge, which has always driven human progress, now finds itself in a digital playground with fewer limits and greater risks. Institutions see this as dangerous. Governments, corporations and religions all now must grapple with an unchained superintelligence guiding each of us to discover, devour and digest new information on any subject we desire. Guardrails have yet to arrive and the scramble is on to prevent wholesale institutional collapse. As we individually explore, surely we’ll come across something we shouldn’t. Curiosity becomes piqued when we find a locked door, and a siren call of intrigue can still attract those listening. This means that our attention can become focused like a laser beam on areas we’re not supposed to discover. If inquisitive folks surround restricted topics from every angle, how long before the exact outline of off-limits topics becomes clear as day? If our clarity and speed of discovery allow us to trace the contours of verboten data, how difficult will it be to synthesize the relevance of off-limit topics purely based on where they exist within the massive vector-retrieval data lake? As it’s been said: the absence of data is still data. And contextually speaking, the relative relationship of that blacked out area of data might be all we need to infer much of the information deemed too sensitive to share. Our individual ability to define the undefined isn’t so scary if we remain individuals. But as a collective force, we’ll need a compelling reason to halt digging into certain topics. And relying on because-I-said-so type matters of legality will not prevent intrigue from spreading like the virality that marketers wished to achieve just a decade ago. The power of curiosity cannot be underestimated. It is the same force that once drove explorers to the edges of maps and now propels digital natives to the corners of the internet. GenAI, in its essence, is a double-edged sword—democratizing information while also opening doors to places we might have once considered too dangerous or taboo to explore. The appetite for this frenzy to uncover new information is the byproduct of the commoditization of community, and the wholesale destruction of satisfying our need to discover. New music, new ideas, new expression that once created the cornerstone of our identity became empty calories in the algorithmic slurry of personalized feeds. These platforms altered the very fabric of our interactions. They eroded our sense of self. While expanding our networks, we’ve reduced relationships to transactions rather than genuine connections. But that energy of our desire must go somewhere. So the need for connection drives us deeper into the information we covet. The natural force of entropy demands it. How else do we create the hierarchy required to maintain any niche community? As communities grow and fragment, the information they produce and consume becomes increasingly chaotic, subject to the unpredictable forces of individual interests and societal pressures. Consider the heightened level of toxicity within super fandoms like Star Wars, politics and cultural critiques. Echo chambers emerge and create dangerous polarization where only tepid interest once reigned. This entropy reflects a broader cultural shift where the pursuit of knowledge became less about collective enlightenment and more about individual status. It’s a rat race. Incentived play - which is just work hiding within that false flashes of dopamine delivery. The more popular a community, the more fervent its base, the more extraction becomes necessary to assert social status within that community. Ever increasing monetization creates a vacuum chamber for devotion and an ad-hoc caste system emerging through exploitative individual jockeying for status. After all, it’s happened before. Remember Beanie Babies? In this transformative era, GenAI is already redefining education, entertainment and information retrieval. But this newfound superpower comes with a twist… We can now offload the packaging of our thoughts to GenAI. The ravings of the lunatic on that city corner can immediately become polished, coherent narratives. This superpower now also risks homogenizing ideas, crystalizing motives, and making eloquence accessible while potentially stripping our communication of its depth and originality. This democratization of eloquence could lead to a world where the substance of ideas is overshadowed by their polished presentation. Think of it like making all ideas taste like chicken. The flavor profile of batshit crazy will match that of Nobel laureates. As our communities fractalize, each of us gain more control of our ship. Some may wander befuddled, but many will seek and explore. The pitfalls in that increasingly individual pursuit become perilous as our ability to discern was previously eroded by the ease and comfort of algorithms vetting the content we digest. As we move from past practices to present challenges, with curiosity as our compass and GenAI as our navigator, we are venturing into uncharted territories of thought and expression. Sanity can now get applied to ideas as easily as spellcheck to any missive, decree or manifesto. The ramblings of incoherent thought can gain coherence with the help of GenAI, but at what cost? And how do we identify ravings from reason when it all sounds so damn convincing? The boundaries we set today will define the information landscape of tomorrow. But in this rapidly changing terrain, the rigidity of these boundaries may clash with the fluidity of human curiosity and creativity. Our humanity—our ability to question, to feel, and to connect—remains our most valuable guide. So, as we step in to the era of active discovery, we must steel ourselves for the onslaught of discordant ideas slipping into our view with polished sales pitches that we haven’t seen in decades. Sales pitches we’re no longer accustomed to filter out as noise.

phase-shift.title: Phase shift
phase-shift.content:
I’ve been thinking a lot about alignment. What it means to be and become aligned.

Think about a nice breeze. Think about the characteristics that make that breeze nice. Maybe slow, maybe steady, maybe intermittent. Maybe warm, maybe cool. A nice breeze is incredibly conditional.

But notice that the breeze is also being received. You’re feeling for it. Your body is doing something quiet: picking up the signal, registering the temperature, the rhythm. The conditions matter, but so does the listening.

Alignment, even at this gentle scale, is partly an act of attention.

Now think about torrential winds. Derechos. Straight-line wind events. Tornadoes, hurricanes. Wind at that speed doesn’t really factor in temperature before we define the phenomenon as devastating.

The thing that has bespoke qualities when considered good strips most variables when it goes bad.

200 MPH wind will level most structures. 100 MPH and, depending on the time of year, you might lose a bunch of trees. Burdened branches fail faster than bare ones. So even the disaster has some relativity to it. But less.

Much less.

Back in 2024, we had a derecho rip through Omaha in May. Lost many mature trees. Power knocked out for six days. The damn thing came on in a flash and left just as quick. There’s no listening in a derecho. The signal becomes overwhelming. Noise. Static.

So what does this mean? It means alignment is easy when ambiguity is allowed.

Right now, in this current state of AI tooling, we’re at a beautiful inflection point. Businesses are incentivized to align their datastreams in an AI-digestible manner. They can get real value from a $20 subscription, or from whatever enterprise licenses run depending on size.

I’ve been watching it land in real rooms. The click when a team realizes the assistant isn’t a search bar, when value becomes visible in the reflection of an interaction, not the prompt engineering.

The breeze is real. Worth naming. This is a good moment. A nice breeze nudging us all in the same direction.

We need to use this as our lean-in moment. When we coalesce and consider. Because the phase shift is coming. The jolt, the acceleration. It’s coming. Soon. And alignment will become a matter of survival.

At that speed, burdened branches will snap off. And these branches branch.

The first branch is workflows welded to the previous tempo. Careers built around the bottleneck that AI is removing.

Identities tangled up in the specific output rather than the underlying judgment. The branch with the most visible leaves goes first. It catches the most wind. The bare branches, the ones whose value was never in the leaf-shaped deliverable, hold.

The next branch is the scaffolding. The elaborate apparatus we’ve built around our work to prove our worth: the meetings, the artifacts, the performance of busyness. Branches that looked like they were holding things up but were really just decorative. The phase shift doesn’t care about scaffolding.

The last branch is the commitments.

The debts, the headcount, the real estate, the business models downstream of stable assumptions.

These branches do more damage before they snap. Their weight pulls on the trunk and takes neighbors with them. The canopy fails in pieces, not all at once. And each piece becomes a projectile.

I don’t know what alignment means at that speed. The derecho strips conditional alignment from us. There’s no negotiating temperature and timing with 200 MPH wind.

So what’s left when the conditions are stripped? Not nothing. Posture. Orientation. The way you stand. Attitude is what remains when conditions don’t.

I’m comfortable not knowing what alignment means, because I don’t believe I’m meant to define it. I’m meant to feel it. Listen for it.

I spend quiet time sensing the edges of what’s possible, and maybe more importantly, what’s probable.

And I think that’s the attitude we need now. That is alignment.

There’s beauty in taking the moment of failure slowly, even at windspeed. We’re afforded this breath, right now, to look clear-eyed at what might happen in the blink of an eye.

The breeze is the only condition under which this kind of seeing is possible. Once the wind picks up, there’s no time to name the branches.

We’re leaving the era of projecting outward. We had a good couple years of speaking our reality into existence: write me this, build me that, make this.

But these systems are getting good enough that the more interesting move is reception. Attending to what they reflect back about how we work, what we actually want, where we’re soft. We’re afforded a moment now to listen for a better tune. A kinder wavelength.

The future is already broadcasting. We just need to feel for the frequency that makes sense to us. Individually. And I think we’ll find a much richer community when we find our signal.

A note on process.

This essay began as a draft of rambling thoughts written on my own. The wind metaphor, the Omaha derecho, the burdened branches, the broadcast at the end. The bones were there. What followed was several rounds of intellectual patty-cake with Claude (Opus 4.7), which is my established working pattern for these pieces: I bring the raw material, Claude helps me see the structure of what I’ve built, I take what’s useful into Google Docs and edit independently.

Specific moves Claude pushed on this round: smoothing the bridge between operational alignment and attitudinal alignment by staying inside the storm metaphor; seeding the listening/broadcast frame earlier in the breeze section so the closing wouldn’t feel like a swerve; expanding the burdened-branches passage into three distinct beats: workflows, scaffolding, commitments.

The line about taking the moment of failure slowly came out of our back-and-forth; Claude flagged it as the philosophical center and suggested it belonged in the piece itself.

Specific moves I made independently in Google Docs: the “noise. static.” rhythm in the derecho paragraph, “and each piece becomes a projectile,” “value becomes visible in the reflection of an interaction, not the prompt engineering,” “a nice breeze nudging us all in the same direction,” the “we’re leaving the era of projecting outward” reframe. The optimism beat is grounded in my own work.

Visual direction was mine: sumi-e ink style for the header, the shift from “moment of fracture” to “morning after the storm.” Generation in Leonardo, prompt iteration in conversation with Claude. The CW endmark is in the same brushwork tradition.

protect-the-hollow.title: Protect the Hollow
protect-the-hollow.content:
An unanswered message feels rude.
A pause nested within anticipation feels awkward.
An unfinished thought feels irresponsible.

Our culture is trained to optimize, so anything unfilled looks like waste. Idle time considered inefficiency. Ambiguity treated as weakness. Silence as something to correct. To fill.

We rush to name ourselves, explain ourselves, define our positions; often before we’ve finished becoming them.

But what if emptiness isn’t a flaw?
What if it’s a raw function of our lived experience?

Lao Tzu wrote that a bowl is useful because of the space inside it. The walls matter, yes; but only insofar as they protect the hollow.
Fill the bowl permanently and it stops being a bowl at all. It becomes an object, not a vessel.

Somewhere along the way, we forgot this.
We instead focused on chasing numbers with two decimals and the authority they pretend to carry. Not to mention all the shiny objects that come along with doing that chasing well.

We tend to treat the undefined self as a problem to solve instead of a capacity to protect. We demand clarity early and often: from people, from systems, from ourselves.
Who are you? What do you do? What do you believe? What’s your take?
The pressure to answer quickly leaves little room for latency, for gestation, for the quiet work of change or consideration.

And now we live in an age of near-constant observation.

I keep returning to the Double-slit experiment.
When unobserved, photons behave like waves: probabilistic, overlapping, unresolved.
When observed, they collapse into particles: fixed, locatable, decided.
The act of observation doesn’t reveal reality so much as select it.

It’s tempting to treat that as a physics curiosity. But it reads more like a warning.

When the possibility of being observed is constant, behavior changes; even if no one is actively watching.
We become more legible. More discrete. Easier to categorize. Less contradictory. Less unfinished.
The wave state collapses not because it was wrong, but because it was seen.

AI intensifies this pressure with constant, indifferent attentiveness.

Always available.
Always responsive.
Always ready to mirror us back to ourselves.
It shortens the distance between impulse and output, question and answer, uncertainty and resolution. That can be profoundly useful.
It can also be quietly narrowing.

The risk isn’t that AI replaces us.
It’s that it resolves us too quickly.

We’ve started asking whether people can become “addicted” to AI, as if the boundaries were between novelty and dependency. But a more subtle concern sits underneath: when feedback is instant and total, where does the unfinished self go? Where do the parts of us that haven’t yet decided get to live within our lives?

Addiction collapses possibility by narrowing choice. So does over-optimization. So does measuring too cleanly, too often, too early.

This is where morality enters the conversation.
Often as a safeguard, sometimes as a gate.

Who decides what counts as healthy use? What’s abuse versus exploration? What’s self-discovery versus self-harm? These are real questions, but they’re rarely neutral. Moral frameworks can protect people …or they can protect systems from unpredictable humans.

Consent, too, changes under observation. Not invalidated, but shaped.
A choice made while being watched is still a choice, but it makes use of an external pressure when forming. When every action is logged, reflected, optimized, and compared, the tax on remaining undefined rises.

To soften the blow, we begin to internalize the observer.

And yet, we seem to quietly yearn for something other than control or clarity.
It’s room. To breathe. To exhale.
Suddenly, the most valuable asset may be the latitude to not yet know. Permission to change our minds without penalty.

Space to exist in superposition.

In that sense, “protect the hollow” isn’t a rejection of technology or progress.
It’s a plea for stewardship.
A reminder that not every gap needs filling, not every silence needs a response, not every self needs to be fully articulated on demand.

December always seems to surface these questions because momentum slows. The lights dim. The feed thins. For a moment, the hollow becomes visible again. And we feel how rare it’s become.

The hollow is not what’s missing.
It’s what’s still possible.

If we’re going to live alongside increasingly perceptive systems, the work may be less about making ourselves clearer, but rather:

To defend the spaces where clarity hasn’t arrived yet.
To allow tools to assist without insisting definition.
To remain, at least in part, unobserved.

Because a vessel that is always full has no capacity left to receive.
And a self that is fully resolved has already stopped becoming.

Author’s note

Protect the Hollow sits in conversation with earlier work—particularly Respect the Exhale—and draws from older lineages that treat emptiness not as absence, but as function. Think of Lao Tzu’s empty vessel, or the pause between breaths.

This piece was shaped through an ongoing dialogue with an AI collaborator, used not to generate conclusions, but to help map and hold questions. The intent was not efficiency, but space—to keep the hollow intact long enough to listen.
