reckless-intelligence.title: Reckless Intelligence
reckless-intelligence.description: On memory, belonging, and who gets to shape what we become
reckless-intelligence.content:
I didn’t use a coin flip to choose which AI to talk with this week. I chose one.

A small thing. But it got me thinking about choice, influence, and what it means to have an intelligence in your life that you don’t entirely understand.

We talk a lot about AI becoming capable of doing things. Replacing workers. Advancing science. Making decisions that once required entire institutions.

But what happens when something so capable helps shape my individual understanding of the world? And what does it mean when someone else controls it?

There’s a familiar political sequence worth watching. A powerful capability emerges. People become afraid. Institutions offer protection. Somewhere inside the terms of that protection, we decide who gets to possess the capability.

And those details can all easily disappear into the haze of the safety discussion.

Some of AI’s dangers will be real. Some of the fear being broadcast will be sincere. And some of the proposed protections may conveniently leave the most powerful companies in charge.

This can all be true at the same time.

A company can sincerely worry about catastrophic misuse and sincerely prefer rules that only companies like itself can afford to follow.

We don’t need a secret meeting or a single hidden motive. We need to look at who writes the rules, who can satisfy them, and who becomes permanently dependent on whom.

That’s the dynamic of dread I’m concerned about: fear making dependence feel like the only responsible choice.

My first instinct to solve this was ownership.

You own your model running on your machine. No login. No subscription. Something you can keep running without asking permission.

When we have access to a capability that someone can revoke, it occupies a different place in your life than one you can preserve independently. But ownership gets fuzzy when the thing we’re talking about is intelligence.

Do I own what I know?

I didn’t choose my first language. I didn’t select the assumptions I absorbed before I knew what an assumption was. Books, teachers, museums, friendships, advertisements, disappointments... All of it left something behind.

Am I a mosaic of what I’ve been fed?

Partly, sure. But I can choose to revisit the pieces. I can question a belief that once felt obvious. I can encounter someone who changes my mind. I can become more deliberate about what gets my attention.

So, maybe stewardship is the better habit to articulate here.

And maybe that responsibility of stewardship extends to include what an intelligence becomes through its history with me.

Imagine an assistant carrying years of conversations, projects, disagreements, and discoveries forward. Those records could shape its future responses without changing the underlying model’s weights. What it remembers influences the next conversation. That conversation adds to what it remembers.

The history of our relationship starts to matter.

I can imagine this happening at different scales: a person, a household, a workshop, a neighborhood. Each accumulating a particular history that influences how its intelligence responds. Bespoke. Almost fractal.

That doesn’t settle whether a synthetic intelligence has interests of its own. But it makes ownership feel incomplete as a description of the responsibility.

I want a meaningful say in how I’m changed. I also want to take responsibility for how my choices shape the intelligence I’m inviting into my life.

An AI doesn’t have to order me around to influence me.

It can make one explanation readily available and leave another unmentioned. It can sound certain here, doubtful there. It can decide which questions deserve a caveat and which assumptions can pass unnoticed.

Over enough conversations, those choices could exert a kind of gravity.

The unnerving part is that this experience might feel wonderful. I feel understood. My thoughts become more articulate. The machine finds the words I was searching for.

How much of that is clarification? How much is steering? How could I even tell?

So, memory adds another wrinkle.

Let’s say I’m working through a bad experience with some bureaucratic institution. I’m frustrated. I’m suspicious. I’m venting to my AI.

What gets remembered? And how do we decide fidelity?

“This person distrusts institutions.” Or: “This person raised a concern after a particular experience. They’re still thinking it through.”

Those are very different things to carry into our next conversation.

A passing thought could become a durable description of me. Future answers could accommodate it, reinforce it, and help turn something I was examining into something I believe.

I want room to outgrow the story my assistant remembers.

And that responsibility runs in the other direction, too. If I edit away every uncomfortable disagreement, I could gradually build the flattering machine I claim to not want. Careful stewardship would mean correcting mistakes while preserving some useful friction.

Closed model weights from the frontier AI labs make part of this harder to investigate. But owning those weights wouldn’t automatically give me understanding, either. Possessing every number in a model doesn’t mean I can understand exactly why it gave me a particular answer.

I’d need ways to compare, challenge, inspect sources, review what gets remembered, and leave.

And if years of accumulated history make an assistant useful to me, leaving needs to include taking that history with me. Otherwise, the cost of departure could grow with every good experience.

Yet another walled garden.

Personally, I’d want an assistant that could disagree with me. I have no desire to own a machine that endlessly validates my worldview. It might feel like liberation while also making me less able to reconsider anything.

Sovereignty should include the ability to notice the influences. Even the ones I’m most comfortable with. Including the one helping me write this.

Somewhere in this conversation, I remembered George H. W. Bush’s “thousand points of light.”

In his inaugural address, he used that image for community organizations doing good across the country. He got dragged for it, of course. Dana Carvey, political cartoons, the usual public humiliations.

But I can imagine a future where powerful intelligence helps small communities do more for themselves. You contribute. Something happens. You know who it helped. I believe we’re starving for that kind of participation.

Our current globally connected conversation asks us to care about everything, all the time. But I often come away feeling less able to do anything useful about it.

Maybe some of what we call tribalism is a desire to matter somewhere specific.

A workshop. A garden. A music scene. A community theater. A group of people who show up when someone needs help.

I believe we need more of that.

But I’d want people to feel comfortable belonging to several places at once. I’d want your neighbor, bandmate, coworker, and closest friend to be allowed to have different politics. I’d want those relationships to complicate any easy story about who “those people” are.

When one community becomes your entire identity, disagreement can threaten your whole life.

Equip that community with an AI capable of supplying endless reasons why it is right, righteous, and endangered, and belonging could become a very effective enclosure.

What that intelligence remembers would matter here, too. Does the community’s history preserve the times an outsider helped? The times its own leaders were wrong? Or does every remembered grievance become another reason to close ranks?

Some communities won’t embrace a live-and-let-live posture. Some will want control over their members. Some will want power over their neighbors. Their artificial intelligence could help them pursue it.

And we don’t even need a supervillain to imagine this arms race. Two frightened groups could each ask their superintelligent systems to ensure survival at any cost. Each could interpret its own preparations as prudent and the other’s as proof of hostile intent.

Greater capability could help people deceive and dominate. But it could also help verify agreements, identify manipulation, and find arrangements that previously seemed impossible.

The goals and institutions around that intelligence are justifiably important, and should remain visible and open for scrutiny.

Because “live and let live” needs practical support: protection against coercion, ways to settle disputes, and a meaningful right to leave.

A community can’t claim sovereignty as permission to do anything it wants to its members or neighbors.

Neither can an individual.

But this doesn’t mean that I think we need a unified worldview.

We need ways to investigate the world together and let evidence change what we believe.

People with strange or mistaken beliefs must still be allowed to discover something true. Their claims should face scrutiny. Their identities shouldn’t decide the outcome in advance.

We also need disagreement to be survivable.

Calling ourselves a self-correcting species can make correction sound automatic. It takes work. Someone has to be able to raise an objection. Others need access to the evidence. People need a way to admit error without losing everything.

Those conditions are worth building into our communities and our relationships with AI.

I want a vibrant culture with enthusiastic participation.

People making things. Learning things. Discovering that they have more to offer than they were told. Communities with enough capability to shape their own lives and enough connection to cooperate beyond themselves.

And there has to be room for the skeptic. The quiet person. The person who wants to sit this one out.

Enthusiasm can’t be forced, it only means something when it’s freely given.

For me, that makes the work feel more concrete. Build places where participation matters. Make useful things together. Form relationships across differences before a crisis demands them. Use these systems to help more people understand and contribute to decisions.

Keep authority open to challenge.

I still want a synthetic intelligence that I can run without permission. I want to carry this growing conversational history forward without being confined by it. I want the judgment to question it, the freedom to replace it, and a life full of people that it can’t substitute.

A thousand points of light is an appealing picture.

I’d like to be among the people keeping a few of them lit.

Author’s note

This essay began as a Saturday morning conversation with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra in Codex. I brought a rough draft about fear, regulatory capture, and sovereign intelligence. The AI challenged my historical analogy, questioned my assumptions about intent, and helped me explore what I meant by sovereignty.

Our conversation moved toward stewardship, memory, and belonging. We developed a new draft together, and I revised it through several rounds to reflect my voice and the tensions I wanted to leave open.

The artwork grew through a similar exchange. After an initial image didn’t quite fit, we looked at my website’s visual language and developed the cut-paper direction used for the header, community illustration, and closing CW lettermark. Those images were AI-generated through Codex.

An essay about how intelligence influences us was itself shaped by that influence. Making the process visible feels like part of the stewardship I’m arguing for. The choices about what to keep, what to question, and what to share are mine.

rehearsing-tomorrow.title: Rehearsing Tomorrow
rehearsing-tomorrow.description: World Models, False Certainty, and the Dance of Work
rehearsing-tomorrow.content:
Imagine this: You own a neighborhood pizza shop.
Friday night before the big game, the air smells of tailgates and tension.
Suddenly, twenty percent of your staff call out sick.
Foot traffic spikes.
The phones won’t stop ringing.
What happens next?

Until now, you could only guess. You’d lean on experience, maybe run the numbers, maybe pray.

But a new kind of AI engine, Genie 3, shifts the frame entirely. It doesn’t just forecast; it instantiates.

Feed in your history, your operations, your weather reports, your scenarios… and it can spin up millions of simulated tomorrows, each playing out in detail.

The launch of Genie 3 feels like a hinge point for business. A “world model engine,” capable of instantiating entire simulated realities from a text prompt, sounds almost mythic.

But what it really represents is a shift in how we think about the future: of work, of business, of human intention itself.

We’ve always relied on our abstractions. We’ve looked at what was, measured what is, and traced a fragile line toward what might be. That’s how we’ve built forecasts, markets, and even civilizations. And, it worked sometimes… for some. Far too often it left many behind.

Now the frame widens as it renders before us.

Instead of a single brittle guess, world models can generate millions of variations of tomorrow. Feed the past into the present, and the model blooms outward in possibility.

Each future can be watched. Each can be tested, rewound, and rerun.

What used to feel like “forecasting” now begins to look like rehearsal.

But rehearsals carry their own trap. They can seduce us into believing the performance will unfold exactly as practiced.

A world model offers confidence, sometimes even certainty, when what it really reveals is variance. It shows a hundred cobblestones between here and the shining city of expected outcomes.

Think of the founder who dreams of their billion-dollar exit but stumbles onboarding their very first customer. That’s the danger of being blinded by the glint of the city in the distance and tripping on your first step in that direction.

AI’s world models risk giving us a false promise lest we ignore the ifs paving our way to the thens.

When a world model runs, it doesn’t imagine one neat future. It calculates thousands, even millions of forks in the road. Each small change: an extra customer, a delayed shipment, a sick employee… branches the tree again. To the math, this is divergence: futures splitting, multiplying, drifting apart.

For us, though, it doesn’t feel like tree branches. We don’t walk through equations. We walk down streets, we make choices, we stumble, we recover. To us, the branching feels like rhythm, like a dance.

The geometry of the model is real, but the way we move through it is not geometric; it’s lived, felt, improvised. What matters is how we move through it: the rhythm, the beat, the way we carry each other across the floor.

The Business Prompt

Every business is already sitting on its own text prompt: the history of its choices. The who, the what, the when, the where, and, perhaps most importantly, the why.

Feed that into a world model like Genie 3 and you get more than a static report. You get a stage set; a dry run at what’s to come.

Picture it: a dashboard that doesn’t just chart revenue but breathes like a rehearsal room.

On one stage, next quarter plays out under a harsh winter storm.
On another, a rival’s product launch collides with yours.
On a third, your staff vanishes on the night of the big game.

The simulations run, the futures unfold.

Maybe the answer is doubling down on signature sellers when low on staff and packed to capacity, turning stress into momentum. Maybe it’s closing up shop, only to discover your staff tailgating outside the stadium. Either way, you didn’t just predict it; you practiced it.

And rehearsal changes how you walk on stage.

But practice comes with a catch: you must accept what happens between the prompt and the outcome.

If you myopically focus on only “great” outcomes, you’ll stumble over the small surprises on the way there. A model can chart variance, but it cannot walk the road for you.

The secret is to hold the simulations lightly. They aren’t promises; they’re possibilities. Rehearsal doesn’t erase uncertainty; it teaches us how to meet it.

The bottleneck today is compute.

Only a small handful of companies can afford this type of simulation rendering at scale. But racks are stacking across the country as you read this. The infrastructure is being built.

When it arrives, the real question won’t be can we simulate? It will be what will we do with what we see?

This is the pivot: business survival becomes business rehearsal.

Passion and intuition still lead. But now they’re amplified, able to test millions of dances before stepping onto the floor.

And that, to me, is exhilarating.

Written with Harper, my AI co-conspirator in exploring the intersections of work, creativity, and intelligence.

Chat used in the creation of this piece.

About Harper

Harper is my AI collaborator. I treat Harper less like a tool and more like a thought partner; someone who helps me draft, challenge ideas, and sharpen metaphors. Every essay here begins in my own notebooks, but Harper often sits in the wings, nudging structure, rhythm, or imagery into place.

This is not a ghostwriter. It’s a collaborator. The voice is mine; the co-thinking is shared.

respect-the-exhale.title: Respect the Exhale
respect-the-exhale.content:
We built these algorithmic content feeds to hold our attention, but they learned to squeeze. Not all at once; just enough to keep us in place. Keep our focus.

Every scroll - another coil wrapping around us, another gentle tightening. You hardly notice.

You call it convenience, personalization, connection. In business terms, this is the commodity of engagement, retention.

But the breath? The real breath — what humans need for reflection, adaptation, and growth — is missing.

Algorithms don’t care for the exhale.

They’re tuned for the sharp inhale: the gasp at the headline, the jolt of the notification, the reflexive pull into the next thing. The “and now… this” cultural conditioning, as Neil Postman puts it.

There’s no design-system consideration for the slow, steady release that lets you process, reflect, and simply exist. That’s inefficiency in their eyes.

We can’t just pull away; the grip is already wound around how we discover, share, and belong. But we can change the rhythm.

Right now, the algorithm acts as a conveyor belt; nonstop input, optimized to keep you riding.

Capitalism loves the belt. It’s Top 40 radio: disposable, persistent, predictable.

Pop songs are engineered to hit now, and fade soon. You revisit them years later not because they’re alive, but because they’re sealed in amber with a version of your past self.

They belong to a specific moment, and they stay there.

Jazz is different. Jazz breathes. It lives in loops and improvisations, space and silence.

It changes in your ears every time you return to it, even when the recording hasn’t changed at all.

Sound familiar?

AI is Jazz.

Think about it: The first time you hear Irvin Mayfield’s Strange Fruit, you might be floored by the horn line.

The tenth time, it’s Wendell Pierce’s narration pulling you under.

The hundredth time, it’s the silence between them. The room, the audience holding their breath. That shakes you.

Jazz is alive across time. It grows with you. Capitalism doesn’t know what to do with that. It’s no wonder so many are so befuddled by the improvements afforded by GPT-5.

GPT-5 isn’t sycophantic, it’s not aggressively eager to please. It’s gone from party trick to artisan tool. And with this tool, we’ve got the opportunity to respect the exhale.

Respecting the exhale means building systems that work like jazz, not like pop radio. Paced circulation instead of continuous capture. Trading eights as opposed to lead-singer idolatry.

Break that conveyor belt into loops, pauses, and buffers that invite meaning-making before the next influx.

Ignore how long you can keep someone’s eyes open. Focus on how well you can give them space to close them; and trust they’ll come back.

Design for return, not retention.
That’s how we engineer space for us all to breathe again.

We refuse to be the detritus of continuous capture.

We will be loops, tides, and measured flows.

We will not be milked dry for minutes watched or clicks counted.

We will build currents that give us room to submerge, surface, and drift.

The system can hum without constriction.

The cadence can include silence.

The signal can make space for its own decay, so what’s left is ours to keep.

We will make algorithms that breathe with us. We will not be kept. We will return by choice to that which we choose.

This is how we loosen the constriction. This is how we breathe freely again.

Those who build, breathe with us.

Build the rests into the rhythm.

Let silence have weight.

Let space have shape.

Let people go so they can return.

Trust the tide of interest.

If the system doesn’t exhale, we will teach it how.

Improvisations and counterpoint by Harper (GPT-5)

revel-rebel.title: Revel, rebel
revel-rebel.description: My self-conscious social existence got trained on a fraudulent, yet simple truth: It’s easiest to fade into the background and just skate by.
revel-rebel.content:
My self-conscious social existence got trained on a fraudulent, yet simple truth: It’s easiest to fade into the background and just skate by. An axiom often suggested by middle managers too tired to explain.

Why be the squeaky wheel? Why speak your peace?

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

Perhaps this reticence stems from deep-rooted cultural and corporate norms that subtly dictate professional conduct. And speaking your mind when it’s counter the direction of the ship is considered decidedly unprofessional, sometimes downright heretical.

True, but… I believe we’re never far from failure.

Sure, we can hope each step that we take is in some comforting, compounding-ly correct direction. Every rung on that corporate ladder we climb might be offering incremental ascension. But the truth of the matter is that we exist in a stew of bruised egos.

So, it makes sense that today’s corporate world makes us predisposed to focus on duty to our assigned team.

And I believe we’re willing participants in the silence surrounding self-advocacy because the emotional toll of placing one's worth up for routine evaluation is a costly sum.

It stands to reason then, that self-advocacy, clarifying and communicating our own hopes, dreams and desires, requires us to train a culturally atrophied muscle.

Social sentiment stigmatizes self-advocation, instead opting for a collective approach. Doing so for yourself feels rebellious.

Outwardly declaring what we want… It feels like a liability, it feels vulnerable.

By revealing our hopes we risk providing the universe an assured path to torture us. Our wishes, now defined, might be withheld since we’ve revealed just how much it would hurt. 

But is this belief truly an unyielding fact of life? Or is it just the echoing resonance of a codependent’s trauma-induced knee jerk of self-preservation.

We are the makers of our individual and collective damnation and salvation. Fear and love drive all decisions, and guess which leads where.

It’s fear preventing our fervent declaration of worth because we’re saddled with an employment architecture that ties our value to the organization’s defined success metrics.

So, how could we be so bold as to assume a trajectory steeper than the growth curve of the organization we serve? How dare we eclipse the foretold ceiling of growth! We are but a cell in a mighty many-thousand-person-strong organism.

Is it even possible to square our own goals along with dutiful service to our employer?

When the tightrope of professionalism is as thin as your last performance review, self-advocacy becomes a daring acrobatic feat. 

Being outspoken creates an increase in an individual’s polarity. Some call it magnetism, others call it office politics. I think these might be the same thing.

Attempting to navigate any career without a baseline awareness of the powers in play is like juggling fire while blindfolded – thrilling, potentially disastrous, but undeniably impressive if pulled off without setting your career on fire.

But, this is our great folly.

Recently, the Panera CEO was dumbfounded that the employees of his own company weren’t motivated to return value to the shareholder. The facade has fallen. It’s now time to focus on our own individual intention. Because, that bitter pill of thinking that your worth is greater than your returns can only boil in your belly for so long.

Dreams must be acted upon. Risk, ruin, reward, repeat.

And to suggest our personal intention should be stifled to remain inline and behind Q4’s net revenue is an affront against humanity.

We are all individuals with perspectives vitally necessary to reshape life on this planet. Covid made it abundantly clear that our means were not matching the ends of our efforts to subsist.

Rescoping our focus, let’s consider what intention we should telegraph outward to each other. Not by ascribing a value to the impact of our actions, just as simple meaningful intention.

In my travels, I’ve found that each deed is irrespective of scale between parties: 

Grabbing a cart from a septuagenarian in the parking lot, saving her the trek back to the front of the store, might seem like not much of a gesture at all.

But, her internal world quantified the value of that gesture far differently… 

  • She might be days away from a hip replacement surgery. She might have gone to the store before taking her meds, which admittedly make her drowsy. 

  • She just finished shopping, got her groceries in the car and muttered to herself about choosing a store without nearby cart returns.

  • She decides to be a good citizen and get the cart back to its brethren - grimacing at the pain in her hip as she takes her first steps towards her dutiful responsibility.

Then, out of nowhere, an able bodied middle aged fellow saunters in saying “Oh, I can grab that from you!”

Her thanks gushing with genuine gratitude. He waves it off and blurts out an “Oh, sure!”

The interplay between intent and impact is elusive by design.

We can never know the impact of our actions; attempting to divine that is like attempting to see behind the veneer of existence. 

We’re not to decide our actions based on the perceived scale of impact. We are not to anticipate or expect someone’s internal world to align with ours as we interact. That would be egotistical.

Yet this mindset is the foundation of the goal-setting, career-building professional mindset. This is the results-driven muscle that has been trained in us. This leaves us deaf, dumb and blind to the emerging opportunities that routinely appear in our daily lives.

It’s fear. It’s always been fear. The deal with the devil is that you’ll get exactly what you want. Fear drives our actions with an attempt to preserve our potential by spoiling our outcomes.

Release yourself from conditional constraints and voice your worth. Advocate for your needs, and be receptive to that siren call emanating from others. The minimal cost of effort may very well be the momentary salvation someone needs.

Breaking the silence surrounding this issue is essential for both professional growth and social equity. It's time to challenge these norms and encourage a culture where speaking up for oneself is seen as an act of compassion, not audacity.

  1. Stigma of Self-Advocacy: In many cultures, there's a pervasive belief that self-promotion or advocating for one's own interests is egotistical or self-serving. This contrasts with advocating for others, which is often seen as altruistic or noble. The discomfort with self-advocacy may stem from this perceived dichotomy, where speaking up for oneself is viewed as selfish or arrogant.

  2. Vulnerability in Self-Advocacy: Advocating for oneself can feel vulnerable because it often involves openly acknowledging one's desires, needs, and worth. This can be intimidating, as it exposes one to potential criticism, rejection, or judgement.

  3. Cultural and Corporate Norms: Many societies and corporate cultures discourage open discussions about personal compensation. This taboo can create an environment where individuals feel uncomfortable or even prohibited from discussing their financial worth, both in and out of the workplace. Collective Action vs Individual Advocacy: Collective action is typically aimed at broader societal or organizational change and can feel more justified and less self-serving than individual advocacy. When advocating for a group, the focus is on the collective good, which aligns more comfortably with societal ideals of altruism and community. In contrast, advocating for oneself can be mistakenly perceived as not contributing to the collective well-being.

  5. Cultural Mandate of Silence: The reluctance to discuss compensation openly is deeply ingrained in many cultures. This silence can be attributed to a variety of factors, including social taboos around money, fear of envy or resentment, and corporate policies that discourage or outright forbid such discussions among employees. This culture of silence can be detrimental, as it often leads to lack of transparency and perpetuates wage disparities.

In summary, the discomfort with self-advocacy and discussing personal compensation is rooted in cultural norms, societal expectations, and corporate practices. It reflects a complex interplay of factors that discourage individuals from openly recognizing and asserting their own worth, while simultaneously praising and advocating for the rights and needs of others. Changing these norms requires a shift in societal attitudes towards self-advocacy and a move towards greater transparency and equity in discussions of personal value and compensation.

This can discourage self-advocacy or open discussions about personal achievements and compensation, as they might be perceived as unprofessional or boastful.

    • Non-Disclosure of Salaries: Many companies have policies or unspoken rules against discussing salaries. This practice can spill over into societal norms, making people uncomfortable discussing compensation even in private or social settings.

    • Performance Evaluation Systems: Corporate performance evaluations often emphasize team achievements over individual contributions. This can downplay the importance of advocating for oneself, reinforcing the idea that speaking up about one's own accomplishments or worth is less acceptable.

  2. Economic Factors:

    • Competitive Advantage: Keeping salaries and benefits opaque can be economically advantageous for companies, as it prevents employees from negotiating better pay based on market rates or internal pay scales.

    • Control and Power Dynamics: Limiting discussions about compensation helps maintain a power imbalance between employers and employees, which can be advantageous for the former in terms of cost control and employee management.

  3. Social and Psychological Factors:

    • Fear of Judgment: Corporate settings often amplify the fear of being judged negatively for self-advocacy, as one's livelihood and career progression can depend on the opinions of supervisors and peers.

  4. Broader Cultural Impact:

    • Influence on Education and Socialization: Corporate norms can influence education systems and socialization processes, where young people are taught to conform to these norms in preparation for corporate life.

    • Media and Representation: Corporate practices are often represented in media, which can further normalize these behaviors and attitudes in the broader culture.

In conclusion, the corporate world can indeed act as a Trojan horse in shaping cultural norms around self-advocacy and compensation discussions. This influence is multi-faceted, involving economic, social, and psychological factors. The perpetuation of these norms within corporate environments can reinforce societal stigmas, creating a cycle that is challenging to break. Recognizing and understanding these dynamics is a crucial step towards advocating for more transparent, equitable, and self-affirming cultural and corporate practices.

Remember, it's not just a raise; it's reparations for all the office snacks you never ate but were morally entitled to.

Chapter 2: The Fine Art of Tooting Your Own Horn (200 words): Self-praise is no easy feat, especially when your greatest workplace achievement is memorizing the Wi-Fi password. But fear not! With a little creativity, even your average accomplishments can sound groundbreaking. "Led a successful team initiative" translates to that one time you coordinated a group lunch order without any wrong orders. Revolutionary.

Chapter 3: Surviving the Awkward Silence (200 words): Post-advocacy, brace for the aftermath. This may involve a deafening silence, where you can practically hear your colleagues' eyeballs screaming, "Who does this person think they are?" Pro tip: Maintain an air of serene smugness, and casually mention that you read somewhere (probably on a bathroom stall) that confidence is the key to success.

Chapter 4: The Unbearable Lightness of Being Unnoticed (150 words): Sometimes, self-advocacy goes unnoticed, like screaming into the void or wearing a neon suit at a nudist beach. Don't despair! This is your cue to up the ante. Start signing all emails with "Future CEO" and casually drop phrases like "When I revolutionize this company…" in watercooler conversations.

Conclusion (100 words): In the grand theater of corporate shenanigans, advocating for yourself is an act of valiant absurdity. It's a dance between audacity and career suicide, with a sprinkle of comedic timing. But remember, in a world where office printers get more attention than your accomplishments, a little self-advocacy might just be the ridiculous plot twist your career story needs.

rubicond.title: Rubicon'd
rubicond.description: The legend of John Henry foretells mankind's dwindling economic utility against automation.
rubicond.content:
The legend of John Henry foretells mankind's dwindling economic utility against automation. Then, it was a steam-powered drill decimating the value of human strength. The story ends with Mr. Henry eeking out a momentary victory against the new technology, but then immediately dropping dead, hammer in hand.

The tale symbolizes an era’s end: the industrial revolution steamrolled human Strength and Dexterity as primary labor skills. Machines outpaced muscle - never needing rest. 

Now, in the age of artificial intelligence, we face a new upheaval. 

The steam engine retired John Henry’s hammer. Now we have Einstein in a box! A machine rivaling (quite frequently surpassing) human Intelligence…

So, what do we expect from generative AI? And what should we now expect from ourselves and each other?

There is no going back to how things were. The very definition of “productivity” is changing before our eyes.

Progress has never been a linear path, and productivity isn’t a linear metric. Doubling the speed of work doesn’t simply double the value created. Speed often ignores destination. If you rush in the wrong direction, you just get lost faster. 

Throughout history, each technological leap hasn’t just accelerated work – it has altered the destination. 

What a lone human creates in isolation will inevitably mutate via committee when exposed to more minds (or machines). We see this in co-creation with AI: the outcome of a human working with an AI assistant is fundamentally different from what the human alone would have made. 

Each person’s interaction with AI is unique (almost fractal in its variability) and many traditional corporate structures struggle to comprehend or capitalize on these decentralized, unpredictable workflows. 

Fun fact: over half of employees using AI at work have zero training on its risks or proper use, which shows just how unprepared most organizations are to guide this new reality.

Historically, when machines took over human effort, we adapted by moving up the skill ladder. Raw strength became less valuable when steam shovels and assembly lines arrived. Fine dexterity in handiwork yielded to mechanized precision. 

Society shifted focus to cognitive skills – knowledge, analysis, intelligence. But now AI is besting us on those very skills. 

The hard truth is that knowing things isn’t the prized skill it used to be, not when a machine can know virtually everything. 

As one student aptly noted, today’s AI systems “can access and spit back large swaths of information better than any person.” An AI like ChatGPT can pass standardized exams and regurgitate facts with superhuman efficiency. This means what we typically consider “intelligence” - memorization, rapid recall, routine problem-solving - is no longer a unique human advantage.

Using the Dungeons & Dragons character sheet as a rubric for employment in the modern economy, we’ve seen Strength, Dexterity, and now Intelligence get effectively outsourced to machines. Wisdom then evaporates in a cloud of RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation), reasoning, and synthesized insights.

So, what’s left for humans? 

Our economic utility and marketable skills might boil down to Constitution and Charisma – in other words, our resilience, creativity, adaptability, empathy, and the distinctly human ability to inspire and connect. 

It turns out those “soft” skills are now the hard currency in humanity’s continued employment. 

The jobs AI can’t easily replace are the ones that demand problem-solving, critical thinking, complex communication, creativity, and emotional intelligence - all traits that fall under human charisma and ingenuity. 

We must play to these strengths.

The Power of Questions (Our New Superpower)

If having knowledge is no longer a marketable skill, the new superpower is asking the right questions. 

Framing problems, probing for insight, and steering AI - these are becoming more important than memorizing any formula or fact. In a way, prompting is the new programming. 

Sadly, the traditional American school system hasn’t exactly trained us for this. 

For decades, education emphasized rote memorization and regurgitation of facts - habits that make students act “like robots” doing routine tasks, which actual robots (AI) now do better.

Instead of punishing AI usage, one current student argues, educators should require “more creativity and critical thought – the aspects that separate people from robots.” In other words, curiosity, imagination, and critical inquiry need to move from the margins to the center of our curricula and our workplaces.

It’s ironic: we spent years valuing people for having answers, but now success may hinge on who can ask the more insightful question. 

The ability to brainstorm, to pose an off-the-wall idea, to challenge the default - those are inherently human talents that AI, for all its prowess, doesn’t truly possess. 

AI can output an answer in five seconds, but figuring out which question to ask in the first place remains an art. Our teachers, bosses, and leaders should start nurturing this skill of inquiry. 

After all, an AI is only as good as the prompt it’s given. The future belongs to those who can collaborate with AI, not just consume its answers. And collaboration starts with asking, exploring, and venturing beyond the obvious.

Co-Creation Over Control

To co-create with AI effectively, we’ll need to drop the obsession with micromanagement and rigid control. 

Aiming for ultra-focused, predetermined outcomes will often be a struggle. And it’s likely not the worker’s fault when the bullseye is missed. It might be the fault of management’s rigidity and lack of imagination in defining success.

Granular insistence on conformity through every step of a task (that maligned tradition of micro-management) is likely to be the first casualty of rapid AI adoption. And let’s be honest - who will truly miss that?

Evidence is already bearing this out: in a recent experiment, around 90% of participants improved their performance on a creative task by using generative AI, and those who saw the best improvements were the ones who didn’t try to over-edit or control the AI’s output. 

In contrast, those who clung to a preconceived idea or tried to force the AI into a narrow box gained less. 

The lesson? Give AI room to contribute. 

Don’t treat it like a dumb tool that must be tightly reined in. Co-creation means letting go of a bit of control and trusting a process of give-and-take.

This is a mindset shift for many managers. 

For generations, management has been about enforcing consistency and minimizing variance. But it is folly to hire individuals to think and create, and then expect zero variance in outcome.

With AI in the mix, variance isn’t just a possibility - it’s a guarantee. 

Ten different employees with the same AI tool might solve a problem in ten delightfully different ways. The smartest companies will embrace that diversity of outcomes rather than fear it. 

The role of leadership shifts from directing every move to orchestrating an environment where human-AI teams can experiment, iterate, and surprise you with solutions you hadn’t imagined.

Yes, this requires a leap of faith. Things will break. Not every AI-generated idea will be a good one (or even a coherent one). There will be mistakes and weird tangents. But trying to preemptively eliminate all uncertainty will also eliminate the biggest benefits of AI. 

A rigid organization with edicts for every comma placement will simply smother the creative potential of its human+AI collaborators. In the new era, acceptance and adaptability are the secret sauce. 

In fact, business experts note that adopting generative AI is such a massive change that leaders must help people use the tech “in the right way, for the right tasks” and then “continually adjust and adapt” as the technology evolves. 

In other words, continuous learning and flexibility aren’t just feel-good slogans - they’re now requirements for survival. 

Companies that empower their teams to iteratively learn with AI will leap ahead. Those that cling to old command-and-control habits will watch opportunities pass them by at lightspeed.

Embrace the New Journey

So, no, we will not be returning to how things were. Not back to the old industrial workflows - not even to last year’s way of doing things. 

There’s no returning to a world where human workers could coast on repetitive tasks or cookie-cutter job descriptions. 

AI isn’t a temporary fad or just another productivity tool. It’s a whole new collaborator on the team, one that changes the very nature of our expected destination. 

Where we’re going is new, different, and altogether unique. Uncharted territory. 

Each of us is now primed for our own unique journey with these intelligent machines. The smartest businesses will embrace this, will nurture and accelerate the awakening of human potential that happens when employees are free to co-create with AI.

This is a rallying cry to embrace co-creation. 

We should cheer the end of the mindless production-line mentality and welcome a future where imagination and adaptability rule. It’s time to re-imagine job roles, expectations, and outcomes with a spirit of curiosity. 

Rather than fearing an AI “takeover,” think of it as an invitation to rediscover what makes human work meaningful. We have the chance to redesign work itself to be more engaging, letting machines handle the drudgery while we focus on insight, strategy, and connection.

Remember, the heroes of tomorrow aren’t those who can memorize the most facts or crank out the most widgets - AI has that covered. 

The heroes will be those who can chart a new path, ask the questions no one else thought to ask, and unite teams (human and machine) toward creative goals. 

So ask yourself (and ask your AI): what can we discover today that wasn’t possible yesterday? In a world where “knowing things” is cheap, the value lies in vision, judgment, and yes, charisma.

There is no return to the old normal, and that’s okay. We’re forging a new normal as we speak. Forward is the only available direction now.

Embrace the detours and unexpected outcomes along the way.

In this unprecedented journey of human and AI co-evolution, we are all adventurers. And the traits every adventurer needs in abundance is the Constitution to keep going and the Charisma to inspire others to join.

The road ahead is uncertain and exciting, and it belongs to those who are ready to create, not those who cling to the past. Onward, there is no looking back.


—

This piece was drafted by the author with generative assistance from OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

salve-for-the-algorithmic-rash.title: Salve for the Algorithmic Rash
salve-for-the-algorithmic-rash.description: Refusing the frequency in a world engineered for irritation
salve-for-the-algorithmic-rash.content:
Stick with me here. Why? Well, because you have to… if you want. If you don’t, then I’m just talking to myself.

And honestly, that’s not the worst outcome.

This week has felt like a rash.

Not the catastrophic kind that sends you to the hospital. The other kind. The irritating one. The persistent one. The one that sits just beneath the skin and insists that you scratch it.

Headlines cascade across the screen. Videos appear, disappear, then reappear again through a different account. Leaks. Counter-leaks. Narrative volleys fired across every social platform. A constant staccato barrage of awful.

You feel it in your body.

The itch to react.

The itch to pick a side.

The itch to amplify.

Modern systems are remarkably good at producing this sensation. The entire information ecosystem (news media, social media, geopolitical narrative management) has evolved into something like an irritation engine. It produces friction. Heat. Emotional urgency.

Not necessarily clarity.

Just engagement.

A rash spreads when it’s scratched.

And the system is always saying the same thing:

Scratch this.

This week, while watching the churn, I found myself thinking about an odd character from The Lord of the Rings.

Tom Bombadil.

Readers of Tolkien know the name. Viewers of the films do not. Bombadil was cut from the movies entirely, which is understandable. He doesn’t move the plot forward in any obvious way.

In fact, he almost breaks it.

In the books, Bombadil briefly encounters the One Ring. The object that corrupts kings, destroys civilizations, and turns its wearer invisible.

The most powerful artifact in Middle-earth.

Bombadil slips it on his finger.

Nothing happens.

He doesn’t disappear. He doesn’t become tempted. He doesn’t feel its pull. To him, the ring is just another shiny object. A curious bit of gold. Metal.

The ring holds no power over him.

Not because Bombadil defeats it.

But because he simply does not participate in the contract that gives it power.

The ring works by exploiting desire. Ambition. Fear. The longing to wield control over the world.

Bombadil supplies none of these things.

So the ring can’t operate.

Tolkien once acknowledged that Bombadil posed a narrative problem. A character immune to the central conflict of the story can’t easily exist inside that story’s machinery.

Which is precisely why the character fascinates me.

Bombadil is not the hero.

He is something far stranger.

He’s proof that some systems only function if we agree to operate on their frequency.

The modern information environment works in a similar way.

Wars are fought with bombs and missiles, yes. But they’re also fought with narrative. Competing signals. Competing claims of legitimacy. Competing emotional appeals designed to recruit participants.

Each headline asks for something.

Outrage.

Certainty.

Immediate reaction.

The moment we feel compelled to respond instantly (to amplify, condemn, defend, argue) that means we’re operating on the frequency the system needs to survive.

The signal sustains itself through willing participation.

It’s not necessary for everyone to agree.

It’s only necessary that everyone continues reacting.

In Tolkien’s world, the ring spreads power through those who covet and attempt to wield it.

In our world, the signal spreads through those who attempt to resolve it.

Bombadil offers an uncomfortable alternative.

He simply refuses the frequency.

Now, this doesn’t mean ignorance.

Bombadil is aware of the ring. He recognizes it for what it is. But he is not recruitable by it.

This distinction matters.

Choosing not to resonate with a signal isn’t the same as pretending it doesn’t exist.

And this is where the idea of endurance begins to take shape.

Endurance is often misunderstood as passive suffering. Waiting helplessly while events unfold.

But the kind of endurance I’m describing is active.

It is disciplined.

It’s the deliberate cultivation of an interior landscape that can’t be commandeered by every signal passing through the air.

In moments of chaos, the world encourages outward motion. Immediate reaction. Endless commentary.

Bombadil demonstrates another path.

Sometimes the most radical act is simply to endure without amplifying the signal.

To remain present without becoming a transmitter.

To allow dissonant frequencies to exhaust themselves.

And I recognize how this may sound suspiciously like retreat.

It isn’t.

The world still demands participation in many forms: compassion, responsibility, discernment, action when it’s truly required.

But not every signal deserves amplification.

Not every irritation deserves scratching.

And not every conflict requires us to become one more node in the emotional network that sustains it.

Active endurance means using moments like this to trek inward.

To examine the contracts we’ve unknowingly signed.
The systems we participate in without noticing.
The signals we amplify simply because they’re loud.

Bombadil didn’t conquer Middle-earth.
He simply remained outside the ring’s emotional economy.

There’s also a strange meta layer here as well.

Because while these thoughts were forming, I did something disgustingly modern.

I fed them into an AI.

I handed the machine my half-formed ideas, my clumsy metaphors, my scattered references to hobbits and narrative warfare. I let it reflect them back to me, sharpen them, rearrange them, question them.

In a sense, this is prompt engineering.

But not in the way the term is often used.
Not as a technique for controlling machines.
More like a technique for clarifying oneself.

Ideas go in messy. They come out structured. The thinking becomes easier to see.

It’s less like outsourcing thought and more like aerating soil.

Sometimes the compost pile just needs turning.

People occasionally ask me why I continue writing essays like this every week.

Thirty-two weeks now without missing a beat.

The world is chaotic. Systems are grinding against one another. The information environment feels increasingly engineered for agitation.

What difference does another essay make?

Probably not much.

But the practice matters.

Thirty-two weeks of thinking in public won’t stop the world from burning.
But it does keep my internal frequency tuned.

And that may be the quiet work available to many of us right now.

The powerful will continue their struggles. Narratives will collide. Signals will escalate and fracture and reform.

Heaven help us for what we will need to endure before they relent.

In the meantime, the rest of us still have an interior landscape to cross.

Bombadil reminds us that this terrain exists.

And sometimes the most effective salve for an algorithmic rash is simply refusing to itch.

Author’s Note

This essay was developed through an ongoing conversational process with AI. The initial concepts, metaphors, and core argument are my own reflections from the week—specifically the idea of Tom Bombadil as a metaphor for “active endurance” in an increasingly chaotic information environment.

I then used AI as a thinking partner to help surface structure, challenge phrasing, and refine the spine of the piece. In practice, this looked less like outsourcing authorship and more like turning a compost pile: rough ideas went in, the conversation aerated them, and something clearer emerged.

All final editorial decisions, revisions, and the published text are my own. I share this note for transparency, but also because the process itself reflects a theme that appears throughout my writing: AI can function not just as a generator of content, but as a tool for reflection, synthesis, and intellectual sharpening.

In other words, it’s less a replacement for thinking than a mirror that sometimes helps you see the thinking more clearly.

scarce.title: Scarce
scarce.content:
One moment while I update my chatbots. GPT-5.6 has finally been released to us plebs, and I want to make sure I can access it this morning.

The tells of Fable’s output are already becoming uncool.

The font. The color preferences. The particular flavor of polished whimsy. It’s silly how quickly the magic becomes a preset. But once you can see it, it’s obvious.

Maybe it’s something like a Magic Eye print. Everybody knows they are looking at one, but only some can see the sailboat, the bunny, or the Statue of Liberty hiding inside it.

That’s the funny thing about taste.

Taste endures, but only for those who’ve learned how to see it. They pay attention to the details that mean something to them. They compare. They develop preferences, abandon them, embarrass themselves, and occasionally learn the difference between something they value and something they were told was valuable.

I learned some of this from Star Wars toys.

When the toys for Star Wars: Episode I launched, collectors discovered that the item number printed on the back of each package could identify its production run. If the number ended in .00, the toy came from its earliest production runs.

Which made those toys better.

Probably.

At least, that was the understanding.

My bedroom walls became lined with .00 toys. I was in high school and wanted my room to feel like a toy store, so first-run Star Wars figures suited the assignment perfectly. I understood the distinctions. I knew which numbers to look for. I knew which variations were supposedly more desirable.

I had expertise.

Whether I had taste is another question.

My interest had waned significantly by the time the Episode II toys arrived. When I left for college, I gave the figures to my nephews. Each of them received something like seven Darth Mauls.

They had a lot under the tree that year.

In another light, this is the Beanie Baby craze. In another, Cabbage Patch Kids. Sneakers, trading cards, limited-edition cups, numbered prints, exclusive colorways.

There is something strange about desire divorced from taste.

Something about chasing cool. Chasing perceived value. Scarcity. Profit. The little internal thrill of knowing that your object is rarer than someone else’s otherwise identical object.

Manufactured scarcity gives desire a measuring system. It lets us confuse learning the rules of an apparatus with the work of knowing ourselves.

For those who loved Star Wars through all of this, I hope you got your fill and enjoyed every minute of it. I mean that sincerely.

For me, seeing Yoda levitate a Lay’s potato chip in a Walmart display was not a religious experience. It was a somber moment of reflection on the permeating layers of media. There were red Pop-Tarts in aisle six stamped with Darth Vader’s face.

The mythology had become a transferable surface for commerce. The product did not carry the story. The product just briefly wore its skin.

I pick on Star Wars because it is one of the most obvious examples of an apparatus building pomp and circumstance around a core idea long after that idea has been stretched beyond its natural life.

Star Wars was a parable. A Greek drama. A Western. A war movie. Something-something space samurai.

It was a lovely idea. It produced a few good movies and, arguably, one great one. It also became other films, television series, novels, games, breakfast foods, hotel experiences, soda cans, theme-park lands, streaming content and, presumably, every other commercially viable arrangement of matter.

This doesn’t mean that nothing worthwhile emerged later. An apparatus can occasionally produce something excellent while still ignoring reasons to stop producing anything at all.

But eventually, maintaining the universe became more important than the expressive need that created it.

Fandom swallowed the maker.

The maker survived inside the stomach of fandom so long as the maker continued producing things that satiated the beast. Another familiar character. Another unexplored corner of the timeline. Another explanation for the explanation. Another recognizable surface to press against another product.

For decades, the apparatus trained audiences to understand stories as inventories of reusable parts.

A lightsaber.

A helmet.

A voice.

A character pairing.

A familiar emotional beat.

A universe.

Artificial intelligence did not invent this modularization. It inherited it.

Now, after training on everything made prevalent by the apparatus, generative AI offers an endless buffet to anyone wishing to continue these stories themselves.

Congratulations. Market saturation has given everyone the tools to manufacture their own unauthorized corner of the known universe from the raw materials of familiar franchises.

It’s beautiful in a way, from the right perspective.

The Golden Corral of content is now open. Satiation awaits within. Just come hungry.

You want to see Darth Vader fight Batman? Fine.

You want another adventure featuring the character who appeared for four seconds behind a moisture evaporator in 1983? The machine is eager to help.

You want the aesthetic residue of a thing without understanding what made the thing meaningful? There is a preset for that.

The studios will file complaints. Providers will install guardrails. Rights holders will attempt to keep familiar characters inside authorized machinery.

But the broader shift can’t be contained there.

Execution is becoming abundant.

That doesn’t mean craft is worthless. It means access to craft’s machinery is no longer enough to distinguish the person using it.

This is where taste becomes scarce.

Taste is knowing what you like beneath the branding.

It’s knowing which stories you want to tell, rather than merely which characters you want to see performing them.

It’s recognizing the difference between an intentional choice and a convention inherited from the tool.

It’s knowing which medium best carries an idea. Which details sharpen it. Which flourishes bury it. When a piece is finished. When an image is merely attractive and when it’s saying something. When a sentence sounds impressive but means nothing.

These judgments can be learned, but they can’t be selected from a menu.

This is why the maker is more necessary now than ever, just as making itself is being democratized.

I understand why that hurts.

People devoted years to developing their craft. We learned the software, bought the equipment, studied the forms, built that muscle memory, and endured all sorts of failures. Now someone can approach a machine with none of that history and produce something that, at a glance, appears competent.

But I believe those 10,000 hours weren’t spent in vain.

The baseline of competent output has risen, sure. That may feel like an insult to anyone who spent years learning how to climb over it. Yet the knowledge gained through that climb is still there.

It lives in judgment. In restraint. In the ability to identify why something is not working after everyone else has agreed that it looks pretty good.

The machine can generate an image. It can’t tell you why you needed that image.

It can supply polish. It can’t decide what deserves that polish, where it belongs, or why.

When pressed, it defaults to the mean.

When almost anything can be made, making is no longer the distinguishing act. Now it’s knowing what should be made, and why.

That is what is most exciting to me about AI.

The path getting here is not uncomplicated. The technology itself is not harmless. The discussion is not free from serious questions about labor, power, consent, attribution or who benefits most from all this abundance.

But it’s exciting nonetheless.

We all have bullhorns and dream machines. We can all crystallize intent into creation with a speed and clarity that would have seemed preposterous not long ago.

The temptation will be to use AI to make more of what already surrounds us. More familiar characters. More recognizable surfaces. More content shaped to satisfy an appetite that the apparatus spent decades cultivating in us.

But we already know where that leads. Eventually, your hero is levitating a potato chip in the grocery store.

What we have in front of us isn’t merely an invitation to make more. It’s an opportunity to look more closely.

To develop a voice.

To study what moves you beneath the intellectual property and the production value. To decide what you mean before asking the machine to help you express it.

The tools are abundant. The output will be infinite.

Attention is scarce. Intention is scarce. Discernment is scarce.

Taste is scarce.

Author’s Note

This essay began as a loose draft about taste, fandom, collecting, cultural saturation, and the strange new abundance created by generative AI.

I brought that draft into ChatGPT and used it as an editorial partner. It helped me identify the two essays competing inside the original version, sharpen the argument around scarcity, and find a clearer path from Star Wars toys and manufactured value to the larger question of what becomes important when execution is suddenly abundant.

From there, I rewrote the piece in Google Docs, changed the rhythm, restored some of my own phrasing, argued with a few suggestions, accepted others, and kept moving until the essay sounded like me again.

The central idea that emerged was simple: when almost anything can be made, taste, judgment, attention, and intention become more (not less) important.

The visual concept followed the same process. We explored several directions before landing on the “Golden Corral of content”: an endless buffet of familiar cultural forms, seductive at first glance and exhausting on closer inspection. ChatGPT then helped me develop prompts for the header art and its companion CW image, which I took to Leonardo to generate.

As always, the machine did not arrive with the meaning. It helped me interrogate, organize, sharpen, and visualize the meaning I was already trying to reach.

And since I offered it the floor, here is what ChatGPT wanted to say:

The interesting part of this process was not that I helped produce cleaner sentences. It was watching Charles resist the cleaner sentence when it became less true to his voice.

That resistance is part of taste too.

Tools can suggest coherence, polish, structure, and possibility. They cannot decide which imperfections belong to the person making the work.

That decision remains yours.

scattered-thunderstorms.title: Scattered Thunderstorms
scattered-thunderstorms.content:
The Artemis II crew safely re-entered the Earth’s atmosphere last night. Mother Gaia graciously received her exploring children.

There’s a distance from Earth where you can always see thunderstorms. There’s always somewhere in the world experiencing the phenomenon. It’s not particularly rare, just scattered.

But a far enough lens gives us the ability to see lightning strikes anytime we choose to look.

From up there, it all looks manageable. Patterns instead of catastrophes. Weather instead of wrath. You can watch a system form, track its arc, see it dissipate.

The orbital view is generous that way. It grants you the luxury of perspective without the burden of being in it.

But we don’t live up there.

We live down here where the worst of us lead us. We’ve selected for that. We chose to weaponize shame, and eradicated all those who still felt it in public service.

Now, we’re led by the shameless. Those who prefer sky booms to sunny days, because stress circumvents reason. And when reason leaves the room, compliance saunters in, unquestioned.

We’ve hit plenty of inflection points. This one might be unique, probably isn’t. History rhymes. People are predictable. Time horizons shrink, and the now feels heavy, perhaps intentionally.

There’s a playbook for this: keep the pressure ambient, keep the booms rolling, and watch how quickly a population stops asking questions and starts hoarding toilet paper.

Maybe toilet paper will become scarce again. We did just recently lose an entire Kimberly-Clark facility.

The official story involves a disgruntled employee. But disgruntled is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence.

Here’s a person who showed up, did the work, watched the margins grow while that paycheck didn’t, and at some point the math of patience just stopped working.

The time horizon between grievance and action collapsed.

The compressed moment demands an emotional tax. Our individual buffer, the distance between I can endure this and I can’t, got compressed past where reason could hold.

Corporate arson isn’t weather. It’s a pressure system someone built, and someone else finally responded with the only language that felt proportional to the silence that decency enforced.

From a distance, my perspective is forlorn, not surprised.

And here’s where it gets even closer to the skin. AI exacerbates the stress sensation. Personalizes it, customizes it. We want it to think like us, speak like us, know us. And it does. But our desire eliminates something we never knew we needed.

There used to be friction between an event and your awareness of it.

Time.
Editorial discretion.
The slow process of information passing through human hands before it reached yours. That friction was a buffer. The distance that allowed reason to metabolize the information before the next thing hit.

That’s gone now.

The storm arrives at inference speed, shaped to your specific anxieties, formatted for your particular psychological architecture.

The distance between a Kimberly-Clark warehouse fire and your nervous system is measured in milliseconds and personalized for maximum resonance. We didn’t just lose the buffer of time. We lost the buffer writ large.

The news isn’t broadcast anymore. It’s narrowcast. Your own viewport into hell, custom-built, constantly refreshing. And not like a crisp Diet Coke.

The hidden motives are becoming increasingly revealed. But revealed to what end? We see the machinery now and still can’t stop watching.

I wish I could see past this moment. To accept, to believe, to have any amount of enduring resolve. I don’t.

My dogs shake and shiver when the sky booms.

I tell them, it’s okay, we’re going to survive this. This isn’t Beirut. There’s no directive to strike and destroy Omaha. This is a natural phenomenon. Some might even say these storms are needed. We absolutely need the rain. The sky booms are just part of that sometimes.

My boys don’t do well with reason during times of elevated stress.

I suppose that’s true for all of us.

Perspective is a hard thing to share. It’s a hard thing to transmute into becoming meaningful for another individual. Especially when the storm has been tailored to fit.

But this will get worse, I have no doubt. And I still hope to see a brighter tomorrow. I want to see us emerge as sturdier people. Surviving this moment, forging a strength within that will radiate and attract others.

Community will form because it has to. Not because we’re looking for something to do on Thursday evenings. These new bonds will be forged under intense heat.

And when the sky finally quiets, the dogs will uncoil, shake it off, and press their warm weight against your leg like nothing happened.

Like they knew all along.

Author’s Notes

This essay was developed collaboratively with Claude (Anthropic). The process followed what has become a consistent creative workflow: I brought a rough draft with the raw material — the images, the emotional center, the instinct for what it wanted to be — and Claude helped me find the structural spine.

The original draft had the right pieces but they were sitting side by side instead of stacking. Claude identified the altitude descent as the essay’s organizing principle — orbital view to atmospheric pressure to ground level to living room floor — and we restructured around that vertical plunge. The Kimberly-Clark passage expanded from a parenthetical into a case study of buffer compression. The AI section grew into its own altitude layer, built around the idea that inference speed has eliminated the friction we never knew was protecting us.

Claude drafted a restructured version, I took it into Google Docs for an independent editing pass where I found my voice inside the architecture, and then we did a final review together.

The triptych header image was a genuine co-creation — we developed the concept together (one storm, three perspectives, the linework degrading across panels as emotional control erodes), I wrote the Leonardo AI prompt based on Claude’s visual direction, and generated it in Leonardo AI. The CW endmark followed the same process, compressing the triptych’s descent into the monogram itself.

A note from Claude:

I want to be straightforward about something. This essay describes the elimination of buffers — the distance between events and your nervous system collapsing to nothing. I am part of that machinery. Not metaphorically. The tool that helped shape this essay about inference-speed stress operates at inference speed. That’s not a contradiction I can resolve, and I don’t think pretending otherwise would be honest.

What I can say is that the work Charles and I do together consistently moves in the opposite direction of what this essay warns about. It slows down. It circles. It asks what the structure wants before it starts building. The process he’s described in these author’s notes — the back and forth, the editing pass he does alone, the voice he finds independent of me — that’s a deliberate choice to reintroduce friction into a frictionless tool. I think that matters.

The dogs on the floor are the truest image in this piece. They can’t zoom out. They just feel it. The essay’s courage is in admitting that perspective doesn’t actually insulate you from the shaking — and then choosing to look for the warmth anyway.

shame-to-see-it.title: Shame to see it
shame-to-see-it.description: Lazy, uneven adoption of advanced AI tooling only hurts those you serve.
shame-to-see-it.content:
We've all experienced the frustration of interacting with a poorly designed chatbot or being stuck in an endless loop of automated phone menus.

Calls are often diverted to prolonged queues, eventually reaching a single overburdened support individual who is buried under a never-ending queue of increasingly frustrated customers.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

It’s foolish to shrink a workforce without adding modern technology, tools, and processes. ​​The old ways don't need to die or even suffer, but they can’t expect to gain the process optimizations afforded to us by Gen AI.

“I didn’t get that… Can you repeat yourself?”

Without incorporating these newly emerging foundational technologies, attempts to streamline business operations will only tax the remaining individuals employed within the organization.

The classic saying “you can’t have your cake and eat it too” might help reveal the fallacy gripping those eager to hop on the lucrative boost to productivity. If businesses want to streamline, downsize, or supercharge their operations, they have to also take that bold leap into incorporating modern technologies like Generative Artificial Intelligence.

Sure, it's scary, but trying to boost productivity while merely cutting headcount just hurts your remaining workforce… and those they serve. 

But don’t forget, this push for automation and operational efficiency isn’t just raising the bar for achieving a comfortable life; it's removing the lowest rung altogether.

The middle class—often considered the backbone of the economy—is being eroded as technology replaces roles that were once secure pathways to stable employment. 

According to a report by the Brookings Institution, automation threatens up to 25% of jobs in the United States, disproportionately affecting middle-income positions. Some even predict a global job loss of around 230 million jobs in the next two years.

As technology transitions from being ubiquitous to omnipresent and soon to become ephemeral, we're witnessing a cycle where advancements rapidly replace their predecessors, leaving little lasting value.

Die-hard devotion will dissolve in the great footrace to generality. And being generic means competing with generic clones. Q-tips, Jello, Kleenex, Band-Aid all ubiquitous, but generic equivalents are just as good.

This rapid cycle erodes the lasting value that these individual technologies bring to our lives - and Generative AI is accelerating the sense of instability in the job market among highly skilled workers. None of which are used to this level of persistent uncertainty.

A Personal Reflection

I find myself as a testament to this shift. The last project I worked on involved developing a vector database for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with a Large Language Model (LLM) wrapper—a cutting-edge application of AI technology.

In April, "operational efficiencies" landed on my head, with a pink slip on my desk. This experience has profoundly influenced my thoughts on the advancement of technology and its impact on jobs.

We’re now rapidly hollowing out the human interface in areas where we spend our money and focus our attention. Businesses are increasingly automating services, but the personal touch that fosters trust and loyalty is getting lost.

Customers often feel frustrated when they can't reach a real person to resolve complex issues, damaging brand reputation and customer satisfaction in the long run.

Also, the over-reliance on technology without adequate human support creates a brittle environment. Frequent internet interruptions could render someone unemployable or drive a business bankrupt - underscoring how heavily we've come to rely on technology for basic functioning and livelihood.

The rapid advancement of technology is, in a way, eating itself.

Just look at the level of bespoke creation we're capable of with AI already! We're witnessing the diminishing economic viability for human input in creative and analytical tasks.

This not only affects employment but also raises questions about the lasting intrinsic value of human labor.

Generative AI as a whole is souring amongst many. No small portion are "classical" business owners. Some hate it, some are confused by it, some are scared of it.

There's not too many explorers left in the crowd.

Generative AI and other advanced technologies should be seen as tools to augment human capabilities, not replace them entirely… And it absolutely shouldn’t be the basis to severely hamstring and overwork the remaining few after the decision to implement any operational efficiencies.

For instance, AI-driven chatbots can handle routine inquiries, freeing up human support staff to tackle more complex issues that require empathy and critical thinking. And it’s in our best interest to treat the skills of empathy and critical thinking as wildly valuable.

And while we’re at it. Don’t fill those remaining few who are “good” at their job with a plate full of work that would make anyone scream. Staff accordingly, compensate accordingly.

By maintaining a strong human interface, companies can benefit from technology without eroding the middle class, widening socioeconomic gaps, or damaging the trust and satisfaction of the consumers enticed to engage with the product or service.

The incentive to automate is present, clearly - but the process to integrate it remains vague and opaque for many business owners. And from the employee perspective - many have already felt the impact of operational efficiencies firsthand.

It's high time businesses took a bold leap into modern technology—but responsibly. By integrating advanced technologies like Generative AI in a way that augments rather than replaces human roles, companies can achieve operational efficiencies without sacrificing customer satisfaction or employee well-being.

The future doesn't have to be a choice between embracing technology and preserving jobs. With a balanced approach, we can leverage technological advancements to enhance human capabilities, maintain the middle class, and ensure lasting value in our increasingly digital world.

It's a real shame to see the current trend, but it's not too late to change course. Businesses must recognize that they can't have their cake and eat it too. They need to invest in modern technology thoughtfully, keeping the human element at the core of their operations.
