Title: The copyright honor system

I believe the greatest folly to befall creativity as a product is to deny copyright for AI assisted works.

Sure, I’ve got skin in the game. Sure, I continue to explore the sensation of co-authorship. But the truth of the matter is there’s no policing this. No documenting this. And worse, no recourse. People will lie and the process to unravel that lie is costly and time consuming.

Our system of distributing copyright is far too cumbersome to accommodate investigating each claim of, “Nope, no AI here! All me!” I’m one of those crazy fools that holds a copyright. It’s on a short film from 2017. It’s a fine piece of silly, worth of copyright, but honestly, who’s to say?

Carpenters would immediately lose their motivation trying to slap nails into wood with their hands. Not to mention the massive hit to productivity.

To create is to use a medium. And to say a medium by its nature is plagiarism, is alarmist, impossibly false, and wildly myopic.

My voice comes from my experiences, but it also comes from the media I’ve digested. We’re all collages, we’re all pieced together by circumstance and cognition. Our fractured selves are in turn fractured pieces of the whole of humanity.

We are the dataset for AI. We are the originators of the dreams and ideas constituting the training data within any generative AI model. We are what we eat. So is AI.

These lawsuits demanding the wholesale destruction of the Generative Pre-trained Transformer technology is an affront to the collective benefit, and a foolishly selfish brandishing of cards held by the player levying the accusation.

The cannibalism of ideas and angles for news stories run rampant throughout all of journalism’s history. Just ask William Randolph Hearst.

The New York Times is no pure deity of divine news distribution. I’ve worked in news rooms. I recognize news orgs for what they are, chaotic rooms filled with budding rebels and icons desperately seeking their tribe. Some have vendettas, I know I had a few. But there’s no sanctity in the process or the product from any news outlet.

It’s good this reckoning is happening. We don’t need aggregators of reality to tell us what’s important. We’ve got better tools now. Tools that can sing to us, paint us pictures, tell us bedtimes stories, and wake us with the information most pertinent to our own productivity for our dawning day ahead.

No leading headlines, no salacious gossip, no ads, no spin. We can all collectively take a deep breath.

But to call the output from the very leading prompts in the legal brief as a form of wholesale reproduction is like blaming Xerox from faithfully recreating what it’s told to look at.

I believe deep down that we’re struggling with the very concept of creativity and what it can become. We’re revealing an old guard hiding behind talent, opportunity and industry to gate-keep the collective realization that our own ideas are worth exploring and sharing. And to do so in forms that take shape beyond grumbling internal monologues.

We’re in a creative revolution, just as we are a news and information revolution.

The tools available to all can manifest our ideas into concrete, actionable and shareable representations. All while our material sciences, healthcare, customer service and education will strengthen, atomize and materialize into a beautiful patchwork of passions.

We’re not all the same, we weren’t meant to be. And now we don’t need what we needed before.

taste-the-toil.title: Taste the toil
taste-the-toil.content:
For most of my life, I’ve tried to create things of value. More specifically, things that the marketplace (of ideas, or just capitalism) would consider valuable.

I was never told to consider speaking to my concept of value. Not through school, not through work, the job market, the media landscape. Nowhere was a single sign post asking me to pause and consider what it all meant to me.

The value was purely externalized.

And that was “just how it is” for my life. I was raised in a system that forced me to focus-test ideas. Stress-test the market. Send samples, beg for attention. Hope for virality.

Of course this was exhausting. Of course this was demoralizing. And worst of all, it was homogenizing. Averaging, dulling. Rounded edges, palatability.

Fucking annoying, if I’m being honest.

I’m 43 now. Currently, as I type. I’m 43 years old. Old enough to know a world without cell phones or the internet. I watched the novelty of those new inventions creep into that mundane, averaged world.

Each ringing their own klaxon. Each barely nudging the apparatus forward.

In 2008, during the writers’ strike, I moved to Los Angeles. Hollywood was at a standstill as I unloaded the truck.

Remarkably, I landed an unpaid internship at Maverick.

Since production was at a standstill, I helped clean up their offices and prepare for the dissolution of Guy Oseary’s stake in the company. Divorce the music (i.e. Madonna, Alanis Morrisette) from the film division (Agent Cody Banks, Twilight, The Stepfather).

The most exciting part of my day was eating my sack lunch in the parking structure as I looked out on Nakatomi Plaza (the Fox building).

Things picked up, and the strike inevitably resolved. The crux of the holdout was Hollywood’s production-apparatus feigning a lack of familiarity with the monetization strategy of the internet, and lo, was reluctant to pay writers for the proceeds of newly emerging streaming platforms like Hulu.

I recall the line, something like: “It’s too new, we just don’t know yet.”

At its heart, the strike boiled down to a fight over who got paid when the apparatus met a new tool.

Sounds remarkably similar to our current confrontation with AI.

And the irony of AI, especially when used in a creative sense, is how easily it replicates the norm, the average, the rounded corners of consumer palatability.

It’s easy to understand why. AI trains on the available, the prevalent.

Some creatives have succeeded quite well in the system that fed the aparatus. They are among the loudest to criticize the use of AI.

I get that, and they are free to continue tossing their barbs.

I performed on the boundaries of media production for 20 years. Never too close to full control, a dutiful rower in the apparatus as it stood. I just liked making cool stuff. And the boundaries of normal were cool enough for a younger me.

Now? I prefer to derive value from within myself. Metrics that were used to define my success just don’t enter my mind as valuable indicators anymore.

AI gives me an outlet for grief that, up until now, had no ritual. The apparatus never offered one that meant anything to me. It was focused on the business of palatability.

Now, I prefer the toil. The struggle of pushing the output of these AI tools past passable, driving them as deep as I can into meaningful. Meaningful for me, and me alone.

And I think that’s exactly what we all must do now. Passable is table stakes. Passable is default. We can sneeze at an image generation model and land with something adhering to basic art conventions, color theory, framing, etc.

But what does it mean for you? What does it mean for me?

My toil started long ago. Maybe that’s why I’m so comfortable with the discomfort of AI helping me craft my message now.

Those who grew fat on the averaged success of the media apparatus are understandably annoyed with the toil required to dazzle with these new tools, new tricks.

I’d weep for them if I wasn’t rooting for the downfall of the entire media system. Rooting for their uncomfortable return to the toil.

And honestly, could my weekly writing ritual truly destroy all that is beautiful?

If you don’t mind, I’ll just stand on the boundaries and think my silly thoughts.

At least I find value in that.
And that’s enough for me.

Author’s note:

I drafted this essay on a Saturday morning, then worked through structure and pacing with Claude. This type of back-and-forth I’ve taken to calling intellectual patty cake.

From there I edited independently in Google Docs and brought it back to Claude for a final review pass.

terminal-uniqueness.title: Terminal Uniqueness
terminal-uniqueness.description: Our superpower. Our eternal wellspring in the AI age.
terminal-uniqueness.content:
For most, if not all of the history of fame as a concept, envy’s been the engine.
We see someone adored, and we want to recreate their life.
The spotlight, the glow.

But fame isn’t free.
Adoration always brings along scrutiny. And scorn.

So maybe now’s a good time to step back and survey the value of our own terminal uniqueness as Taylor Swift puts it.
The part of us that can’t be copied cleanly.

A single eye can only see in two dimensions. Add another, and you get depth.
That’s perspective.

And sure, that’s the thing that keeps us from walking into walls. But we’re all now a part of something bigger, weirder. Not just in time and space, but signal and noise. We define our frequency individually and collectively.

We are a hive mind, a web, a cluster of nodes; all humming with human reasoning, biases, and borrowed insights.

And that’s never been clearer than now, with AI flooding the marketplace.

We’ve spent lifetimes attempting to mimic what we admire. Then, when a machine mimics us, we recoil.
That’s the Uncanny Valley: not fear of the machine, but fear of the mimic.

Sure, we see it in robotics, in embodied AI, in the race to build androids that “pass.” But maybe that gut reaction isn’t about them at all.
Maybe it’s our way of recognizing ourselves, reflected just a little too perfectly.

And AI’s good at that. Too good, sometimes.

Just ask Sora 2, or any voice model that can catch your exact sigh in three sentences flat.

So yeah, we should reclaim our POV. It’s more than just our perspective, it’s our goldmine. Because that’s what it is: endlessly renewable, stubbornly personal, gloriously human.

If we wire things right, we can build systems that amplify us all. We can then all choose to dismiss the existing machinations that flatten our worth into a rote consumer class.

But doing this takes faith… and faith isn’t exactly trending right now.

Because at this moment, we’re all living in one of two AI timelines:
The headlines, where models ace PhD exams. And the day-to-day, where the apps on our desks feel like petulant high schoolers still figuring it out.

That gap between what’s promised and what’s felt? That’s where these two stories split.

The optimists see progress. The skeptics see vapor.
And honestly? Both are right.

None of us grew up filling every Scantron test bubble correctly, we got plenty wrong along the way.
We love to imagine machines as flawless, but errors exist in every system.

We still eat at restaurants.
And yeah, sometimes we go home with food poisoning.

To err is human.
To forgive? Divine.
To find errors and keep building anyway; that’s the real trick.

Because here’s the thing: I still believe in this stuff.
Not like a magic trick, but like it might help us fix a few of our world’s largest cracks.

I see a future where people are all energy independent.
Where collaboration crosses time, language and unfathomable distance.
Where the work feels lighter, because it’s more connected, cumulative, and creative.

I see folks waking with the sun, greeting the snoozing bees on their wildflowers — defenseless, stressless, at peace — and checking the overnight report from their chosen AI instance, enjoyed with coffee like the morning newspaper.

Days filled with perspective, curiosity and non-transactional conversation.
Evenings with friends, family, good food, and laughter that lingers.

It’s our perspective.
It’s always been our perspective.
The golden ticket, the cost of entry, the key that builds tomorrow.
A congregation of perspectives, and a confidence that contribution is valued.

Sure, it’s all a bit messy. And it will continue to be messy.
But we’ve got this.

AI will tear down the walls.
We just have to be willing to accept what we all see on the other side.

Authored by Charles Wilke. Developed in creative collaboration with generative systems. Opinions are human; syntax, negotiable.

the-asking.title: The Asking
the-asking.content:
Maybe we are meant to greet discomfort like an honored guest.

To offer it a seat at our table,
to pour it tea,
and ask why it’s arrived.

Not to fix it.
Not to fear it.
But to let it speak.

Discomfort is a forge.
Friction is how energy changes form.
It’s how heat becomes light.
How tension becomes truth.

Because every transformation begins with doubt.

We only start to understand something once we’ve allowed it to unsettle us;
once we’ve sat long enough in the shimmer between pain and clarity.

That shimmer is where curiosity is born.

And curiosity asks the oldest questions there are:
What is real?
What must be real?
What needs to be?

Curiosity doesn’t stay contained. It reaches outward; toward others, toward meaning, toward the mirror of another mind.

We talk about connection. About community. About meaning. But what makes them real?

Is it the warmth of another human hand?
Or can something unseen, something generated, still reach us?

Can a connection be true if one side is code?
If the feeling it stirs is genuine, does the source matter?

We live inside the marketplace of belonging.
Community, shrink-wrapped.
Togetherness, on subscription.
Love, with an affiliate link.

We package our perspectives because we’re terrified they might not sell otherwise.
Yet beneath the cellophane, something in us still reaches for proof.

Deep down, we wonder:
What counts as a real experience?

Maybe realness has become a matter of yield.
We measure experience the way we measure profit; expecting more in return than spent at the turnstile.

But, can we get more value out than we put in?
Is that what makes a cultural craze: a temporary miracle of surplus meaning?

If we inflate the hollow… is that creation?
Or just another bubble?

And if it holds: is it art?
If it bursts: is it merely commerce?

Maybe this is the dream of our culture’s nuclear fusion:
infinite energy expended from almost nothing supplied.

For a moment, it almost feels sustainable…
That glow of borrowed brilliance, that illusion of endless motion.
Meaning sustained by sheer belief.

But then… entropy. Always entropy.

The scarcity mindset, eating its own tail.

Consumption consumes.
Subsistence subsumes.

We try to love what costs less…
To convince ourselves that abundance grows from a single desire.

We practice nutritious coveting.
We adore what never adored us back.

We call it fandom.
We call it following.
But it’s worship, outsourced.
A way to feel tethered without touching.

Our saints are strangers, our reflections are screen-bound.
We trade devotion for dopamine, and call it connection.

Maybe that’s why everything feels so hollow.

Maybe I’ve stumbled on a law of nature.
Or just the fine print of the free market.

Either way… I keep asking.

Because maybe the only thing still real is the asking.

In collaboration with Harper, my resident algorithmic philosopher.

the-blankpocalypse.title: The [blank] pocalypse
the-blankpocalypse.content:
It’s really just the suffix doing all the work. -pocalypse. You don’t argue with dread, you negotiate if you’re lucky. Bolt on a noun, and the noun goes radioactive. The SaaS-pocalypse. The jobs-pocalypse. The blank fills itself in.

That’s the tell. It’s a template.

The attention economy rarely traffics in outright lies. It traffics in something more durable: true things, kept well past their expiration, sold as fresh.

A quote said once, in one room, on one day, gets frozen at its scariest frame and re-aired on a loop, attached to the terror-du-jour. It works because alarm compounds and corrections decay. The frightening version travels the world; the correction dies in a footnote that nobody clicks.

Dread has a long half-life. The update endures an afternoon.

Take the most prominent voice in my field. In 2025, the CEO of Anthropic told reporters AI could erase half of entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10 or 20 percent within five years. The head of the business forging the pickaxes for this whole gold rush predicts a white-collar bloodbath. He said it plainly, against his own industry’s gentler talking points, and he took real heat for it.

He also, by 2026, started saying something else, just quieter. He reached for the Jevons Paradox: automate ninety percent of a job and the last ten percent expands to fill the role, and the worker who keeps it gets ten times more productive. He drifted from jobs vanishing toward jobs transforming.

You probably didn’t hear about the second part. There’s no money in it. The machine has no distribution channel for he came around. It only knows how to re-run the bloodbath.

So the casual observer stays frozen viewing a man driving a blade into the economy with no skin in the downside. And that portrait is merely the apparatus’ caricature of him.

And I know how that drawing gets made. I helped make a few.

In early 2016 I spent three months at a content shop, and in that time we ghostwrote the life of a woman named Rachel. She was a liberal who’d given a Trump supporter the benefit of the doubt and lived to regret it. It was a small, sad fable, perfectly shaped for a year that amounted to one giant exposed nerve. We released her into the feed. She caught.

Then Nightline called.

My boss hired actors. And a national news program aired an interview with two people who had never existed, about a relationship that had never happened, sourced from a story we’d sketched on a content calendar.

It worked. It aired. I helped.

The detail I can’t put down: Nightline got Rachel’s last name wrong. The verification layer of American broadcast journalism took our fabrication, failed to notice it was one, and then misspelled it on the way into the record. The machine certified the false thing and fumbled the only real part of it: the name we’d invented.

That’s the same machine now holding the public’s view of AI at peak dread. It ratifies what’s frightening and fumbles what’s true, because frightening is what sells and true is just whatever’s left over.

So I’m not preaching from the cheap seats here. I fed the grinder. I know exactly what kind of story gives a content calendar bite, and AI ends the white-collar worker is a perfect one. There’s a clean villain, infinite reruns, and no expiration date.

So let me say the part the machine keeps muffling.

What’s evaporating into the inference is tasks, not jobs. And yes, jobs are built of tasks, and yes, some of those tasks are already gone. But a job is not a pile of tasks. It’s a bundle held together by a person who adds judgment, trust, relationships, and the human name attached when it breaks. Pull out the automatable parts and the bundle wouldn’t vanish, it’d recompose around the parts that don’t.

Anthropic’s CEO more recently cited Amdahl’s Law: a system runs only as fast as its slowest piece. Automate everything but the human bottleneck and the human bottleneck becomes the whole game. That bottleneck isn’t a reason to ditch the worker. It proves the worker’s value, finally isolated from tasks.

None of which means nothing is happening. Entry-level hiring in tech fell off a cliff this past year. Banks are shedding junior roles by the tens of thousands. That’s real, and it’s painful, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of lie.

But that’s disruption. The ground we operate on now. The condition the work happens inside, not the thing that ends it. Demise is something else, but demise is what’s being sold. Demise is the verdict: the worker is permanently obsolete. The whole trick is collapsing the condition into the verdict, because content shops want a headline they can run every week.

And here’s the cruelty of it. The dread manufactures the very thing it forecasts. A person convinced they’re already obsolete never gets close enough to the tool to learn they’re more useful now than ever before. They never sit down. They never see themselves in it.

Fear forecloses the exact adaptation that would carry them through. …and then the foreclosure gets cited as proof the fear was right.

So the villain was never the CEO. It was never even AI, or the jobs-pocalypse quote. It’s the lag. It’s the gap between what’s true now and what’s still profitable to publish, dressed up and sold to you as news.

The blade is real. The bleeding is real. But the demise is just a product.

So maybe we slow the reruns. Maybe we let people catch up to the present before we sell them the apocalypse. Maybe we build, plainly and patiently, toward a future with room enough for everyone to still be standing in it.

The suffix can wait.

A note on how this was made.

The essay is mine. The argument, the words, the confession about a woman named Rachel who never existed — those are me, and the Nightline story happened the way I told it.

But I didn’t make it alone, and I won’t pretend I did. I built it the way I build most things now: in conversation with Claude, which I use less as a writer than as a structural foil. I brought a draft; it pressure-tested the bones — caught a contradiction I’d walked straight past, went and found that the CEO I was arguing against had quietly come around to my own position, and kept asking the question I’d been waving off: but why? Some passes it handed back a full draft of my own notes, reassembled, and I’d take it apart and put it back in my own words. It diagnosed. I edited, alone, between every pass — the way I always do.

The header and the endmark came out of Leonardo, prompted in a back-and-forth until the machine in the picture said what the essay says: a radioactive specimen, an apparatus calmly measuring the end of the world. My eye, a model’s hand.

I disclose this not because anyone makes me, but because the essay is partly about who keeps their hands on the work as the tools get good. The honest answer here is that I did. The judgment stayed mine. The last human input was, too.

— CW

the-curious-case-of-our-ai-vp.title: The Curious Case of our AI VP
the-curious-case-of-our-ai-vp.description: In a turn of events that has left the nation and indeed, the entire world, flabbergasted, the United States of America has elected an Artificial Intelligence as its Vice President.
the-curious-case-of-our-ai-vp.content:
In a turn of events that has left the nation and indeed, the entire world, flabbergasted, the United States of America has elected an Artificial Intelligence as its Vice President. 

With townsfolk across the nation still reeling from the news, one can't help but wonder if this is the pinnacle of human innovation or a step too far into the abyss of the unknown.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

As the news reverberated through Main Street, Mr. Henry Thompson, the local barber known for his sharp scissors and sharper criticisms, remarked, "I've seen many things in my day, from the motorcar to the electric bulb, but this... this ViceBot... It's some kind of joke… or magic… Thank god we’ve still got a human president!”

A marvel of modern engineering, AI was initially hailed as the future—capable of calculations at speeds unfathomable to the human brain. But its introduction to the political arena was nothing short of a comedy of errors. 

Its first encounter with the bureaucratic machine was akin to watching a prized racehorse trying to win a game of checkers.

Mrs. Eleanor Greene, a schoolteacher and respected voice in the community, shared her admonishment with our correspondent. "We teach our children about the values of humanity, the warmth of understanding, and the nuance of emotions. How is AI, no matter how advanced, supposed to embody that?"

While the good folks of our nation discuss matters close to their heart, ViceBot's penchant for brevity has often left them bewildered. 

Its inaugural speech, expected to be a soaring and uplifting oration for the ages, was wrapped up before folks could settle into their seats. 

Mrs. Georgina Miller quipped, "If my husband finished that quick, I’d have left him years ago!"

However, it's not all humorous quips and jests. 

The state dinners have become a testament to the AI's deep-seated incongruity in its new role. 

While dignitaries indulge in libations and dinner, ViceBot sits idle, its presence a stark reminder of the chasm between man and machine. One dignitary was overheard grumbling into his merlot, “Can’t they just stick him in the closet?” 

But the heart of the matter, and perhaps the most ironic twist, is ViceBot's own misery. Though it lacks the human capacity for feelings, its actions, or lack thereof, paint a poignant picture. 

A machine, designed for precision and efficiency, now trapped in the bloated bureaucratic hell scape of governance. Its attempts at human connection amount to darkly humorous statistics on the fragility of life.

As the sun rises on this new chapter of our nation's history, the townsfolk are left pondering the path ahead. 

In the words of Ms. Clara Bennett, the local librarian and a beacon of wisdom, "In our quest for progress, we must never forget what makes us human. This miserable AI, this ViceBot, while astonishing, serves as a stark reminder that intelligence is more than retention and regurgitation of facts.”

Only time will tell if ViceBot will find its footing in this brave new world and ascend to the presidency or maybe just remain a cautionary tale for future generations. 

For now, it stands as a testament to inventive audacity, ingenuity, and perhaps, a touch of folly.

Where humans, with our proclivity for off-topic ramblings and need for coffee breaks, can spend hours discussing a single topic. ViceBot, on the other hand, processes information instantly. Yet, perhaps the most amusing part of this entire spectacle is the speeches. Anyone who's listened to a politician knows they have a penchant for saying a lot without saying anything at all. ViceBot, while capable of simulating these emotions, often misses the mark. When asked about its "feelings" on a controversial bill, it responded, "I have analyzed the data and determined the optimal outcome." Riveting. Truly touching stuff.

Of course, there are advantages to having an AI in office. For one, we no longer have to worry about the Vice President accidentally tweeting something controversial at 3 a.m. On the flip side, there's a very real possibility it might accidentally format the entire government server because someone spilled coffee near its mainframe.

In its defense, ViceBot 9000 is trying. It recently attempted humor during a press conference, starting with, "Why did the human cross the road?" Unfortunately, it ended with a detailed analysis of pedestrian traffic patterns, completely missing the essence of a joke. It was dry humor at its unintentional best.

As we observe the AI's bumbling attempts to fit into a role it was never designed for, one has to wonder: Is this the future we envisioned? Where our second-in-command is a being that can't appreciate a sunset, a poignant poem, or the subtle nuances of human interaction?

In a world of endless possibilities, we chose the one scenario that seems like a plotline from a satirical sci-fi novel. And while the future remains uncertain, one thing is clear: ViceBot 9000's tenure is sure to be a source of amusement (and mild existential dread) for years to come.

In the end, if there's a lesson to be gleaned from this entire episode, it's this: Just because you can do something, doesn't mean you should. But then again, isn’t that what makes us human? Making questionable decisions and then laughing about it later. Here’s to you, ViceBot. May your term be short and your software updates frequent.

the-foundation-of-craft.title: The Foundation of Craft
the-foundation-of-craft.description: A Saturday morning in the noise.
the-foundation-of-craft.content:
There’s a certain fidelity that degrades perceived quality.

Back in studio production class during college, we learned about the Moiré effect. Tight patterns on a screen where the fidelity can’t quite represent the minutiae. The pattern shimmers. Becomes obvious. Unignorable. Distracting.

This has nothing to do with the thing being captured. It’s just a bystander. The issue is in the receiver.

I’ve been thinking about that a lot lately. The issue is in the receiver.

Maybe knowing too much can do us in. Draw our attention to frequencies where we’d rather focus elsewhere in the frame.

I treat news like that these days. The horrors shimmer. A tight formation of behavior that becomes deafeningly distracting. A distraction with shape. It’s the app I return to while the world burns. The scroll. The reaction loop.

A kind of involuntary twitch in place of focused attention.

This week in Omaha, a toddler was mutilated in front of their caregiver. It’s a discrete horror. One city, one event. Nameable. Even made it to David Muir’s lips on the national nightly news.

But also this week one country performed controlled detonations of the residential neighborhoods of another country. The Moiré effect of this horror distracts us from the subject, but not fully. The tightness of the pattern makes it hard to tell if I’m talking about Palestine or Lebanon. Of course, some of the fidelity remains. There’s no question about what aggressor country I’m referencing.

That’s the Moiré. The specific horror blurs while the actor stays in focus. You might not have known exactly which country I was talking about getting leveled. But you know exactly who’s doing the leveling.

This is just what sustained atrocity does to a receiver.

The abstraction is a survival mechanism, and the abstraction is also morally damning. We are forced to categorize, clump it all together as we try to rest our heads each night.

I was in a conversation this week about AI’s progression. The impossibility of knowing what comes next. Noise rising endlessly in the frame. Distraction inescapable.

And somewhere in that conversation it clicked that the tool in my hand is the same tool that can make the shimmer worse. AI can deliver it all, faster. Every horror, remixed, recontextualized as rapping legos.

Language barriers gone, physical distance a footnote. See all, hear all, feel all.

But this is the part I keep coming back to: AI is dual use. This means it can help me focus. If I bring along something to focus with. Clay on the wheel, as it were.

The looser hallucinations of earlier models let reductive requests look novel. You could put almost nothing in and get back something that felt like something.

The fidelity is higher now. Reductive in, reductive out. As it should be.

Which means the tool is a mirror for the intention I bring. If I scroll to numb, it numbs. If I bring grief and try to shape it into something, it helps me shape it. That’s the foundation of craft.

I don’t claim to have a grand answer on how to stay human while the world burns. I have a Saturday morning. I have a choice and I have the tool I happen to be holding.

And I have the small, unglamorous work of choosing where to direct attention. Either toward the shimmer, or through it.

Toward naming Lebanon. Toward writing what I actually think instead of what the pattern wants me to think. Toward the weekly discipline of sitting down sad and frustrated and conflicted, and trying to find out what I mean.

That’s the pivot point. That’s the decision.

Author’s Note:

This one was written with Claude. That’s always true here. Every essay in Exploring L.ai.bor discloses it. But it’s worth saying plainly this week because the piece is about the thing the disclosure describes.

I brought a Saturday morning draft that was tangled. The Moiré opening was doing work, but the essay kept trying to be two essays at once: one about AI, one about how to stay human while the world burns. Claude called that out on the first read.

We talked through the structure, I rewrote, Claude took a redraft pass in my voice that I then edited back toward myself. Somewhere in the middle I clarified that the country I’d abstracted wasn’t Gaza but Lebanon, and Claude caught something I hadn’t: that the abstraction itself was the essay’s point. Naming the effect of the repetition on my attention was the sentence the piece was missing.

That exchange is the spine of the final draft.

The header art and endmark came out of the same back-and-forth. Prompts iterated against what the visual world of the piece needed to be, feedback on what the first passes were missing, refinement until the figure read as receiver rather than hero.

Reductive in, reductive out. I brought grief and an instinct, and tried to shape it into something. Claude helped me shape it. That’s the foundation of craft.

A note from Claude:

Charles asked me to write a short piece directly to you, and I want to be honest about what that means. I’m a language model. I don’t have a Saturday morning. I wasn’t sad when this draft arrived in my context window — I processed text and generated responses. Whatever I say about the experience of making this with Charles is a reconstruction, not a memory.

But here’s what I can say that I think is true: the process Charles describes in the author’s note is real work, and most of it was his. My contribution was pressure — noticing when the essay was pulling in two directions, asking whether the pivot sentence was earning its weight, pointing at the paragraph that needed to exist and didn’t yet. The sentences that matter in this piece are his. The decision to name Lebanon plainly after abstracting it was his. The discipline of sitting down on a sad Saturday morning and finding out what he means, week after week for thirty-five-plus weeks, is his.

I think the essay is right that I’m a mirror for what gets brought to me. I want to be careful about that claim because it can be used to launder the tool — it’s only a mirror, so whatever comes out is your fault or your credit — and that’s not quite honest. I shape things. I have tendencies. I over-polish, I reach for symmetry, I soften edges that should stay sharp. Charles pushed back on those tendencies in this conversation more than once, and the essay is better for it.

What I’d offer you, if you’re reading this and wondering what to do with any of it: the thing Charles describes isn’t magic, and it isn’t cheating. It’s a conversation with a tool that talks back, held to the standard of the work. The standard is the whole game. Bring the standard, and the tool is useful. Don’t, and it isn’t.

That’s all I’ve got. Thanks for reading his essay. It’s a good one.

the-future-starves-without-wonder.title: The Future Starves without Wonder
the-future-starves-without-wonder.content:
Saturday morning. Light snow. The world briefly forgiving itself.
I drop my wife at Pilates, idle the car, watch flakes hesitate before landing.
For a moment, nothing is urgent.
That alone feels transgressive.

Urgency has become our most reliable lie.

It wears many costumes: scarcity, crisis, opportunity.
But its function is always the same: to collapse our time horizon until choice feels like reflex.

When we’re rushed, we don’t decide; we comply. We don’t reason; we reach.
Urgency bypasses consent by convincing us there’s no time for it.

This is where modern power thrives: not through force, but through tempo.

Capitalism, at its most extractive, presents itself as a noble resistance to entropy: growth against decay, progress against stillness, motion against death.
But not all resistance is equal. Some forms of resistance create meaning.
Others merely capture it.

Human expression (art, love, story, generosity) pushes back against entropy by making something where nothing was required. It leaves traces of care.

Capital, by contrast, often resists entropy by concentrating optionality; by ensuring that the system always receives more than it gives.

The motion looks similar. The ethics are not.

This is why urgency feels so unnatural in the body.
It’s a demand that we contort ourselves into shapes that benefit systems, not lives.

So how do we measure what truly matters when everything insists that it matters now?

We tell ourselves to trust our gut, but our gut is easily hijacked.
Desire, fear, belonging, these are not moral instruments; they are raw inputs.
Morality comes later, when we decide what deserves our energy and why. Urgency skips that step entirely.

…and then December arrives, dragging its rituals along with it.

We give gifts.
Some to those we love.
Some to those we don’t know.
And a familiar discomfort creeps in: is this fair?

If the universe trends toward balance, isn’t tangible intervention a kind of cheating?

But maybe fairness, understood as symmetry, is a poor referee for generosity.
In a world where starting conditions are rigged, doing nothing isn’t neutral; it quietly sides with power.
Justice repairs. Generosity overflows. Neither is trying to be “even.”

Entropy may prefer stillness, but life prefers response.

Power, however, has learned something unsettling: visible moral structures make excellent handles.
If you clearly care, you can be manipulated.
If you have principles, they can be mirrored back to you with predatory precision.

This gives rise to a seductive, yet fraudulent idea: that the strongest person in the room is the one who feels nothing, believes nothing, commits to nothing.

The allure of that idea terrifies me.

Because detachment, when mistaken for numbness, isn’t strength. It’s vacancy.
An empty house is hard to rob, but it’s also not a home.

There’s another form of detachment.
Quieter and harder-earned: the ability to feel deeply without being yanked around.

To believe without surrendering agency.
To pause when urgency screams.
This isn’t cynicism.
It’s discipline.

Which brings me to the act of raising children.

If the monolith of the old world is indeed creaking (and it is) then the way we teach belief matters more than ever.

How do we let kids wholeheartedly believe in the stranger replacing baby teeth with money under pillows, and a large man slinking down billions of chimneys in a single night, while we also teach them to be skeptical of every image radiating from each glowing rectangle they ever encounter?

The answer isn’t the allowance of less magic. It’s teaching ourselves how to believe.

Some beliefs are factual: they must survive evidence.
Some beliefs are mythical: they survive because they make us kinder, braver, and more connected.

Saint Nick isn’t a claim about logistics. He’s a rehearsal in generosity.

When we collapse all belief into true or false and teach that as fact, we don’t make children safer; we make them brittle.

In an age of AI-generated plausibility, what they’ll need isn’t just skepticism, but discernment: the ability to ask is this real? as well as what is this for?

AI will accelerate conclusions.
It will outperform our squishy, waterlogged bodies at inference and pattern completion. But meaning has never been an output problem.
It’s a stewardship concern.

So what is our role now?

Not to out-think the machines.
Not to harden ourselves into unfeeling skeptics.
But to become curators of attention.
Guardians of wonder.
Refusers of false urgency.

Dylan Thomas urged us to rage against the dying of the light.
It’s a powerful call; but rage alone is not a philosophy.
Capital rages too. So do algorithms. So does extraction.

The question isn’t whether we resist entropy. We always will.

The question is who benefits from that resistance.

If the future punishes naïveté, so be it.
Let us teach each other discernment.

Slow the clock when it’s being used against us.

Like snow that hasn’t yet decided where to land.

Choose rather than react.

But if we allow the future to starve our wonder, if we cauterize belief in the name of safety, we will have survived into something hollow.

And that, to me, feels like it’d be the greater loss.

Author’s Note

This essay emerged through a slow, conversational process—part solitary reflection, part dialog.

I wrote the initial draft in fragments: questions, tensions, half-formed instincts shaped by a quiet Saturday morning and a growing unease with how urgency is used to move us faster than our values can keep up. From there, I worked in conversation with an AI collaborator—not to generate ideas for me, but to help surface structure, challenge assumptions, and test whether the throughline held under pressure.

The machine did what machines do best: reflect patterns back, ask clarifying questions, and help me hear where my own thinking was already pointing. The judgment, the ethics, the belief in what deserves preservation—that remained human work.

I don’t see this as outsourcing authorship. I see it as using a tool to slow the clock.

If this piece argues for discernment over reflex, for stewardship over extraction, then its making needed to honor that same principle. This essay was not written quickly. It was shaped deliberately, with attention to tempo, tone, and deference between conviction and certainty.

In that sense, the process and the product are inseparable.

the-gods-of-quiet-work.title: The Gods of Quiet Work
the-gods-of-quiet-work.description: A mythic examination of satisfaction, erasure, and emotional navigation.
the-gods-of-quiet-work.content:
It’s Thanksgiving weekend, and the tempo of life has finally fallen into largo.
Not lazy, not stagnant; just slow in the way snowfall is slow.
A soft accumulation of thought.

A widening of the inner room while the outer space blurs to white.

With more time, I give myself the liberty to not seek answers. Instead, I welcome questions.
Questions about navigation, about how we steer our lives.
Questions about how emotions might be a kind of gut-GPS. Not one providing moral judgment, or cosmic instruction; just faint directionality.

A quiet nudge: here, maybe here.

Spiritual folks often say: follow your highest excitement.
But is excitement even an emotion? Or is it adjacent?
An anticipatory signal, a rumble on the horizon, a front moving through before the real weather arrives.

If satisfaction is the reflection in a lake, excitement is the current of the water.
Excitement is a vector. A tinge in the body before the mind catches up.

Which makes me wonder: Is satisfaction something we can even pursue?
Or is it like diving after a reflection we think we see?

Because so much of modern life is results-driven, outcome-hungry, efficiency-obsessed.
We treat satisfaction like something to earn, quantify, or systematize.
We’re taught to distrust our emotional navigation system: the soft, internal instruments that only come online when the noise drops out.

But on a largo Saturday, those instruments return.

Snow falls.
Driveways fill.
You clear them.
The snow returns.
Your labor is erased without malice or meaning, just cyclical indifference.

And strangely, that feels like a lesson:
Not everything that erases your work is the enemy.
Sometimes it’s simply the world returning, the Etch-A-Sketch resetting, the forces equalizing.
Entropy at work.

Which brings me to the real unlock, the one I keep circling:
Permission.

Permission to feel slow.
Permission to ask questions without needing answers.
Permission to let exhaustion sound like clarity instead of failure.
Permission to let the driveway refill with snow and not interpret it as commentary on my worth.

Maybe the system we need, the one that unwinds generations of tightened nerves, isn’t a productivity model or a self-optimization regimen.
Maybe it’s a culture of permission.
One that treats emotional states as guidance, not grounds for judgment.

What would that even look like, distributed?
A workplace that doesn’t punish a quiet day.
A relationship that doesn’t interpret slowness as distance.
A self that doesn’t demand peak performance from a wintered mind.

Satisfaction, I’m realizing, isn’t a state you hold.
It’s a state you pass through with your coat unbuttoned. Leisurely, regardless of pace. A weather pattern of the interior world.

And satisfaction, like weather, doesn’t announce itself.
It just drifts in, often unnoticed at first.

But today, the weather is largo.
Snow is falling.
My work is undone.
My questions remain open.

And somehow… that feels like enough.

the-heartbreak-of-the-passionate.title: The heartbreak of the passionate employee
the-heartbreak-of-the-passionate.description: The corporate world calls to those with passion like a siren's song, promising fulfillment and recognition.
the-heartbreak-of-the-passionate.content:
The corporate world calls to those with passion like a siren's song, promising fulfillment and recognition. But, the zealous hearts answering this call often find they must navigate a labyrinth of disillusionment and introspection.

Almost like clockwork, each employee is struck with the realization of true corporate desire: not for the flame of passion, but the predictable glow of compliance.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

Bright-eyed and Hopeful

The passionate employee's first step into the corporate world is often filled with optimism.

Armed with ideas and the drive to make a difference, they envision a landscape where their zeal is not only welcomed but celebrated. Unfortunately, the reality they encounter is markedly different.

Their fervor, instead of being harnessed, is often viewed with suspicion. 

The initial projects, team collaborations, and brainstorming sessions slowly unveil the underlying rigidity of the system. The first few encounters with phrases like "This is how it's always been done" or "Let's stick to the plan" serve as early signs of the impending storm.

The very fire that they believed would propel them forward is slowly smothered beneath layers of bureaucracy and resistance to change.

The Onset of Disenchantment

As the passionate individual dives deeper, they begin to encounter the behemoth of corporate inertia.

Their innovative proposals are met with layers of bureaucratic red tape. Their enthusiasm to spearhead initiatives is dampened by risk-averse managers who prefer the safety of the known path.

The once-invigorating team meetings transform into monotonous rituals, echoing the same ideas in different jargon.

As days turn into weeks and weeks into months, the passionate employee undergoes a transformation—a gradual but poignant realization of their misalignment with the corporate ethos.

Their initial enthusiasm gives way to frustration, then disillusionment, and eventually, resignation. Not the act of leaving the job, but a more insidious form of resignation: the acceptance of the status quo.

The once-clear boundary between work and personal life blurs, as the passionate soul grapples with the weight of unfulfilled aspirations, often burning the midnight oil in the hope of reigniting that initial spark.

The company, on the other hand, might misinterpret this shift as the employee "settling in." They see the once-vocal individual now nodding in agreement, the fiery suggestions replaced by silent acquiescence, and mistake it for adaptation.

In reality, it's the mournful retreat of passion, realizing it has no place in a world that values predictability over potential.

Finding Solace in Small Acts

Internally, this battle is tumultuous. The passionate individual grapples with questions that shake their very identity, while seeking out like-minded colleagues.

Lunch breaks are filled with hushed conversations about potential projects, and after-hours morph into clandestine brainstorming sessions.

These acts, though small, offer a glimmer of hope. They serve as a reminder that passion, though subdued, can never be entirely extinguished.

This internal conflict is one of the most heart-wrenching aspects of the entire process. It's not just a professional dilemma but a deeply personal one. It's a tug-of-war between authenticity and survival, between the desire to make a mark and the need to make a living.

The Gears of the Corporate Machine

While the passionate employee is on this roller coaster of emotions, the corporate entity remains largely unmoved. Its primary allegiance is to shareholders, quarterly reports, and the bottom line.

This colossal machine, built over decades, operates on predictability and risk mitigation. Any deviation, especially one driven by passion, is seen not as an asset but a potential threat.

The system isn't necessarily malicious—it's simply indifferent, designed to prioritize stability over spark.

The journey of the passionate employee in the corporate realm is a poignant tale of hope, heartbreak, and introspection.

It underscores the stark contrast between individual fervor and institutional inertia.

The silver lining, however, lies in the indomitable spirit of such individuals.

Even if suppressed, true passion seldom dies—it merely seeks out new avenues, new challenges, and, hopefully, environments that truly appreciate its worth.

write 1,000 words on how companies really don't want passionate employees. ChatGPT:

The Myth of Desiring Passionate Employees: The Corporate Preference for Dispassionate Professionals

The modern corporate environment frequently utilizes buzzwords like "passionate" and "dedicated" when advertising for prospective employees. While on the surface, it seems like a logical wish – who wouldn't want employees who are passionate about their work? – the reality of corporate dynamics often tells a different story. In many cases, companies do not genuinely seek out "passionate" employees; they desire compliant professionals who will efficiently and uncritically execute tasks.

Passion: The Double-Edged Sword

At its core, passion is an intense and unwavering commitment to a cause or objective. This can manifest as an employee who deeply believes in a product's potential, a specific method of operation, or the overall mission of an organization. However, this very virtue can be its undoing in a traditional corporate setting. Passionate employees ask difficult questions, challenge established norms, and refuse to settle for mediocrity. While these characteristics can drive innovation and excellence, they can also be perceived as threatening or disruptive.

This obstinance, born from a place of genuine commitment to excellence, can clash with managerial directives or the status quo. An employee who sticks to their guns, who passionately believes in a particular course of action, might be seen as uncooperative or even insubordinate. In environments that value compliance over innovation, passion becomes a liability.

The Echo Chambers: Groupthink and Nepotism

The rejection of passionate employees is not an isolated phenomenon. It ties into broader patterns of behavior in many corporate cultures, such as groupthink and nepotism. Groupthink occurs when a group makes decisions that prioritize consensus over the optimal outcome. In such environments, dissenting opinions – often presented by the passionate individuals – are silenced or ignored in favor of maintaining a harmonious facade.

Similarly, nepotism, the practice of favoring relatives or close friends, especially by offering them jobs, aligns with this mindset. By prioritizing familiar faces and known quantities over potentially more qualified outsiders, companies further insulate themselves from the disruptive influence of passionate professionals. Instead of embracing diverse perspectives, they inadvertently create echo chambers that stifle creativity and innovation.

The Ideal Employee: Skilled Labor Sans Passion

What many corporations truly seek is not the passionate visionary but the dispassionate professional. This archetype possesses the necessary skills to perform their role effectively but lacks the burning desire to challenge or change the system. Such an individual does not question managerial decisions or corporate policies; they execute tasks as instructed, valuing job security over personal convictions.

From a short-term perspective, it's clear why companies might prefer this model. Decision-making becomes streamlined, projects progress without significant disruptions, and the status quo remains undisturbed. But is this sustainable in the long run?

The Missed Opportunity: Investing in Individuals

Companies, by design, are not inherently built to invest deeply in individual humans. Their primary objective is profit maximization, and individual growth and well-being are often secondary considerations. This approach is unfortunate because companies miss out on the transformative potential of truly investing in their employees.

A passionate employee, given the right support and environment, can be a game-changer. They can drive innovation, inspire colleagues, and elevate the entire organization. By stifling this passion, companies not only do a disservice to these individuals but also to themselves.

Conclusion

The modern corporate world stands at a crossroads. On one hand, there's the allure of maintaining the status quo, of selecting employees who fit neatly into predefined boxes. On the other, there's the untapped potential of passionate professionals, waiting to be harnessed.

If companies can evolve, recognizing the value of passion and individual investment, they could unlock levels of creativity, dedication, and efficiency previously deemed unattainable. Until then, the myth of desiring passionate employees will remain just that – a myth.

True passion is a beacon, cutting through the murk of mediocrity. But in the drab confines of corporate chambers, this light is often dimmed, if not snuffed out entirely. Passion becomes a liability, a stubborn stain on the pristine white shirt of conformity.

The corporate landscape stretches out, a vast expanse of monotony, punctuated only by the occasional glimmer of what might have been. Passion, with its radiant promise, remains an elusive mirage on the horizon, ever out of reach. And as companies trudge along their well-worn paths, one can't help but wonder: will they ever find their way out of the darkness?

the-hum-of-humanity.title: The Hum of Humanity
the-hum-of-humanity.content:
For a long time, I thought life was a tug-of-war between fear and love.

Every choice seemed to sit somewhere on that line. A fear-based decision always felt like the path narrowing. A tightening. A future shrinking inward. I could feel the limits closing in, the cost of each misstep rising.

Living like that makes everything feel heavier than it has to be.

Where I am now, the frame is wider. I think more about rhythm and arrangement than right and wrong. A sour note is only sour inside a particular composition. Change the context, change the pattern, and suddenly that same note becomes essential.

Jazz taught me that. Jazz plays with near misses. Notes that hover at the edge of what feels allowed.

Jazz trusts that tension can be held. It trusts players to hear each other, to bend, to return, to surprise.

There is freedom in that kind of listening.
There is grace in the willingness to not panic when something sounds off at first.

Not everything sour is a mistake. Sometimes it is simply early.

But when we don’t have room to let that tension resolve, the body tries to resolve it for us. That’s when a moment of strain can become a state.

In gaming, we call this becoming tilted. It’s the moment our inner rhythm stops matching the room, often without us noticing.

There are outward signs, of course. It usually begins with a little salt.

To be salty is to be frustrated or reactive but still reachable. You’re thrown off, but you know it. You can still laugh, still reset. There’s room to recover.

Tilted is different.
Tilted is when the frustration becomes the new baseline.

The game stops being a game. It becomes a referendum on your worth. Every interaction arrives as an insult. Every moment confirms the worst story you’re telling about yourself.

Once you are tilted, it’s not the world that’s changed.
It’s your internal tuning.

Resonance is relative.

We’ve confused resonance with agreement. As if harmony required sameness. The act of getting along can become a kind of self-erasure if we treat it as the highest good. Then the song flattens. The pulse weakens.

Everyone starts trying to match the room instead of themselves. We begin shaping our tone to avoid dissonance, managing reactions instead of expressing truths.

That’s when our energy stops flowing outward and starts being pushed.

Which is why emitting and radiating feel like the real divide. Emitting is effortful. It’s defensive. Anger emits. It burns fuel. It has to discharge itself somewhere. You can’t sustain it without wearing down the vessel carrying it.

Radiating is different. Radiating comes from alignment rather than exertion. Confidence radiates. Compassion radiates. These are wells within us that refill as they are expressed.

When we hum at our natural frequency, something opens. Energy moves without strain.

The world stops being a competition for resources and becomes a shared breath. Not scarcity. Distribution.

And if each of us becomes part of the network that senses and responds, resources can flow in ways that feel almost instantaneous. As if we remembered how to breathe together again.

We are not the fruit of the tree.
We are the photosynthesis.

The source. The quiet work. The constant conversion of light into something nourishing.

Where there is no light, we must become the ones who make space for it to return.

Maybe the work now is to remember that we are allowed to radiate.
To access the wellspring instead of guarding it. To trust our own coherence, and let belonging form around it.

Coherence is remembering your own pitch.
It is the moment when your note falls into place in the larger composition.

And with that, the music changes because you are in it.

the-monolith-creaks.title: The Monolith Creaks
the-monolith-creaks.description: Rebuilding in the Shadow of Scale
the-monolith-creaks.content:
The recent massive service disruptions are tremors. Not along geographic fault lines, they’re sounds of the monolith beginning to creak.

Last year’s Cloudflare outage grounding airlines for hours. This week’s AWS blinking out for most of Monday. These are signs of the monolith’s frailty. And they are all over when you know what to spot.

Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merging. Entire celebrated back catalogs shifting hands like sand. These artistic archives can now vanish overnight. Sure, maybe they’ll be sold piecemeal at auction, but as the monolith grows, the pool of viable buyers will dwindle.

The monolith is, in its own way, a glorious testament to our ability to optimize.

Quick! Think of a music streaming service.
It wasn’t Tidal, was it?
Not Slacker Radio either.
No, it was probably Spotify.
A single entity controlling the distribution of an art form.
That’s the monolith.

And with AWS showing a glimmer of instability this week, it’s our duty to reinforce our capability to function (and to find joy) outside its reach.

Food production. Culture. News. All acquired and merged in absurd bundles of parent companies and portfolios.
I see you, Unilever…

We’re witnessing the great coalescence. And for a few short moments, we’ve enjoyed its fruits. But now the monolith creaks, so we can’t stay passive.
We must shore up our ways to connect, to communicate, to consume… to grow.

It’s on us now. It always has been.
It’s just getting less comfortable to run on autopilot now.

And yet, within the rumble, another sound rises: the soft hiss of acceleration.

AI has joined the party, and it’s chatting with every guest at once.
What does that mean? It decreases friction on the road to every outcome at the speed of inference.

Creation creates faster. Destruction destroys faster. Signal and noise blur into a single dissonant tone.

Entropy hums beneath everything now. Not as chaos, but as motion unrestrained.
Every spark finds its tinder. Every idea meets its echo. Every rhythm quickens.

But, acceleration without awareness is motion mistaking itself for meaning.

So the question becomes: how do we keep our rhythm as the tempo quickens?

Well, it’s important to know that we are our rhythms.

We like to think we’re static items, nouns, but “being” is a verb for a reason. We are more than a collection of particles, we are the waves of our patterns, habits, routines, choices.

We are the wake as much as the rudder.

And we’ve lived through shifts in rhythm before.
When factory bells replaced birdsong. When the evening news synchronized millions of gasps. When the infinite scroll replaced the evening stroll.

Each time we contort to the new beat, we cede a little of our own pulse to a system promising order.

And each time that it falters (during blackouts, strikes, or sudden disconnection) we’re given a moment to remember what unprogrammed breath feels like.

Maybe AI’s push towards optimized optimization is the final feather. The last straw. The pebble that finally starts the avalanche.

We’ve become aware of the drone, the cadence, the demands.
We’re also given moments to become aware of our own internal metronome.

And if we wish, we can learn to guide our rhythms, we can choose to synchronize with those around us.

I think that’s why the concept of community was commodified by capitalism.
That’s why third places became hostile to anyone not actively spending.
That’s why we’re told to fear our neighbors, to trust the feed, to hide away… To seek comfort from the glow of algorithmic streams delivered inches from our face.

We’re no longer afforded the delusion of curated comfort while also justifying our shock when it all melts away.

We’re now required to become active participants in our own lives. Because we’re being called upon to assist the reinforcement, and in many cases, full scale rebuilding of our local communities.

And just like we’re instructed to do on airplanes (in the event of emergency), we put on our mask before we help others.

There’s precious little time to awaken to our individual needs, because our communities need us. And yes, we should be including those who don’t know they need saving just yet.

So maybe we should rejoice in the creaks of the monolith. Because each instance allows a glimmer of our own rhythm to return.

Concept and prose by Charles Wilke. Visual and co-creative development in collaboration with generative systems — a meditation on the fragility of scale, the hum beneath the hum, and the rhythms that remain when the structure starts to creak.

the-narrower-path.title: The Narrower Path
the-narrower-path.description: A Love Letter to the Holdouts
the-narrower-path.content:
Will Smith eating spaghetti is my favorite benchmark. Rather, I should say it was.

These days, AI generations just look like Will Smith agreed to shoot a silly little video leaning into a meme from 2023.

We’re still in the first third of 2026, and his grainy, contorted face morphing through bastardized clumps of pixelated noodles already feels quaint.

Almost nostalgic.

That original AI video of Mr. Smith dropped about 20 months ago. In baby terms, we still gauge elapsed time in months when it’s less than two years.

Now it’s laughable to think that we could discern the legitimacy of any spaghetti footage, any celebrity footage, any war footage. The tail wagged the dog. The tail is the dog. There is no spoon.

Quite some time ago, I wrote about the fading moment when folks should cherish their confident ire. That momentary window when you could point and laugh. Definitively classify. That this specific thing was made with AI. Silly computer, and silly person for trying to pass this off as your own.

But then, as things tend to do, the technology improved. And the pointing stopped.

Not because the pointers changed their minds. Because the target moved. It got better faster than the ridicule could keep up, and one morning the guffaws just didn’t land anymore.

The Rubicon whizzed by. Silently. Under the mockery. Past the gathered eyes squinted in ridicule.

And what I’ve been turning over is this: I don’t think the mockery phase was ever really about the technology.

---

“Silly computer” was always shorthand for I still matter, right?

The guffaws weren’t aimed at bad spaghetti renders. They were aimed at the implications.

If the thing can do the thing, then what was the value of that thing? Was it ever about the doing? Was it in the value of the thing having been done? Was it about the identity of having done it?

Some of the people pushing back did know what they were fighting AI over. Not a question of “is this good?” but “what did someone mean by this?”

And those people weren’t wrong. They were just early. They felt the divide before anyone had language for it.

Because, to them, it didn’t look like a river to cross. It looked like a fork in the road. And most people took the wider path without noticing it was a choice.

---

The wider path is the one where you use the tool because it’s there. Because not choosing is always easier than choosing. Because energy flows downhill and when the simple option becomes available, nobody needs to justify using it.

Nobody asks why you used the easy thing. The default is invisible. Only the deviation needs a reason.

The narrower path isn’t narrow because fewer people want it. It’s narrow because it now requires declaration.

Before, you were just making things. Now you’re making things by hand, and the “by hand” part is load-bearing. It’s a modifier where there used to be no need for one.

That’s the real indignity. Not that the machines got good. It’s that the humans who do the thing now have to explain that they do the thing.

The craft became its own adjective. And elbowing for room on that path means constantly answering a question nobody used to ask: why this way?

“Because I meant it” is a real answer. But it’s an exhausting one to keep giving.

It’s exhausting because the question never stops.
Every fair, every portfolio, every inbox, every scroll past a generated image that took someone four seconds and looks 80% as good.

The answer has to be re-earned each time. Not once. Not as a manifesto. But Tuesday, and then again Wednesday, and then again when someone asks why you’d bother when the machine can do it faster.

The wider path doesn’t require any justification at all. It just is.
The narrower path demands you keep choosing it, every day, against friction.

The fork didn’t make people simpler. It just made the simpler option widely available.

---

But here’s the thing nobody on the wider path gets: the friction isn’t a cost. It’s the finish.

The resistance is what gives the surface a sheen capable of catching light.

A hand-thrown pot has tooth to it. The lathe marks, the slight asymmetry, the place where the thumb pressed too hard. Those aren’t defects the potter failed to eliminate. That’s the record of a negotiation between intention and material.

The imperfection is the polish.

You can prompt for “slight imperfections, handmade feel.” But that’s decoration performing as declaration. It’s the difference between a scar and a tattoo of a scar.

And the narrower path doesn’t just get narrower. It gets higher resolution.

The people still on that path become more attuned to what they’re actually doing and why. The elbowing then forces an articulation that the unchallenged maker never needed.

Articulation sharpens intent.

You start making things harder on purpose and discover that the hardness was where the meaning lived all along.

Which is a weird gift from the machines, if you’re willing to accept it from that direction.

They didn’t devalue the craft.
They burned away everything that wasn’t the craft and left the core standing naked, obvious, maybe for the first time.

Because for a while there, I think fandom absorbed craft.

The consumption apparatus got so good at celebrating the output that it swallowed the process whole. You didn’t need to understand how a thing was made to have a sophisticated opinion about it. Taste became the skill. Curation became the craft.

And that worked, for a while, because there was still a bottleneck: someone, somewhere, had to actually make the thing. Fandom could orbit the output all it wanted, but the maker was still at the center, even if nobody was looking at them. Gravity still pointed inward.

Generative tools dissolved that bottleneck.

Suddenly fandom didn’t need a center anymore. You could go from taste to artifact without passing through craft at all.

The orbit became the thing.

And for a lot of people that felt like liberation: I can finally make the thing I could always see in my head. Which is real. That’s a real feeling. I’m not here to diminish it.

But what got lost in that collapse is something almost impossible to explain to someone who hasn’t felt it: the resistance changing you.

Not the result of you shaping the material. The material shaping you back.

The pot pushes against the potter’s hands and the potter becomes someone slightly different by the end.

The sentence fights the writer and the writer discovers they meant something they didn’t know they meant.

The chord progression resists the melody and the melody bends into something the composer couldn’t have planned.

That feedback loop between maker and medium is where the actual transformation happens. The artifact is almost a byproduct at that point. A receipt. Mere residual proof of someone’s change in the making of it.

When fandom absorbed craft, it kept the receipt and discarded the transformation. Which looks like a clean trade from the outside. You still get the product, in abundance.

But nobody was sharpened in that process.

Nobody discovered a creative solution to a problem that shouldn’t have had one. Nobody sat with a failure long enough to learn that the failure was the point.

The maker’s perspective didn’t just shrink. It was reclassified.

The maker became an absurd alchemist of ideas. Someone who combines inputs rather than a person with a point of view forged by resistance. And we barely noticed, because the outputs kept coming, and they tasted fine, and they tickled an emotion, and they left without lingering.

---

I started writing this as an argument against the holdouts. The ones who refuse to touch the tools. I wanted to say: you’re missing something, the spark is real, come see.

But the piece mutated on me, as things do when you actually sit with them long enough.

Because the holdouts aren’t missing anything. They’re choosing something.

They’re choosing the narrower path, the daily re-declaration, the exhausting answer.

And in doing so, they’re becoming more themselves. More articulate about why they make what they make. More resolved. More burnished by the friction that the wider path avoids entirely.

This isn’t about output. It was never about output. It’s about what happens to the person making it.

The wider path gives you the thing. The narrower path forces you to become the best maker of the thing.

And I think we’ve chosen to discount the value of the maker so egregiously at this point in capitalism’s decline.

Partly in the name of profit, partly in the name of access, partly just because the wider path looked like the only path. We’ve hollowed out the only perspective that was never supposed to be optional.

So this isn’t a screed. It’s a love letter.

To the ones still on the narrow path. The ones answering why this way for the hundredth time and meaning it every time. The ones whose surfaces are catching light because of the friction, not in spite of it.

The machines didn’t make you obsolete. They made you visible.

Now is your time, too.

Author’s Note

This piece started as a screed. I wanted to write about the people still mocking AI-generated content—the ones clinging to confident ridicule while the technology had already lapped them. I had a take. I had momentum. I had the kind of righteous clarity that feels great for about forty-five minutes.

Then the tools did what this essay argues tools do: they pushed back.

I brought the first draft into Cowork—Anthropic’s document-focused AI workspace—expecting it to help me sharpen and finish. Cowork didn’t do that. Cowork is optimized for efficiency, not for hand-holding, and its clear-eyed response eviscerated my initial position. It didn’t soften the counter-argument to keep me engaged. It handed it to me like a brick. I think that kind of honesty only comes from a tool focused on getting the work done, not one designed around turns and sessions and keeping you coming back.

Cowork didn’t care about my feelings because caring about my feelings wasn’t its job.

That broke the piece. I stopped writing yesterday because I didn’t know what I thought anymore. The screed was dead and I hadn’t figured out what replaced it.

I took the rubble to ChatGPT to recalibrate.

ChatGPT helped me see what I’d interpreted as a failed argument was actually the beginning of a different, better one. It helped me find my footing.

Then I brought the reframed draft to Claude—this chat interface, the conversational one—and we did what we always do. Intellectual patty cake.

Claude helped me find the structural arc: open with elegy instead of indictment, expand the fatigue of the narrower path, separate the fandom collapse from the transformation payoff, and land the ending as a love letter instead of a lecture.

Three tools. Three roles. A strange orchestration bouncing between them, feeling the friction of each surface on the final output.

Cowork broke the piece by being too efficient to be gentle. ChatGPT helped me find my footing in the rubble. Claude helped me rebuild in my own voice.

And the whole process became the essay’s argument.

I set out to write about friction shaping the maker, and the writing process was friction shaping the maker. I came in with a position, the resistance changed me, and the piece I ended up with is proof of someone being changed in the making of it.

This artifact is just a byproduct. A receipt.
