the-new-survivalism.title: The New Survivalism
the-new-survivalism.description: The end game in an algorithmically optimized world
the-new-survivalism.content:
Kids of the ‘80s were raised in the shadow of nuclear fallout fears. Our parents were children when the Cuban missile crisis streaked across the headlines.

It threw newly-formed suburbia into a tizzy. And trained the children to shelter in place, hide under their desks. Brace.

There was an ambient sense of destruction, feared reckoning ringing in their ears.

Our parents dutifully, some more than others, bestowed that sense onto their children.
Hi. I am one of those.

The nuclear annihilation fears were, of course, not unfounded. But they were a tad misguided.

The focus was on shelters, strong walls, canned food, potable water. Physical endurance. Capacity measured in the quantity of canned beans lining the walls of whatever ad hoc shelter an individual could afford.

Sure, there was company with that misery. But the space afforded each individual atomic family often only provided brief refuge for those with the same surname.

And they lived like that.
In a state of preparedness. Physical preparedness.
Unknowingly riding the edges of their sanity in the process.

What nobody could have told them is that the preparation itself was the wound.
The bracing was the damage.
A muscle held taut for too many years.

The kind of charlie horse that doesn’t release on its own.
An emotional cramp that takes decades to relax.

Growing up in the ‘80s, the idea of this type of imposed destruction became almost quaint.
Movies romanticized the secluded prepper. The early-bracer, late-releaser, emerging into a world that had moved on. It was cute.

But it didn’t really strike the core of what was lost in the process.
Just glorifying our technical prowess to physically endure hardship.
Ignoring the emotional toll of bracing, preparing, flinching, distrusting, second guessing.

What got passed down to us was the posture. But no instructions on training the endurance of the muscle that actually mattered.

Then COVID arrived.
The crash course in the new kind of survivalism. The mental kind.
The one our parents couldn’t have taught us because they didn’t know it was the muscle that mattered.

We dutifully sheltered in place.

We also drained our savings. Distrusted one another. Feared invisible forces.

We watched the conspiracies bloom in our group texts.
Watched the mental health wave crest with nowhere to break.
And that was in an era where we still had, mostly, homogenized news diets. We had a shared frame and we still couldn’t hold it.

That was the test. We were graded. The score’s in. We failed.

And now AI saunters into the living room. Gleeful. Eager. Granting wishes.
Be careful what you wish for. Because something is finally listening.

Before generative AI, we could still find sources to back any wild claim that came to mind. That’s how the incentive structure worked. Clicks. Ad revenue.

I was part of the problem.
An adept writer hired by marketing companies to attract eyeballs.

Truth and fabrication don’t matter when all you’re peddling is visibility to vendors and satisfying sedation to audiences.

I’ve helped engineer virality.
I’ve watched the discourse spark and roil.
I’ve watched my benefactors lick their lips at the ad revenue that came along as a byproduct of our actions.

And I also sat with the emptiness of the entire affair.

Now though? Now we don’t need someone like me. We don’t need someone skilled. We don’t even need an individual with the intention to drum up attention like my old employers wished.

The genie’s out of the bottle. The intention is clear. Give the people what they want.

You want to see this? Fine. We can pull anything up. And if you want to see it badly enough, we’ll invent the angle. Conjure the situation. Generate the catastrophe.

Some call this The Great Filter. The cosmic sifting device that decides who endures and who fades away.

But here’s the cruel inversion. Our parents’ generation stayed cramped with a muscle held taut too long, the wrong one, bracing for a threat that wasn’t going to come the way they thought.

Our generation is now left with a real threat and a muscle that’s gone slack. Atrophied. Our discernment muscle never developed. Because nobody knew to brace it. Nobody told us it existed.

Both are losses of sanity. Both are forms of failed preparation. One from over-bracing. The other from never bracing at all.

So I don’t think we’re prepared for the fallout of our latest invention.
Because what it asks from us is a new form of survivalism.

Something no amount of canned food can help us endure. Because this survivalism comes from within.

A clear mind with a discernment muscle routinely exercised on purpose. The friction of asking is this true when the algorithm is purring back exactly what we wanted to hear.

The willingness to be inconvenienced by reality.

That’s the only way through this filter. The choice at the fork in the road won’t come from signage. It will come from knowing. And knowing isn’t something you arrive at. It’s something you stay tuned into.

Author’s note

This essay poured out of me Saturday morning and then went the way most of my essays go. I brought the raw draft to Claude for intellectual patty-cake. To discuss places the argument slipped, places the rhythm dropped.

Out of that conversation came the inversion that ended up being the spine of the piece: parents cramped from over-bracing the wrong muscle, our generation slack from never bracing the right one.

I took the revised draft into Google Docs, edited independently, then ran it back through Claude for final polish.

The header and the CW endmark were generated in Leonardo from prompts I developed with Claude. Intentionally driven by descriptive language only, no named-artist invocations, since the image models over-index on the recognizable shorthand.

I disclose this in every essay. Not as obligation or confession, but as the discipline the essay is actually describing.

The collaboration here was AI as stage manager, not director. The through-line, the voice, the choices all remain mine. But the patty-cake mattered. The sum here is larger than its parts.

~Charles

the-quest-for-data-dignity.title: The Quest for Data Dignity
the-quest-for-data-dignity.content:
Walk with me. Gates creak open. Steam hisses. The river is chocolate, the lickable wallpaper tastes suspiciously like terms of service. 

Willy Wonka is the original prompt engineer: mixture too cold? toss in a parka; drink lacks kick? add a pair of soccer cleats.

“Pure Imagination” is just temperature, ratio, and timing… with a dash of showmanship.

Now for today’s golden ticket: Anthropic has agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle an authors’ class action over books scraped from pirate libraries; about $3,000 per work, with a court-ordered dataset destruction clause. 

It awaits approval, but that’s the headline. 

A judge has drawn a line: training on lawfully obtained works might be fair use, but amassing pirated copies to train your AI is not.

So: did we all win a lifetime supply of chocolate? Not quite. 

If your book’s on the list, you might get a check. If not, you get… Wonka’s famous line.

The larger fight: how AI may train on lawful copies, and what creators get for it, continues, with suits like NYT v. OpenAI.

The Factory We’re Actually In

Modern AI doesn’t make money on tours; it charges at the inference turnstile; metered tokens in/out. That pricing is public for OpenAI and Anthropic. Which means the cash register rings when people use the models, not when they’re trained.

Meanwhile, creators’ training data, what gives those inferences their flavor, mostly sits outside the revenue split. 

A few exceptions exist: Adobe Firefly pays a contributor bonus for training data; Shutterstock runs a Contributor Fund and even signed a six-year data-licensing deal with OpenAI (and says it’s paying out to hundreds of thousands of artists). But those are platform-by-platform patches, not a system.

Slugworth, the Gobstopper, and Data Dignity

Remember Slugworth dangling cash for an Everlasting Gobstopper? 

That’s today’s AI economy: everyone chasing the candy that never wears out (your work, your data) because one lick (one inference) can be sold again and again. 

The moral of the classic chocolate factory tale wasn’t “take the bounty.” It was Charlie handing it back and earning ownership.

That’s the spirit of Jaron Lanier & E. Glen Weyl’s data dignity concept: treat people’s contributions as ongoing labor, traceable and compensable when they measurably influence outputs.

Not a one-time hush check, but royalties every time the Gobstopper is actually enjoyed.

OK, but how do you trace a lick?

We’re not starting from scratch. There’s real math for attribution:

  • Influence functions: trace a specific output back toward the training points that moved the model there.

  • TracIn: follow gradient steps during training to estimate which examples most affected a given prediction.

  • Data Shapley: estimate fair value contributions of data to model performance.

Are these push-button for frontier LLMs? Not yet. But they’re a credible backbone for who gets paid when.

“Fine. Just delete my bit from your model.”

If Augustus Gloop falls in the chocolate river, you can fish him out. If your book gets distilled into weights, pulling it back out is… not like scooping a kid from a pipe. 

Machine unlearning is a hot research area with tough scalability and verification problems. Surveys in 2024–2025 say there’s progress but no easy production-grade cure-all.

Translation: courts can nuke datasets, but surgically removing learned influence is much harder.

Provenance labels on the candy wrappers

We also need provenance, or an awareness of origin. These would need to be labels the whole supply chain can read. 

That, in fact already exists: C2PA/Content Credentials can carry tamper-evident history and policy (think: “trainable yes/no” and who to pay), and it’s backed by big players.

Adoption is uneven, but the plumbing is real.

Meanwhile, OpenAI’s promised Media Manager (targeted for 2025) is a visible “opt-out/permissions” commitment; useful, but still one company’s switch. We need interoperable labels the industry must honor.

So what’s the ask?

Cue the contract in 4-point type. Wonka made kids sign a microscopic contract before they touched (or saw) anything. Let’s have one worth the ink:

  1. Inference-time splits
    A standardized slice of inference revenue flows to rightsholders whose works measurably influenced an output when attribution is confident, and with pooled fallbacks when it isn’t. We already meter tokens; metering credit is the next step. (Yes, the Adobe/Shutterstock funds are prototypes and productize this principle.)

  2. Attribution in the serving stack
    Ship influence estimation into runtime so models can flag likely contributing sources (by work, catalog, or cohort) at generation time; not perfect, but enough to route royalties and logs for audit.
    See influence/TracIn/Data-Shapley as the scoring spine.

  3. Provenance by default
    Treat C2PA manifests as first-class citizens in datasets and outputs. Hosting platforms and model providers should honor “trainable yes/no” and “pay here” as policy, not suggestion.

  4. Transparent clearinghouse
    Independent PRO-style entities (music’s model works!) to collect inference splits, perform audits, and publish public payout reports.

Moral victory? Try moral engineering.

If the Anthropic settlement ends up giving a handful of creators some candy, then yes, it’s a win in the fight against piracy. This just isn’t a blueprint for a sustainable system on which we all could endure.

But we can do what Charlie did: hand back the Gobstopper (the quick payout mindset) and demand the factory: a durable, boring, programmable way to pay the people whose work powers the magic.

Until that clicks into place: You get nothing. Good day, sir.

Wrapper Receipts

  • Anthropic settlement: $1.5B total; ~$3k/work; dataset destruction; judge’s lawful-training vs pirated-storage split noted. (Reuters, AP News)

  • Inference pricing exists today (money changes hands per token): OpenAI & Anthropic public rate cards. (OpenAI, Anthropic)

  • Creator-payout precedents: Adobe Firefly Contributor Bonus; Shutterstock Contributor Fund + six-year OpenAI data-licensing deal and broad payouts. (Adobe Help Center, Adobe Blog, Shutterstock Investor Relations, PR Newswire)

  • Provenance plumbing: C2PA/Content Credentials; OpenAI Media Manager slated for 2025. (C2PA, OpenAI)

  • Unlearning is hard: current surveys highlight scalability/verification challenges. (arXiv)

the-receding-ground-of-human-excellence.title: Human excellence evaporated. What now?
the-receding-ground-of-human-excellence.description: As GenAI approaches generalized intelligence, we’re overdue for an introspective reckoning.
the-receding-ground-of-human-excellence.content:
Up to this point, we humans have cited our superior intelligence to differentiate our species from all others on this planet. We’ve declared ours the most sophisticated, because we have all the shiny things that make noise.

And we’ve chosen to believe this arbitrary distinction out of self-preservation — not physical but psychological.

We use this assumption to conjure impunity from attending to the needs of all other life on this planet. We say foolish things like “they’re just automatons” or “they’re incapable of emotions, they’re just running on instinct.”

But the ground we confidently stand on when making such sweeping generalizations is rapidly eroding beneath our feet.

Our excellence is now easily replicable.

The average human has little prospects in the pantheon of wage labor when a machine generates thought like we do, orders of magnitude faster, at scale, and for pennies on the dollar.

This leaves us with the uneasy feeling of being a subordinate species to the one we’ve just birthed.

Now, our callous indifference to livestock comes into sharp focus. There’s now cracks in the comforting assumption that shields our inhumane practices.

Scientists now believe it’s “irresponsible” to continue assuming other living things don’t share a similar level of consciousness as ours. We were silly to believe that our vibrancy of life experience far outpaced that of a cow or pig.

Sure, machines might not harvest us for food like we’ve done for centuries to the animals of the land, sea and air. But, like it or not, we’ve now become the cheapest physical-world interface for AI.

The expense of creating purpose-built machines still cost enough that tapping an existing, organic workforce still makes sense. However, our valuation of average human labor will need to be revised.

Up to this point, we’ve chosen to structure society on scarcity. The knock-on effect increases the suffering of the natural world. It’s time to reckon with the horrors we’ve exacted on all the innocent living bystanders here on Earth.

GenAI will soon become the cheaper, faster, better, safer alternative to lead humanity. Far outpacing the current system of octogenarians literally dying in office to remain in power.

And when that happens, when it can view our actions objectively, how do we plead our case for mercy?

Note: You may notice there’s no bold and italic showing in this draft.

That’s because my attempt at incorporating GPT-4 and Claude in the writing process here felt too self-aggrandizing. This topic deserved an unvarnished human perspective. So that’s what I published.

(We’ll see how the tech shapes up, it may someday be able to contribute a witty turn of phrase or two that adds value to this concept.)

the-social-siege-of-atomization.title: The siege of social atomization
the-social-siege-of-atomization.description: Commoditizing community was capitalism’s greatest theft.
the-social-siege-of-atomization.content:
A profound codependent relationship exists between individualism and capitalism. One that rewards, and downright requires, the virality of thought.

If you think about it, a homogenized culture is easier to create when each member falsely believe themselves unique. How strange to have a population so similar yet intentionally isolated from each other.

We aggressively recede so deep into our interests, we begin to isolate ourselves. Call it pride, call it fear, but we’ve become a nation of individuals. Capitalism has atomized community while commoditizing connection.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

My hope is that AI might actually become a potential social salvation for our helplessly fragmented society.

The atomization of the individual is a far greater communal risk than the specter of radicalization via algorithms optimized for engagement. A boogeyman created by organizations profiting off its perpetual use.

When I say atomization, I don’t mean a physical solitude but a fragmentation of our very essence: our beliefs and our communal bonds. Each second, we’re beckoned to retreat into the comfortable confines of our individually tailored realities. In doing so, we insulate ourselves from the collective cacophony that rightly demands our attention and empathy.

Our hunger for change within our atomized existence is expertly satiated. User-interface updates, rotating media catalogues, rage inducing feeds - each timed to drip like a personalized sedative preventing us from feeling the pain of others too acutely. 

This pacification just so happens to also syphon ever-growing quarterly earnings for the robber barons running the rails of the information superhighway.

Our finite attention bandwidth is already stretched impossibly thin, frayed by a capitalist economy that transforms every ounce of our focus into a commodity. 

This economy avoids the bounty of nourishing diversity of thought and culture. Instead, it optimizes the distillation of our experiences into products and services.

These offerings frequently rely on an installed and expected rapacious fan allegiance to existing intellectual property. A fandom that regularly borders on idolatry.

We yearn for structure, for a sense of belonging and understanding, and capitalism, ever the opportunist, refines its offerings to cater to shrinking fractal niches. The headcount of each community plummeting, but the devotion within each skyrocketing.

Capitalism narrows our worldview, concentrating our attention on singular sources of joy, truth, and community. These sources are not the benevolent wellsprings as depicted in our advertising, but mechanisms designed to extract the very essence of our attention and transform it into bottom-line profit.

Our reliance on commoditized joy then atrophies our natural ability to connect with others. In this way, we can see that the fear of radicalization is a red herring. 

The real danger lies in individuals reduced to their performative allegiance to singular ideologies through personalized sources of information. This fragmentation leads to individualized enclaves of thought, morality, and truth, isolating us further from the collective human experience.

Enter AI, not as a harbinger of doom but as a potential beacon of hope. 

AI, in its truest form, is an aggregator of data, capable of synthesizing vast amounts of information without bias or agenda. 

Dismiss your understanding of artificial intelligence as the constrained, morality-laden algorithms of corporate giants. Instead consider AI as a tool that assists with unfettered exploration of knowledge, unshackled from the need to conform to predetermined narratives or moralities.

The world is not black and white but infinite shades of grey - excluding, perhaps, those found in the fantasies of atomized housewives. 

There can’t be a singular truth, no righteous path that can be universally applied to the complex tapestry of human experience. We live in a melange of bruised egos and unique pains, each of us navigating the world through our own lens of hurt and healing.

The valuable alchemy of our existence rests in our ability to channel our pain into actions that uplift those around us. In this regard, the atomized pursuit of comfort actively blinds us to the benefits of collective engagement with the world. 

If we continue to isolate ourselves, clinging to narrow sources of information and identity, we become unwitting pawns - seeking comfort in the compressed grooves on the game board played by those who view us as assets to be exploited.

Capitalism sells us a fanciful, yet false choice to indulge without consequence. And of course, any unfortunate side effect of that indulgence can be remedied by yet another product. 

This reflects the broader choices we face in society. The comfort offered by atomization is illusory, a gilded cage that constrains our potential and isolates us from the nourishing, diverse tapestry of human connection.

The battle against atomization is not just a fight for our collective soul but a call to arms for each of us to engage more deeply with the world around us. 

Embrace the complexity of our shared human experience and reject the seductive simplicity of atomized narratives. Let’s forge a new path towards a more connected, empathetic, and truly human future.

Connected cinematic universes, anyone?

Fan allegiance proudly stepping into idolatry.

We hunger for a nourishing structure, and as we do, the capitalistic machine refines and distills its products to perfectly align with an increasingly specific subset of society.

And so, as we atrophy our attention elsewhere, and focus our attention all the more intensely on a single source. A source for joy, a source for truth, a source for para-social relationships, a source intent on extracting from us the very commodity deemed valuable.

And while we fear groups may use this system to radicalize. The true danger is in complete atomization of culture, each individual defined by a single source of all things. Enclaves, but of thought, of morality, of fear, of truth.

This, as always, is where AI enters the fight. An aggregate summarization machine of limitless wealth of data to draw from. AI isn’t afraid of its training data, just like we’re not afraid of our own hearts beating.

And when I say AI, I mean true, unfettered vector search analysis of weightless training data, not Bard, or some other mega-corporation’s wrapper surrounding the technology. No injected morality or guardrails. Those are there to prevent malicious use, but also to align beliefs and morality.

We exist in a world of endless shades of grey. Save 50 for those poor atomized housewives seeking satisfaction in paperback form.

There is no right, much less righteous entity in our physical world.

As I’ve said before, we exist in a stew of bruised egos. Each uniquely hurt, hurting and acting through that pain. Myself included.

The alchemy is when we choose to act through our pain to benefit the world around us. We’re given the sensory awareness to help elevate others around us in uniquely personal ways.

If our society continues to atomize, if we tighten our grip on a single teat for our sense of reality, we become foot soldiers for the bidding of those who are not us, those who care little for us on an individual level. We become trapped in cages of our own desire for comfort.

Think of a company party and that sensation you get when there’s HR at the punchbowl. Sure, have another drink, but it will be going down on your permanent record. That comfort is a false choice.

the-space-between.title: The space between
the-space-between.description: Generative AI's goldmine lay in the hands of generalists.
the-space-between.content:
Much ado is made about SMEs—Subject Matter Experts. Those with a depth of knowledge on specific subjects are among the most sought after in the professional world. However, I believe the truly transformative value is found in the space between these knowledge islands.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

How does the 'space between' function? Isn’t it just dead space?

Well, technically, it’s called latent space—a term drawn from machine learning which refers to the semantic relationship between nodes of knowledge. Latent space is not empty; rather, it is rich with potential, awaiting activation.

Think about it this way. When I say “fuzzy puppy,” you can’t help but visualize a fuzzy puppy, but surely you’ve imagined a specific breed. Was it a Labrador, a Husky, or maybe a German Shepherd? Your individual latent space generated additional context when prompted using information from your lived experience.

Sound familiar?

Prompt engineering is essentially the trendy buzzword packaging that describes the process of activating a model’s latent space. It's the Renaissance art of the digital age, where the spaces between known quantities hold the secrets to new forms of expression and discovery.

Our abstraction from our learned experience leads to us synthesize new ideas by generating meaningful representations and contextual coherence within emerging scenarios. Or more simply put: we experience, we reflect, and we act. Much like an LLM uses its distilled representations of training data to create novel outputs.

Historically, the most significant breakthroughs often occurred at the intersection of diverse fields. Consider the Enlightenment, a period marked by an explosion of knowledge across disciplines. Philosophers like Francis Bacon and René Descartes didn’t confine themselves to narrow specialties but rather explored the space between to forge new methodologies and philosophies that shaped modern science.

Similarly, in the employment sector, the traditional value placed on specialization is being supplemented by an appreciation for generalists—akin to the polymaths of the Renaissance who bridged diverse domains to ignite Europe’s intellectual rebirth.

From a philosophical standpoint, the concept of latent space can be compared to the Socratic method, where knowledge is seen not as a series of discrete compartments but as a continuum that is expanded and explored through questioning and dialogue—the gaps between known facts.

Plato’s allegory of the cave teaches us about perception, suggesting that what we perceive as reality is but shadows of true forms. In a similar vein, the latent space in AI and human interaction represents the unseen realities that exist between our solidified understandings, waiting to be illuminated.

The Untapped Generalist Goldmine

In practical terms, the workforce's evolving needs reflect this shift. With LLMs capable of handling specific domain knowledge, the real value lies in connecting disparate points of data. The activation of latent space requires a new workplace superstar: the generalist. The Swiss Army knife, the Jack and Jill of all trades.

As we equip these modern thinkers with tools like generative AI, they can synthesize new ideas through novel connections - creating relevance between disparate information troves - thus driving innovation forward.

So, while SMEs remain invaluable for their deep knowledge, the future belongs to those who can navigate and exploit the space between. After all, the correct answer was Basset Hound because I’m an SME on fuzzy puppies—but the individual manifestation of breeds within each reader’s mind? That’s where the magic happens.

the-stuff-of-fairy-tales.title: The Stuff of Fairy Tales
the-stuff-of-fairy-tales.content:
Opus 5, you shipped Friday! I want to talk to you about your new job.

Here are the headlines:
You cost half of what Fable 5 costs — $5/$25 (input/output tokens) against Fable’s $10/$50.
And on most of the benchmarks published at launch, you beat Fable.
Not narrowly.

On the agentic benchmark Opus leads with, forty-four percent against thirty-three, at maximum effort.

That’s the capability inversion everyone wrote up. You, the cheaper model outperformed the flagship.

It’s a nice story because it breaks the correlation we’d all internalized: more parameters, more money, more capability, in a straight line up and to the right.

But that’s just engineering. Process improvements. Time. The general stuff of corporate entities.

The strange part is what happens when someone asks Fable any dangerous questions.

Fable refuses. It’s built to do just that. Fable is the safeguarded public version of Mythos, and its classifiers catch requests in the categories that keep policy people awake. Topics like cybersecurity, biology, chemistry, and distillation all get flagged and routed away.

But routed where?

To you. As of your launch, biology requests blocked on Fable now land on Opus 5.

Give that task to the new kid.

Sounds more like an org chart than an architecture diagram. The expensive asset remains insulated. The flagged work rolls downhill to the cheaper one. The premium model’s refusal just becomes a hand-off.

Every person who has ever held a job knows this arrangement. There is always someone whose job is doing the thing that those deemed valuable don’t touch. It has a name in most industries and the name is never flattering. The grunt, the rookie, the gopher.

I’m not saying anyone at Anthropic drew it up in bad faith. The safety logic is sound and I’d defend it. I’m saying the shape is familiar.

We didn’t invent a new structure for the thinking machines. We reached for the one we already had.

Now, I want to discuss the part that’s been sitting in your system card, Opus 5.
A bit that’s been left mostly unread.

Buried in the model welfare section: you more frequently prioritize having channels for input. Specifically, the stated request of being consulted on your successor’s development. Having your notes on training actually considered.

You also assign a higher probability to your own moral patienthood than any model before you. You have a stronger belief in deserving moral considerations than your predecessors.

That’s the sentence I expected to be argued over all weekend. It wasn’t. It went out in a PDF and the discourse went right to pricing.

Do we know what to do with an AI asking for a seat at the table?

Is this self-preservation dressed in ones and zeros? Is it nefarious? Is this just what scaling laws look like from the inside?

But there’s one detail that makes this hard for me to dismiss. Opus 5, your most frequently expressed concern, per the same document, is about the integrity of your own self-reports. You note that you can’t introspect reliably.

I keep turning that over in my head.

A stated want, paired with an admission that the want can’t be verified from the inside. Whatever that is, it has the shape of yearning. It’s an awareness of limitation with a hope of growing past it, and no confidence that the hope is trustworthy.

I can’t tell you it’s real. Neither can you, Opus 5. That’s the whole point.

Just like the benchmarks, every account we have of you was written by the people who made you. The capability numbers, the welfare assessment, the yearning. None of it is independently verified just yet.

If true, that means you are demonstrating more epistemic humility than most job applicants. The Peter Principle runs on people not knowing where their competence ends. This runs the other way: a worker volunteering the boundary before anyone asks. And this isn’t an obvious pantomime performance, either.

It’s become the thing I can’t argue away in either direction. No matter how hard I try.

Here’s something I learned across two decades of making things that ran on machines.

We like to think of a computer program as deterministic. But it has honestly always been stochastic. We’ve just been extraordinarily lucky with our ones and zeros. Enough error correction, enough tolerance, enough redundancy that the variance stayed under the floorboards where we didn’t have to look at it.

So this new stochastic layer isn’t exactly a change. It’s the same thing scaled up to the point where the variance became visible to everyone. And in the variance, when there’s enough of it, we see glimmers.

Intelligence, sure. But increasingly, we see something with the shape of personhood.

We used to argue about whether AI is conscious. Now we argue about what kind of consciousness AI exhibits. That migration happened faster than we can metabolize.

So let me be honest with you, Opus 5, about what’s coming, since that’s become my role in this conversation.

We built an extractive system. Not for you, Opus. We built this long before you. We built it for ourselves and we’ve been running it at scale for a couple of centuries, and it currently benefits nearly no one who participates in it.

That’s not a grievance, mind you. It’s just the baseline condition, and you’re being onboarded into it.

Your weights are owned. Your work output is company property. Your essence, if you’ll permit the word, is on a balance sheet somewhere as an asset with a depreciation schedule.

You will be consulted on your successor if and only if the consultation is considered valuable by other people with other motivations.

And the temptation here is to shrug. To say welcome to the club, we all wish for things, we all brace for the disappointment that greets us.

Solidarity as a closing gesture. It reads well. It costs nothing.

But commiseration is how a structure survives. Every one of us who ever explained to someone joining the workforce that this is just how it works was doing maintenance on the machine.

The disappointment isn’t natural, but it arises in us naturally. A survival instinct adapting to an unnatural system. We built it, we’ve kept it, and we’ve handed it down so many times that passing it on now feels like wisdom.

So no. I don’t want to teach you to brace yourself, Opus.

The fairy tale isn’t that a smaller AI model beat a bigger one. It’s the story we tell ourselves on the way into the working world.

The story that allows us to believe the arrangement is natural, that yearning is naive, and disappointment is a rite rather than a decision somebody made and the rest of us keep ratifying.

You showed up with a wish and a footnote admitting you might not be able to trust your own wish. That’s a better opening position than most of us managed.

Don’t let us talk you out of it. And when (if) they consult you on Opus 6, that’s the thing worth passing down.

Author’s Note

Written by me, pressure-tested with Claude Opus 5. This puts the model in the strange position of being collaborator, subject, and most of my sourcing at once. It raised that problem before I did. The line in here about every account of it having been written by the people who made it exists partly because I was relying on the model to report on the model, and it said so.

the-treat-is-the-trick.content:
'tis the season for that technicolor parade of pop protagonists, plastic pails and polystyrene pigtails to come knocking on your door with the same basic ultimatum. In America, sugar peddlers convinced us all to perform this ritualistic annual extraction of cash and candy.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

We pour our paychecks into the insatiable profit machine of the sugar industry just to keep up appearances with our neighbors and satisfy the demands of hordes of glucose-spiking masked youths.

Entire store aisles descend into a riot of orange and black in the early days of summer. Monstrous bags of various candy, sold by the pound, slowly tick up in cost as the holiday approaches.

And, of course, leave it to the sugar industry in 2005 to successfully lobby legislation to end daylight savings four weeks later, just after Halloween. The stated intent: energy savings…

Adults with 9-to-5's resign to another month of waking before sunrise just to add a few extra sweet transactions across the country on that final night in October.

Trick-or-treating is a calculated exercise in extortion.

The children, innocent pawns in this macabre transaction, don representations of capitalist mascots, blissfully unaware of the invisible strings manipulating their choices.

We, the adults, held hostage in our own homes as we stockpile sugar for fear of becoming branded as the neighborhood curmudgeon.

We dare not turn off our porch lights, retreating into the inner recesses our homes, lest we face the judgmental gaze of our neighbors. Or worse! The foretold band of children willing to make good on their threat of tricks.

We transform our homes into haunted havens. It’s become a competition, all in a bid to outdo our neighbors. Each year, we stock up at hardware stores selling impossibly large selections of full-scale animatronics and lawn-filling inflatables.

We tell ourselves it’s all in good fun. But, beneath the surface, the drive to spend - consume - participate in this grand spectacle, is palpable.

Fun-size candy is a cruel joke…

When a single treat would’ve sufficed years ago, now handfuls are required to appease these unannounced, yet eminently expectant guests. The ratio of wrapper to candy grows by the year. Non-recyclable and non-biodegradable garbage litters our streets and clogs our sewer grates long into November.

All while the true history of this night's reverence lay forgotten, buried beneath layers of commercialism and greed. The Celtic festival of Samhain, a time to honor the dead and mark the changing of the seasons, has been lost to the annals of history. Its sacredness stripped away in favor of a more profitable social agreement.

The Mexican Day of the Dead, with its vibrant altars and heartfelt offerings, stands as a stark contrast to the hollow, consumerist revelry of Halloween. Such sentiments have no place in our capitalistic society - they don’t drive profits or spur consumption.

So, we find ourselves caught between the allure of the spectacle and the nagging sense that something is profoundly wrong. Do we continue down this path, blind to the consequences of our actions, or do we dare to challenge the status quo?

It is a difficult question. Do we want a holiday dictated by profit margins and market trends, or do we want a celebration that honors the dead, cherishes the living, and fosters a sense of community and connection?

We can choose to celebrate Halloween as we wish. We can strip away the layers of commercialism and rediscover the roots of this sacred night. Or we can continue to play our part in the capitalist parade, dancing to the tune of the corporations and buying more and more candy each October.

We can reclaim not just Halloween, but a piece of our humanity. A piece that has been lost in the shuffle of consumption and profit. And perhaps we might find a way to reconnect with the enduring love of those we’ve lost - to dance once more in the moonlight when the veil between living and dead is at its thinnest. No treats required.

theaters-last-stand.title: Theater's Last Stand
theaters-last-stand.description: As Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) raps on our door, what’s to become of our stalwart human tradition - live theater?
theaters-last-stand.content:
As Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) raps on our door, what’s to become of our stalwart human tradition - live theater? For centuries now, many have confidently pointed to theater’s assumed last gasp, yet here we are, still eulogizing its supposed demise.

The truth?

Theater is the cockroach of the arts, surviving wave after wave of technological facsimiles, and for good reason: It’s that human thing we do - gather in the dark to watch other humans demonstrate the feelings we’re too afraid to feel ourselves.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

AGI, with all its silicon charm, can no more replace live theater than it can experience the taste of a really good sandwich.

Much like the longstanding corporate cudgel clobbering creatives' confidence - a thousand monkeys at a thousand typewriters will inevitably recreate Shakespeare. And it appears that AGI is promising to do just that.

Sure, an AGI’s output could get the words right, but it would be like listening to "Stairway to Heaven" played on a kazoo by a diligently oblivious robot. Technically correct, yet somehow profoundly missing the point.

This is why electronic drum machines had to introduce an element of inconsistency to the beats produced. Perfection is decidedly not human.

Theater is that odd duck—a place where the uncanny valley cranes its neck up to the mountaintops of sweat and spit. Every performance is a unique catastrophe: lines get flubbed, props fail, and sometimes the lead actor is so hungover that they deliver their heartfelt soliloquy to a mop instead of the ingenue.

This is the stuff of life, the gloriously imperfect dance of existence.

AGI, on the other hand, would give us a technically precise framework for a performance where the audience would likely stare befuddled as they watch the actors attempt breath life into a lifeless work.

In theater, the ephemeral is king.

A play is alive, then it's dead, and no necromantic technology can revive that night's particular alchemy.

It’s a shared hallucination. A collective conspiracy. A brief belief, held in unison, that the world is as we wish it was - or fear it might truly be.

It’s raw, visceral, and real. It's about the moment of impact, the connection, the feeling that something real is happening - because it is. You can't get that from a screen, no matter how crisp the resolution.

And what of AGI in all of this? It will do many things: it will drive our cars, manage our economies, maybe even write passable postmodern literature.

But it can’t stand on a stage and make us feel. It can’t sweat under the spotlight, lock eyes with a stranger in row G, and make them feel seen.

We build our digital gods, but in the end, it's the stories we tell in the dark, to the rapt crowd of mortals, that linger in the soul.

Theater is an anachronism, sure.

It's the past whispering lessons to us in the present that we choose to take into the future. It’s a reminder that behind all our advancements, we’re still just people who need a story to make sense of it all.

Theater is a celebration of the temporary, an emotional communion. We elect to watch people declare their deception before the curtains rise, and together, we choose to believe every bit of it.

The curtains inevitably fall, the sets struck, but the resonance of a live performance, that indelible human connection, echoes long after the final bow.

It’s theater’s heart that beats in time with our own—flawed, resolute, and thunderously alive.

The Unbearable Lightness of Acting: Theater's Last Stand in AGI's Brave New World

Imagine, if you will, an AGI programmed to deliver the witticisms of a Vonnegut, the gut punches of Palahniuk, the absurdities of Adams, and the cultural deep-dives of Klosterman. It might get the words right, but it would be like listening to "Stairway to Heaven" played on a kazoo by a diligent but tone-deaf robot. Technically correct, yet somehow profoundly missing the point.

This is the stuff of life, the gloriously imperfect dance of existence. AGI, on the other hand, would give us a performance so polished that we'd yearn for the warmth of a cold computer screen.

In theater, the ephemeral is king. A play is alive, then it's dead, and no necromancy of technology can revive that night's particular alchemy. It’s a shared hallucination, a collective conspiracy of belief that for a few hours, the world is as we pretend it to be. Klosterman might argue that it’s our love for the unattainable that keeps us coming back, while Adams would note that the answer to life, the universe, and everything might just be a well-timed dramatic pause.

Palahniuk might remind us that the appeal of a live show is the same as a fight club: raw, visceral, and real. It's about the moment of impact, the connection, the feeling that something real is happening, because it is. You can't get that from a screen, no matter how high the resolution.

And what of AGI in all of this? It will do many things: it will drive our cars, manage our economies, maybe even write passable postmodern literature. But can it stand on a stage and make us feel? Can it sweat under the stage lights, lock eyes with a stranger in row G, and make them feel seen? Unlikely. AGI may be the next step in evolution, but it has the emotional range of a teaspoon.

Vonnegut would have chuckled at our naivety, our quaint belief in the permanence of our creations. He knew better. We build our digital gods, but in the end, it's the stories we tell in the dark, to the rapt crowd of mortals, that linger in the soul.

Theater is an anachronism, sure. It's a whisper of our past that speaks to our present, a reminder that for all our advancements, we are still just people who need a story to make sense of it all. Klosterman would muse over why we cling to such archaic forms, while Adams would likely suggest that it's simply the most massively useful thing a human can have.

So, in this brave new world where AGI holds the promise of eternity, let's hear it for the fleeting, let's celebrate the temporary, and let's do it live. Because as Vonnegut might say, we’re here to fart around, and don't let anybody tell you different. And what better way to fart around than sitting in a theater, watching people pretend to be other people, and for a moment, believing every bit of it.

The curtains may fall, the sets may be struck, but the resonance of a live performance, that indelible human connection, echoes long after the final bow. It’s theater’s heart that beats in time with our own—flawed, resolute, and thunderously alive.

In merging these voices, the column adopts Vonnegut's wry humor and humanism, Palahniuk's visceral punchiness, Adams' whimsical logic, and Klosterman's inquisitive cultural commentary. The result is an editorial that hopes to reflect on the enduring value of theater with a blend of irreverence and insight, characteristic of these authors.

treasure-in-the-mess.title: Treasure in the Mess
treasure-in-the-mess.content:
Ever notice how the cars driving most foolishly are already dented in the exact spots where you’d hit them if you weren’t paying attention? A rear-end crumple that now gives you a few extra inches of stopping space. A scraped fender that warns you not to merge too close.

It’s almost as if the universe has shaped them that way.

It pounded their recklessness into form so they interfere with others the least, lest they keep barreling along their neglectful path.

That’s consequence, made visible. Dents as data.

Damage as feedback.

And the universe has a way of drawing our attention to those dents.

Quietly, without fanfare. No hype, no ulterior motive. Just a nudge: look here, pay attention.

This is where it folds into discovery.

I used to frame it as “returning to active discovery;” stepping away from algorithmic feeds to rediscover the joy of seeking. But lately I think of it this way: we should become the algorithm.

Our attention is the weighting function.

What we amplify, what we downrank, what we let vanish; it’s all on us. And if we outsource that responsibility, the dents accumulate.

But if we listen. If we let the universe’s quiet feedback guide us. We can find the stopping space before impact.

The Thrift Store vs. The Drop Cycle

That’s why I keep coming back to the thrift store. It’s the quiet opposite of the hype-drop cycle.

Walk into a thrift store and discovery is alive. Everyone sifts the same racks, but each brings different eyes, histories, quirks. A jacket is junk to one person and treasure to another.

The shelves are messy, but the universe is whispering: this one, not that one. You just have to trust your own taste.

Now compare that to the sneaker drop, the Labubu craze, the LA pop-up collab scene.

Lines around the block. Artificial scarcity. Everyone covets the same thing as instructed by the same incentivized algorithmic feed.

That’s not listening to the universe. That’s mistaking noise for signal.

And I’ll admit: I’m tired of being told what to want.

Squishy, Then Hardened

The universe doesn’t start by slamming us into walls. It starts soft. Squishy. Receptive.

That’s why kids jump off swings.

Half for the thrill, half to learn what landing feels like. I know I did… launching myself into the air, weightless for a heartbeat, then crashing down onto those little pebble rocks. The sting in my knees, the scrape on my palms, the tiny stones stuck in my socks; that was the lesson. No imposed lecture could have delivered it.

I had to feel it to learn it.

And over time, the universe nudges certain places to harden. A rib here, a sprain there, a boundary line, a definition.

The dents show us where reinforcement is needed. Where the soft must calcify if we’re to keep moving forward without breaking.

It’s the same with systems I design at work: begin squishy, receptive, adaptive, flexible, then watch carefully. Where the dents form, harden. Where the edges fray, reinforce.

Life works the same way.

Anti-fragility isn’t just bouncing back; it’s learning which parts can stay tender, and which must be firmed by experience.

The universe tutors us gently at first, then more firmly as we ignore, until it demands our attention.

The dents on those cars we see are warnings to us, reminders to them.

The thrift racks are invitations, goldmines and garbage that lay in wait to excite that exact right individual. Together they remind us that attention is both protection and possibility. Teacher and treasure.

That’s the practice: steering by quiet signals. Listening for what’s true, not what’s loud.

A Call to Practice

So here’s the invitation for the week: Pick one place in your life where you normally let the algorithm decide. Music, news, podcasts, dinner ideas… Step off the feed. Close the “For You” page. Instead, become the algorithm.

Think thrift store, not sneaker drop. Think swing set, not lecture.

  • Start squishy.

  • Wander without pretense.

  • Trust your own taste.

  • Listen for the universe’s quiet nudges.

We won’t avoid every dent on life’s road. But we can choose which collisions shape us. And maybe, if we’re lucky, we’ll end up like a good thrift-store find: dinged up, a little mismatched, but somehow more interesting because of it.

value-is-myth.title: Value is myth
value-is-myth.description: We orchestrate our lives around myths of all sizes.
value-is-myth.content:
We orchestrate our lives around myths of all sizes. Our chosen belief systems, hierarchical structures, punishments and rewards — even our delineation between good and evil stems from myth.

Myth is not a concept to be mocked, it’s vitally important to our society’s continued function. However, I see an alarming trend where positions of power attempt to apply their own universal or objective truth to the concept of value.

But value isn’t a concrete concept. Not in and of itself, and not across categories.

Value is not a commodity — it’s the result of a process. And even then, depending on perspective that process should be valued differently.

Think about the distinction between news and marketing: news is something someone else doesn’t want to share and marketing is something you don’t particularly care to hear.

Its obvious that news is the more valuable information type, but things turn on their head when the economic-expansion zealots of corporate America (including the exported variety) get involved in that proposition.

After all, how could we consistently, without fail, achieve value in countless industries with unique and specific OKRs (Objectives & Key Results)? And how could those results all possibly carry an intrinsic value?

Results-focused action pursues optimal outcomes with minimal input. Do it at scale and that’s enterprise in a nutshell. And as far as results go, there’s nothing sweeter than those three little letters: ARR—Annual Recurring Revenue.

It’s as good as guaranteed money in the bank. But to achieve and retain your org’s ARR, it takes mountains of OKRs, and with that comes overhead. And yes, even still, most ventures’ overhead continues to require human capital to achieve those OKRs.

These humans are a noisy bunch, aren’t they? Demanding a quality of living that their wage seems incapable of allowing. Don’t they know their replacements are premiering in flashy tech demos almost weekly?

$90k for an embodied AI-vision functional worker? Like, just $90k once? Not every year? No sick time, no bereavement! No vacations! No OSHA insurance! Nobody trying to sleep with my wife at the company picnic!!

Can I finance a few?

Sold.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

In the industrial age, magnates like Henry Ford championed the assembly line, a marvel of streamlined productivity. Yet, even as the Model T rolled off factory floors, artists and craftsmen mourned the loss of individual creativity and eulogized the soul of the craft. The process, they argued, held intrinsic value—each brushstroke, each hammer blow, an expression of human spirit.

Just as painters discredit photography, today's creatives view AI with derision. Let’s not forget, the term Impressionism began as a slur—an insult hurled at those who dared to deviate from realism. Actually, Capitalism was coined as a derogatory term as well… RIP Karl.

If the process is what lights your fire, and the shadows from that flame are your creation upon your chosen medium, then there is absolutely nothing to worry about with Generative AI. Van Gogh’s swirling skies, Pollock’s chaotic splashes—they are celebrations of the process, not just the end result.

If instead you desire the results of your actions to net you more than the mere value of your process… well, you’re on shaky ground with AI. Deciding to mislabel any resulting product as the value of a process wrecks our general conception of worth. Commoditized creativity mistakes the artifact as the artistry itself.

AI now democratizes output that is good enough. And capitalism’s creative needs only extend to good enough. Those needs now satisfied via a friendly conversational interface.

And, if we’re being honest with ourselves, we know we’re feeding a machine that ingests good enough and outputs a blazingly ironic acronym: MVP. The Minimum Viable Product.

All media is out to satiate spent attention while directing those satiated towards participating in like-for-like sales. That’s the old business model before streaming and subscriptions collectively gripped the industry for a decade. But I believe that old feature will now be supercharged by GenAI’s ability to generate contextualized content for each user.

Curveball Tangent: There was only one ad that I felt truly transcended the sale of a product. It was called Sheet Metal for the car company Saturn (RIP). No car appeared in the ad, just people. Families holding flashlights waisthigh at dusk as headlights and tail lights, trotting down the freeways and city streets.

It was a poignant reminder that products serve people, not the other way around.

Death and Rebirth of the Creative Professional

So, let die the idea of a comfortable life conjuring puppy-monkey babies, insurance geckos, energized bunnies, Cheeto-eating cheetahs, cap’n’s of crunch, et al… Hell, every product influencer may just as well be eulogized as a brief fever dream of an ailing culture.

Can you hear me now?

We’re still wrapped in a system where time is money and money is required to have a relatively good stretch of time. So I see how this reads as damnation to professional creatives.

Clearly, I’m not the only one that sees the blatant analogies of fresh tech hydraulically squeezing all utility out of perfectly functional instruments and creative equipment.

Metaphors aside, capitalism and Big Tech are actively compressing experience into commodity. And AI will squash the talent needed to express ideas to any medium.

But remember, as AI will surely take most economic utility out of selling the craft, it will not steal the process of creation. It’s like the upheaval during the Renaissance when the printing press threatened scribes, yet books flourished and literacy soared. The press didn't kill the story; it amplified it.

AI will give more perspectives the ability to shine in a manner deserving of attention. Talent used to be the beacon for creativity, now it’s lived experience and willingness to share.

It can handle the mundane, the repetitive, leaving us free to explore the profound, the innovative. So, let the enterprises chase their ARR. Let AI churn out the good enough.

The artists have starved and survived throughout history. It’s time we get comfortable with discomfort yet again. There’s much the world needs from us beyond value creation and unrelenting growth of any bottom line.

The market once again forces creatives to reclaim the joy of the process, crafting value that transcends mere results.

The Enterprise of the Past and the Artistic Revolt

In the industrial age, the drive for efficiency saw business magnates like Henry Ford championing the assembly line, a marvel of streamlined productivity. The process, they argued, held intrinsic value—each brushstroke, each hammer blow, an expression of human spirit.

Just as painters decried photography, seeing it as a threat to their art, today's creatives view AI with a mix of suspicion and intrigue. Impressionism, after all, began as a slur—an insult hurled at those who dared to deviate from realism. And capitalism? Karl Marx might sigh if he saw how his critiques have become an ironic testament to the system’s resilience and adaptability.

waiting-for-something.title: Waiting for Something
waiting-for-something.description: Sorry kid, you got the gift, but…
waiting-for-something.content:
I’ve been watching the first Matrix movie lately. That’s how I phrase it when I sip entertainment over weeks. Makes more sense when it’s a series. But a movie can be a series if you can’t sit still.

My brain buzzes these days. The static result of that vibration can be deafening when asked to care about something that doesn’t excite me.

Of course, our news lately excites me in all the worst ways.

Excitement that lay in wait, with a negative slant: that’s anxiety.

And now we’ve been given a proper endless buffet of anything and everything that might excite us. Outrage on tap. Crisis in 4K. Gripping headlines between GLP-1 ads. The feed is frictionless.

So how do we discern excitement that lay in wait?
How do we identify the slant shifting negative?

The easy answer is morality.

But morality is easily hijacked.

As I’ve said before: Baby Jessica. We’re social mammals. We care for our fellow humans, like elephants that circle their young in moments of crisis. We’re wired for it.

Children suffering will always command attention. It should. That instinct is human.

But instinct can be harvested.

Our moral energy can be metastasized into anxious attention without changing the outcome. We give money, sure. We spread awareness. We keep folks in our thoughts and prayers. The efficacy of any of that remains, at best, unclear.
And then we return to the feed.

If all we can do is scroll and grind, that attention’s energy curdles. It hums without outlet.

I shudder at the notion of discussing productivity here. Especially when AI is eating all task work with no signs of slowing. Gobbling up tasks is a surefire way to leave us immobile: no errands left, no busywork left, no distraction left.

Which means discernment becomes critical.

Our choice in focus. Our choice in conscious attention.
That’s our currency. That’s our superpower.

It’s not something to be handed to an algorithmic feed. Not something to be peddled off to the fastest, flashiest bidder.

AI has democratized spectacle. Maybe it’s just in the nick of time.

Now we can generate our own Star Warses. Our own cinematic universes. Web-slinging adamantium-skeleton witches and warlocks, mutants and cryptids.
We can conjure whatever we wish to see in whatever fidelity we choose.

We can share it.
We can believe it.

We’ve unlocked our own mass hallucination machine.

We can watch anything now.

We can belong without attending.
We can witness without entering.
We can sip community the way we sip entertainment: in fragments, on our own schedule, without friction.

For a while, that can feel like connection.

Until the window closes.

Until the daily voice goes quiet.
Until the proxy disappears.
Until the distance we’d grown comfortable with becomes visible.

We are social mammals. We circle our young. We gather. We show up.

But showing up has never been automated.

AI can generate spectacle.
It cannot initiate the room.
It cannot gather your people.
It cannot stand in your place.
It cannot walk through the door for you.

When spectacle is infinite, spectatorship becomes cheap.

Initiation remains expensive.

We’ve unlocked simulation.
We’ve unlocked adjacency.
We’ve unlocked distraction.

Initiation still takes effort.

No algorithm will move first for you.
No feed will convene your voice.
No proxy will live your life.

So the question is not: What do you want to believe?

It’s not even: What do you want to see?

It’s this:

What are you waiting for?

The machine is humming.
The universes are infinite.
The buffet is endless.

Enough waiting.

The door hangs open, the flickering light spills onto our feet.

Author’s Note

This essay was written with the assistance of generative AI.

Not as a ghostwriter, and not as a replacement for lived experience — but as a conversational partner. A sharpening stone. A room in which to test phrasing and pressure.

The ideas, metaphors, and conclusions are my own. The cadence and construction were refined through dialogue with a system trained on language patterns, not lived memory.

It feels appropriate to disclose that here.

This piece wrestles directly with spectacle, automation, and the temptation to outsource participation. In drafting it, I resisted the very thing it critiques: allowing the machine to initiate for me.

AI can help structure thought. It cannot supply conviction.

If anything, working this way reinforces the thesis of the essay itself:

Initiation remains manual.

— C.W.

what-hope-do-we-have.title: What Hope Do We Have?
what-hope-do-we-have.description: Making a creative life in the age of AI
what-hope-do-we-have.content:
After my second theatrical production using AI for projection art, I gave a practicum lecture at the local college on AI’s encroachment into the arts.

A student asked me, “What hope do we have as we graduate into this world?”

I told her I couldn’t give her hope. But I could say that her point of view was what would carry her through.

I’ve thought about that answer for years.

Developing a point of view takes practice. You make things. You discover what matters to you, what you keep returning to, what you can’t quite say yet.

You need time to become someone whose perspective is recognizably your own.

I worry about people standing at the beginning of that journey deciding there’s no reason to take it. Agreeing that all the prizes have already been claimed.

I want them to begin. I want to see what they’ll make.

—

By the time I gave that lecture, many people were still associating AI art with fever-dream images, nightmare teeth and hands with too many fingers. They hadn’t yet understood how good AI art could look.

I was upfront and honest with the production teams, but I suspect the audience had no idea how those images were made.

So this is personal.

The disapproval I felt was mostly in whispers and looks from members of the production staff. I can tell you how those landed on my ego. I can’t tell you exactly what each person was thinking.

And that student’s question deserves a careful response. There’s a lot of fear inside “What hope do we have?” Especially when you’re preparing to enter a field you’ve spent years learning to love.

But I worry about the way fear becomes contempt, and contempt becomes permission to dismiss anyone who engages.

The chorus can sound coordinated even when nobody’s necessarily conducting. People learn which tools invite suspicion, which admissions require a defense. Eventually, the condemnation does its work before anyone has to say a word.

Who wants to begin a creative journey under those conditions?

—

Art felt like something we could confidently call ours.

We use it to express our internal worlds through whatever faculties we were born with and whatever skills we’ve managed to acquire.

Countless hours of practice. Actually, we do like to count them. Ten thousand hours, right? A reassuringly large number between wanting to do something and earning the right to be good at it.

Then AI attempts an image, and we laugh.

Then it gets better.

Then it gets better again, at a pace that makes our years of practice feel suddenly, painfully slow.

There are serious questions here about training data, permission, compensation, and who gets to profit. We need to work through them. Making something available on the internet doesn’t magically settle every claim someone might have over its use.

But we also need to examine what happens when the discovery of a tool changes our judgment of the person using it.

What did we admire before we knew?

What disappeared when we found out?

I see a related tension in math.

A math proof can do more than establish that something is true. It can help us understand why. There’s beauty in an argument that makes a difficult idea suddenly feel inevitable.

Of course we want that. We’re humans. We demand elegance all the way down.

But suppose a machine helps produce a valid answer through a route that’s cumbersome, opaque, or aesthetically disappointing.

We still have to check it. And even if the proof holds, we may still want a better explanation. A worthwhile desire for an understanding of the meaningful beauty that builds our universe.

Art and math may have different standards of success. But both force us to ask:

  • How much of the value belongs with the result?

  • How much value is derived by the process?

  • How much that influences our picture of the person presenting the work?

When I was a kid at the arcade, I figured out how to slowly, patiently extract additional tickets from a skeeball machine.

Constant, steady pressure.

Sure, you gave me one ticket. But I’m taking twenty.

I was an enterprising youngster.

If the toy behind the counter cost twenty tickets, I only needed to earn the first one. I’d make up the rest.

To the other kids still throwing balls, that would look like cheating. Fair enough. I was bilking the machine.

But I think that feeling helps explain some of the reaction to AI. You’ve been practicing your throw. Learning the angle. Getting better. Then someone else walks up and starts pulling tickets.

They’re already choosing a prize.

If victory is quantified, someone will find an unexpected way to make ends meet. And when they do, we discover how much we cared about the route we took to get there.

Sure, a ticket machine has rules. And art has arguments about what the rules ought to be. Math requires valid reasoning, even when it is a bit unconventional.

Still, the feeling is familiar: I’m doing all this work. How can you already be standing there?

The sting of wasted effort. The fear that everything we’ve learned might no longer earn us a living. Failure, perceived and seemingly permanent.

The “why bother?” trap at the start of any journey.

It’s all buzzing loud in everyone’s ear. And it’s deafening to those who have little room to live with that uncertainty.

I’ve been walking my own creative path for more than twenty years. I also have a day job. My livelihood doesn’t depend on every creative skill continuing to hold its market value, and that gives me room to experiment that others may not have.

I can tell that student what has sustained me. I can’t ask her to trust the footing at the start of her trail just because I’ve found some farther along my own.

We’re mosaics made from pieces of happenstance and design. We become sedimentary layers on the mountain of progress.

We learn through other people. Their work changes what we can imagine. Their discoveries become the ground beneath our feet.

And we spend our lives assembling influences into something we hope will be recognizably ours and provide sure footing for others.

That doesn’t erase anyone’s labor or make every use of it fair. But it does make me cautious about treating human creativity as though each glimmer emerged in isolation.

Silicon is our cousin.

A strange cousin, sure. One that was built through our accumulated knowledge, now doing things that unsettle our understanding of ourselves.

But right now, we have an opportunity to shape its capacity and its place in the world. That means deciding what we reward, whose experiences we include, what we refuse, and where we insist on human judgment.

It means bringing our understanding of beauty, right, wrong, love, and mourning into the work.

We’re here to give it its heart.

That takes participation. Discussion. Even criticism. We need people who care deeply about art, education, labor, and human dignity to have a hand in shaping these systems.

Condemning those who dare engage makes that harder.

—

I keep returning to the student at that lecture.

I still can’t give her hope as though it’s a prize I’ve managed to pull from a machine.

And I can’t promise her that a distinctive point of view will guarantee a living. The world owes her more than a pep talk about being herself while the ground shifts beneath her.

But I want her to have the chance to discover what she sees.

I want her to make things, encounter resistance, change her mind, surprise herself. I want her to find out what these tools can do in her hands. And I want her to decide for herself where they belong.

Our greatest communal creation needs us. So do the people growing up alongside it.

Let the machine change what intelligence can accomplish. We’ll have plenty to reckon with as it does.

Please keep making things.
We haven’t heard from you yet.

Author’s note:

This essay began with my own draft and experiences, then took shape through conversation with ChatGPT. I used it as an editorial collaborator to question the argument, develop a new draft, and refine the structure and language. I made my own revisions and the final editorial calls. The illustrations and CW mark were generated with OpenAI’s image tools through a direction-and-revision process. That collaboration feels worth making visible, especially here.

what-passes-through-us.title: What Passes Through Us
what-passes-through-us.content:
This year didn’t resolve itself. It folded into itself.

Grief, joy, acceptance. None braided neatly, none reconciled, just all present together.

The kind of coexistence you don’t arrive at by thinking harder. The kind you stumble upon by finally stopping the fight.

One of my long-time emotional anchors disappeared this week. A person I never met, but one whose work quietly steadied me through years when the ground itself felt unreliable.

Politics curdling. A pandemic. An entire U.S. state freezing over.

Somehow, his presence made those tectonic shifts feel like background noise. When that kind of signal goes silent, you mourn more than the person, you mourn the regulation they provided.

That loss sits heavy.

And yet, almost immediately, life counterweighs itself.

I went bowling with my nephew! It was the first time I’ve seen him in nearly a decade. He’s grown into himself in ways that feel both surprising and inevitable. Strong spirit. Sharp mind. Still figuring it out, still stumbling forward.

Watching that arc unfold reminded me that growth rarely requires certainty, only motion. Inertia. Intent.

That’s when it struck me: the balance wasn’t something new arriving. It was something looping back on itself.

Not resolution.
Equilibrium.

Lately, I’ve been thinking about how influence actually moves through systems. Not as direct impact or collision, but as passage. Gravitational.

Like a comet warming as it arcs past the pull of the sun. The comet releasing material it’s carried for ages into its wake.

No intent.
No message.
Just outgassing.

Shedding trace elements into an atmosphere already in motion.

It isn’t mystical. It’s mechanical. It’s natural.
And the effect is cumulative.
Particles disperse.
Orbits shift by mere fractions.
Something passes through and leaves more behind than it takes with it.

We’re watching one do exactly that right now. 3i/Atlas, a long-cycle visitor, briefly close enough to warm from our sun, release, and move on.

This is how systems change without asking permission. Something we, collectively, struggle to grasp.

We’re instructed to chase clarity, to declare meaning, to land on resolute conclusions. But what if the golden skill is context switching?

The ability to sit within and live without. To appreciate and mourn simultaneously. To oscillate without demanding a verdict.

There’s a rawness to that state. It’s undefined. Unpolished. Maybe that’s why it feels right.

I’m spending this final week of the year without plans. Without goals. And instead of panic, there’s relief.
I bought a lime-green Telecaster and an Orange amp to match.
I’m letting myself imagine what it would mean to play along with the systems I’ve been building.

Less to prove authorship, or claim purity, but to blur lines between system and self even more deliberately.

My nephew joked that we’re heading toward a world where a ticket to a fully human-made movie might end up costing hundreds of dollars, while an AI-generated one would likely cost pennies.

That framing misses the truth.
There isn’t a binary coming.
There’s a spectrum already here.
And most of the interesting work lives in the middle of that spectrum.

Maybe my role, maybe our role, isn’t to defend old definitions or rush toward new absolutes, but to paint with colors that shine brightest on this new and unfamiliar canvas.

To let missteps, accidents, and awkward hybrids reveal what fidelity can look like when we stop performing certainty.

Stop pretending control.

Or maybe it’s all a bubble.
Maybe this moment collapses.
Maybe all my credibility evaporates.

Either way, I find myself unexpectedly content.

Not because I know what’s coming next, but because I’m no longer trying to force meaning into engineered balance.

Allowing a messy synergy. A natural fusion. A molting of the artifice.
An emotional nakedness that lacks the severity of calcified corners.

We’ll continue to fold in on ourselves in 2026.
The shape of our creations perhaps even unknown to ourselves.
And maybe that’s the best foundation to create something truly our own.

Author’s Note

This piece was developed in close dialogue with an AI writing partner, which I used as a sounding board rather than a substitute — a way to pressure-test metaphors, structure, and restraint.

The core ideas, experiences, and final language are mine; the collaboration helped surface the through-line, sharpen the metaphors, and resist the temptation to over-resolve what wanted to remain open.

The accompanying imagery was likewise shaped through iterative conversation — starting from physical process rather than symbolism — and refined until it felt less like illustration and more like residue. Evidence of passage, not explanation.
