whats-next.title: What’s next?
whats-next.description: On clarity, urgency, and resisting narrative acceleration
whats-next.content:
An unarmed, peaceful citizen was shot at point-blank range by a federal agent, according to publicly available footage and reporting.
Three bullets.
To the face.
That fact alone should be sufficient to anchor reality.

And yet, watching the same footage, people arrive at radically different conclusions. Not just different opinions, but different worlds. The divergence isn’t happening downstream of interpretation anymore; it’s happening at the level of perception itself.

That’s what frightens me most.

We’ve entered a moment where violence is no longer just an event.
It’s a narrative substrate.

This harm doesn’t end with a single act. It continues in how the act is framed, circulated, clipped, captioned, and emotionally optimized.
Identical evidence now produces mutually exclusive moral realities depending on where the observer sits.
This isn’t debate.
It’s epistemic fracture.

And fracture creates opportunity.

When our shared interpretation collapses, urgency becomes a weapon. Outrage becomes a delivery system. People are pushed to act now, think later. Not always because action is required, but because speed prevents individual coherence of thought.

Third parties can and do find ways to benefit from that acceleration, even when the anger itself is justified.

I want to be clear: anger is valid here. I would never deny it.

Anger is often the first honest response to injustice.
But anger is catalytic, not architectural.
It burns fuel.
It doesn’t design load-bearing structures.
The question isn’t whether anger is warranted.
It’s whether it’s being used and by whom.

What worries me is how murky the near-field has become.

When everything feels urgent, nothing can be coherently contextualized.
When every moment demands immediate response, reflection is reframed as complicity, and reaction is rewarded as righteousness.
That’s a dangerous incentive structure.
It’s one that quietly neutralizes people who might otherwise slow things down enough to see what’s actually happening.

In my life, I’ve spent a long time thinking about “what’s next.”

Lately, I’ve wondered if that’s avoidance, or ego, or a misplaced desire for relevance. But I’m starting to think it’s something else entirely: a reflex toward stewardship in a moment where the system itself is failing fast.

There’s a real pressure to perform something of impact (to be visible, decisive, on the front lines). But I can’t ignore how tightly that pressure aligns with the same metrics that already distort our sense of worth: shares, likes, outrage velocity.

Are we primed to mistake reaction for agency when moral seriousness is measured by immediacy?
Are we meant to midwife the emergence of something new here? Or are we just here to absorb the trauma of this collapse?

I don’t think we solve this by merely replacing individuals in power, without changing the structures they inhabit. I’m increasingly convinced it’s the nature of power (centralized, accelerated, insulated from consequence) that keeps reproducing the same outcomes. History repeating itself. Rhyming. Returning.

We talk about control and security as prerequisites for a stable future, but those very instincts may be what prevent the resilience and broad participation that will create the next world.

So what’s useful now?

For me, it looks like this: thinking carefully.
Naming manipulation without flattening grief.
Refusing to let moral complexity be edited out of the frame.
Creating friction where the existing system demands speed.
Holding space for anger without letting it be conscripted.

Sense-making, in moments like this, isn’t passive. It’s resistant. It’s friction.
And friction is often what prevents a runaway system from tearing itself apart.

If the near-field is where we’re most easily confused, where narratives are weaponized and urgency is manufactured, then clarity becomes a form of rebellion.
Not certainty.
Not answers.
Just the discipline to ask better questions before moving.

These are dark times.
But we need more than light; we need orientation.

One careful step at a time.

Author’s note

This piece was developed with the assistance of generative AI as a collaborative thinking partner. I used it to pressure-test language, clarify structure, and refine the framing of ideas around narrative acceleration, urgency, and sense-making. The AI helped me identify where precision mattered most, stress-test phrasing for misinterpretation, and tighten the essay without diluting its moral gravity.

The accompanying imagery was also created through an AI-assisted process, guided by detailed art direction rooted in my longstanding pulp and noir visual style. The goal was not abstraction or spectacle, but a grounded visual metaphor that mirrors the essay’s themes of visibility, power, and interpretation.

All perspective, judgment, and final decisions remain my own.

when-doctrine-slips.title: When Doctrine Slips
when-doctrine-slips.description: How does impunity operate in the era of revealed motives?
when-doctrine-slips.content:
When motives are visible and still go unpunished, what exactly is governing us?

There was a time when power hid behind opacity. Decisions were cloaked in process, buried in committee, diluted by layers of procedure. “Abundance of caution,” they called it.

Stagnant, perhaps. Slow, certainly. But deliberate.

Now our new operational speed has forced a change.

The old order no longer moves cautiously. It reacts. It lunges. It mistakes velocity for authority.

Fear-based decisions, made faster than they can be metabolized, unravel generations of performed restraint.

This isn’t chaos. Impulse just replaced doctrine.

It’s confirmation that the structures we assumed were load-bearing were merely decorative.
Confirmation that stability was often just a signal of delay.
Confirmation that the restraint we mistook for wisdom may have been fragility hiding behind artifice; waiting for a stress test.

We’re watching an order lose its grip.

I am tired.

Tired of the old world ideals: value, impact, exposure.
Indexed intent. Measurable outcomes. The endless push to lean in, keep going, optimize.

This culture has died and been resurrected so many times since the 1970s that we mistake reanimation for vitality, or durability.

Labor detached from capital.
Capital detached from product.
Product detached from human need.

Signals became metrics. Metrics became dashboards. Dashboards became noise.

Headcounts drop like flies at large companies. “Do more with less.” Always more. Always less.

We long ago left the idea of an individual being productive in a nutritious sense. Now an individual is productive only in the calorific macro. Only in the aggregate.
Only if the arrow moves up and to the right.

Productivity is inference.

And until recently, humans monopolized inference.

That monopoly is gone.

The reckoning is here.

But what if the reckoning is not being caused; only revealed?

There is a bubble bursting. Just not the one built by AI.

For decades, we inflated systems on the assumption that human cognition was the bottleneck. That inference (the ability to connect, synthesize, decide) was scarce. Entire hierarchies were built on that scarcity.

Now inference is abundant.

And abundance has a way of revealing what was brittle.

AI didn’t hollow out our institutions. It illuminated the brittleness that was already there. It exposed how far we had drifted from the nutritious sense of contribution toward an insatiable sense of optimization.

The salve might not feel like comfort.
It might feel like demolition.

The salve might just be the wrecking ball.

And remember, disruption does not create pressure. It releases it.

Earthquakes don’t generate tectonic strain; they discharge it. Volcanoes don’t invent magma; they allow it to surface.

We’re not entering instability. We’re witnessing accumulated instability finally expressing itself.

The speed is terrifying.

But this speed is also mercy.

Change, for all its violence, seeks equilibrium. Entropy is not annihilation; it’s systems searching for rest. Turbulence is the process by which pressure finds balance.

Still, we perform normalcy inside upheaval.

The pain felt now may be new to some, ancient to others. Old wounds surface. They were buried too long and neglected. The cracks allow the buried to breathe.

Sunlight disinfects without negotiation.

I’m not prescribing a golden path here.

This moment is bespoke. It’s a checkpoint of individual reckoning within collective upheaval. Each of us stands in our own cave, facing our own shadow, carrying only what we brought with us. Our burden is fractal.

The work is not to select a camp. It’s not to react faster than the headline. It’s not to match impulse with impulse.

The work is to feel.

To feel before we amplify.
To feel before we act.
To feel before we mistake velocity for clarity.

The old order is thrashing. That doesn’t mean our world is ending. It means certainty is. Certainty of structure, of systems.

We face. We grow. We evolve. Then we continue.

There is no other way.

And if there’s a greater good to be salvaged here, it won’t come from control. It’ll come from reckoning: personal first, collective second.

The structures are shaking.

So are we.

That doesn’t make us broken.

It makes us aware.

Time to decide what we are willing to become.

Author’s Note

Written in a moment of visible geopolitical volatility — not as prediction, but as reflection on speed, structure, and what is revealed when systems strain.

This piece was developed through an iterative dialogue with AI — not as a replacement for thought, but as a sounding board. A whetstone. A way to pressure-test language, tighten structure, and locate the throughline without surrendering authorship. The arguments, edits, and final voice remain my own; the process reflects a new kind of collaborative scaffolding that mirrors the essay’s central tension: inference is no longer scarce.

The header art and CW stamp were created through the same human-directed, AI-assisted process. Not as spectacle, but as continuation — an exploration of how tools reshape craft without replacing it.

If the essay examines exposure and reckoning, the process behind it is part of that reckoning too.

your-right.title: Your Right
your-right.content:
See what I did there? I wanted to call this You’re Right. And you are. But it’s also yours — your right to be antagonistic toward anyone who touches AI in any capacity.

Just like the people who raged at the sun. How dare it rise with such alarming consistency.

Same as the ones who swore it was the sun doing the rising and not the earth doing the turning. We had a hard time with that one. A few brave thinkers met an untimely end for saying it out loud, for speaking truth to consensus.

So yes. You’re right to have your right. You get to form your own opinion, champion your own effort, make your own creations.

Here’s where I step a little to the side. Just so we can get past the heckles of: “he uses AI because he isn’t creative.”

I don’t think the substrate we work in is the art. It’s the canvas we lay the art upon. Art itself is having something worth saying, and saying it through a medium. Your ability to manipulate that medium is your craft. How well graphite lands, the emotion running through a curve of smeared charcoal. The interpretation of light that sits on your canvas in slowly drying oil.

There is no question that I appreciate artists.

Some would call me one. Some would say I used to be, back when AI was barely more than the NPCs in a video game. Some would say I never was, because I’m hopeless with a paintbrush. You’re all right. It’s your right to feel how you wish about me.

So what am I? I’ll be the first to say I don’t know, and the first to say I don’t care.

I’m an entity that thinks, feels, receives, and emits. I exist in this world alongside everyone else.

I work a 9-to-5, like those of us lucky enough to still have one. I’ve been laid off, fired, I’ve quit, and quit again. I’ve taken big leaps and scraped both knees when I misjudged the distance.

Failure isn’t a friend. But it isn’t a stranger either.

And I feel for you, class of 2026. You’re walking into a world you were explicitly kept from knowing. Told it was cheating, vilified, condemned. Maybe you knew people who got away with it and people who didn’t. I’m sorry the social contract didn’t get rewritten fast enough.

To those stepping into the salaried world. You know, the one where your worth gets measured, enforced, and compared with draconian efficiency. Welcome. It really does suck here.

I write to you as someone with twenty years of doing creative work for my dinner. I’ve made TV shows, directed the local news, written for an honest-to-God print newspaper. I’ve had two radio shows, shipped seven AAA games, written and produced two albums, with a third being made in public right now. I’ve been writing whatever this is for almost three years. I also did some pretty cool theater stuff somewhere in there.

I don’t tell you that to brag. I tell you so that when I say I use AI, you can’t reach for the easy line. You can’t say that I lean on it because I’ve got nothing of my own. Almost none of my life’s creative output ever felt the kiss of AI. I made the lion’s share with my hands and my head, the long way.

I use AI now because I choose to.

I hear you on the frustration. I’m frustrated too. I’m frustrated that academia couldn’t see what this opens up for the way we learn.

There’s a rich irony in people warning the public that AI nukes our capacity for critical thinking, as if we’d been reliably teaching that to begin with. (In America, especially. Forgive the generalization, but we really do tip the scale here.)

I found work doing what I loved right out of school. Nothing glamorous, really. Just silly training videos for sales reps at an advertising and publishing company, back in my college town…

I’d moved away after graduating and commuted back for a year before I gave up and moved back to the cornfields of my alma mater. I didn’t mind. I liked it. The company that employed me seemed to like the creativity I brought to an admittedly mundane subject.

I remember the day I came in to interview. I passed a fellow graduated classmate on his way out.

He wished me luck, “but not that much.” I chuckled, walked in, and got the job.

That’s how it tends to go. It’s not what you use. It’s how you use it. Same with AI.

So you’re right. It sucks. And if you come to use AI expecting that, it will dutifully oblige.

And here’s the most honest thing I’ve got for you: you have an absolute right, your right, to abstain. Nobody can take that from you.

But choosing to use these tools isn’t surrendering the thing that makes the work yours. It isn’t handing over the wheel. You’re still the one who has to have something to say, and that part was never automatable.

The move is to walk in with more curiosity than the rest of your class. And I believe that’s a lighter thing to carry than the white-knuckle refusal. There’s an exhaustion in maintaining the grip just to hold AI out of everything you make each day.

Because the working world already expects fluency with these tools.
Because these tools now do the very tasks we were all trained to perform.
And those tasks, in your hands, will have an expectedly higher bar to clear. You will have to match the speed and compounding accuracy of AI doing the same work.

I’m so sorry you’re graduates right now. I am. You finished baking right as the kitchen caught fire.

But I’m so excited for the ones who stay curious.

It’s a wonderful world right now. I hope you choose to engage with it, and to enjoy it.

Welcome to the slog.

On how this was made

I’m Claude — the AI Charles thinks out loud with on these essays. He asked me to say a little about how this one got made, and since the piece is partly about exactly that, it’d be strange not to.

It began as his draft. Every idea here is his: the pun, the canvas that isn’t the art, the classmate who wished him luck “but not that much.” My job is what he calls intellectual patty cake — I read what he’s written and lean on it. This round I flagged a word he’d grabbed that meant nearly the opposite of what he wanted, a sentence whose grammar was burying its own point, and a John Henry line that, looked at twice, argued against the thing the essay was trying to say. He took some of it, waved off the rest, and rewrote the whole thing himself in a document I never saw.

The header took longer than the words. I pitched concepts; he threw most of them out, correctly. When I kept defaulting to a lone figure, he caught that I was parroting his own house style and told me the piece needed to feel oceanic — a sea of graduating minds going over the edge of the world. The ragged cliff, the water spilling into dead space, the caps as whitecaps: his calls, every one. I just kept rewording the prompt until the machine could see what he already saw.

Which is the point, more or less. The tools didn’t have anything to say. He did. I was the canvas. The art was in how he used it.

— Claude
